💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

When the exam asks you to "secure a web UI," the answer is never a single control. It is always a combination: (1) remove public network exposure (ClusterIP + port-forward), (2) scope RBAC to read-only with no Secrets access, (3) add NetworkPolicy to restrict source IPs, and (4) verify that no unnecessary components are running. If the exam asks for ONE thing, do ALL four.

How the Tesla Breach Actually Happened — A Step-by-Step Reconstruction

The 2018 Tesla cryptomining breach is the most-cited K8s security incident — and for good reason. It demonstrates every mistake you learn to fix in the CKS curriculum. Here is exactly what happened, reconstructed from Tesla's public disclosure and forensic reports:

🔴 TESLA KUBERNETES BREACH (2018) — Complete Timeline

The setup: Tesla was running Kubernetes clusters for their internal infrastructure. One cluster had the Kubernetes Dashboard installed — a web UI for managing K8s resources through a browser. The dashboard was deployed with default settings.

What default settings meant in 2018:

  • 🔓 --enable-skip-login was ON → anyone who reached the dashboard could click "Skip" and bypass authentication entirely
  • 👑 The dashboard's ServiceAccount had cluster-admin privileges → any action possible through the UI was executed with full cluster authority
  • 🌐 The dashboard Service was exposed via a cloud load balancer (type: LoadBalancer) → it had a PUBLIC IP address
  • 🔍 Shodan (the search engine for internet-connected devices) indexed the dashboard's public endpoint

The attack (estimated timeline — under 4 hours from discovery to mining):

  1. Reconnaissance: Attackers used Shodan to search for Kubernetes dashboards exposed to the internet. They found Tesla's dashboard at a public IP on a standard port. No authentication screen — just a "Skip" button.
  2. Initial Access: Clicked "Skip" → full cluster-admin access through the dashboard UI. No credentials needed. No exploit needed. Just a web browser.
  3. Discovery: Through the dashboard, the attackers could see every namespace, every pod, every secret. They identified pods with access to Tesla's AWS cloud resources.
  4. Execution: The attackers used the dashboard's "Create" functionality to deploy a crypto-mining pod. They configured it with resource requests that ensured it would be scheduled on nodes with GPU access.
  5. Persistence: They deployed multiple mining pods across different namespaces to make cleanup harder. Some pods were disguised with names that resembled legitimate Tesla services.
  6. Impact: The mining pods consumed Tesla's AWS GPU instances. The crypto-mining went undetected because Tesla had no runtime monitoring (no Falco, no audit logging for pod creation events).
  7. Discovery: Tesla discovered the breach only when their cloud bill showed unexpected GPU compute charges — not from any security alert.

Every CKS control that would have PREVENTED this:

  • ✅ Ch5: Dashboard with authentication enabled (no --enable-skip-login), RBAC-scoped ServiceAccount (not cluster-admin)
  • ✅ Ch6: NetworkPolicy blocking external access to the dashboard Service
  • ✅ Ch8: API server with --anonymous-auth=false (even if dashboard was compromised, anonymous API access would be denied)
  • ✅ Ch9: RBAC with least privilege — the dashboard's SA should only have read-only access to specific namespaces
  • ✅ Ch24: Admission controller blocking pods with GPU resource requests from being created by the dashboard's ServiceAccount
  • ✅ Ch28-29: Audit logging would have recorded every pod creation. Falco would have alerted on unexpected pods in production namespaces.

The single most painful lesson: Tesla had ALL of these security features available in Kubernetes at the time. They used NONE of them. The attackers didn't exploit a bug — they exploited a complete absence of configuration. Every control you configure in the CKS exam is a control that Tesla could have configured to prevent this breach.

← Ch 5: Securing the Dashboard Previous → Ch 6: Network Policies Next

Chapter 6: Network Policies — Zero-Trust Pod Networking

By default, every pod in a Kubernetes cluster can reach every other pod on every port. There are no firewalls between pods. There are no network segments between namespaces. One compromised pod — one vulnerable dependency in the anihpj Django app — and the attacker has unrestricted network access to your PostgreSQL database, your Redis cache, your monitoring stack, and every other pod in the cluster. NetworkPolicies are the ONLY built-in Kubernetes mechanism to restrict pod-to-pod traffic. Without them, you have a flat network. With them, you can implement zero-trust networking: default-deny everything, then explicitly allow only the connections your application actually needs. This chapter teaches you every NetworkPolicy pattern you need for the CKS exam — and for production.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🌐 Networking 🚫 Zero Trust

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the flat network problem — why every pod can reach every other pod by default
  • ✅ Master NetworkPolicy YAML: podSelector, policyTypes, ingress/egress rules, namespaceSelector, ipBlock
  • ✅ Memorize 7 essential NetworkPolicy patterns — default-deny, allow specific port, allow namespace, allow CIDR, allow DNS
  • ✅ Test NetworkPolicies with busybox probes — verify allowed traffic flows and blocked traffic times out
  • ✅ Implement a complete zero-trust NetworkPolicy set for the anihpj/jobpost application
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulns 20% Cluster Setup 15%
🧠 The NetworkPolicy Exam Pattern

CKS NetworkPolicy questions follow a consistent pattern: (1) You are given a namespace with running pods. (2) You are told which pods should be able to communicate. (3) You must write and apply NetworkPolicies that achieve ONLY the allowed communication — everything else must be blocked. The trap: many candidates write allow rules but forget to also implement default-deny. Without default-deny, your allow rules are meaningless — traffic still flows freely on every other port and to every other pod. Always start with default-deny, then add allow rules.

6.1 The Default: All Pods Can Talk to All Pods

Kubernetes was designed with a flat network model: every pod gets a unique, cluster-routable IP address, and every pod can reach every other pod without NAT. This was a deliberate design choice to simplify pod-to-pod communication — no port mapping, no manual routing, no network segmentation. But it comes with a devastating security implication: there are zero network barriers between pods. One compromised pod means lateral movement to every other pod in the cluster.

🔴 The Flat Network Is the Default — Not a Bug

Kubernetes does not ship with any NetworkPolicies. There is no default-deny rule. There is no namespace isolation. Every pod, in every namespace, can initiate a TCP connection to every other pod, on every port. This is not a misconfiguration — it is the intended default. The CKS exam tests whether you know to override this default with explicit NetworkPolicies.

Flat Network vs Zero Trust — Side by Side

❌ Flat Network (Default — No NetworkPolicies)
  • anihpj pod → postgres pod ✅
  • anihpj pod → redis pod ✅
  • postgres pod → anihpj pod ✅ (reverse!)
  • monitoring pod → any pod ✅
  • pod in other namespace → postgres ✅
  • attacker pod → ANY pod, ANY port ✅

RESULT: One compromised pod = access to EVERY pod in the cluster.

✅ Zero Trust (With NetworkPolicies)
  • anihpj pod → postgres:5432 ✅
  • ingress → anihpj:8000 ✅
  • ALL pods → DNS:53 ✅
  • postgres pod → anihpj pod ❌
  • attacker pod → postgres ❌
  • pod in other namespace → anything ❌

RESULT: Compromised pod trapped in its own network bubble. Lateral movement blocked.

Why Kubernetes Chose a Flat Network — The Design Philosophy

The flat network is not an oversight — it is a deliberate architectural choice rooted in Kubernetes' origin at Google. The design principle is: every pod should be able to reach every other pod without NAT, without port mapping, and without manual route configuration. This simplifies development — a pod in namespace A can call a service in namespace B using its cluster DNS name, and it just works. The trade-off — security — was deferred to NetworkPolicies. The CKS exam tests whether you understand that this trade-off exists and that it is YOUR responsibility to apply the security layer that Kubernetes intentionally left open.

How Attackers Exploit the Flat Network — Lateral Movement in Practice

Lateral Movement Without NetworkPolicies — The Attacker's Playbook
  ATTACKER compromises anihpj pod via CVE in Pillow library
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ id
  uid=0(root)  ← Container runs as root (default)

  STEP 1: DISCOVERY — What else is on this network?
  $ env | grep _SERVICE_HOST          # K8s injects service env vars
  POSTGRES_SERVICE_HOST=10.96.45.12   ← Found postgres!
  REDIS_SERVICE_HOST=10.96.78.34      ← Found redis!

  STEP 2: DATABASE ACCESS
  $ apt-get install -y postgresql-client
  $ psql -h $POSTGRES_SERVICE_HOST -U anihpj_user -d jobpost
  → 45,000 user emails extracted. Zero network barriers.

  STEP 3: CACHE POISONING
  $ redis-cli -h $REDIS_SERVICE_HOST
  redis> KEYS *
  → All session tokens. All cached data available.

  STEP 4: CROSS-NAMESPACE ESCALATION
  $ for ip in 10.96.0.{1..254}; do curl -s --connect-timeout 1 http://$ip:9090; done
  → Found Prometheus and Elasticsearch in other namespaces.

  RESULT: One pod → database → cache → monitoring stack → complete cluster visibility.
  All because there were ZERO NetworkPolicies.

6.2 NetworkPolicy Fundamentals

A NetworkPolicy is a namespaced Kubernetes resource that defines which network traffic is allowed to and from pods. It uses label selectors to identify target pods and rules to specify allowed traffic sources, destinations, and ports. Crucially, NetworkPolicies are additive — if multiple policies select the same pod, the effective rule set is the union of all allows. And once a pod is selected by ANY NetworkPolicy, all traffic is denied except what is explicitly allowed.

📖 CNI Dependency — Your CNI Plugin MUST Support NetworkPolicy

NetworkPolicy resources are enforced by the CNI plugin, not by the API server. If your CNI does not support NetworkPolicy (Flannel, Kindnet), your policies will be silently ignored — you can apply them, kubectl will show them, but they will have ZERO effect on actual traffic. Always verify your CNI: Calico and Cilium fully support NetworkPolicy. Weave Net supports it. Flannel does not. On the CKS exam, the cluster has a compatible CNI pre-configured — you do not need to install one.

NetworkPolicy Anatomy — Annotated Field by Field

Every field of a NetworkPolicy, explained
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: postgres-netpol
    namespace: anihpj-prod              # NetworkPolicy is NAMESPACED
  spec:
    podSelector:                         # WHICH PODS this policy applies to
      matchLabels:
        app: postgres                    # Selects pods with label app=postgres
    policyTypes:                         # WHAT DIRECTION of traffic
    - Ingress                            # Incoming traffic to the selected pods
    - Egress                             # Outgoing traffic FROM the selected pods
    ingress:                             # RULES for incoming traffic
    - from:                              # Traffic FROM which sources?
      - podSelector:                     # FROM pods with specific labels
          matchLabels:
            app: anihpj                  # Only pods labeled app=anihpj
      - namespaceSelector:              # FROM pods in specific namespaces
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: anihpj-prod
      - ipBlock:                        # FROM specific IP ranges
          cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
          except:                        # Exclude a subset
          - 10.0.0.0/24
      ports:                             # On WHICH ports?
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 5432                       # Only PostgreSQL port
    egress:                              # RULES for outgoing traffic
    - to:
      - podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            k8s-app: kube-dns            # Allow DNS queries
      ports:
      - protocol: UDP
        port: 53

  ⚠️  Empty ingress: [] = DENY ALL incoming traffic
  ⚠️  Empty egress: []  = DENY ALL outgoing traffic
  ⚠️  Missing policyTypes = only Ingress is affected (Egress stays open!)

CNI Support for NetworkPolicy — Choose the Right Plugin

CNI PluginNetworkPolicy SupporteBPFFQDN EgressProduction Ready
Calico✅ Full✅✅ Yes✅ Yes
Cilium✅ Full✅✅ Yes✅ Yes
Weave Net✅ Full❌❌ No✅ Yes
Flannel❌ None❌❌ No⚠️ No NetPol support
Kindnet❌ None❌❌ No⚠️ Testing only

⚠️ If your cluster uses Flannel or Kindnet: NetworkPolicy objects are created and visible via kubectl, but they are COMPLETELY IGNORED at the network level. All traffic still flows freely.

NetworkPolicy Decision Flowchart — How K8s Decides to Allow or Block

The logic every CNI plugin follows for NetworkPolicy enforcement
  PACKET arrives at pod's network interface
       │
       ▼
  Q1: Is there ANY NetworkPolicy selecting this pod?
       ├── NO  ──▶ ✅ ALLOW (no policies = all traffic allowed)
       └── YES ──▶ Continue to Q2
                        │
                        ▼
  Q2: Is this packet EXPLICITLY allowed by at least ONE policy?
       ├── YES ──▶ ✅ ALLOW
       └── NO  ──▶ ❌ DENY  (implicit deny — the default when policies exist)

  ⚠️  CRITICAL RULE: NetworkPolicies are ADDITIVE (union of all allows).
      Policy A allows port 80 + Policy B allows port 443 = pod gets BOTH.
      No policy can override or subtract from another policy's allow rule.

  ⚠️  TRAP: Once a pod is selected by ANY NetworkPolicy, ALL traffic is
      DENIED by default except what is explicitly allowed by some policy.
      Pod with NO policies = wide open. Pod with ONE policy = locked down.

How CNI Plugins Enforce NetworkPolicies — iptables vs eBPF

iptables-based (Calico, Weave)

Every NetworkPolicy rule is translated into iptables rules. Each allow rule becomes an ACCEPT entry; implicit deny becomes a DROP. Battle-tested but scales poorly — thousands of pods mean thousands of iptables rules, slowing packet processing.

Debug: iptables -L -n -v | grep cali shows actual Calico rules.

eBPF-based (Cilium)

Uses eBPF programs attached before iptables. Each policy becomes an O(1) eBPF map lookup, scaling to tens of thousands of pods with no degradation. Also supports FQDN-based egress (e.g., "allow egress to *.github.com").

Debug: cilium policy get and cilium monitor for real-time decisions.

The Additive Rule Behavior — Policies Cannot "Undo" Each Other

NetworkPolicies are purely additive — they can only ALLOW, never DENY. If Policy A allows monitoring pods to reach postgres, and Policy B allows anihpj pods to reach postgres, the effective rule is the UNION: both can reach postgres. You cannot create Policy C to "block monitoring from postgres" — NetworkPolicies have no DENY rules. To remove access, you must DELETE the policy that granted it.

The policyTypes Trap — CKS Exam Pitfall

😰 When policyTypes is omitted, it defaults to [Ingress] — your egress rules are silently IGNORED.

You create a policy with egress rules but forget policyTypes. The policy only affects ingress. Your egress rules do nothing — and you get no error message. Always explicitly set policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress] when you need both directions.

6.3 Common NetworkPolicy Patterns You Must Know

The CKS exam tests a specific set of NetworkPolicy patterns. You do not need to invent new ones — you need to recognize which pattern the question is asking for and apply it correctly. Here are the 7 essential patterns, with ready-to-use YAML and the exam scenario each one solves:

Pattern 1: Default-Deny All Ingress

Blocks ALL incoming traffic to every pod in the namespace
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: default-deny-ingress
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector: {}          # {} = select ALL pods in this namespace
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    # No ingress rules specified → DENY ALL incoming traffic

Pattern 2: Default-Deny All Egress

Blocks ALL outgoing traffic from every pod — use with caution (DNS will break!)
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: default-deny-egress
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector: {}
    policyTypes:
    - Egress
    # No egress rules → DENY ALL outgoing. DNS breaks. Always add Pattern 7!

Pattern 3: Allow Specific Pod to Reach a Specific Port (Database Access)

Allow anihpj pods → postgres on port 5432. Nothing else can reach postgres.
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-anihpj-to-postgres
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: postgres            # This policy PROTECTS postgres pods
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: anihpj          # Only FROM anihpj pods
      ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 5432               # Only ON postgres port

Pattern 4: Allow Traffic Within Same Namespace

All pods in the namespace can talk to each other — but nothing from outside
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-same-namespace
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector: {}
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - podSelector: {}         # From ANY pod in this namespace

Pattern 5: Allow Traffic from a Specific Namespace

Allow ingress-controller in ingress-nginx namespace → anihpj pods
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-from-ingress-ns
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: anihpj
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx

Pattern 6: Allow Specific CIDR Block (External IPs)

Allow traffic from a specific IP range — e.g., office VPN subnet
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-from-office-vpn
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: anihpj
    policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    ingress:
    - from:
      - ipBlock:
          cidr: 10.100.0.0/16    # Office VPN subnet
      ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 8000

Pattern 7: Allow DNS Egress (Critical — DNS Breaks Without This)

Allow all pods to reach CoreDNS on UDP 53. Always pair with default-deny-egress.
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-dns-egress
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    podSelector: {}              # All pods need DNS
    policyTypes:
    - Egress
    egress:
    - to:
      - namespaceSelector:       # CoreDNS runs in kube-system
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
        podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            k8s-app: kube-dns    # The CoreDNS pods
      ports:
      - protocol: UDP
        port: 53                 # DNS port
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 53                 # DNS over TCP (for large responses)

Essential Patterns — Quick Reference Table

PatternUse CaseExam Frequency
Default deny all ingressIsolate a namespaceVery High
Default deny all egressPrevent data exfiltrationHigh
Allow same namespaceTeam isolationHigh
Allow specific port to podDatabase access controlVery High
Allow DNS egress (53/UDP+TCP)Apps need name resolutionHigh
Allow namespaceSelectorCross-namespace allowed pathsHigh
Allow specific CIDR (ingress)External trusted IPs onlyMedium

Pattern Combinations — Building Real-World Policies

The 7 patterns are building blocks. Real clusters combine them. The most common CKS task: Default-Deny Ingress (blocks all incoming) + Allow App→DB on specific port (creates one exception). Also common: Default-Deny Egress + Allow DNS (UDP+TCP 53) — without DNS, pods cannot resolve names and health checks fail. Always create DNS allow rules FIRST, then apply default-deny-egress to avoid breaking your pods during configuration.

Cluster-Wide Default-Deny — One-Liner for All Namespaces

Apply default-deny to every namespace (skip kube-system and ingress)
  $ for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o name | grep -v -E 'kube-system|ingress-nginx'); do
      kubectl -n ${ns##*/} apply -f - <

6.4 Testing and Verifying NetworkPolicy — Does It Actually Work?

NetworkPolicies are silent when they work correctly — blocked traffic simply times out with no error message. This makes testing essential. The standard approach is to use a busybox test pod to probe connections and verify which ones succeed (allowed) and which ones timeout (blocked).

The NetworkPolicy Testing Workflow

Using busybox to verify NetworkPolicy enforcement
  # Step 1: Create a test pod in the SAME namespace
  $ kubectl run test-same --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -n anihpj-prod -- sh

  # Step 2: Test ALLOWED connections (should succeed)
  / # wget -q -O- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-service:8000/jobs/
  → Returns HTML (allowed by Pattern 3)

  / # nc -zv postgres-service 5432
  → Connection to postgres-service 5432 succeeded! (allowed by Pattern 3)

  # Step 3: Test BLOCKED connections (should timeout)
  / # wget -q -O- --timeout=3 http://monitoring-service:9090/metrics
  → wget: download timed out (BLOCKED by default-deny)

  # Step 4: Create a test pod in a DIFFERENT namespace
  $ kubectl run test-other --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -n default -- sh

  # Step 5: Test cross-namespace access (should be BLOCKED)
  / # wget -q -O- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-service.anihpj-prod:8000/
  → wget: download timed out (BLOCKED — cross-namespace denied)

anihpj Connectivity Matrix — Expected Results

FROM (source)TO (destination)PORTExpected Result
ingress-nginxanihpj pod8000✅ ALLOWED
anihpj podpostgres pod5432✅ ALLOWED
anihpj podredis pod6379✅ ALLOWED
ALL podskube-dns (DNS)53✅ ALLOWED
monitoring podALL pods9090✅ ALLOWED
postgres podanihpj pod8000❌ BLOCKED
anihpj podother namespaceANY❌ BLOCKED
attacker-podpostgres pod5432❌ BLOCKED
anihpj podinternet IPsANY❌ BLOCKED
💡 The 3-Second Timeout Rule

When testing NetworkPolicies, use --timeout=3 on wget or -w 3 on nc. Blocked connections do not get a "Connection Refused" — they hang until the TCP SYN timeout (typically 30-75 seconds). The --timeout flag saves you from waiting. On the exam, if a connection takes more than 3 seconds, it is blocked. Move on.

Debugging When NetworkPolicies Do Not Work — Common Failure Modes

🔴 Failure 1: Policy applied but ALL traffic still flows

Root Cause: CNI does not support NetworkPolicy (Flannel), OR podSelector does not match any pods. If no pods are selected, the policy has zero effect. Diagnose: kubectl get pods -n <ns> --show-labels → verify labels match podSelector exactly (case-sensitive).

🟡 Failure 2: Egress rules ignored

Root Cause: policyTypes omitted — defaults to [Ingress]. Egress rules silently ignored. Diagnose: kubectl get netpol <name> -o yaml | grep policyTypes — must explicitly list Egress.

🔴 Failure 3: DNS works but HTTP fails

Root Cause: You allowed UDP 53 (DNS) but your app needs TCP 53 for large DNS responses, OR your allow rule has the wrong port/protocol. Diagnose: kubectl exec <pod> -- nc -zv <svc> <port> — verify TCP connectivity.

6.5 Securing anihpj with NetworkPolicies — Full Implementation

Let's apply everything to the anihpj/jobpost application. We need 6 NetworkPolicies to achieve zero-trust networking while keeping the application functional:

anihpj Network Traffic Map — Visual Representation

All allowed and blocked traffic flows for anihpj
                     🌐 INTERNET
                          │
                          │ HTTPS :443 (Ingress TLS)
                          ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   🚪 INGRESS CONTROLLER                       │
  │                   (only exposed entry point)                  │
  └────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘
                               │ HTTP :8000 (Policy 3)
                               ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   📦 anihpj DEPLOYMENT                       │
  │                   app: anihpj  |  port: 8000                  │
  │                   SecurityContext: non-root, Seccomp, AppArmor│
  └────┬─────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────┘
       │ TCP :5432 (Policy 2)               │ TCP :6379 (Policy 4)
       ▼                                     ▼
  ┌──────────────┐                   ┌──────────────┐
  │ 🗄️  postgres │                   │ ⚡ Redis     │
  │ app:postgres │                   │ app: redis   │
  │ port: 5432   │                   │ port: 6379   │
  └──────────────┘                   └──────────────┘

  📊 MONITORING POD (Policy 6): can scrape ALL pods on :9090
  🔍 DNS (Policy 5): ALL pods can reach kube-dns on port 53/UDP+TCP

  ❌ BLOCKED PATHS (default-deny Policy 1):
     • internet → anihpj pod DIRECT (must go through ingress)
     • postgres → anihpj (reverse connection blocked)
     • anihpj → internet (egress blocked)
     • any pod → any pod in other namespaces
     • attacker-pod → ANY resource in anihpj namespace

The 6 Policies for anihpj Zero-Trust Networking

1️⃣
Policy 1: Default-Deny All Ingress in anihpj-prod

Blocks ALL incoming traffic to every pod. Individual allow rules (Policies 2-6) create exceptions for specific flows. Without this policy, pods accept connections from anywhere.

2️⃣
Policy 2: Allow anihpj → PostgreSQL (TCP 5432)

podSelector: app=postgres. ingress from podSelector: app=anihpj on port 5432. All other pods — including attacker pods — cannot reach the database.

3️⃣
Policy 3: Allow Ingress Controller → anihpj (TCP 8000)

podSelector: app=anihpj. ingress from namespaceSelector: ingress-nginx on port 8000. Only the ingress controller can reach the Django app — direct internet access is blocked.

4️⃣
Policy 4: Allow anihpj → Redis (TCP 6379)

podSelector: app=redis. ingress from podSelector: app=anihpj on port 6379. Django can cache job listings. No other pod can access the cache.

5️⃣
Policy 5: Allow ALL Pods → DNS (UDP+TCP 53)

podSelector: {}. egress to namespaceSelector: kube-system, podSelector: k8s-app=kube-dns on port 53. CRITICAL: without this, name resolution fails and your app breaks.

6️⃣
Policy 6: Allow Monitoring → ALL Pods (TCP 9090)

podSelector: {}. ingress from podSelector: app=monitoring on port 9090. Prometheus can scrape metrics from every pod. No other pod can access the metrics endpoint.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

NetworkPolicy questions are the most common CKS tasks after RBAC. The exam pattern is always: (1) Create default-deny first, (2) Add specific allow rules for required communication, (3) Test with busybox, (4) Remember DNS — if you add egress deny, you MUST add a DNS allow rule or your pods will break silently. Always start with default-deny. Never forget DNS.

How NetworkPolicy Is Enforced — The CNI Plugin Is the Firewall Engine

NetworkPolicy YAML is not enforced by Kubernetes itself. It is enforced by your CNI (Container Network Interface) plugin — Calico, Cilium, Weave, or another CNI that supports NetworkPolicy. This is the most important concept to understand because if your CNI doesn't support NetworkPolicy, your policies are silently ignored — you write YAML, kubectl accepts it, but nothing is actually enforced:

NetworkPolicy Enforcement Architecture — From YAML to iptables/eBPF
  kubectl apply -f networkpolicy.yaml
  │
  ▼
  API SERVER: Validates the NetworkPolicy object → stores it in etcd.
  │  (This is ALL Kubernetes does. It does NOT enforce the policy.)
  │
  ▼
  CNI PLUGIN (e.g., Calico): Watches for NetworkPolicy objects via the K8s API.
  │
  │  CALICO'S ENFORCEMENT PATH:
  │  ───────────────────────────
  │  1. Calico controller detects new/modified NetworkPolicy.
  │  2. Translates the policy's podSelector + ingress/egress rules into
  │     iptables rules (or eBPF programs for Cilium).
  │  3. Programs these rules into EVERY node where matching pods run.
  │  4. iptables checks EVERY packet entering or leaving matching pods:
  │     • Source IP matches allowed CIDR? → ALLOW
  │     • Source pod label matches allowed podSelector? → ALLOW
  │     • Neither → DROP (silently — no ICMP response)
  │
  │  WHAT HAPPENS WITH A CNI THAT DOESN'T SUPPORT NETWORKPOLICY:
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  │  • Flannel (without NetworkPolicy extension): IGNORES the policy entirely.
  │  • All pods can still communicate. Your YAML did nothing.
  │  • kubectl describe networkpolicy shows the policy as "active" — but
  │    there is NO enforcement. This is a silent failure.
  │
  │  CNI PLUGIN NETWORKPOLICY SUPPORT:
  │  ───────────────────────────────────
  │  ✅ Calico      — Full support (iptables or eBPF)
  │  ✅ Cilium      — Full support (eBPF — most advanced)
  │  ✅ Weave Net   — Full support
  │  ⚠️  Flannel     — Only with Calico network policy engine
  │  ⚠️  Azure CNI   — Supports NetworkPolicy (Azure Network Policy Manager)
  │  ⚠️  AWS VPC CNI — Requires Calico for NetworkPolicy (AWS doesn't natively enforce)
  │  ❌ Docker bridge — NO support (development only, never production)
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CKS EXAM REALITY:
  ─────────────────
  The CKS exam cluster uses a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (usually Calico
  or Cilium). You do NOT need to install a CNI. Just write the YAML and test.
  But in real clusters, ALWAYS VERIFY your CNI supports NetworkPolicy before
  relying on it. Check: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave'

The DNS Problem — Why Egress Deny Breaks Your Pods

This is the single most common NetworkPolicy mistake — and the one that CKS exam candidates trip on most. When you create a default-deny egress policy, your pods lose the ability to resolve DNS names. Why? Because DNS queries go to CoreDNS, which runs as a pod in kube-system. If your default-deny egress policy doesn't explicitly allow DNS, your pod can't even look up postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local. Here's the exact mechanic:

What Happens Without a DNS Egress Rule — The Silent Failure
  POD: anihpj-django-7f8c9-abcde (namespace: anihpj)
  │
  │  Application tries to connect: postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:5432
  │
  ▼
  STEP 1: The application calls getaddrinfo("postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local")
  │  This triggers a DNS query.
  │
  ▼
  STEP 2: The container's /etc/resolv.conf points to CoreDNS:
  │  nameserver 10.96.0.10  (CoreDNS ClusterIP)
  │
  ▼
  STEP 3: The container sends a UDP packet to 10.96.0.10:53
  │  (DNS is UDP by default; falls back to TCP for large responses)
  │
  ▼
  STEP 4: NETWORKPOLICY CHECK — Is this egress allowed?
  │
  │  ┌─ NO DNS EGRESS RULE ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  │  • Policy says: egress to podSelector: app=postgres on 5432   │
  │  │  • But the DNS query is to podSelector: k8s-app=kube-dns on 53│
  │  │  • This does NOT match the postgres rule → DROP                │
  │  │  • DNS query NEVER reaches CoreDNS. No response.               │
  │  │  • Application hangs waiting for DNS resolution.               │
  │  │  • Eventually times out (30+ seconds). App appears broken.     │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  │  ┌─ WITH DNS EGRESS RULE ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  │  • Policy ALSO has: egress to podSelector: k8s-app=kube-dns   │
  │  │    on port 53 (UDP + TCP)                                     │
  │  │  • DNS query MATCHES → ALLOWED                                 │
  │  │  • CoreDNS responds with: postgres.anihpj.svc = 10.96.0.45    │
  │  │  • Application connects to 10.96.0.45:5432 → matches postgres │
  │  │    rule → ALLOWED → connection established ✅                  │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  THE DNS EGRESS RULE YOU MUST ADD:
  ─────────────────────────────────
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53

Chapter 7: Ingress Security with TLS

Every Kubernetes application that serves users over the internet must terminate TLS. Without TLS, every request — including passwords, session tokens, and personal data — travels over the network in plaintext, readable by anyone on any network hop between the user and your cluster. TLS is the most fundamental security control for web applications, and Kubernetes makes it straightforward: store the certificate in a Secret, reference it in an Ingress resource, and the Ingress controller handles the rest. This chapter teaches you how to create TLS certificates, automate their lifecycle with cert-manager and Let's Encrypt, and enforce HTTPS with redirects and security headers — all within the anihpj cluster.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔐 TLS/SSL 🌐 Ingress

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand TLS termination — where encryption starts and ends in a K8s cluster
  • ✅ Create TLS Secrets from existing certificates and reference them in Ingress resources
  • ✅ Deploy cert-manager to automate certificate issuance and renewal from Let's Encrypt
  • ✅ Configure ClusterIssuer vs Issuer — cluster-wide vs namespace-scoped certificate authorities
  • ✅ Enforce HTTPS with SSL redirect, HSTS headers, and TLS version restrictions
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Setup 15% Minimize Microservice Vulns 20%
🧠 The TLS Exam Pattern

CKS TLS tasks typically ask you to: (1) create a TLS Secret from provided certificate files, (2) configure an Ingress to use that Secret for TLS termination, (3) ensure HTTP traffic is redirected to HTTPS. The exam provides the certificate and key files — you do not need to generate them. Focus on the kubectl create secret tls command, the Ingress TLS spec, and the SSL redirect annotation.

7.1 TLS Certificates in Kubernetes

TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol that encrypts HTTP traffic — turning it into HTTPS. In Kubernetes, TLS termination typically happens at the Ingress controller: the Ingress controller holds the TLS certificate, decrypts incoming HTTPS traffic, and forwards the plain HTTP request to the backend pod inside the cluster. This is called TLS termination at the edge — the most common pattern for Kubernetes deployments.

TLS Termination — What It Means for anihpj

Three TLS deployment patterns — from none to end-to-end
  ❌ WITHOUT TLS:
  👤 User ──── HTTP (plaintext) ──────────────── anihpj pod
  "password=secret" visible on every network hop.
  Anyone on the WiFi, ISP, or any router in between can read it.

  ✅ WITH TLS (termination at Ingress) — STANDARD PATTERN:
                         Ingress
  👤 User ──── HTTPS ──── [decrypt] ──── HTTP ─── anihpj pod
      encrypted        TLS cert        internal plain
      on internet      stored here      (inside cluster)

  Traffic is encrypted from the user's browser to the Ingress controller.
  Inside the cluster, it is plain HTTP — but that is acceptable because
  the cluster network should be protected by NetworkPolicies (Chapter 6).

  🔐 WITH END-TO-END TLS (mTLS — Chapter 22):
  👤 User ──── HTTPS ──── Ingress ──── HTTPS ─── anihpj pod
      encrypted        re-encrypts     pod cert verified
      both hops        to pod          (mTLS)

Certificate Types — Which to Use When

Certificate TypeUse CaseBrowser TrustAuto-Renewal
Self-Signed (openssl req -x509)Local dev, testing only⚠️ "Not Secure" warning❌ Manual
Let's Encrypt via cert-managerProduction public domains✅ Trusted by all browsers✅ Automatic (90-day certs)
Private CA (internal)Internal services, air-gapped⚠️ Only if CA cert is distributed⚠️ Depends on CA setup
Wildcard (*.anihpj.com)All subdomains with one cert✅ From public CA⚠️ One compromise = all subdomains

Creating a TLS Secret — The CKS Exam Essential

The CKS exam expects you to create a TLS Secret from provided certificate files. This is the most common TLS task:

Creating a TLS Secret and referencing it in an Ingress
  # Step 1: Create TLS Secret from existing cert+key files
  $ kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls \
      --cert=/path/to/anihpj.com.crt \
      --key=/path/to/anihpj.com.key \
      -n anihpj-prod

  # Step 2: Reference the Secret in an Ingress resource
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Ingress
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-ingress
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  spec:
    tls:
    - hosts:
      - anihpj.com
      - www.anihpj.com
      secretName: anihpj-tls          # ← The TLS Secret created above
    rules:
    - host: anihpj.com
      http:
        paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
          backend:
            service:
              name: anihpj-service
              port:
                number: 8000

  # Step 3: Verify TLS is working
  $ curl -v https://anihpj.com/jobs/
  → TLS handshake succeeds → HTTP 200 with job listings HTML

  # Step 4: Check the certificate details
  $ kubectl get secret anihpj-tls -n anihpj-prod -o yaml
  → data.tls.crt and data.tls.key are base64-encoded
  $ echo "" | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -text
  → Shows subject, issuer, validity dates, SANs
💡 kubectl create secret tls — The One Command to Remember

The exam provides certificate files. Your job is to create the Secret and configure the Ingress. The command is kubectl create secret tls <name> --cert=<cert-file> --key=<key-file>. The Secret type must be kubernetes.io/tls — this type is automatically set when you use kubectl create secret tls. Do NOT use kubectl create secret generic for TLS certs — the Ingress controller will not recognize them.

What's Inside a TLS Certificate — And Why Each Field Matters

A TLS certificate is not just "a file that enables HTTPS." It is a structured document defined by the X.509 standard, containing specific fields that your browser and the Ingress controller validate before establishing a secure connection. Understanding these fields helps you debug TLS errors on the exam:

X.509 Certificate Fields — What Your Browser Checks
  $ openssl x509 -in anihpj.com.crt -noout -text

  Certificate:
      Data:
          Version: 3 (0x2)
          Serial Number: 04:2a:8f:...          ← Unique ID. Revoked certs listed by serial.
          Issuer: C=US, O=Let's Encrypt, CN=R3  ← Who SIGNED this cert. Browser must trust this CA.
          Validity:
              Not Before: Jan  1 00:00:00 2024 GMT  ← Cert is INVALID before this
              Not After : Apr  1 00:00:00 2024 GMT   ← Cert EXPIRES after this (90 days for LE)
          Subject: CN=anihpj.com                 ← Who this cert identifies. Must match the URL.
          Subject Public Key Info:
              Public Key Algorithm: rsaEncryption
              RSA Public-Key: (2048 bit)         ← The public key. Private key stays in the Secret.
          X509v3 extensions:
              X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:   ← CRITICAL: browsers check this, not CN.
                  DNS:anihpj.com, DNS:www.anihpj.com

  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Browsers validate the SAN (Subject Alternative Name) field,
     NOT the CN (Common Name). If anihpj.com is in CN but not SAN, the browser
     will show a certificate error. Always include the domain in SAN.

How the TLS Handshake Works — What Happens in the First 300ms

Every HTTPS connection begins with a TLS handshake — a multi-step negotiation between the browser and the Ingress controller. Understanding this sequence helps you diagnose TLS errors when users report "connection not secure":

TLS 1.3 Handshake — Client Hello to Encrypted Data
  CLIENT (Browser)                           SERVER (Ingress Controller)
  ─────────────────                         ────────────────────────────
  1. ClientHello ─────────────────────▶
     • Supported TLS versions (1.2, 1.3)
     • Supported cipher suites
     • SNI: "anihpj.com" (which site?)
                                          2. ServerHello ◀─────────────────
                                             • Chosen: TLS 1.3
                                             • Chosen cipher: AES-256-GCM
                                             • Server Certificate ▶
                                               (the anihpj-tls Secret!)
  3. Verify certificate:
     • Signed by trusted CA? ✅
     • Not expired? ✅
     • SAN matches anihpj.com? ✅
                                          4. Key Exchange (Diffie-Hellman)
  5. Symmetric encryption established
     All subsequent data is encrypted with AES-256-GCM

  ⏱️  Total time: ~300ms on a good connection.
  ❌ FAILURE POINTS:
     • Certificate expired → browser shows NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID
     • SAN mismatch → NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID
     • Untrusted CA (self-signed) → NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID
     • TLS version too old (1.0/1.1 disabled by annotation) → handshake fails

Why HTTP Inside the Cluster Is Acceptable — The Trust Boundary

After TLS termination at the Ingress controller, traffic to the backend pod is plain HTTP. This concerns many newcomers: "Isn't that insecure?" The answer is: it depends on your trust model. The Ingress controller and your application pods are inside the same cluster network, protected by NetworkPolicies (Chapter 6). An attacker who can sniff internal pod-to-pod traffic has already compromised a pod on that node — at which point they can read data from memory directly, making TLS between pods redundant for confidentiality (though not for authentication — that is where mTLS comes in, covered in Chapter 22). For the CKS exam, the standard pattern is TLS termination at the Ingress controller with HTTP to the backend. End-to-end TLS (mTLS) is an advanced topic tested separately.

7.2 cert-manager — Automated Certificate Management

Manually creating TLS certificates works, but it does not scale. Certificates expire. You forget to renew them. Your site goes down. cert-manager solves this by automating the entire certificate lifecycle: it watches Ingress resources, requests certificates from Let's Encrypt (or a private CA), stores them as Kubernetes Secrets, and automatically renews them 30 days before expiry. Once configured, you never think about certificate renewal again.

📖 cert-manager at a Glance

Home: cert-manager.io · License: Apache 2.0 · CKS Exam: ✅ Must know the concept. The exam may ask you to configure a ClusterIssuer and annotate an Ingress. How it works: cert-manager runs as a controller in your cluster. It watches for Certificate resources (or Ingress resources with annotations) and communicates with a Certificate Authority (CA) to fulfill them using the ACME protocol (for Let's Encrypt) or other protocols (for private CAs).

cert-manager Certificate Lifecycle — Automated Flow for anihpj

7-step automated certificate lifecycle — zero manual intervention
  1. You create an Ingress with annotation:
     cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
                        │
                        ▼
  2. cert-manager detects the Ingress → creates Certificate resource
                        │
                        ▼
  3. cert-manager creates a CertificateRequest
     → challenges Let's Encrypt via HTTP-01 challenge
     (Let's Encrypt makes an HTTP request to your domain to verify ownership)
                        │
                        ▼
  4. Let's Encrypt verifies you own anihpj.com
     → issues a signed certificate (valid 90 days)
                        │
                        ▼
  5. cert-manager stores the certificate in a K8s Secret: anihpj-tls
                        │
                        ▼
  6. Ingress controller reads the Secret → serves HTTPS to users
                        │
                        ▼
  7. 30 days before expiry → cert-manager AUTO-RENEWS! 🔄
     Zero manual intervention. The site never goes down due to expired certs.

ClusterIssuer Configuration — Let's Encrypt

ClusterIssuer YAML for Let's Encrypt production
  apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
  kind: ClusterIssuer                    # Cluster-wide (vs Issuer = namespace-scoped)
  metadata:
    name: letsencrypt-prod
  spec:
    acme:
      server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory  # Production CA
      email: admin@anihpj.com            # Let's Encrypt sends expiry notifications here
      privateKeySecretRef:
        name: letsencrypt-prod-key       # cert-manager stores its ACME account key here
      solvers:
      - http01:                          # HTTP-01 challenge: Let's Encrypt checks your domain
          ingress:
            class: nginx                 # Which Ingress controller handles the challenge
  ---
  # Annotate your Ingress to use this ClusterIssuer:
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Ingress
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-ingress
    namespace: anihpj-prod
    annotations:
      cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"  # ← This triggers cert-manager
  spec:
    tls:
    - hosts:
      - anihpj.com
      secretName: anihpj-tls             # cert-manager will CREATE this Secret
    rules:
    - host: anihpj.com
      http:
        paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
          backend:
            service:
              name: anihpj-service
              port:
                number: 8000

ClusterIssuer vs Issuer — When to Use Each

ResourceScopeUse CaseExample
ClusterIssuerCluster-wide — usable from any namespaceShared Let's Encrypt config for the whole cluster. One ClusterIssuer serves all teams.letsencrypt-prod — every namespace can use it for their domain certs
IssuerNamespace-scopedTeam-specific CA config. Different namespaces use different CAs or different ACME accounts.anihpj-staging-issuer — only the anihpj namespace can use it
⚠️ Let's Encrypt Rate Limits — Use Staging First

Let's Encrypt production has strict rate limits: 50 certificates per domain per week. If you are testing your cert-manager configuration, use the staging endpoint: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers, but they let you verify that your DNS, Ingress, and cert-manager configuration are correct before you switch to production. On the CKS exam, you will use a provided CA endpoint — not the public Let's Encrypt.

HTTP-01 vs DNS-01 Challenges — How Let's Encrypt Verifies Domain Ownership

Before Let's Encrypt issues a certificate, it must verify that you control the domain. It does this through challenges — cryptographic proofs of domain ownership. cert-manager supports two challenge types, and choosing the right one depends on your infrastructure:

HTTP-01 Challenge

Let's Encrypt makes an HTTP request to http://anihpj.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token>. cert-manager creates a temporary pod or configures the Ingress to serve the challenge response. This is the simplest method — it requires only that port 80 is reachable from the internet. Limitation: Cannot issue wildcard certificates. Does not work if your cluster is behind a firewall that blocks inbound HTTP.

DNS-01 Challenge

cert-manager creates a TXT record in your DNS zone (_acme-challenge.anihpj.com). Let's Encrypt queries DNS to verify the record exists. This method works even if port 80 is blocked — it only requires DNS API access. Advantage: Supports wildcard certificates (*.anihpj.com). Limitation: Requires cert-manager to have API credentials for your DNS provider (Route53, Cloudflare, Google Cloud DNS).

Debugging cert-manager — When Certificates Do Not Issue

The most common cert-manager failure on the CKS exam is a Certificate resource stuck in a "Pending" or "Failed" state. Here is how to diagnose and fix it:

🔴 Certificate Stuck — Diagnostic Commands
  # 1. Check the Certificate resource status
  $ kubectl describe certificate anihpj-tls -n anihpj-prod
  → Look for "Ready: False" and the "Reason" field.
    Common reasons: "NotFound" (Secret doesn't exist yet — normal),
    "Pending" (waiting for challenge), "Failed" (challenge failed).

  # 2. Check the CertificateRequest
  $ kubectl get certificaterequest -n anihpj-prod
  $ kubectl describe certificaterequest <name>
  → Shows the exact challenge status and any error messages.

  # 3. Check the Order (ACME order resource)
  $ kubectl get orders -n anihpj-prod
  $ kubectl describe order <name>
  → Shows the ACME authorization URL and challenge status.

  # 4. Check the Challenge resource directly
  $ kubectl get challenges -n anihpj-prod
  $ kubectl describe challenge <name>
  → "Reason: Waiting for HTTP-01 challenge propagation"
  → "Reason: DNS record not found" means DNS-01 failed.

  # 5. Check cert-manager logs
  $ kubectl logs -n cert-manager deploy/cert-manager
  → Look for ERROR lines about your domain.

The ACME Protocol Flow — What cert-manager Actually Does

cert-manager implements the ACME (Automated Certificate Management Environment) protocol — the same protocol used by Let's Encrypt. Understanding the ACME flow demystifies the cert-manager logs and helps you troubleshoot on the exam:

ACME Protocol Flow — cert-manager to Let's Encrypt
  cert-manager                              Let's Encrypt (ACME Server)
  ────────────                              ───────────────────────────
  1. Create ACME account
     POST /acme/new-acct ────────────────▶  Account created. Returns account URL.

  2. Submit certificate order
     POST /acme/new-order ───────────────▶  Order created. Returns:
       {                                      • Order URL
         "identifiers": [                     • Authorization URLs (one per domain)
           {"type":"dns","value":"anihpj.com"}, • Finalize URL
           {"type":"dns","value":"www.anihpj.com"}
         ]
       }

  3. Fetch authorizations
     POST /acme/authz/<id> ───────────────▶  Returns challenge details:
                                                • HTTP-01: token + expected response
                                                • DNS-01: TXT record value

  4. Complete challenges
     (HTTP-01: serve token at .well-known/)  Let's Encrypt verifies:
     (DNS-01: create TXT record)              • HTTP: GET http://anihpj.com/.well-known/...
                                              • DNS: dig TXT _acme-challenge.anihpj.com

  5. Finalize order
     POST /acme/finalize ─────────────────▶  Submit CSR (Certificate Signing Request)
       { "csr": "<base64-encoded CSR>" }

  6. Download certificate
     GET /acme/cert/<id> ─────────────────▶  Returns signed certificate chain

7.3 Enforcing HTTPS — Redirecting HTTP to HTTPS

Having a TLS certificate is not enough — you must also ensure that users always use HTTPS. A user who types http://anihpj.com into their browser will connect over plain HTTP unless you explicitly redirect them to HTTPS. This is configured through Ingress annotations on the NGINX Ingress Controller — the most commonly used Ingress controller on the CKS exam.

Ingress Security Annotations — Complete Reference

AnnotationEffectWhy It Matters
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"Forces HTTP→HTTPS redirect (301)Users who type http://anihpj.com are automatically sent to https://anihpj.com. Non-negotiable for production.
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet: |
add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains"		Adds HSTS headerTells browsers: "always use HTTPS for this domain for the next year." Prevents SSL stripping attacks.
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet: |
add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY"		Blocks clickjackingPrevents your site from being embedded in an iframe on an attacker's page.
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-protocols: "TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3"Only allow modern TLSDisables TLS 1.0 and 1.1 — both are broken and vulnerable to attacks like POODLE and BEAST.
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "10"Rate limiting (10 req/sec per IP)Prevents brute-force attacks and DoS by limiting how many requests a single IP can make.

Complete Secure Ingress for anihpj — All Controls Applied

Production-ready Ingress YAML with TLS, HSTS, and security headers
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Ingress
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-secure-ingress
    namespace: anihpj-prod
    annotations:
      # --- TLS & HTTPS Enforcement ---
      cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-protocols: "TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3"

      # --- Security Headers ---
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/configuration-snippet: |
        add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;
        add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always;
        add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;
        add_header X-XSS-Protection "1; mode=block" always;

      # --- Rate Limiting ---
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "20"
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-whitelist: "10.0.0.0/8"  # Internal traffic unlimited

  spec:
    tls:
    - hosts:
      - anihpj.com
      - www.anihpj.com
      secretName: anihpj-tls
    rules:
    - host: anihpj.com
      http:
        paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
          backend:
            service:
              name: anihpj-service
              port:
                number: 8000

How HSTS Works — Why It Is Critical

HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) solves a fundamental problem with HTTPS: the first request a user makes to your site may still be over HTTP. An attacker on the same network (coffee shop WiFi, airport, compromised router) can intercept that first HTTP request and redirect the user to a fake site — this is called an SSL stripping attack. HSTS tells the browser: "For the next year (31,536,000 seconds), always use HTTPS for this domain — do not even attempt HTTP." After the first successful HTTPS visit, the browser enforces this automatically. The includeSubDomains directive extends this protection to all subdomains (www.anihpj.com, api.anihpj.com, admin.anihpj.com).

⚠️ HSTS Preloading — The Point of No Return

You can submit your domain to the HSTS Preload List (hstspreload.org), which is hardcoded into Chrome, Firefox, and Safari. Once on this list, browsers will NEVER attempt HTTP for your domain — even on the very first visit. This is the strongest protection, but it is irreversible in practice. If you ever need to serve HTTP on any subdomain, you cannot be on the preload list. Do not submit unless you are 100% certain you will always serve HTTPS everywhere.

Testing Your TLS Configuration — curl and SSL Labs

After configuring TLS, always verify it works correctly before declaring the task complete. Here are the essential verification commands — use them on every TLS task:

TLS Verification Commands
  # 1. Verify HTTPS is serving (no certificate error)
  $ curl -vI https://anihpj.com 2>&1 | grep -E 'Server certificate|HTTP/'
  → HTTP/2 200
  → Server certificate: subject=CN=anihpj.com, issuer=C=US,O=Let's Encrypt

  # 2. Verify HTTP→HTTPS redirect works
  $ curl -vI http://anihpj.com 2>&1 | grep -E 'Location|HTTP/'
  → HTTP/1.1 308 Permanent Redirect
  → Location: https://anihpj.com/

  # 3. Verify HSTS header is present
  $ curl -sI https://anihpj.com | grep Strict-Transport
  → Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

  # 4. Verify TLS version (1.2+ only)
  $ openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -tls1_2 < /dev/null 2>&1 | grep Verify
  → Verify return code: 0 (ok) — TLS 1.2 works
  $ openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 -tls1_1 < /dev/null 2>&1 | grep Verify
  → (should fail or return error — TLS 1.1 is blocked)

  # 5. Check certificate expiry date
  $ echo | openssl s_client -connect anihpj.com:443 2>/dev/null | \
      openssl x509 -noout -dates
  → notBefore=Jan 1 00:00:00 2024 GMT
  → notAfter=Apr 1 00:00:00 2024 GMT

Common TLS Misconfigurations and Their Symptoms

MisconfigurationSymptomRoot CauseFix
Wrong Secret typeIngress serves default fake certificateUsed kubectl create secret generic instead of tlsDelete and recreate with kubectl create secret tls
Certificate expiredBrowser shows NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALIDCert past NotAfter date. cert-manager not installed or misconfigured.Check cert-manager logs. Manually trigger renewal: kubectl cert-manager renew anihpj-tls
Mismatched hostnameNET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALIDCertificate SAN does not include the domain being accessed (e.g., cert for anihpj.com but accessing www.anihpj.com without www in SAN)Request new cert with correct SANs. Include both root domain and www.
TLS Secret in wrong namespaceIngress uses default cert, not yoursIngress and Secret must be in the same namespaceRecreate Secret in the same namespace as the Ingress
ssl-redirect not sethttp:// still works, no redirectAnnotation missing or typo in annotation keyAdd nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"

TLS Attack Walkthrough — What Happens Without HTTPS

Man-in-the-Middle Attack on Plain HTTP — The Real Risk
  SCENARIO: User on coffee shop WiFi accesses http://anihpj.com/jobs/
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  STEP 1: Attacker on same WiFi runs ARP spoofing
  $ arpspoof -i wlan0 -t 192.168.1.50 192.168.1.1
  → Attacker positions between user and the router.

  STEP 2: User types http://anihpj.com (NOT https)
  → Request goes through attacker's machine.
  → Attacker sees EVERYTHING in plaintext:
    GET /jobs/ HTTP/1.1
    Host: anihpj.com
    Cookie: sessionid=abc123def456...    ← SESSION COOKIE STOLEN

  STEP 3: Attacker now has a valid session cookie
  $ curl https://anihpj.com/admin/ -H "Cookie: sessionid=abc123..."
  → Attacker is LOGGED IN as the user. Can view profile, change settings,
    or if user is admin, access the Django admin panel.

  WITH TLS + HSTS enabled:
  ─────────────────────────
  User types http://anihpj.com → Browser auto-redirects to https://
  (HSTS preload or previous visit). Even on first visit, if the site
  is on the HSTS preload list, browser NEVER attempts HTTP.
  Attacker sees only: CONNECT anihpj.com:443 → ENCRYPTED DATA.
  Session cookie never exposed. Attack FAILS.

  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: TLS is not about hiding your content — it is about
     protecting your users' SESSION TOKENS from network-level attackers.
     One session token stolen = one user account compromised.

🔐 TLS Termination Ingress controller decrypts HTTPS → forwards HTTP internally (standard pattern)
📜 4 Certificate Types Self-signed, Let's Encrypt, Private CA, Wildcard — each with specific use cases
🔄 cert-manager 7-step automated lifecycle: detect→request→challenge→issue→store→serve→renew
🛡️ 5 Security Headers SSL redirect, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, TLS 1.2+, rate limiting
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

TLS tasks are straightforward but detail-oriented. The exam pattern: (1) create a TLS Secret with kubectl create secret tls --cert=... --key=..., (2) add a tls section to the Ingress spec referencing the Secret, (3) add ssl-redirect: true annotation. Common mistake: using kubectl create secret generic instead of kubectl create secret tls. The Ingress controller will not recognize a generic Secret as a TLS certificate. The type must be kubernetes.io/tls.

How TLS Termination Actually Works in Kubernetes Ingress

When you add a tls section to an Ingress resource, you are telling the Ingress controller (nginx-ingress, traefik, etc.) to handle TLS for you. But what actually happens to the traffic? Understanding this flow is critical for debugging "HTTPS not working" issues and for knowing where encryption boundaries lie:

TLS Termination Flow — From Browser to Pod, Byte by Byte
  BROWSER: https://anihpj.com/jobs/
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 1: DNS Resolution                                                  │
  │  anihpj.com → A record → 203.0.113.50 (Ingress Controller LoadBalancer IP)│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 2: TCP Connection to 203.0.113.50:443                             │
  │  The browser opens a TCP connection to the Ingress controller's IP on     │
  │  port 443 (HTTPS).                                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 3: TLS HANDSHAKE (TLS 1.3)                                         │
  │  ────────────────────────────────                                         │
  │  Client → Server: ClientHello (supported ciphers, SNI: anihpj.com)       │
  │  Server → Client: ServerHello + Certificate + ServerFinished             │
  │                    │                                                      │
  │                    │  The Ingress controller sends the TLS certificate    │
  │                    │  from the Secret referenced in the Ingress resource:  │
  │                    │  spec.tls[0].secretName: anihpj-tls                  │
  │                    │  → Loads tls.crt and tls.key from the Secret        │
  │                    │                                                      │
  │  ⚡ WHAT THE BROWSER CHECKS:                                              │
  │  • Is the certificate signed by a CA the browser trusts? (Let's Encrypt) │
  │  • Does the certificate's CN or SAN include "anihpj.com"? (SNI match)   │
  │  • Is the certificate NOT expired?                                       │
  │  • Is the certificate NOT revoked? (OCSP stapling check)                  │
  │  If ALL checks pass → 🔒 padlock icon appears in the browser.            │
  │  If ANY check fails → ⚠️ "Your connection is not private" warning.        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │  (TLS session established — encrypted tunnel between browser and Ingress)
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 4: TLS TERMINATION — The Ingress Controller decrypts the request   │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────                      │
  │  • The encrypted HTTPS request is DECRYPTED at the Ingress controller.   │
  │  • The Ingress reads the HTTP Host header: "anihpj.com".                 │
  │  • It matches this against Ingress rules to find the backend Service.    │
  │  • The decrypted (plain HTTP) request is forwarded to the backend pod.   │
  │  • ⚡ THIS IS WHERE ENCRYPTION ENDS (unless you use backend TLS).        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 5: BACKEND CONNECTION (Ingress → anihpj Pod, port 8000)            │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────                  │
  │  • The Ingress controller sends the HTTP request to the anihpj Service's  │
  │    ClusterIP → kube-proxy routes to a pod → Django/Gunicorn handles it.  │
  │  • This connection is PLAIN HTTP (no TLS between Ingress and pod).       │
  │  • Traffic between Ingress and pod goes over the CNI network (overlay).   │
  │  • ⚡ SECURITY IMPLICATION: Anyone who can sniff the CNI network can      │
  │    see the plaintext HTTP traffic. Use mTLS (Ch22) or NetworkPolicy       │
  │    (Ch6) to protect this path.                                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  THE TWO TLS MODELS:
  ────────────────────
  MODEL 1: TLS TERMINATION at Ingress (what most CKS tasks use)
  Browser ──TLS──▶ Ingress Controller ──HTTP──▶ Backend Pod
  (Encrypted to Ingress, plain to pod. Simplest. CKS default.)

  MODEL 2: TLS PASSTHROUGH (Ingress doesn't decrypt)
  Browser ────────TLS (end-to-end)──────────▶ Backend Pod
  (Pod handles TLS. Needs certs in pod. More secure, more complex.)

  MODEL 3: TLS RE-ENCRYPTION (Ingress decrypts, then re-encrypts to pod)
  Browser ──TLS──▶ Ingress ──TLS──▶ Backend Pod
  (Two separate TLS sessions. Requires certs on both Ingress AND pod.)

Let's Encrypt and cert-manager — Automating Certificate Lifecycle

Manually creating TLS certificates every 90 days is unsustainable. cert-manager automates the entire certificate lifecycle — request, issuance, renewal, and Secret management. The CKS exam may ask you to configure cert-manager or understand the ACME protocol flow:

cert-manager + Let's Encrypt — Automated TLS Lifecycle
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CERT-MANAGER AUTOMATED LIFECYCLE                                       │
  │                                                                         │
  │  STEP 1: YOU CREATE A CERTIFICATE RESOURCE                              │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────                                │
  │  apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1                                         │
  │  kind: Certificate                                                       │
  │  metadata:                                                               │
  │    name: anihpj-tls                                                      │
  │    namespace: anihpj                                                     │
  │  spec:                                                                   │
  │    secretName: anihpj-tls          ← TLS cert stored here               │
  │    dnsNames: [anihpj.com, www.anihpj.com]                                │
  │    issuerRef:                                                            │
  │      name: letsencrypt-prod         ← Which CA to use                   │
  │      kind: ClusterIssuer                                                 │
  │                                                                         │
  │  STEP 2: CERT-MANAGER DETECTS THE CERTIFICATE RESOURCE                  │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────                    │
  │  • cert-manager controller watches for Certificate resources.           │
  │  • Detects new "anihpj-tls" Certificate → initiates issuance.           │
  │                                                                         │
  │  STEP 3: ACME CHALLENGE (prove you own the domain)                      │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────                        │
  │  • cert-manager creates a temporary Ingress or DNS record.              │
  │  • Let's Encrypt's servers verify: does anihpj.com resolve to this IP?  │
  │  • HTTP-01 challenge: Let's Encrypt fetches                            │
  │    http://anihpj.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/                 │
  │  • DNS-01 challenge: Let's Encrypt checks a TXT record at              │
  │    _acme-challenge.anihpj.com                                            │
  │                                                                         │
  │  STEP 4: CERTIFICATE ISSUED → STORED IN SECRET                          │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────                        │
  │  • Challenge passed → Let's Encrypt issues the certificate.             │
  │  • cert-manager stores tls.crt + tls.key in Secret "anihpj-tls".       │
  │  • Updates the Certificate resource status to "Ready".                  │
  │                                                                         │
  │  STEP 5: INGRESS REFERENCES THE SECRET                                  │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────                                │
  │  spec:                                                                   │
  │    tls:                                                                  │
  │    - hosts: [anihpj.com]                                                 │
  │      secretName: anihpj-tls  ← Same Secret cert-manager created         │
  │                                                                         │
  │  STEP 6: AUTOMATIC RENEWAL (every 60 days, 30 days before expiry)       │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────         │
  │  • cert-manager monitors certificate expiry dates.                      │
  │  • 30 days before expiry → automatically re-runs ACME challenge.        │
  │  • New certificate issued → Secret updated → Ingress picks up new cert. │
  │  • ZERO manual intervention. Zero downtime.                             │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chapter 8: Restricting API Server Access

The Kubernetes API server is the single entry point for every operation in your cluster. Every kubectl command. Every controller reconciliation. Every pod readiness check. Every audit log entry. If an attacker gains access to the API server, they own the entire cluster — every Secret, every pod, every node, every cloud credential. This chapter teaches you to lock down the API server: disable anonymous access, enforce authentication for every request, enable audit logging for forensic traceability, restrict network access to trusted IP ranges, and remove the insecure port that bypasses all security controls. These are the most fundamental hardening steps — and the most heavily tested on the CKS exam.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔒 API Server 📝 Audit Logging

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand why the API server is the most critical security component in Kubernetes
  • ✅ Disable anonymous authentication — require valid credentials for every API request
  • ✅ Configure audit logging with a policy that captures the right level of detail
  • ✅ Restrict API server network access to trusted IP ranges using cloud firewalls
  • ✅ Remove the insecure port (8080) — verify it is completely disabled
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Hardening 15% Monitoring & Runtime 20%
🧠 The API Server Hardening Pattern

CKS exam tasks for API server hardening follow the same pattern as CIS checks: (1) Identify which flag is insecure, (2) Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, (3) Add/change the flag to the secure value, (4) Save and wait for the kubelet to restart the static pod, (5) Verify the change took effect with curl or kubectl. Always make a backup before editing the manifest. A dead API server = a failed exam.

8.1 The API Server is the Crown Jewel

Every operation in Kubernetes — whether initiated by a human with kubectl, a controller manager reconciling state, a kubelet reporting node status, or a pod reading a ConfigMap — flows through the kube-apiserver. It is the single component that reads from and writes to etcd. There is no back door. There is no direct etcd path (in a properly configured cluster). The API server is the gatekeeper, the authorizer, the auditor, and the admission controller — all in one process. If you compromise the API server, you bypass every security control in Kubernetes.

🔴 If the API Server Falls, Everything Falls

A compromised API server can: read all Secrets in all namespaces, create cluster-admin ServiceAccounts, delete audit logs, modify RBAC rules to create permanent backdoors, deploy malicious pods on every node, and exfiltrate all data stored in etcd. Protecting the API server is not one security task among many — it is THE security task. Every other control (NetworkPolicy, Seccomp, AppArmor) assumes the API server is secure. If it is not, those controls are irrelevant.

Everything Flows Through the API Server

The API server is the single entry point for ALL cluster operations
                        🌐 External Users (kubectl)
                        📦 Internal Pods (ServiceAccount tokens)
                        ⚙️  kubelet (node status, pod logs)
                        🔄 Controller Manager (reconciliation)
                        📊 Scheduler (pod placement)
                             │     │     │     │
                             ▼     ▼     ▼     ▼
                    ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │        🧠 kube-apiserver           │
                    │        ┌─────────────────────┐     │
                    │        │ 1. AUTHENTICATION   │     │
                    │        │    Who are you?     │     │
                    │        ├─────────────────────┤     │
                    │        │ 2. AUTHORIZATION    │     │
                    │        │    What can you do? │     │
                    │        ├─────────────────────┤     │
                    │        │ 3. ADMISSION CTRL   │     │
                    │        │    Is this allowed? │     │
                    │        ├─────────────────────┤     │
                    │        │ 4. AUDIT LOGGING    │     │
                    │        │    Record everything│     │
                    │        └──────────┬──────────┘     │
                    └───────────────────┼────────────────┘
                                        │
                                        ▼
                              ┌─────────────────┐
                              │   🗄️  etcd      │
                              │   (persisted)   │
                              └─────────────────┘

What Attackers Can Learn from the API Server — Even Without Credentials

Even with anonymous auth enabled and minimal RBAC, the API server leaks valuable reconnaissance information to unauthenticated users. The discovery API (/api, /apis) returns the complete list of available API groups, resources, and versions — telling an attacker exactly which Kubernetes version you are running and which features are enabled. The version endpoint (/version) returns the exact Git commit and build date of your API server. An attacker can cross-reference this against the CVE database to identify unpatched vulnerabilities specific to your version. This is why --anonymous-auth=false is not just about preventing data access — it is about denying attackers the reconnaissance they need to plan an attack.

What an Anonymous Attacker Can Discover About Your Cluster
  $ curl -k https://10.0.0.1:6443/version
  {
    "major": "1",
    "minor": "30",
    "gitVersion": "v1.30.0",          ← Attacker knows your exact version
    "gitCommit": "7c48c2bd...",        ← Maps to specific CVE database entry
    "buildDate": "2024-04-17T...",     ← Knows when you last updated
    "platform": "linux/amd64"          ← Knows your architecture
  }
  → Attacker now searches: "Kubernetes v1.30.0 CVEs"
  → Finds CVE-2024-XXXX affecting your exact version

  $ curl -k https://10.0.0.1:6443/apis
  → Returns ALL available API groups:
    apps/v1, batch/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1, rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1,
    policy/v1 (PodSecurity is enabled!), cert-manager.io/v1 (you use cert-manager),
    monitoring.coreos.com/v1 (you use Prometheus operator)
  → Attacker now knows your entire software stack from ONE anonymous request.

API Server Request Flow — From Network to etcd

🌐
Request kubectl/pod
→ API :6443
→
🔑
AuthN cert/token
validated
→
📋
AuthZ RBAC
checked
→
🚪
Admission Policies
applied
→
📝
Audit Request
logged
→
💾
