persisted

🔒 If anonymous-auth=false, unauthenticated requests are rejected at Step 2 (AuthN) with 401.

8.2 Disabling Anonymous Authentication

By default, Kubernetes allows anonymous requests — requests that carry no authentication credentials. These requests are assigned the username system:anonymous and the group system:unauthenticated. While the default RBAC rules grant anonymous users almost no permissions, a misconfigured cluster may have accidentally granted access — and even without RBAC permissions, anonymous users can still query the API server's version, health endpoints, and discovery APIs, leaking valuable information about your cluster version and available resources.

📖 CIS 1.2.1 — The Most Fundamental Check

The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark's very first API server check is: "Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false." This is check #1.2.1 — and it is the most common FAIL on default clusters. Fixing it is the first thing you do on any hardening task.

Fixing Anonymous Authentication — Step by Step

Edit the API server manifest to disable anonymous access
  # Step 1: Back up the manifest (ALWAYS do this first)
  $ cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml \
       /root/kube-apiserver.yaml.backup

  # Step 2: Edit the manifest
  $ vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

  # Find the command section and ensure this flag exists:
  spec:
    containers:
    - command:
      - kube-apiserver
      - --anonymous-auth=false          # ← ADD or CHANGE this to false

  # Step 3: Save and exit. kubelet detects the change and restarts
  # the API server automatically (10-30 seconds).

  # Step 4: Verify anonymous access is blocked
  $ curl -k https://localhost:6443/api/v1/namespaces
  {
    "kind": "Status",
    "status": "Failure",
    "message": "Unauthorized",          # ← 401 Unauthorized ✅
    "reason": "Unauthorized",
    "code": 401
  }

  # Step 5: Verify authenticated access still works
  $ kubectl get namespaces
  → Returns namespace list (using valid kubeconfig credentials) ✅
⚠️ After Disabling Anonymous Auth — What Breaks?

Most things keep working because they already use valid credentials: kubectl uses client certificates, controllers use ServiceAccount tokens, kubelets use bootstrap certificates. However, liveness and readiness probes configured with HTTP GET requests to the API server health endpoint will fail if they do not include authentication. The health endpoints (/healthz, /livez, /readyz) are exempt from authentication by default, but custom probes targeting other API paths will break. Always test after disabling anonymous auth.

What system:anonymous Can Actually Do — Testing Anonymous Permissions

Before disabling anonymous auth, it is valuable to audit what an anonymous user could have accessed. This tells you whether the cluster was already compromised through this vector:

Audit anonymous permissions before locking down
  # Check what anonymous can do RIGHT NOW
  $ kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:anonymous
  Resources   Non-Resource URLs   Resource Names   Verbs
  *.*         []                  []               []
  → Empty = no permissions (good!).

  # Check if anonymous was given any ClusterRoleBinding (BAD!)
  $ kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o yaml | grep -A5 system:anonymous
  → If ANY results appear, anonymous has been granted permissions.
    This is a critical finding — remove those bindings IMMEDIATELY.

  # Test anonymous access explicitly
  $ kubectl get pods --as=system:anonymous
  → Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden
  → If this SUCCEEDS, your cluster is already compromised.

  # Test anonymous access to the version endpoint
  $ curl -k https://localhost:6443/version
  → If this returns JSON, anonymous can see your version.
  → After fix: should return 401 Unauthorized.

8.3 Enabling Audit Logging on the API Server

Audit logging records every API request — who made it, what resource they accessed, what action they performed, and whether it succeeded or failed. Without audit logs, a security incident is a mystery: you have no way to determine which credentials were compromised, what data was accessed, or how long the attacker was in your cluster. With audit logs, you have a forensic timeline of every action. This is not optional for production — it is a requirement for PCI-DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA, and virtually every compliance framework.

Audit Policy Levels — How Much to Log

LevelWhat It LogsWhen to UseDisk Impact
NoneNothing — the event is not recorded at allNoisy events (e.g., watch connections, health checks) that would flood the logsZero
MetadataWho, what resource, what verb, when, source IP, response code — but NOT the request/response bodyMost events. Sufficient for compliance and most investigations.Low
RequestMetadata + the full request bodyEvents where you need to see WHAT was submitted (e.g., pod specs, ConfigMap data)Medium
RequestResponseMetadata + request body + response bodyCritical resources (Secrets access, RBAC changes) where you need the full pictureHigh — use sparingly

Audit Policy YAML — Annotated Example

Complete audit policy — what to log and at what level
  # /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
  apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Policy
  rules:
  # Don't log noisy events (saves disk space)
  - level: None
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["events"]
  - level: None
    userGroups: ["system:nodes"]
    verbs: ["get"]
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["nodes/status", "pods/status"]

  # Log Secret access metadata (who accessed which Secret, but NOT the values)
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]

  # Log full RBAC changes (who changed permissions)
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
    - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
      resources: ["*"]

  # Log pod exec with full request (captures the command executed)
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["pods/exec"]

  # Default: log metadata for everything else
  - level: Metadata

  # API server flags to enable this policy:
  # --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
  # --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
  # --audit-log-maxage=30      (retain logs for 30 days)
  # --audit-log-maxbackup=10   (keep up to 10 rotated files)
  # --audit-log-maxsize=100    (rotate at 100 MB per file)
💡 Audit Best Practice: Log RBAC Changes at RequestResponse

If an attacker modifies RBAC to create a backdoor, you need to see exactly what they changed. Always log rbac.authorization.k8s.io resources at RequestResponse level. This captures both the RBAC manifest that was submitted AND the API server's confirmation response. Combined with Metadata logging for Secrets access, you have full forensic coverage of the most critical attack paths.

Reading Audit Logs — Understanding the JSON Format

Audit logs are written as JSON objects — one per line — to the file specified by --audit-log-path. Understanding the JSON structure lets you query logs with jq to answer forensic questions like "who deleted that pod?" or "which IP tried to access Secrets?":

Anatomy of a Single Audit Log Entry
  {
    "kind": "Event",
    "apiVersion": "audit.k8s.io/v1",
    "level": "RequestResponse",          ← Which audit level captured this
    "auditID": "abc123-def456",          ← Unique ID to correlate request+response
    "stage": "ResponseComplete",         ← When in the request lifecycle
    "requestURI": "/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/secrets/anihpj-db",
    "verb": "get",                        ← What action (get, create, delete, list)
    "user": {
      "username": "system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-sa",  ← WHO
      "groups": ["system:serviceaccounts", "system:authenticated"]
    },
    "sourceIPs": ["10.0.1.23"],           ← WHERE from
    "userAgent": "anihpj-app/v2.1.0",     ← WHAT client
    "objectRef": {
      "resource": "secrets",               ← WHAT resource
      "name": "anihpj-db",
      "namespace": "anihpj-prod"
    },
    "responseStatus": {
      "metadata": {},
      "code": 200                          ← SUCCESS (403 = denied, 401 = unauthenticated)
    },
    "requestReceivedTimestamp": "2024-06-15T14:23:07.123456Z",
    "stageTimestamp": "2024-06-15T14:23:07.234567Z"
  }

  # QUERY EXAMPLES with jq:
  # Find all Secret access events
  $ cat audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="secrets")'

  # Find all failed (403) requests
  $ cat audit.log | jq 'select(.responseStatus.code==403)'

  # Find requests from a specific IP
  $ cat audit.log | jq 'select(.sourceIPs[]=="10.0.1.23")'

  # Find all delete operations
  $ cat audit.log | jq 'select(.verb=="delete")'

Audit Log Disk Management — Don't Fill the Control Plane Disk

Audit logs at RequestResponse level can generate gigabytes per day on a busy cluster. If the audit log fills the control plane disk, the API server cannot write logs and may stop accepting requests. This is a self-inflicted denial of service. The API server flags --audit-log-maxage, --audit-log-maxbackup, and --audit-log-maxsize control log rotation — but they only rotate the file, they do not enforce total disk usage. For production, always pair file-based audit logging with an audit webhook backend that streams logs to an external system (Elasticsearch, Splunk, or a cloud SIEM) where they can be properly stored, indexed, and queried without consuming control plane disk space.

8.4 Restricting API Server to Specific IP Ranges

Authentication and authorization control WHO can access the API and WHAT they can do. But there is a prior question: who can even reach the API server in the first place? If the API server's port 6443 is exposed to the public internet, attackers can attempt authentication, probe for misconfigurations, and launch brute-force attacks — even if they never successfully authenticate. Network-layer restriction adds a critical first barrier: the attacker's packets never reach the API server at all.

API Server IP Restriction — The 4-Layer Approach

Defense in depth for API server network access
  LAYER 1: Cloud Firewall / Security Group
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  Rule: ALLOW TCP 6443 FROM 10.0.0.0/8 (internal network)
  Rule: DENY  TCP 6443 FROM 0.0.0.0/0  (internet)
  → Attacker on the internet cannot even establish a TCP connection.
  → Port 6443 is invisible to port scanners like Shodan and Masscan.

  LAYER 2: Kubernetes Authentication
  ───────────────────────────────────
  --anonymous-auth=false
  → Even if an attacker gets past the firewall (e.g., compromised internal host),
    they must present valid credentials to make any API call.

  LAYER 3: Kubernetes RBAC
  ─────────────────────────
  → Even if an attacker has valid credentials (e.g., a stolen kubeconfig),
    RBAC limits what those credentials can do to a specific namespace and verbs.

  LAYER 4: Audit Logging
  ───────────────────────
  → Every access attempt — successful or failed — is recorded with timestamp,
    source IP, username, and the exact API call. Forensic evidence for
    investigation and compliance.

API Server Authentication Methods — Comparison

MethodHow It WorksUse CaseSecurity Level
X.509 Client Certificatekubectl uses cert from kubeconfig; API server verifies against cluster CAHuman administrators (kubeadm default)✅ Strong (cert-based)
Bearer Token (ServiceAccount)SA token in Authorization header; signed by K8s token controllerPods calling the API from inside the cluster⚠️ Tokens can be long-lived
OIDC (OpenID Connect)External IdP (Google, GitHub, Azure AD) issues JWT; API server validatesEnterprise SSO for human users✅ Strong (supports MFA)
Webhook Token AuthExternal server validates token via HTTP callbackCustom authentication systems⚠️ Depends on webhook security
Bootstrap TokensShort-lived tokens for new nodes joining the clusterkubeadm join — temporary use only✅ Auto-expiring
Static Token FileTokens stored in CSV file on control plane disk❌ NEVER use in production🔴 Tokens never rotate, stored in plaintext

Cloud Firewall Integration — Putting Theory into Practice

The 4-layer model works, but implementing it requires knowing the exact cloud-specific commands. Here is how to restrict API server access on the three major cloud providers — and the equivalent for on-premises clusters using iptables:

Restricting Port 6443 — Cloud Provider Commands
  # AWS: Security Group Rule
  $ aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
      --group-id sg-abc123 \
      --protocol tcp --port 6443 \
      --cidr 10.0.0.0/8
  # Also: REVOKE the 0.0.0.0/0 rule if it exists!
  $ aws ec2 revoke-security-group-ingress \
      --group-id sg-abc123 \
      --protocol tcp --port 6443 \
      --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

  # Azure: Network Security Group Rule
  $ az network nsg rule create \
      --nsg-name k8s-nsg \
      --name AllowApiServer \
      --priority 100 \
      --source-address-prefixes 10.0.0.0/8 \
      --destination-port-ranges 6443 \
      --access Allow

  # GCP: Firewall Rule
  $ gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-api-server \
      --network k8s-vpc \
      --allow tcp:6443 \
      --source-ranges 10.0.0.0/8

  # On-Premises / Generic Linux: iptables
  $ iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 6443 -s 10.0.0.0/8 -j ACCEPT
  $ iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 6443 -j DROP    # Default deny
  $ iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4           # Persist

8.5 Insecure Port — Removing the Back Door

Older versions of Kubernetes (prior to 1.20) exposed an insecure API port on 8080 that accepted requests with no TLS and no authentication. Anyone who could reach port 8080 could perform any API operation as cluster-admin — no credentials needed, no encryption, no audit log. This port was removed in Kubernetes 1.20, but some clusters running older versions or custom configurations may still have it enabled. The CKS exam expects you to verify it is disabled.

🔴 The Insecure Port — Complete Bypass of All Security

Port 8080 bypasses authentication, authorization, admission control, and TLS. If it is enabled, every other security control in this chapter — anonymous auth disabled, audit logging, RBAC — is meaningless. An attacker who can reach port 8080 can do anything. This is not a vulnerability. This is a deliberate feature that was removed because it is inherently insecure.

API Server Ports — Which Are Safe, Which Are Dangerous

PortPurposeSecurity StatusAction Required
6443Secure API (TLS + auth)✅ Safe — this is the only port you should exposeRestrict with firewall to trusted IPs
8080Insecure API (no TLS, no auth)🔴 DANGER — removed in 1.20+Verify --insecure-port=0 or flag absent
10250kubelet API⚠️ Must be locked with webhook authAnonymous auth disabled, webhook enabled
10255kubelet read-only (no auth!)🔴 DANGER — disablereadOnlyPort: 0
2379etcd client⚠️ API server onlyFirewall: allow only from control plane IPs
2380etcd peer⚠️ etcd members onlyFirewall: allow only between etcd nodes

Verifying the Insecure Port Is Disabled

Check and confirm port 8080 is gone
  # Step 1: Check the API server manifest for the insecure port flag
  $ grep insecure-port /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  → Should show: --insecure-port=0
  → OR: the flag should be completely absent (removed in 1.20+)

  # Step 2: Verify no process is listening on 8080
  $ netstat -tlnp | grep 8080
  → Should return NOTHING (no process listening)

  # Step 3: Verify 8080 is not reachable
  $ curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/namespaces
  → curl: (7) Failed to connect — Connection refused ✅

  # Step 4: Confirm the secure port works (6443)
  $ curl -k https://localhost:6443/healthz
  → ok ✅

  # If port 8080 IS listening:
  # 1. Edit kube-apiserver.yaml, add/change: --insecure-port=0
  # 2. Save and wait for kubelet to restart the static pod
  # 3. Re-run netstat -tlnp | grep 8080 → must be empty

API Server Before vs After — Security Posture Comparison

🔴 Default API Server (no hardening) — Security Score 12% — anonymous access, no audit, insecure port open
🟡 With Anonymous Auth Disabled Only 35% — credentials required but still no audit trail
🟡 With Auth + Audit Logging Enabled 65% — authenticated access + forensic record
🟢 Fully Hardened (Auth + Audit + IP Restriction + No Insecure Port) 95% — multi-layer defense, CKS target state

API Server Attack Walkthrough — What an Attacker Sees

Scenario: API server on public internet with anonymous auth enabled
  ATTACKER scans the internet for open K8s API servers
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ shodan search 'port:6443 product:"Kubernetes"' --fields ip_str
  203.0.113.42   ← Found: anihpj cluster API server

  $ curl -k https://203.0.113.42:6443/version
  { "major":"1", "minor":"30", "gitVersion":"v1.30.0", ... }
  → Attacker knows your EXACT version. Searches CVE database for v1.30.0.

  $ curl -k https://203.0.113.42:6443/api/v1/namespaces
  { "items": [ "anihpj-prod", "anihpj-dev", "kube-system", ... ] }
  → Anonymous access WORKED. Attacker can LIST namespaces with NO credentials!

  $ curl -k https://203.0.113.42:6443/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/secrets
  → 403 Forbidden (anonymous can't read Secrets by default)
  → But if RBAC was misconfigured... 200 OK + ALL SECRETS returned.

  ATTACKER'S NEXT STEPS (even with just anonymous version + namespace access):
  1. Cross-reference v1.30.0 against CVE database → find exploitable CVEs
  2. Brute-force ServiceAccount tokens (if weak token generation)
  3. Look for exposed etcd (port 2379) on the same IP range
  4. Search GitHub for leaked kubeconfig files containing the same IP

  WITH --anonymous-auth=false:
  $ curl -k https://203.0.113.42:6443/version
  { "kind":"Status", "status":"Failure", "message":"Unauthorized", "code":401 }
  → Attacker learns NOTHING. No version. No namespace list. No CVEs to exploit.

📊 Chapter 8 Visual Summary

🧠 API Server Single entry point for ALL operations — protect it above everything else
🚫 Anonymous Auth OFF --anonymous-auth=false — CIS 1.2.1. Every request must carry valid credentials.
📝 Audit Logging ON 4 audit levels: None → Metadata → Request → RequestResponse. RBAC at RequestResponse.
🔥 Insecure Port OFF Port 8080 must be disabled. --insecure-port=0. Verify with netstat.
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

API server hardening tasks always follow the same workflow: (1) Backup the manifest. (2) Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. (3) Add/change the flag. (4) Wait for the kubelet to restart the static pod. (5) Verify with curl or kubectl. Never skip the backup. If you add a typo to a flag, the API server will not start — and kubectl will not work to fix it. The only recovery is to restore the backup via SSH to the control plane node.

The Authentication → Authorization → Admission Pipeline — How the API Server Processes Every Request

The kube-apiserver is not a monolithic handler. It is a pipeline of independent stages, each with its own configuration flags and each separately testable. Understanding the exact order of these stages is critical because a misconfiguration in one stage can silently bypass later stages. Here is the exact pipeline:

kube-apiserver Request Pipeline — Every Stage, Every Flag, Every Chapter
  REQUEST: kubectl get pods -n anihpj
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 1: TLS Termination & Client Certificate Validation           │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────                    │
  │  Flags: --tls-cert-file, --tls-private-key-file, --client-ca-file   │
  │  • API server presents its TLS certificate to the client.           │
  │  • Client presents its certificate. API server verifies it against  │
  │    the CA in --client-ca-file.                                       │
  │  • If --client-ca-file is not set → client certs are NOT validated  │
  │    → anyone with any cert can connect (but still needs AuthN).      │
  │  ⚡ CKS: Chapter 8 — TLS mutual authentication                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 2: Authentication (Who are you?)                              │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────                             │
  │  Flags: --anonymous-auth, --oidc-issuer-url, --token-auth-file,      │
  │         --authentication-token-webhook-config-file                    │
  │  • The API server extracts identity from the request:                │
  │    - Client certificate CN = username, O = groups                    │
  │    - Bearer token → validated against OIDC, webhook, or static file  │
  │    - ServiceAccount JWT → validated by built-in SA authenticator     │
  │  • If NO identity is provided AND --anonymous-auth=true:              │
  │    → Authenticated as "system:anonymous" with group "system:unauthenticated"│
  │  • If --anonymous-auth=false: → 401 Unauthorized                     │
  │  ⚡ CKS: Chapter 8 — disable anonymous auth, Chapter 10 (SA tokens)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 3: Authorization (What can you do?)                           │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────                            │
  │  Flags: --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC,ABAC,Webhook                  │
  │  • API server asks EACH authorizer in order:                         │
  │    - Node authorizer: is this a kubelet requesting its own pods?     │
  │    - RBAC authorizer: check RoleBindings/ClusterRoleBindings         │
  │    - ABAC: check static policy file (deprecated — don't use)         │
  │    - Webhook: ask external service                                    │
  │  • First authorizer that says DENY → request REJECTED (403)          │
  │  • First authorizer that says ALLOW → SHORT-CIRCUIT (next authorizers│
  │    are skipped).                                                      │
  │  • If NO authorizer says ALLOW → REJECTED (default deny).            │
  │  ⚡ CKS: Chapter 9 (RBAC), Chapter 11 (Node authorization)           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 4: Admission Control (Mutating → Validating)                  │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────                    │
  │  Flags: --enable-admission-plugins, --admission-control-config-file   │
  │  • RUNS ONLY for mutating requests (create, update, delete, connect) │
  │  • SKIPPED for read requests (get, list, watch).                     │
  │  • TWO PHASES (in order):                                            │
  │    a) MUTATING plugins: can MODIFY the object (add defaults,         │
  │       inject sidecars, set securityContext).                          │
  │    b) VALIDATING plugins: can ACCEPT or REJECT the (possibly         │
  │       mutated) object. Cannot modify it.                              │
  │  • Key CKS plugins: NodeRestriction (Ch11), AlwaysPullImages,        │
  │    PodSecurity (Ch17).                                                │
  │  ⚡ CKS: Chapter 11 (NodeRestriction), Chapter 24 (webhooks)         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 5: etcd Persistence                                           │
  │  ────────────────────────                                             │
  │  • Object (after mutation + validation) is serialized and stored.    │
  │  • If encryption is configured (Ch19), the object is encrypted       │
  │    BEFORE writing to etcd.                                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STAGE 6: Audit Logging                                              │
  │  ────────────────────────                                             │
  │  • AFTER the request is processed, the audit event is generated.     │
  │  • This is NOT on the critical path — audit logging failure does     │
  │    NOT block the request (by default).                                │
  │  ⚡ CKS: Chapter 28 (Audit Logging)                                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CKS MENTAL MODEL: Every exam task maps to one of these 6 stages.
  Stage 1 = TLS (Ch7-8). Stage 2 = AuthN (Ch8,10). Stage 3 = AuthZ (Ch9,11).
  Stage 4 = Admission (Ch11,24). Stage 5 = Encryption (Ch19). Stage 6 = Audit (Ch28).

Chapter 9: RBAC — Role-Based Access Control for Security

RBAC is the authorization engine of Kubernetes. After a user or ServiceAccount authenticates, RBAC determines what they can do — which resources they can access, which verbs they can perform, and in which namespaces. Misconfigured RBAC is the most common Kubernetes security vulnerability after exposed dashboards. A single wildcard * in a ClusterRole, a cluster-admin binding to the wrong subject, or an escalate verb granted to a non-admin — any of these gives an attacker full cluster control. This chapter teaches you to design, implement, and audit RBAC from a security-first perspective: least privilege by default, explicit allow rules only, and continuous verification that no subject has more permissions than they need.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 👥 RBAC 🔐 Authorization

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Master the 4 RBAC resources: Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding
  • ✅ Identify and fix the 5 most dangerous RBAC misconfigurations
  • ✅ Design least-privilege RBAC for the anihpj team: developers, CI/CD, ops, security, monitoring
  • ✅ Verify RBAC configurations with kubectl auth can-i and impersonation
  • ✅ Automate RBAC auditing to find over-permissioned subjects
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Hardening 15% Minimize Microservice Vulns 20%
🧠 The RBAC Exam Mindset

CKS RBAC questions typically ask you to: (1) create a Role/ClusterRole with specific permissions, (2) bind it to a user, ServiceAccount, or group, (3) verify the permissions work correctly, (4) ensure the subject cannot do anything beyond what is specified. The trap: using ClusterRole when a namespaced Role would do, or forgetting to verify that the subject CANNOT access resources outside their scope. Always test both positive (allowed) and negative (denied) cases.

9.1 RBAC Refresher — The Security Lens

RBAC in Kubernetes is built from four resource types, and understanding how they connect is the foundation of every RBAC task on the CKS exam. Think of it as a sentence: "WHO (subject) is BOUND (via RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding) to WHAT (Role/ClusterRole) allowing them to DO (verbs) on WHICH resources."

RBAC 4-Resource Anatomy — How They Connect

The RBAC relationship model — Subjects → Bindings → Roles → Permissions
  WHO                        BINDING                    WHAT CAN DO
  (Subject)                  (Connects who to what)     (Role / ClusterRole)

  👤 User: alice   ──────▶  RoleBinding          ──▶  Role
  🤖 SA: anihpj-sa           (namespace-scoped)         (namespace-scoped)
  👥 Group: devs   ──────▶                             verbs + resources
                             RoleBinding can ALSO
                             refer to a ClusterRole
                             → grants ClusterRole perms
                               in ONLY that namespace

  👤 User: bob     ──────▶  ClusterRoleBinding   ──▶  ClusterRole
  🤖 SA: monitoring           (cluster-wide)            (cluster-wide)
                                                         verbs + resources

  SCOPE RULES:
  • Role           = permissions within ONE namespace
  • ClusterRole    = permissions across ALL namespaces OR cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs, namespaces)
  • RoleBinding    = binds a Role (or ClusterRole) to a subject in ONE namespace
  • ClusterRoleBinding = binds a ClusterRole to a subject CLUSTER-WIDE

RBAC Verb × Resource Permission Matrix — anihpj Team Roles

Rolecreateget/listupdatedeleteexec/logs
anihpj-dev (Developer)podspods, logs——pods/log, pods/exec
anihpj-deployer (CI/CD)—deployments, podsdeployments——
cluster-viewer (Ops read-only)—all———
security-auditor (Security)—roles, secrets———
cluster-adminALL 🔴ALL 🔴ALL 🔴ALL 🔴ALL 🔴

🔴 cluster-admin should be granted to NO ONE except the cluster provisioning tool (kubeadm) and emergency break-glass accounts with full audit logging.

anihpj Team — RBAC in Practice

Four personas, four different RBAC scopes — least privilege for each
  👨‍💻 DEVELOPER (Alice)                  🤖 CI/CD PIPELINE
  Role: anihpj-developer                 Role: anihpj-deployer
  Namespace: anihpj-dev                  Namespace: anihpj-prod
  Verbs: get, list, create              Verbs: get, list, update
  Resources: pods, logs                  Resources: deployments
  Can exec into pods for debugging.      Can update deployments only.
  Cannot: access prod, read secrets.     Cannot: delete, read secrets, exec.

  🔧 OPS (Bob)                          🛡️ SECURITY (Carol)
  ClusterRole: cluster-viewer            ClusterRole: security-auditor
  Verbs: get, list, watch               Verbs: get, list
  Resources: nodes, namespaces, pods     Resources: roles, rolebindings, secrets
  Read-only across all namespaces.       Read-only audit of permissions.
  Cannot: create, update, delete.        Cannot: modify RBAC, read Secret values.

The RoleBinding + ClusterRole Trick — Namespace-Scoping Cluster-Wide Permissions

One of the most useful and most misunderstood RBAC patterns is using a RoleBinding to reference a ClusterRole. This grants the ClusterRole's permissions but scoped to ONLY the namespace where the RoleBinding exists. This is how the built-in edit, view, and admin ClusterRoles work: they are cluster-wide role definitions, but each namespace creates a RoleBinding referencing them, granting those permissions only within that namespace. For the anihpj team, you could create ONE ClusterRole called "anihpj-developer" and then create a RoleBinding in each developer's namespace referencing it — instead of duplicating the Role YAML in every namespace. Exam trap: a ClusterRoleBinding referencing a ClusterRole grants permissions cluster-wide. A RoleBinding referencing the SAME ClusterRole grants permissions ONLY in that namespace. The binding type determines the scope, not the role type.

Aggregated ClusterRoles — Labels That Auto-Combine Permissions

Kubernetes supports aggregated ClusterRoles: you can create a ClusterRole with the label rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-admin: "true", and its rules are automatically merged into the built-in admin ClusterRole. This is how custom resources (CRDs) automatically appear in the admin/edit/view roles — the CRD controller creates an aggregated ClusterRole with the appropriate permissions, and it merges into the built-in roles without anyone editing them. The CKS exam does not heavily test aggregation, but understanding it prevents confusion when you see permissions appearing in roles you did not explicitly configure.

9.2 RBAC Misconfigurations — The Top Security Risks

Most RBAC vulnerabilities are not complex exploits — they are simple misconfigurations that grant far more access than intended. The CKS exam tests your ability to identify these patterns and fix them. Here are the five most dangerous RBAC anti-patterns:

Dangerous RBAC Patterns — Red Flags to Find and Fix

❌ DANGEROUS — Never Use in Production
  • Wildcard verbs: verbs: ["*"] — grants ALL actions including escalate and impersonate
  • Wildcard resources: resources: ["*"] — grants access to every resource including Secrets
  • Wildcard API groups: apiGroups: ["*"] — exposes all API groups including RBAC itself
  • Binding to system:masters: — this group has cluster-admin permanently, cannot be revoked by RBAC
  • escalate verb: allows creating Roles with more permissions than the creator has — privilege escalation vector
✅ SECURE — Specific, Minimal Permissions
  • Specific verbs: verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"] — read-only, explicitly listed
  • Specific resources: resources: ["pods", "services"] — only what is needed
  • Specific API groups: apiGroups: [""] (core) or ["apps"] — scoped to one group
  • Named subjects only: bind to specific users and ServiceAccounts, never system:masters
  • No escalate: never grant escalate to non-admin users — it is a privilege escalation vector

The escalate, bind, and impersonate Verbs — Privilege Escalation Vectors

Three RBAC verbs are uniquely dangerous because they allow a subject to increase their own privileges. These are not bugs — they are designed features that must be carefully controlled:

⬆️
escalate

Allows creating or updating a Role/ClusterRole with MORE permissions than the creator currently has. A user with escalate can create a ClusterRole that grants them cluster-admin — then bind it to themselves. Never grant escalate to non-admin users.

🔗
bind

Allows creating or updating a RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding. A user with bind can bind an existing powerful ClusterRole (like cluster-admin) to their own user account — even if they cannot create new Roles. Never grant bind without also restricting which roles can be bound.

🎭
impersonate

Allows acting as another user, group, or ServiceAccount. A user with impersonate can make API calls AS any other user — including cluster-admin. Audit logs will show the impersonated user, not the impersonator. Only grant to audit and debugging service accounts.

RBAC Authorization Flow — The Complete Decision Path

From API request to allowed/denied — every check in sequence
  👤 USER or 🤖 SA makes an API request
       │
       ▼
  STEP 1: AUTHENTICATION — "Who are you?"
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Validates certificate / token / OIDC claim.
  Extracts: username, groups, extra attributes.
  FAIL → 401 Unauthorized (stops here).
       │ ✅ Authenticated
       ▼
  STEP 2: AUTHORIZATION — "What can you do?"
  ───────────────────────────────────────────
  Combines ALL Roles + ClusterRoles bound to this user/group.
  Checks: does ANY bound role allow {verb, resource, namespace}?
  ALLOW if any rule matches → 200 OK.
  DENY if no rule matches → 403 Forbidden.
  ⚠️  RBAC is ALLOW-only. If no rule explicitly allows, it is denied.
       │ ✅ Authorized
       ▼
  STEP 3: ADMISSION CONTROL — "Should we allow this change?"
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Mutating webhooks modify the request.
  Validating webhooks accept/reject.
  Built-in plugins: NodeRestriction, PodSecurity, etc.
       │ ✅ Admitted
       ▼
  ✅ REQUEST PROCESSED

  COMMON EXAM QUESTION:
  Q: "User Alice can get pods in ns1 but not ns2. Why?"
  A: Alice has a Role (not ClusterRole) with a RoleBinding in ns1 only.
     Roles are namespace-scoped. A RoleBinding in ns1 does not grant
     access in ns2. She would need a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding
     for cluster-wide pod access.

How RBAC Misconfigurations Lead to Real Breaches

These are not theoretical risks. Every Kubernetes security incident that involved RBAC followed one of these patterns. The Shopify 2020 incident: a rogue employee with legitimate pod access used kubectl exec to move laterally across namespaces because RBAC was not namespace-scoped — each namespace should have had its own RoleBinding, but a ClusterRoleBinding was used instead, granting pod access everywhere. The Capital One 2019 incident: the pod's ServiceAccount had overly broad IAM role permissions because RBAC was not configured to restrict which pods could read which Secrets — the Secrets contained cloud credentials, and any pod in the namespace could read them. Lesson: never use ClusterRoleBinding when a RoleBinding would suffice. Never put cloud credentials in Secrets that are readable by pods that do not need them.

Detecting Wildcard RBAC at Scale — Beyond Manual Inspection

A single wildcard ClusterRoleBinding can grant cluster-admin to hundreds of ServiceAccounts. Finding these manually in a cluster with dozens of namespaces and hundreds of bindings is impossible. Here is a one-liner that finds every wildcard binding and the subjects it affects:

One-Liner: Find All Wildcard Permissions
  # Find every subject that has wildcard access (verbs:["*"] OR resources:["*"])
  $ for binding in $(kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o name); do
      kubectl get $binding -o json | jq -r \
        'select(.roleRef.name as $role | .subjects[]? |
         if ($role == "cluster-admin") then
           "🔴 CLUSTER-ADMIN: \(.kind)/\(.name) via \($binding)"
         else empty end)'
    done

  # Sample output:
  # 🔴 CLUSTER-ADMIN: ServiceAccount/default/anihpj-sa via clusterrolebinding/anihpj-admin
  # 🔴 CLUSTER-ADMIN: User/admin@anihpj.com via clusterrolebinding/cluster-admin
  # → Each line is a security finding that must be investigated.

RBAC Request Flow — The Complete Path from User to Decision

👤
User/SA Makes API
request
→
🔑
AuthN Who are
you?
→
📋
AuthZ What can
you do?
→
🚪
Admission Is this
allowed?
→
💾
etcd Persist
state

🛡️ RBAC is checked at the AuthZ step — if no Role/ClusterRole allows the verb+resource, the request stops at 403.

9.3 RBAC for the anihpj Application

Let's implement least-privilege RBAC for the entire anihpj team. Each role grants exactly the permissions needed for that persona's job function — and nothing more:

Complete RBAC Manifest Set for anihpj Team
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # ROLE 1: Developer — can debug pods in dev namespace
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Role
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-developer
    namespace: anihpj-dev
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods/exec"]
    verbs: ["create"]            # kubectl exec uses "create" verb on pods/exec
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list"]
  ---
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # ROLE 2: CI/CD Deployer — can update deployments in prod
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Role
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-deployer
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "update", "patch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]    # Read pods to verify deployment
  ---
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # CLUSTER ROLE: Read-only ops viewer (all namespaces)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: ClusterRole
  metadata:
    name: cluster-viewer
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["nodes", "namespaces", "pods", "services", "persistentvolumeclaims"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  ---
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # CLUSTER ROLE: Security auditor (read-only RBAC + Secrets audit)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: ClusterRole
  metadata:
    name: security-auditor
  rules:
  - apiGroups: ["rbac.authorization.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["roles", "clusterroles", "rolebindings", "clusterrolebindings"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]        # Can audit who has what permissions
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]        # Can see Secret names (not values by default)
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["serviceaccounts"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

Troubleshooting RBAC — When kubectl auth can-i Says "yes" But Your Command Fails

This is the most frustrating RBAC debugging scenario: kubectl auth can-i returns yes, but the actual kubectl command returns 403 Forbidden. The root cause is almost always one of these three issues:

😰 Reason 1: Wrong namespace

kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=alice checks permissions in the default namespace (if -n is not specified). But the actual command kubectl get pods -n anihpj-prod runs in anihpj-prod. Alice may have a Role in anihpj-dev but not in anihpj-prod. Always specify -n in both the test and the actual command. They must match.

🟡 Reason 2: Sub-resource permissions missing

kubectl logs anihpj-pod requires get on pods/log, not get on pods. kubectl exec requires create on pods/exec (yes, it uses the create verb, not get!). kubectl port-forward requires get on pods/portforward. If your Role only has permissions on pods but not the sub-resources, the parent resource check passes but the sub-resource fails.

🔴 Reason 3: Impersonation headers stripped by API server

If you are using --as to impersonate a user, your own credentials must have the impersonate verb on the users resource for that specific user. Without impersonate permission, the API server strips the impersonation headers and the request is processed as YOU, not as the impersonated user. The exam typically sets up the necessary impersonation permissions, but in production debugging, you may need to grant them to your admin account temporarily.

9.4 Verifying RBAC — kubectl auth can-i

kubectl auth can-i is the most important RBAC command on the CKS exam. It tests whether a specific subject can perform a specific action — without actually performing it. Use it to verify both positive cases (the subject CAN do what they need) AND negative cases (the subject CANNOT do anything beyond their scope).

kubectl auth can-i — Verification Table for anihpj Team

CommandExpectedWhy
kubectl auth can-i get pods -n anihpj-dev --as=aliceyesAlice has developer role in dev namespace
kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n anihpj-dev --as=alicenoDeveloper role does not include delete
kubectl auth can-i get pods -n anihpj-prod --as=alicenoAlice's role is only in dev namespace
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n anihpj-dev --as=alicenoDevelopers should never read Secrets
kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n anihpj-prod --as=ci-pipelineyesCI/CD deployer role in prod namespace
kubectl auth can-i delete deployments -n anihpj-prod --as=ci-pipelinenoCI/CD can update but not delete
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-sanoanihpj pod SA should have NO API access
kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=bobyesBob has cluster-viewer ClusterRole

Impersonation — Testing RBAC As Another User

Using --as and --as-group to impersonate any subject
  # Impersonate a user
  $ kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=alice -n anihpj-dev
  → yes (if Alice's RBAC allows it)

  # Impersonate a ServiceAccount
  $ kubectl auth can-i get secrets \
      --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-sa -n anihpj-prod
  → no (if SA has no API permissions — as it should!)

  # Impersonate with group membership
  $ kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=bob --as-group=ops-team -n default
  → yes (if bob or ops-team group has a binding)

  # List ALL permissions for a subject
  $ kubectl auth can-i --list --as=alice -n anihpj-dev
  Resources   Verbs
  pods        [get list watch]
  pods/log    [get list watch]
  pods/exec   [create]
  configmaps  [get list]
  → This is Alice's COMPLETE permission set. No surprises.

  # Audit: find subjects that CAN access Secrets
  $ kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:anonymous
  → MUST return "no". If "yes", you have a critical RBAC misconfiguration.

9.5 Automatic RBAC Audit — Finding Overpermitted Subjects

Manual verification with kubectl auth can-i works for individual checks, but in a cluster with hundreds of Roles, ClusterRoles, and Bindings, you need automation to find over-permissioned subjects. The CKS exam tests your ability to use RBAC audit tools to identify dangerous configurations:

Automated RBAC Audit — Finding Dangerous Permissions
  # 1. Find ALL subjects with cluster-admin
  $ kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r \
      '.items[]|select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin")|.subjects[]|"\(.kind)/\(.name)"'
  → system:masters (normal — kubeadm uses this)
  → User/admin (⚠️  review: does admin need cluster-admin?)
  → ServiceAccount/default/anihpj-sa (🔴 ALERT: pod SA should NEVER have cluster-admin!)

  # 2. Find ALL ClusterRoles with wildcard (*) verbs
  $ kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq -r \
      '.items[]|select(.rules[]?.verbs[]=="*")|.metadata.name'
  → cluster-admin (built-in — expected)
  → anihpj-wildcard-role (🔴 CUSTOM wildcard role — investigate!)

  # 3. Find ALL RoleBindings referencing cluster-admin
  $ kubectl get rolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r \
      '.items[]|select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin")|"\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'
  → anihpj-dev/anihpj-admin-binding (🔴 RoleBinding to cluster-admin in dev!)

  # 4. Find subjects with escalate, bind, or impersonate verbs
  $ kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq -r \
      '.items[]|select(.rules[]?.verbs[]?|select(.=="escalate" or .=="bind" or .=="impersonate"))|.metadata.name'
  → system:kube-controller-manager (built-in — expected)
  → security-auditor (🔴 AUDIT: does security-auditor need impersonate?)

RBAC Audit Tools — Beyond kubectl

🔍
kubectl-who-can

A kubectl plugin that answers: "Who can perform this action?" kubectl who-can get secrets --all-namespaces returns every subject with Secret read access — much faster than manually tracing RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings.

📊
rakkess

Shows an access matrix: for each resource, which verbs are available to the current user. Useful for verifying: "After my RBAC changes, can I still do my job?" rakkess --as=alice -n anihpj-dev shows Alice's complete access matrix.

RBAC Audit Automation — A Script for Continuous Compliance

Manual RBAC audits are not sustainable. Integrate RBAC auditing into your CI/CD pipeline or run it as a CronJob. This script generates a human-readable audit report that you can run before every deployment:

RBAC Audit Script — Generate a Compliance Report
  #!/bin/bash
  # rbac-audit.sh — Run before every deployment
  echo "=== RBAC AUDIT REPORT — $(date) ==="
  echo ""
  echo "1. SUBJECTS WITH CLUSTER-ADMIN:"
  kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r \
    '.items[]|select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin")|.subjects[]|"  \(.kind)/\(.name)"'
  echo ""
  echo "2. CLUSTERROLES WITH WILDCARD VERBS:"
  kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq -r \
    '.items[]|select(.rules[]?.verbs[]=="*")|select(.metadata.name!="cluster-admin")|.metadata.name'
  echo ""
  echo "3. ROLEBINDINGS TO CLUSTER-ADMIN (namespace-scoped admin):"
  kubectl get rolebindings -A -o json | jq -r \
    '.items[]|select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin")|"\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'
  echo ""
  echo "4. SUBJECTS WITH ESCALATE/BIND/IMPERSONATE:"
  kubectl get clusterroles -o json | jq -r \
    '.items[]|select(.rules[]?.verbs[]?|select(.=="escalate" or .=="bind" or .=="impersonate"))|.metadata.name'
  echo ""
  echo "=== AUDIT COMPLETE ==="

  # Run this as a CronJob or in CI/CD before deploy.
  # If any unexpected subjects appear, BLOCK the deployment.

RBAC Hardening Impact — Before vs After

🔴 Default RBAC (no hardening) — Subjects with wildcard access 28% of bindings use wildcards — cluster-admin everywhere
🟡 With Wildcard Audit + Removal 5% — only intentional wildcards remain (kubeadm defaults)
🟢 Least-Privilege RBAC (CKS target) — No wildcards, namespace-scoped 0% — every subject has only exactly needed permissions

📊 Chapter 9 Visual Summary

👥 4 RBAC Resources Role + ClusterRole + RoleBinding + ClusterRoleBinding — subjects → bindings → permissions
⚠️ 5 Dangerous Patterns Wildcard verbs/resources/API groups, system:masters binding, escalate/bind/impersonate verbs
✅ kubectl auth can-i Test permissions with --as and --as-group. Always test positive AND negative cases.
🔍 RBAC Audit Tools jq queries + kubectl-who-can + rakkess — find over-permissioned subjects automatically
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

Every RBAC exam task should end with kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<subject> -n <ns>. This shows you the subject's complete permission set — and reveals if you accidentally granted more than intended. Never submit an RBAC task without verifying both positive cases (allowed) AND negative cases (denied). If the exam asks you to restrict access to Secrets, verify that kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=<subject> returns no.

RBAC Deny-by-Default — How the Authorization Engine Thinks

Kubernetes RBAC is deny-by-default. If no RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding grants a specific permission, it is automatically denied. There is no "deny" rule in RBAC — you cannot explicitly deny a permission. You can only grant or not grant. This has profound implications for how you design and audit RBAC:

RBAC Authorization Logic — How the API Server Decides ALLOW vs DENY
  REQUEST: User "alice" wants to DELETE pods in namespace "anihpj-prod"
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 1: FIND ALL BINDINGS for this user                             │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────                            │
  │  The RBAC authorizer searches ALL RoleBindings in "anihpj-prod"      │
  │  AND ALL ClusterRoleBindings (cluster-wide).                          │
  │                                                                       │
  │  Found bindings for user "alice":                                    │
  │  • RoleBinding "pod-reader" in anihpj-prod → Role "pod-reader"       │
  │    verbs: [get, list, watch]                                          │
  │    resources: [pods]                                                  │
  │  • ClusterRoleBinding "namespace-admin" → ClusterRole "admin"         │
  │    verbs: [get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete]          │
  │    resources: [pods, deployments, services, ...]                      │
  │                                                                       │
  │  STEP 2: UNION all permissions from all bindings                     │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────                    │
  │  Combined permissions:                                                │
  │  pods: [get, list, watch] (from pod-reader)                           │
  │  pods: [get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete] (from admin) │
  │  → Effective: pods: [get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete] │
  │                                                                       │
  │  STEP 3: CHECK if the requested verb is in the effective set         │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────            │
  │  Requested: [delete] [pods] in [anihpj-prod]                          │
  │  Effective set contains "delete" for "pods" → ALLOWED ✅              │
  │                                                                       │
  │  STEP 4: IF NOT FOUND → DENY (no explicit deny needed)               │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────               │
  │  If alice had ONLY the "pod-reader" binding:                          │
  │  Effective set: pods: [get, list, watch]                              │
  │  Requested: [delete] → NOT in set → DENIED ❌                           │
  │  No "deny delete" rule was needed. The absence of permission = denial.│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CRITICAL RBAC PROPERTIES:
  ─────────────────────────
  1. Permissions are ADDITIVE. Two bindings = UNION of permissions.
  2. There is NO deny rule. You CANNOT say "alice can do everything EXCEPT delete pods."
     You must list exactly what alice CAN do. If you grant *, she gets delete.
  3. ClusterRoleBindings grant cluster-wide access. RoleBindings grant
     namespace-scoped access. Both apply simultaneously.
  4. The "*" wildcard in verbs means ALL verbs (including escalate, bind, impersonate).
     Granting "*" to a non-admin is effectively giving them cluster-admin.

The Three Most Dangerous RBAC Verbs — escalate, bind, and impersonate

These three verbs are special. They allow privilege escalation. Granting any of them to a non-admin user is equivalent to giving them cluster-admin — because they can use these verbs to give themselves cluster-admin:

⬆️
escalate

Allows creating/updating ClusterRoles even if you don't have the permissions those ClusterRoles grant. Attack: User creates a ClusterRole that grants themselves * on * → now they're cluster-admin. Never grant escalate to non-admins.

🔗
bind

Allows creating RoleBindings/ClusterRoleBindings even if you don't have the permissions in the role you're binding. Attack: User binds the existing cluster-admin ClusterRole to their own user account. Never grant bind to non-admins.

🎭
impersonate

Allows acting as another user via kubectl --as=other-user. Attack: User impersonates system:admin or a ServiceAccount with cluster-admin. All audit logs show the impersonated user, not the attacker. Restrict impersonate tightly.

← Ch 9: RBAC for Security Previous → Ch 10: Service Accounts Next

Chapter 10: Service Accounts — Securing Pod Identity

Every pod in Kubernetes has an identity — a ServiceAccount. By default, every pod gets the default ServiceAccount in its namespace, and that ServiceAccount's JWT token is automatically mounted into the pod at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. Any process inside the pod can read this token and use it to authenticate to the Kubernetes API. If the ServiceAccount has RBAC permissions — even accidentally — every pod using it inherits those permissions. If the token is stolen (via a compromised container, a leaked log, or a misconfigured volume), the attacker has a permanent, non-expiring credential. This chapter teaches you to control pod identity: disable token auto-mounting for pods that do not need API access, create dedicated ServiceAccounts with minimal RBAC, and use bound tokens that automatically expire — eliminating the risk of stolen credentials granting persistent access.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🤖 ServiceAccounts 🔑 Pod Identity

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand how every pod authenticates to the API server using a mounted ServiceAccount token
  • ✅ Recognize the dangers of the default ServiceAccount — one shared identity for all pods
  • ✅ Create dedicated ServiceAccounts with minimal RBAC for each workload
  • ✅ Disable automountServiceAccountToken for pods that never need API access
  • ✅ Use bound (projected) tokens that auto-expire — eliminating permanent credential theft
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Hardening 15% Minimize Microservice Vulns 20%
🧠 The ServiceAccount Exam Pattern

CKS ServiceAccount tasks follow a consistent pattern: (1) Identify which pods need API access and which do not, (2) For pods that do NOT need API access, set automountServiceAccountToken: false, (3) For pods that DO need API access, create a dedicated ServiceAccount with minimal RBAC, (4) Verify the pod can (or cannot) access the API. The exam always tests both cases: pods that should have access AND pods that should not.

10.1 How Pods Authenticate to the API Server

Every pod, when it starts, has a specific set of files mounted into it by the kubelet. These files are the pod's identity documents — and any process inside the container can read them:

What the kubelet mounts into every pod — the identity files
  $ kubectl exec anihpj-pod -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
  ca.crt       ← Cluster CA certificate (to verify the API server's TLS cert)
  namespace    ← The pod's namespace (plain text: "anihpj-prod")
  token        ← THE JWT TOKEN — this IS the pod's identity

  $ kubectl exec anihpj-pod -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IiJ9.eyJpc3MiOiJrdWJlcm5ldGVzL3NlcnZpY2VhY2NvdW50Iiwia3ViZXJu
  ZXRlcy5pby9zZXJ2aWNlYWNjb3VudC9uYW1lc3BhY2UiOiJhbmlocGotcHJvZCIsImt1YmVybmV0ZXMuaW8vc2Vy
  dmljZWFjY291bnQvc2VydmljZS1hY2NvdW50Lm5hbWUiOiJkZWZhdWx0Iiwic3ViIjoic3lzdGVtOnNlcnZpY2Vh
  Y2NvdW50OmFuaWhwai1wcm9kOmRlZmF1bHQifQ...

  # Decode the JWT payload (middle section between the dots):
  $ echo "eyJpc3Mi..." | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 -d | python -m json.tool
  {
    "iss": "kubernetes/serviceaccount",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/namespace": "anihpj-prod",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/secret.name": "default-token-xxxxx",
    "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/service-account.name": "default",
    "sub": "system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:default"
  }
  → This pod identifies as: system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:default

How the Pod Uses Its Token — The Full Flow

From pod to API — authentication, authorization, response
  1. Pod starts → kubelet creates the token volume mount
     Mount path: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
     Files: token (JWT), ca.crt (CA cert), namespace

  2. App inside pod reads the token file
     $ cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token

  3. App calls the K8s API with the token as a Bearer header
     $ curl https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/pods \
         --cacert /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt \
         -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/.../token)"

  4. API server receives the request:
     a. Validates the JWT signature (signed by the SA token controller)
     b. Extracts: username = system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:default
     c. Looks up RBAC: does this SA have "list pods" in anihpj-prod?
     d. If RBAC allows → returns pod list. If not → 403 Forbidden.

  IF automountServiceAccountToken: false:
     Step 1 never happens → /var/run/secrets/ is EMPTY
     → Pod CANNOT call the K8s API at all ✅

How the ServiceAccount Token Controller Works — Behind the Scenes

Three Kubernetes components collaborate to make ServiceAccount tokens work. Understanding this chain helps you diagnose token issues and understand why bound tokens are fundamentally more secure:

The ServiceAccount Token Pipeline — 3 Components
  1. SERVICEACCOUNT CONTROLLER (kube-controller-manager)
     ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
     Watches: ServiceAccount creations
     Action: Creates a Secret (type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token)
             containing a signed JWT for the SA.
     ⚠️  This is LEGACY behavior — for STATIC tokens only.
         Bound tokens are NOT created by this controller.

  2. TOKEN CONTROLLER (kube-controller-manager)
     ─────────────────────────────────────────────
     Watches: ServiceAccount deletions
     Action: Deletes all Secrets associated with a deleted SA.
     Also: Signs the JWT using the cluster's ServiceAccount private key
           (--service-account-private-key-file on kube-controller-manager).

  3. KUBELET (on every node)
     ────────────────────────
     Action: Mounts the token into every pod's filesystem.
     For STATIC tokens: reads the Secret, writes the token file.
     For BOUND tokens: calls the TokenRequest API to get a fresh,
     time-limited token on every pod start AND on rotation.

  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Bound tokens NEVER touch a Secret. The kubelet
     calls the TokenRequest API directly, gets a JWT with an expiry,
     and writes it to a tmpfs volume. No Secret. No persistence.
     When the token expires, the kubelet gets a new one automatically.

The TokenRequest API — How Bound Tokens Are Created

The TokenRequest API is the modern replacement for static ServiceAccount tokens. Instead of creating a permanent Secret, you request a temporary token with a specific audience and duration. This API is what the kubelet uses internally for projected tokens — and you can use it directly to generate short-lived tokens for CI/CD pipelines or debugging:

Using the TokenRequest API — Generate a Short-Lived Token
  # Create a 1-hour token for the anihpj-sa ServiceAccount
  $ kubectl create token anihpj-sa -n anihpj-prod --duration=1h
  eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6Ii...truncated...

  # Use it directly with curl
  $ TOKEN=$(kubectl create token anihpj-sa -n anihpj-prod --duration=1h)
  $ curl -k https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/pods \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
  → Returns pods if SA has RBAC, 403 if not.

  # This token expires in 1 hour. No Secret exists. Nothing to clean up.
  # This is the recommended way to generate tokens for CI/CD, not static Secrets.

  ⚠️  kubectl create token requires K8s 1.24+. For older versions,
      use kubectl create token -- requested via the raw API.

10.2 The Dangers of the Default Service Account

Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount — created automatically by the namespace controller. Unless a pod explicitly specifies serviceAccountName, it uses this default SA. The danger: every pod in the namespace shares the same identity. If you grant any RBAC permissions to the default SA, every pod inherits them. If one pod is compromised and its token is stolen, the attacker can impersonate every other pod in that namespace.

❌ Default ServiceAccount — Shared Identity
  • All pods → "default" SA
  • Grant permissions to default → ALL pods get permissions
  • One compromised pod = all pods' identity stolen
  • Token never expires (old-style static token)
  • Default SA appears in every namespace

Compromised anihpj pod → can read Secrets as default SA → can access API across namespace.

✅ Dedicated ServiceAccounts — Isolated Identity
  • anihpj pod → anihpj-sa
  • postgres pod → postgres-sa
  • Each SA → minimal, specific RBAC permissions
  • Tokens can be time-limited (projected tokens)
  • Automount disabled for pods that don't need API

Compromised anihpj pod → can only do what anihpj-sa allows → nothing else.

🔴 The Default SA Is Shared — Never Give It Permissions

The default ServiceAccount should have zero RBAC permissions in every namespace. If you need a pod to access the API, create a dedicated ServiceAccount for that specific workload and grant permissions only to that SA. Never create a RoleBinding that references the default SA. If you see system:serviceaccount:<ns>:default in any RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding, that is a security finding that must be remediated immediately.

Auditing Default ServiceAccount Permissions — Find the Gaps

Use these commands to audit every namespace for default SA permissions. Any non-empty result is a security finding:

One-Liner: Find All Permissions Granted to Default ServiceAccounts
  # Find every RoleBinding that references a default SA
  $ kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o json | jq -r \
      '.items[] | select(.subjects[]? | select(.kind=="ServiceAccount" and .name=="default")) |
       "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name) → default SA"'

  # Sample output (each line is a FINDING):
  # anihpj-prod/anihpj-admin-binding → default SA 🔴
  # kube-public/default-view → default SA 🟡 (intentional for kube-public)

  # Check what the default SA can actually do in a namespace
  $ kubectl auth can-i --list \
      --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:default -n anihpj-prod
  → Must return NO permissions. If any appear, investigate immediately.

  # Find namespaces where the default SA has ANY RBAC binding
  $ for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o name | cut -d/ -f2); do
      count=$(kubectl get rolebindings -n $ns -o json | jq \
        '[.items[]? | select(.subjects[]? | select(.kind=="ServiceAccount" and .name=="default"))] | length')
      if [ "$count" -gt 0 ]; then
        echo "🔴 $ns: default SA has $count RoleBinding(s)"
      fi
    done

Attack Scenario: What Happens When a ServiceAccount Token Is Stolen

Understanding the risk requires seeing the attack. Here is exactly what happens when an attacker compromises an anihpj pod and extracts its ServiceAccount token — and how the outcome differs dramatically depending on whether the SA has permissions and whether the token is static or bound:

Scenario A: Pod with DEFAULT SA + Accidental RBAC Permissions
  ATTACKER compromises anihpj pod via CVE → gains shell as root
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ whoami
  root     ← Container runs as root

  $ cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6Ii...   ← THE POD'S IDENTITY

  $ curl -s https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/secrets \
      --cacert /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/.../token)"
  {
    "items": [
      {"metadata":{"name":"anihpj-db-credentials"}},
      {"metadata":{"name":"anihpj-tls"}},
      {"metadata":{"name":"aws-s3-backup-key"}}
    ]
  }
  → Attacker can LIST all Secrets in the namespace!
    Because someone granted "get secrets" to the default SA.

  $ curl .../secrets/anihpj-db-credentials ...
  → Returns DATABASE_URL with username and password.
  → Attacker now has production database credentials.

  IMPACT: Full database access. All user data. All job listings.
  CAUSE: Default SA + accidentally granted Secret read permission.
Scenario B: Pod with DEDICATED SA + Zero Permissions
  ATTACKER compromises anihpj pod via CVE → gains shell as root
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ whoami
  root

  $ cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  → FILE NOT FOUND (automountServiceAccountToken: false)

  $ ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
  → DIRECTORY EMPTY

  $ curl https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj-prod/secrets
  → curl: (77) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate
  → Cannot even verify the API server's TLS cert (no ca.crt mounted)

  IMPACT: Zero. No token. No API access. No lateral movement via K8s API.
  CAUSE: automountServiceAccountToken: false + dedicated SA with no RBAC.
  Attacker must find another path — and NetworkPolicies (Ch 6) block that too.

ServiceAccount Lifecycle — From Creation to Token Rotation

📝
Create SA kubectl create
serviceaccount
→
🔑
Token Gen kubelet calls
TokenRequest API
→
📦

to tmpfs volume
→
🌐

in header
→
🔄

at 80% life

🔑 With automountServiceAccountToken: false, the flow stops at Step 1 — no token is ever generated.

10.3 Bound Service Account Tokens (Projected Tokens)

Legacy ServiceAccount tokens (the kind stored as Kubernetes Secrets) are non-expiring, non-revocable, and valid for any API server audience. If an attacker steals one — from a compromised container, a leaked log file, or a misconfigured volume — they have permanent API access. Bound tokens (also called projected tokens) solve this: they are time-limited, audience-scoped, and automatically rotated by the kubelet. No Secret is created. No permanent credential exists.

Old vs New ServiceAccount Tokens

FeatureOld (Static) TokenNew (Bound) Token
Stored asKubernetes Secret (auto-created per SA)Projected volume (tmpfs, never on disk)
ExpiryNever expires 🔴1 hour (default), configurable ✅
AudienceAny K8s API server 🔴Specific audience (e.g., "vault") ✅
RotationManual only 🔴Automatic (kubelet rotates before expiry) ✅
RevocableOnly by deleting the Secret 🔴Expires automatically ✅
If stolenPermanent access 🔴Access expires within 1 hour ✅
Available sinceKubernetes 1.0Kubernetes 1.21+ (enabled by default in 1.24+)

Configuring a Bound Token — Pod Spec

Pod YAML with a projected ServiceAccount token (1-hour expiry)
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-secure
  spec:
    serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa         # Dedicated SA, not default
    automountServiceAccountToken: false    # Disable the default token mount
    containers:
    - name: anihpj
      image: anihpj:v2
      volumeMounts:
      - name: token
        mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens # Custom path, not the default
        readOnly: true
    volumes:
    - name: token
      projected:
        sources:
        - serviceAccountToken:
            path: token                    # The token file name
            expirationSeconds: 3600        # 1 hour expiry ← KEY FIELD
            audience: api                  # Audience claim in the JWT
  # ⚠️  The old default mount at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/
  #     is EMPTY because automountServiceAccountToken: false.
  #     Only THIS projected token exists, and it expires in 1 hour.

What Happens When a Bound Token Expires Mid-Request

A common concern with bound tokens: "What if my pod is in the middle of a long-running operation and the token expires?" The answer depends on your Kubernetes version and configuration. In K8s 1.22+, the kubelet automatically rotates the token BEFORE it expires — typically at 80% of its lifetime. The new token is written to the same file atomically, and any process that re-reads the file gets the new token. For HTTP clients that reuse connections (keep-alive), the existing connection continues to work — token validation only happens at connection establishment. For new connections, the pod reads the updated token file and presents the fresh token. Best practice: set expirationSeconds to at least 3600 (1 hour) to give the kubelet time to rotate. Avoid very short expirations (less than 600 seconds) unless your application explicitly handles token refresh.

Disabling Legacy Tokens Cluster-Wide

Even after you configure bound tokens for your pods, the old static token Secrets may still exist — and they never expire. The CKS exam may ask you to ensure that legacy tokens are not in use. The API server flag --service-account-extend-token-expiration=false (K8s 1.24+) prevents the legacy token controller from creating auto-mounted Secrets for new ServiceAccounts. Combined with --service-account-issuer and --service-account-signing-key-file (which configure the bound token issuer), you can ensure that all new tokens are bound tokens — no static Secrets created, no permanent credentials lingering in your cluster.

10.4 Securing anihpj Service Accounts

Let's apply everything to the anihpj application. We have four workloads, each with different API access needs:

anihpj ServiceAccounts — Each with least privilege
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # SA 1: anihpj-sa — Web application (NO API access)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ServiceAccount
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-sa
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  automountServiceAccountToken: false   # No API access needed
  # The Django app serves HTTP — it never calls the K8s API.
  # Even if Django is compromised, there is no token to steal.

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # SA 2: postgres-sa — Database (NO API access)
  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ServiceAccount
  metadata:
    name: postgres-sa
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  automountServiceAccountToken: false   # No API access needed

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # SA 3: anihpj-operator-sa — Needs to read ConfigMaps

    name: anihpj-operator-sa

    name: anihpj-operator-sa
  roleRef:
    kind: Role
    name: anihpj-operator-role
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

  # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════

  kind: ServiceAccount
  metadata:
    name: ci-deployer-sa
    namespace: anihpj-prod

    name: ci-deployer-role
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  rules:

    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "update", "patch"]
  ---
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: RoleBinding
  metadata:
    name: ci-deployer-binding
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  subjects:
