Verifying anihpj ServiceAccounts — What Each Can Do

ServiceAccountAPI Access?PermissionsToken Auto-Mount?
anihpj-sa❌ NoNonefalse ✅
postgres-sa❌ NoNonefalse ✅
anihpj-operator-sa✅ Yesget/list/watch ConfigMaps in anihpj-prod onlytrue (needed)
ci-deployer-sa✅ Yesget/list/update/patch Deployments in anihpj-prod onlytrue (needed)

Decision Tree: Does My Pod Need API Access?

Walk through this decision tree for every pod in your cluster. The most common CKS mistake is either disabling the token on a pod that needs it (breaking functionality) or leaving the token mounted on a pod that does not need it (leaving a credential exposed):

🔍 Does this pod call the Kubernetes API? (kubectl, client-go, any /api/ endpoint?)
❌ NO → automountServiceAccountToken: false. Create a dedicated SA with zero RBAC. The anihpj web app does NOT call the K8s API — it serves HTTP.
✅ YES → Continue. The pod needs a token.
📋 Does it need read-only access (get/list/watch) to specific resources?
✅ YES → Create dedicated SA + Role with only get/list/watch on only the needed resources. Example: anihpj-operator-sa → ConfigMaps only.
❌ NO → Continue.
✏️ Does it need to modify resources (create/update/delete)?
✅ YES → Create dedicated SA + Role with only the needed verbs on only the needed resources. Example: ci-deployer-sa → update deployments only. Use bound tokens with 1-hour expiry.
🎉 Your pod needs API access but NOT to modify resources. Verify with kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>. Every verb listed beyond get/list/watch is a finding.

ServiceAccount Security Maturity Model

Where is your cluster on the ServiceAccount security maturity curve? Each stage eliminates a class of attack:

🔴
Stage 0
Default Everywhere

All pods use the default SA. Token auto-mounted in every pod. Static tokens never expire.

❌ Extremely vulnerable
🟠
Stage 1
Dedicated SAs

Each workload has its own SA. Default SA has zero RBAC. But tokens are still static and auto-mounted everywhere.

⚠️ Still using static tokens
🟡
Stage 2
Auto-Mount Disabled

automountServiceAccountToken: false on all pods that do not need API access. Token only present where needed.

⚠️ Static tokens still expire never
🟢
Stage 3
Bound Tokens

All tokens are projected, time-limited, audience-scoped. Auto-rotated. No static Secrets. CKS target state.

✅ CKS Hardened

📊 Chapter 10 Visual Summary

🔑 Pod Identity Every pod has a ServiceAccount. Token mounted at /var/run/secrets/ — any process can read it.
🚫 Default SA Danger One shared identity for all pods. Never grant permissions to the default SA.
⏰ Bound Tokens Time-limited (1hr), audience-scoped, auto-rotated. No permanent credentials.
✅ Least Privilege SAs 4 dedicated SAs for anihpj — two with zero API access, two with minimal RBAC.
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

Every CKS ServiceAccount task has two parts: (1) disable the token for pods that do not need it (automountServiceAccountToken: false), and (2) create a dedicated SA with minimal RBAC for pods that do. Always verify BOTH: kubectl exec <pod> -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ — if the directory is empty, the token is disabled. If it contains a token, verify the SA has only the expected permissions with kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>.

JWT Token Lifecycle — How ServiceAccount Tokens Work at the Kernel Level

A ServiceAccount token is a JSON Web Token (JWT) — a signed, base64-encoded JSON document that proves the pod's identity. Understanding the token lifecycle explains why long-lived, non-expiring tokens are so dangerous and why bound tokens are the fix:

ServiceAccount JWT Token — Creation, Mounting, and Validation
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LEGACY TOKEN (pre-1.22, still default in many clusters)                  │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────                    │
  │  • Created: Automatically when the SA is created.                         │
  │  • Stored: As a Secret (type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token).       │
  │  • Expiry: NEVER. The token is valid forever.                             │
  │  • Revocation: ONLY by deleting the Secret. Changing RBAC does NOT       │
  │    invalidate an existing token — it already passed auth.                 │
  │  • Mounted: Token is mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/          │
  │    serviceaccount/token via a projected volume.                           │
  │  ⚡ DANGER: If this token is stolen (log file, compromised pod, leaked   │
  │    ConfigMap), the attacker has PERMANENT API access as that SA.          │
  │    The only fix is to delete the Secret (revoking the token) AND           │
  │    change the RBAC bindings (in case the attacker already used the token  │
  │    to create backdoor credentials).                                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  BOUND TOKEN (TokenRequest API, 1.22+) — CKS exam standard               │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────                       │
  │  • Created: On-demand when the pod is created, via the TokenRequest API. │
  │  • Stored: NOT stored in etcd. Generated on-the-fly and mounted.         │
  │  • Expiry: Configurable — typically 1 hour, renewable.                    │
  │  • Bound to: The specific POD that requested it. Cannot be used by any   │
  │    other pod, even if the token string is copied.                         │
  │  • Revocation: Automatic on expiry. No cleanup needed.                    │
  │  • Mounted: Same path, but kubelet rotates the token BEFORE expiry.      │
  │  ⚡ ADVANTAGE: A stolen token is useless after 1 hour. A token stolen     │
  │    from Pod A cannot be used by Pod B (pod-bound).                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  TOKEN PROJECTION MECHANICS (how the token file stays fresh):
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • kubelet mounts a PROJECTED VOLUME at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/
    serviceaccount/.
  • The projected volume contains a symlink: token → ..data/token
  • ..data/token is a NEW file each time kubelet rotates the token.
  • The symlink updates ATOMICALLY (rename()) — the pod always reads
    the current token without needing to restart.
  • Token rotation happens at 80% of the token's TTL (e.g., at 48 min
    for a 60-min token).

Default vs Dedicated ServiceAccount — Security Comparison

Why You Should NEVER Grant Permissions to the Default ServiceAccount
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  ❌ DEFAULT SERVICEACCOUNT   │   │  ✅ DEDICATED SERVICEACCOUNT │
  │                              │   │                              │
  │  All pods → "default" SA    │   │  anihpj pod → anihpj-sa     │
  │  Grant permissions to default│   │  postgres pod → postgres-sa │
  │  → ALL pods get permissions  │   │  Each SA → minimal permissions│
  │                              │   │                              │
  │  Compromised pod:            │   │  Compromised anihpj pod:     │
  │  → can access API as default │   │  → can only do what         │
  │  → may reach secrets across  │   │    anihpj-sa is allowed     │
  │    the namespace             │   │  → nothing else              │
  │                              │   │                              │
  │  🔴 If default SA has        │   │  🟢 anihpj-sa has NO        │
  │     cluster-admin binding:   │   │     permissions at all.     │
  │     EVERY pod = cluster-admin│   │     Postgres-sa also none.  │
  │     → CATASTROPHIC breach   │   │     Least privilege.        │
  └──────────────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────────────┘

Service Account Token Flow — How a Pod Uses Its Identity

Pod → Token → API Server → RBAC Check — The Complete Flow
  1. Pod starts → kubelet creates projected volume
     Mount path: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
     Files: token (JWT), ca.crt (cluster CA), namespace

  2. App inside pod reads the token file
     $ cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
     → eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...

  3. App calls K8s API with Authorization: Bearer <token>
     $ curl https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/pods \
       -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/.../token)"

  4. API server validates token → extracts SA identity → RBAC check → respond

  IF automountServiceAccountToken: false:
     Step 1 never happens → /var/run/secrets/ is EMPTY
     → Pod cannot call K8s API at all ✅

  🔑 THE CKS EXAM PATTERN: Tasks often ask you to create a pod that CANNOT
     access the API. The answer is always: ServiceAccount with
     automountServiceAccountToken: false.

Chapter 11: Node Restriction & Hardening Authorization

Every Kubernetes node runs a kubelet — the agent that starts pods, reports node status, and manages container lifecycles. The kubelet communicates with the API server to register its node and update pod statuses. If a kubelet is compromised — through a container escape, a node-level exploit, or stolen credentials — it can wreak havoc: modify other nodes' labels, evict pods from healthy nodes, or impersonate other kubelets to redirect traffic. NodeRestriction is the admission plugin that limits each kubelet to only its own node and its own pods. Combined with the Node authorization mode, which restricts what kubelets can even request, these controls form a critical defense layer that the CKS exam tests heavily.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours ⚙️ Kubelet 🔐 Authorization

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Enable and verify the NodeRestriction admission plugin — limit kubelets to their own node
  • ✅ Understand the Node authorization mode and why it must be paired with RBAC
  • ✅ Compare all authorization modes and know which ones to NEVER use in production
  • ✅ Harden SSH access to nodes — disable root login, enforce key-only authentication
  • ✅ Protect the kubelet API (port 10250) from unauthorized access
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Hardening 15% System Hardening 10%

11.1 The NodeRestriction Admission Plugin

NodeRestriction is an admission plugin — it intercepts API requests from kubelets and validates that each kubelet is only modifying resources it owns. Without NodeRestriction, a compromised kubelet on node-worker-2 can modify labels on node-worker-1 (impersonating another node), evict pods from node-worker-3, or modify pod labels to bypass scheduling constraints. With NodeRestriction, each kubelet is strictly limited to its own node object and the pods scheduled on it.

🔴 Without NodeRestriction — One Compromised Kubelet = Cluster-Wide Chaos

A compromised kubelet can: modify ANY node's labels (redirecting workloads), evict pods from ANY node (causing denial of service), modify pod labels to bypass affinity rules, and update node statuses to disrupt scheduling. NodeRestriction prevents ALL of this by enforcing: "kubelet on node-X can only modify node-X and pods on node-X."

NodeRestriction — What Each Kubelet Can and Cannot Touch

❌ WITHOUT NodeRestriction

Scenario: kubelet on node-worker-2 is compromised.

  • 🔴 Modify labels on node-worker-1 (impersonate other nodes)
  • 🔴 Evict pods from node-worker-3 (disrupt other nodes)
  • 🔴 Modify pod labels it doesn't run (bypass scheduling)
  • 🔴 Update any node's status to NotReady
  • 🔴 This enables privilege escalation across the entire cluster
✅ WITH NodeRestriction

Scenario: kubelet on node-worker-2 is compromised.

  • ✅ Can read its own node object (node-worker-2) — only
  • ✅ Can modify its own node status and labels — only
  • ✅ Can read/write pods scheduled ON node-worker-2 — only
  • ✅ Cannot touch node-worker-1 or node-worker-3 at all
  • ✅ Blast radius contained to ONE node

Enabling NodeRestriction — API Server Configuration

Add NodeRestriction to the admission plugin list and verify
  # Step 1: Edit the API server manifest
  $ vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

  # Find --enable-admission-plugins and add NodeRestriction:
  - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,AlwaysPullImages,...

  # Step 2: Save → kubelet restarts API server (10-30 seconds)

  # Step 3: Verify NodeRestriction is active
  $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system kube-apiserver-* -o yaml | grep NodeRestriction
  → --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,...  ✅

  # Step 4: Test — a kubelet CANNOT modify another node's labels
  $ kubectl label node node-worker-1 test=value
  → (From the compromised kubelet on node-worker-2)
  → Error: node "node-worker-1" cannot be modified (NodeRestriction)

How NodeRestriction Actually Works — The Internal Mechanism

NodeRestriction is not magic — it is a specific set of validation rules hardcoded into the API server's admission chain. Understanding exactly what it checks helps you diagnose when it blocks legitimate kubelet operations (rare, but possible during cluster upgrades or node replacements):

NodeRestriction Validation Rules — What Gets Checked
  RULE 1: kubelet identity is derived from the username "system:node:<nodeName>"
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  If a request comes from user "system:node:worker-2", NodeRestriction
  enforces that the kubelet can ONLY modify:
  • Node object: "worker-2" (its OWN node — not worker-1, not worker-3)
  • Pod objects: only pods where spec.nodeName == "worker-2"
  • Any attempt to modify worker-1 → REJECTED with "node 'worker-1' is not
    managed by node 'worker-2'"

  RULE 2: kubelet cannot modify taints on its own node with
          NoSchedule or NoExecute effects
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  A compromised kubelet CANNOT taint its own node to attract or repel
  specific workloads. Only the API server (via scheduler) or cluster-admin
  can modify taints. This prevents a compromised kubelet from making its
  node a "preferred" target for sensitive pods.

  RULE 3: kubelet cannot set labels prefixed with
          "node-restriction.kubernetes.io/" on its own node
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  This label prefix is RESERVED. Only the NodeRestriction admission
  plugin itself can set these labels. Kubelets cannot modify them.

  RULE 4: kubelet can only update its own node's status sub-resources
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Node status updates (Ready, MemoryPressure, DiskPressure) are
  restricted to the kubelet's own node. A kubelet on worker-2 cannot
  mark worker-3 as NotReady.

What Happens When You Try to Bypass NodeRestriction

The CKS exam may present a scenario where NodeRestriction is disabled and ask you to enable it — or present a scenario where it IS enabled and ask you to diagnose why a kubelet operation is failing. Here is exactly what the API server returns when NodeRestriction blocks a request:

NodeRestriction Blocks — Error Messages and What They Mean
  ATTEMPT 1: Kubelet on worker-2 tries to label worker-1
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ kubectl --as=system:node:worker-2 label node worker-1 test=value
  Error: nodes "worker-1" is forbidden: node "worker-2" is not allowed
  to modify node "worker-1"
  → FIX: Legitimate. The kubelet should NOT touch other nodes.

  ATTEMPT 2: Kubelet on worker-2 tries to evict a pod on worker-3
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ kubectl --as=system:node:worker-2 delete pod anihpj-pod --grace-period=0
  Error: pods "anihpj-pod" is forbidden: node "worker-2" is not allowed
  to modify pods not assigned to it
  → FIX: The pod is on worker-3, not worker-2. This is NodeRestriction working correctly.

  ATTEMPT 3: Kubelet tries to set taint with NoSchedule
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ kubectl --as=system:node:worker-2 taint node worker-2 dedicated=user:NoSchedule
  Error: node "worker-2" is forbidden: node "worker-2" is not allowed to
  modify taint "dedicated"
  → FIX: Only cluster-admin can modify taints. The kubelet cannot.

Kubelet Request Authorization Flow — Node Authorizer in Action

🔒 Three-layer defense: Node Authorizer (scope) → RBAC (permissions) → NodeRestriction (admission). All three must pass.

11.2 Authorization Modes — Understanding the Chain

Kubernetes supports multiple authorization modes simultaneously, checked in order. When a request arrives, each mode is evaluated. The first mode that explicitly ALLOWS the request stops the chain — the request proceeds. If no mode ALLOWS, the request is DENIED. This means the order matters, and a poorly placed AlwaysAllow mode would grant every request before RBAC ever gets checked.

Authorization Mode Comparison

ModeHow It WorksSecurity LevelWhen to Use
AlwaysAllowAllow every request, no checks🔴 NEVER IN PRODUCTIONTesting only — REMOVE before going live
AlwaysDenyDeny every request⚠️ Testing onlyTesting admission plugins — blocks everything
RBACRoles + RoleBindings define permissions✅ StandardAll production clusters — the primary mode
NodeRestricts kubelet API access by node✅ RequiredAll production clusters — paired with RBAC
WebhookExternal service decides allow/deny via HTTP✅ AdvancedCustom authorization logic, OPA integration
ABACAttribute-based, policy file on disk⚠️ Legacy — avoidLegacy clusters — migrate to RBAC

Secure Authorization Configuration

The only authorization mode combination you should use
  # API server flag — secure configuration:
  --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC

  # What this does (checked in order):
  # 1. Node authorizer: kubelet requests checked first
  #    → Is this kubelet authorized to access this node/pod?
  #    → If ALLOW: request proceeds. If DENY: passes to RBAC.
  # 2. RBAC: all other requests checked against Roles/Bindings
  #    → Does this user/SA have a binding allowing this action?
  #    → If ALLOW: request proceeds. If no rule: DENIED.

  # ❌ NEVER DO THIS:
  --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow,RBAC
  # → AlwaysAllow matches FIRST → ALL requests allowed → RBAC NEVER checked.
  # → This is equivalent to having NO authorization at all.

  # ✅ THE ORDER MATTERS:
  --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
  # → Node checked first (kubelet-specific rules), then RBAC (everything else).
  # → If Node and RBAC both DENY, the request is denied.
😰 Real-World Scenario: When AlwaysAllow Was Left Enabled

A cluster was deployed with --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow,RBAC during development for convenience. The cluster went to production without removing AlwaysAllow. Every API request — from every user, every ServiceAccount, even anonymous requests — was allowed. RBAC rules existed but were never consulted. The cluster ran for six months with effectively zero authorization. An attacker who gained a single pod's ServiceAccount token had full cluster-admin access — because AlwaysAllow granted it before RBAC could say no. Lesson: Always audit your authorization mode. One typo disables all authorization.

Authorization Mode Decision Tree

⚙️ What does your --authorization-mode flag contain?
AlwaysAllow present → 🔴 REMOVE IMMEDIATELY. This disables all authorization.
No AlwaysAllow. Continue.
📋 Does it include Node AND RBAC?
❌ Missing Node → Add it. Kubelets need Node authorization. Missing RBAC → Add it. This is your primary authorization.
✅ Node,RBAC present → This is the CKS-recommended configuration.
🔍 Is ABAC or static token file present?
⚠️ ABAC/static tokens → Legacy. Plan migration to RBAC. Remove ABAC policy file and --token-auth-file flag.
✅ Clean — only modern authorization modes. CKS target state.

How the Node Authorizer Works — Internal Rules

The Node authorization mode is a special-purpose authorizer designed exclusively for kubelets. Unlike RBAC (which matches arbitrary rules to arbitrary subjects), the Node authorizer has a fixed set of rules based on the kubelet's identity. Understanding these rules helps you diagnose when the Node authorizer ALLOWS a request (and RBAC is never checked) vs when it passes the request to RBAC:

Node Authorizer — Built-in Permission Rules
  IDENTITY: A kubelet authenticates as "system:node:<nodeName>"
  GROUP: The kubelet is in the group "system:nodes"

  NODE AUTHORIZER ALLOWS (without consulting RBAC):
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Read services, endpoints, nodes (to discover cluster topology)
  • Read/write pods bound to its OWN node
  • Read/write node status for its OWN node
  • Read/write events for its OWN node's pods
  • Read ConfigMaps, Secrets referenced by pods on its node
  • Read PVs, PVCs referenced by pods on its node
  • CertificateSigningRequest: create/update for its own node cert

  NODE AUTHORIZER PASSES TO RBAC (no opinion):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Any request NOT listed above → passed to the next authorizer (RBAC)
  • This means: if a kubelet tries to read ALL Secrets in a namespace,
    Node passes → RBAC checks → DENIED (unless RBAC explicitly allows)

  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: The Node authorizer is DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH for kubelets.
     It GRANTS the minimum permissions kubelets need to function, AND
     it RESTRICTS them from requesting anything beyond that.
     Even if RBAC somehow granted a kubelet cluster-admin (a catastrophic
     misconfiguration), the Node authorizer would still DENY requests
     to modify other nodes — because Node authorizer operates BEFORE RBAC.

11.3 Protecting Node-Level Access

Node-level access — SSH, console, and kubelet API — represents the deepest level of compromise. If an attacker gains SSH access to a node, they can read all Secrets mounted on that node, access the container runtime directly, modify static pod manifests, and potentially compromise the entire control plane if they land on a control plane node. Node-level hardening is the last line of defense in the CKS model.

Node Access Hardening Checklist

SSH and Node-Level Security — Every Control
  □ SSH: Disable root login
      $ grep PermitRootLogin /etc/ssh/sshd_config
      → PermitRootLogin no

  □ SSH: Key authentication only — no passwords
      $ grep PasswordAuthentication /etc/ssh/sshd_config
      → PasswordAuthentication no

  □ SSH: Restrict to specific users/groups
      $ grep AllowUsers /etc/ssh/sshd_config
      → AllowUsers admin@10.0.0.0/8

  □ SSH: Audit all login attempts
      $ grep sshd /var/log/auth.log | grep Accepted
      → Review regularly for unauthorized access

  □ Kubelet API (10250): Anonymous auth disabled
      $ grep anonymous /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
      → enabled: false

  □ Kubelet API (10250): Webhook authorization
      $ grep authorization /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
      → mode: Webhook

  □ Kubelet read-only port (10255): DISABLED
      $ grep readOnlyPort /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
      → readOnlyPort: 0

  □ IAM roles (cloud): Minimal permissions for node instances
      AWS: Node IAM role should NOT have s3:* or iam:* permissions
      → Only ec2:DescribeInstances, ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, etc.

  □ Remove stale user accounts from all nodes
      $ awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1}' /etc/passwd
      → Audit: every human account must be justified.

Kubelet API Protection — The Last Network Barrier

How an attacker exploits an exposed kubelet API (port 10250)
  ATTACKER gains network access to node IP on port 10250
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  WITHOUT kubelet hardening:
  $ curl -k https://node-worker-2:10250/pods
  → Returns ALL pods running on this node — full pod specs, labels, env vars
  $ curl -k https://node-worker-2:10250/stats/summary
  → Returns CPU, memory, network stats for every container
  $ curl -k https://node-worker-2:10250/run/.../anihpj-pod/anihpj?cmd=whoami
  → Executes "whoami" inside the anihpj container → returns "root"

  WITH kubelet hardening (anonymous=false + webhook auth):
  $ curl -k https://node-worker-2:10250/pods
  → 401 Unauthorized — kubelet requires authentication
  $ curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer <stolen-SA-token>" .../pods
  → 403 Forbidden — SA token not authorized for kubelet API (RBAC denies)
  $ curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer <valid-admin-token>" .../pods
  → 200 OK + pod list — only authorized users can access kubelet API

  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: With webhook authorization, the kubelet sends EVERY request
     to the API server for a SubjectAccessReview. No local decision-making.
     The API server's RBAC controls who can access every kubelet.

Cloud IAM Role Minimization — Node Instances Should Have Zero Power

When Kubernetes nodes run on cloud providers, each node inherits the IAM role attached to its VM instance. A common security mistake is attaching broad IAM roles (like AdministratorAccess) to nodes "to make things easier." This means any pod on that node can access those cloud permissions via the instance metadata service. Here is what proper node IAM minimization looks like:

Cloud ProviderMinimum Required PermissionsNEVER Include
AWSec2:DescribeInstances, ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, ecr:BatchGetImages3:*, iam:*, sts:*
AzureMicrosoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read, ACR pull permissionsContributor role, Storage Account keys
GCPcompute.instances.get, artifactregistry.readerEditor role, Service Account Token Creator

🔴 CKS Rule: If a node IAM role includes s3:*, an attacker who compromises ANY pod on that node can read ALL S3 buckets in the account. This is exactly how Capital One was breached.

Node Compromise Attack Walkthrough — What Happens Step by Step

Scenario: Attacker escapes container → gains node access → what now?
  ATTACKER has root on node-worker-2 (via container escape). Now what?
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  STEP 1: Read all Secrets on this node
  $ for secret in $(ls /var/lib/kubelet/pods/*/volumes/kubernetes.io~secret/); do
      cat /var/lib/kubelet/pods/*/volumes/kubernetes.io~secret/$secret/* 2>/dev/null
    done
  → ALL Secrets from ALL pods on this node — DB passwords, API keys, TLS certs.

  STEP 2: Access kubelet credentials
  $ cat /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem
  → kubelet's client certificate — can authenticate to API server as "system:node:worker-2"

  STEP 3: Try to modify other nodes (WITHOUT NodeRestriction)
  $ curl -k https://kube-apiserver:6443/api/v1/nodes/worker-1 \
      --cert /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem \
      --key /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-key.pem \
      -X PATCH -H "Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json" \
      -d '{"metadata":{"labels":{"compromised":"true"}}}'
  → SUCCESS (without NodeRestriction) — attacker now controls worker-1 labels!

  STEP 4: WITH NodeRestriction enabled
  → Same request returns: "node worker-1 is not allowed to modify by node worker-2"
  → BLOCKED. Attacker trapped on worker-2.

  BLAST RADIUS COMPARISON:
  Without NodeRestriction: worker-2 compromise → ALL nodes compromised
  With NodeRestriction:    worker-2 compromise → ONLY worker-2 compromised

Node Hardening Impact — Before vs After

🔴 Default Node (no hardening) — Security Score 8% — anonymous kubelet, no NodeRestriction, root SSH
🟡 With kubelet Auth + NodeRestriction 55% — kubelet locked down, nodes isolated
🟢 Fully Hardened (kubelet + SSH + IAM + AuthZ = Node,RBAC) 92% — multi-layer node defense, CKS target state

📊 Chapter 11 Visual Summary

🔒 NodeRestriction Limits kubelets to their own node + pods. One compromised kubelet = one node at risk, not the cluster.
⚙️ AuthZ Modes Node,RBAC is the only safe combination. AlwaysAllow disables ALL authorization.
🔑 SSH Hardening No root login. Key-only auth. Restricted users. Audit all access. Remove stale accounts.
🚪 Kubelet API Anonymous=false, webhook auth, readOnlyPort=0. Every request → SubjectAccessReview.
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam expects you to configure THREE things for node security: (1) NodeRestriction admission plugin on the API server, (2) --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC on the API server, and (3) kubelet hardening (anonymous=false, webhook auth, readOnlyPort=0). These three controls work together — missing any one leaves a gap. Always verify all three: kubectl describe pod -n kube-system kube-apiserver-* | grep -E 'NodeRestriction|authorization-mode' AND grep -E 'anonymous|webhook|readOnlyPort' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.

How the Node Authorizer Works — The Allowlist That Protects Node Identity

The Node authorizer is a special-purpose authorizer that runs BEFORE RBAC in the authorization chain. It allows kubelets to perform the specific operations they need — but ONLY on resources belonging to their own node. This prevents a compromised kubelet on node-01 from accessing pods or secrets on node-02:

Node Authorizer Logic — What Each Kubelet Is Allowed to Do
  REQUEST: Kubelet on "worker-01" (authenticated as system:node:worker-01,
           group system:nodes) wants to UPDATE pod status for a pod
           running on "worker-02".

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  NODE AUTHORIZER CHECK (runs BEFORE RBAC)                                │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────                                 │
  │  Step 1: Is the requester in group "system:nodes"?                       │
  │  → YES (system:node:worker-01 is in system:nodes)                         │
  │                                                                           │
  │  Step 2: Is the requested operation in the kubelet allowlist?             │
  │  Kubelets are allowed to:                                                 │
  │  ✅ Read: services, endpoints, nodes (their own)                          │
  │  ✅ Write: node status (their own), pod status (their own pods),          │
  │     events (for their own pods)                                            │
  │  ✅ Auth: CertificateSigningRequests, TokenReviews                        │
  │  ❌ NOT allowed: Read/Write pods on OTHER nodes, secrets, configmaps,     │
  │     deployments, RBAC objects                                             │
  │  → Request is: UPDATE pod status for a pod on "worker-02"                 │
  │  → Node authorizer checks: Is this pod scheduled on "worker-01"?          │
  │  → NO — the pod is on worker-02, and worker-01's kubelet is asking.      │
  │  → DENY. (The kubelet cannot touch pods on other nodes.)                  │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CONTRAST: If the SAME kubelet requests pod status for a pod on           │
  │  worker-01 → the pod IS on worker-01 → ALLOW by Node authorizer.         │
  │  The request NEVER reaches RBAC (Node authorizer short-circuits).         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WHAT NODERESTRICTION ADDS ON TOP:
  ──────────────────────────────────
  Node authorizer = AUTHORIZATION (can the kubelet make this API call?)
  NodeRestriction = ADMISSION (even if authorized, can the kubelet modify
                    THIS specific field of THIS specific object?)

  NodeRestriction limits kubelets to ONLY modifying:
  • Their own Node object (node "worker-01" can only modify "worker-01")
  • Pods bound to their node (pod.spec.nodeName = "worker-01")
  • Labels prefixed with "node-restriction.kubernetes.io/"

  Without NodeRestriction: A compromised kubelet on worker-01 could change
  worker-02's labels (e.g., remove a taint), causing pods to schedule on a
  compromised node. WITH NodeRestriction: label modification is DENIED at
  admission time.

NodeRestriction — What Each Kubelet CAN and CANNOT Touch

Compromised Kubelet: Without vs With NodeRestriction
  SCENARIO: node-worker-2's kubelet is compromised

  WITHOUT NodeRestriction:
  Compromised kubelet on node-worker-2 CAN:
  ❌ Modify labels on node-worker-1 (impersonate another node)
  ❌ Evict pods from node-worker-3 (disrupt other nodes)
  ❌ Modify labels on pods it doesn't run (bypass scheduling)
  ❌ This enables privilege escalation across the entire cluster

  WITH NodeRestriction enabled:
  Compromised kubelet on node-worker-2 CAN ONLY:
  ✅ Read its own node object (node-worker-2)
  ✅ Modify its own node status and labels
  ✅ Read/write pods scheduled ON node-worker-2 only
  ✅ Cannot touch anything on node-worker-1 or node-worker-3

  🔑 CKS EXAM: CIS Benchmark 1.2.17 requires NodeRestriction.
     Flag: --enable-admission-plugins=...,NodeRestriction
     Verify: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep apiserver
             → check the command line flags

Authorization Mode Comparison — Complete Reference

ModeHow It WorksSecurity LevelCKS Notes
AlwaysAllowAllow everything, no checks🔴 NEVER useExists only for bootstrapping. Disable immediately.
AlwaysDenyDeny everything (testing only)⚠️ TestingUseful for testing RBAC policies in dry-run mode.
RBACRoles + RoleBindings + ClusterRoleBindings✅ Use thisThe primary authorization mode. Chapters 9, 33 cover this.
NodeKubelet access control — restricts kubelets to their own objects✅ RequiredAlways pair with NodeRestriction admission plugin.
WebhookExternal authorization service (HTTP callback)✅ AdvancedFor integrating with external auth systems (OPA, custom).
ABACAttribute-based, file-based policy⚠️ LegacyDeprecated. Use RBAC instead. Appears in older CKS materials.

Recommended configuration: --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC. The order matters — Node is checked FIRST. If a kubelet request passes Node authorization, RBAC is never evaluated (efficiency). If Node denies it, RBAC is checked as a fallback (but should also deny it).

Node Access Hardening Checklist

🔑
SSH Access

Use SSO (not shared keys). Audit SSH keys monthly. Remove stale users. Disable root SSH login: PermitRootLogin no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.

🌐
Kubelet API

Never expose port 10250 to the internet. Bind to localhost only if possible. Use firewall rules: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 10250 -j DROP (except from control plane).

☁️
Cloud IAM

Use node groups with minimal IAM roles. Cloud-managed nodes should have read-only access to container registry + logging. Never grant ec2:* or equivalent to node roles.

Chapter 12: Kubernetes Version Management for Security

Running an outdated Kubernetes version is not a performance issue — it is a security vulnerability. Critical CVEs are disclosed regularly for Kubernetes components. Each CVE is patched in a new version. If you are not upgrading, you are running known vulnerabilities with publicly available exploit code. The CKS exam tests your understanding of the K8s release cycle, the upgrade process using kubeadm, and the security implications of running unsupported versions. This chapter teaches you how to keep your cluster secure through disciplined version management — how to plan upgrades, how to execute them safely, and how to distinguish between urgent security patches and routine minor upgrades.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours ⬆️ Upgrades 🛡️ CVE Response

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the Kubernetes support window (N, N-1, N-2) and why running EOL versions is dangerous
  • ✅ Recognize notable Kubernetes CVEs and map them to the versions they affect
  • ✅ Execute a safe cluster upgrade using kubeadm — control plane first, then workers
  • ✅ Distinguish between patch releases (apply immediately) and minor releases (test, then upgrade)
🎓 CKS Relevance
Cluster Setup 15% Cluster Hardening 15%

12.1 Why Keeping Kubernetes Updated Is a Security Requirement

Kubernetes releases follow a strict support policy: the latest 3 minor versions (N, N-1, N-2) receive security patches. Versions older than N-2 are End of Life (EOL) — no patches, no CVEs fixed, no support. If your cluster runs v1.27 when v1.30 is the latest, any CVE discovered today for v1.27 will never be patched. Your only remediation is to upgrade to a supported version. Running an EOL version is not a configuration issue — it is a security incident waiting to happen.

🔴 EOL = No Security Patches — Ever

Kubernetes releases approximately every 4 months. Each minor version is supported for approximately 14 months. After that, the release branch is permanently closed. If CVE-2025-XXXX is discovered affecting v1.26 today, there will be NO patch for v1.26 because v1.26 is EOL. You MUST be on a supported version (v1.28, v1.29, or v1.30 as of mid-2025) to receive the fix.

Notable Kubernetes CVEs — Real Vulnerabilities, Real Consequences

CVESeverityAffected VersionsImpact
CVE-2018-1002105 "The Big Bird"CRITICAL 9.8< 1.10.11, < 1.11.5, < 1.12.3Privilege escalation to cluster-admin via API server proxy — unauthenticated RCE
CVE-2019-11247HIGH 8.1< 1.13.9, < 1.14.5RBAC bypass: access cluster-scoped resources as if they were namespace-scoped
CVE-2021-25741HIGH 8.1< 1.19.15, < 1.20.11, < 1.21.5Symlink attack: hostPath volume escapes its restricted directory
CVE-2022-3294HIGH 7.6< 1.25.4, < 1.24.8Node address type confusion → MITM attack between nodes

Every one of these CVEs was patched in a new Kubernetes version. Every unpatched cluster running an affected version was — and still is — vulnerable to these attacks. The fix is always the same: upgrade.

Kubernetes Support Window — Know When to Upgrade

Version lifecycle — which versions get security patches
  If latest version is v1.30:

  v1.30 → ✅ Supported (latest) — receives all patches + new features
  v1.29 → ✅ Supported (N-1) — receives security patches only
  v1.28 → ✅ Supported (N-2) — receives security patches only
  v1.27 → ❌ EOL — NO patches. Vulnerable forever until upgraded.
  v1.26 → ❌ EOL — NO patches.
  v1.25 → ❌ EOL — NO patches.

  RULE: When v1.31 is released, v1.28 goes EOL. Always have an upgrade plan
        to stay within the N-2 window — that gives you ~14 months per upgrade.

  ⚠️  The CKS exam tests your awareness of this support window.
      If a question mentions a cluster on v1.25, the answer includes UPGRADE.

Attack Scenario: What Happens When You Run an EOL Version

Scenario: Cluster on v1.26 (EOL). CVE-2024-XXXX disclosed with CVSS 9.8.
  DAY 0: CVE ANNOUNCED
  ────────────────────
  CVE-2024-XXXX: "Unauthenticated RCE via kube-apiserver proxy"
  CVSS: 9.8 (CRITICAL). Affects: Kubernetes < 1.28.5, < 1.29.2, < 1.30.0
  Exploit published on GitHub same day. Mass scanners deploy within hours.

  YOUR CLUSTER: v1.26 (EOL — NO PATCH COMING)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ kubectl version --short
  Server Version: v1.26.10    ← EOL. No patch will ever be released.

  DAY 1: ATTACKERS SCANNING
  ──────────────────────────
  $ shodan stats --facets version:100 'product:"Kubernetes" version:"1.26"'
  → 12,847 clusters still running v1.26 exposed on the internet.
  → Every single one is vulnerable to CVE-2024-XXXX with NO patch available.

  DAY 2: COMPROMISE
  ─────────────────
  Attacker sends crafted API request to your cluster.
  → Exploits CVE-2024-XXXX via kube-apiserver proxy → RCE as cluster-admin.
  → Deploys crypto-mining pods. Extracts all Secrets.
  → Your only defense was being on a SUPPORTED version that received the patch.

  THE FIX (if you HAD been on a supported version):
  $ apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.29.5-00 kubelet=1.29.5-00
  → CVE patched. Exploit blocked. Upgrade took 30 minutes.

  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: The difference between a secure cluster and a compromised
     one was NOT your security expertise — it was running a supported version
     that received the CVE patch. Version management IS security management.

Version Security Posture — Where Does Your Cluster Stand?

🔴 EOL (v1.26 or older) — No patches, known CVEs exploitable 0% security — every CVE is a permanent vulnerability
🟡 Supported but outdated (N-2, e.g., v1.28) — Gets patches but missing features 50% — patched but may lack newer security features
🟢 Current (N or N-1, e.g., v1.29-1.30) — All patches + latest features 95% — fully patched, all security features available

12.2 Upgrade Strategy for a Running Cluster

Upgrading a Kubernetes cluster is a multi-phase operation that must follow a specific order: control plane first, then worker nodes. This order ensures the API server is always at a version equal to or higher than the kubelets — kubelets cannot be at a higher minor version than the API server. Breaking this rule causes the kubelet to be unable to communicate with the API server.

⚠️ One Minor Version at a Time — No Skipping

Kubernetes only supports upgrading one minor version at a time. You cannot jump from v1.28 to v1.30 — you must go v1.28 → v1.29 → v1.30. The CKS exam tests this explicitly: if a cluster is on v1.27 and you are asked to upgrade to v1.29, you must upgrade to v1.28 first, THEN to v1.29. Attempting to skip a version will fail.

Safe Cluster Upgrade Sequence — Step by Step

The complete kubeadm upgrade workflow
  PHASE 1: PREPARE
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  □ kubeadm upgrade plan → shows available versions
  □ Backup etcd: etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-pre-upgrade.db
  □ Check addon compatibility (Calico, Ingress, cert-manager)
  □ Read release notes for breaking changes and deprecations

  PHASE 2: UPGRADE CONTROL PLANE (one node at a time)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  □ apt-get update && apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.29.x-00
  □ kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.x
  □ apt-get install -y kubelet=1.29.x-00 kubectl=1.29.x-00
  □ systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
  □ kubectl get nodes → control plane shows v1.29.x ✅

  PHASE 3: UPGRADE WORKER NODES (one at a time)
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  □ kubectl drain <worker-node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
  □ SSH to worker: apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.29.x-00
  □ kubeadm upgrade node
  □ apt-get install -y kubelet=1.29.x-00 kubectl=1.29.x-00
  □ systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
  □ kubectl uncordon <worker-node>
  □ Wait for node to become Ready → repeat for next worker

  PHASE 4: VERIFY
  ─────────────────
  □ kubectl get nodes → ALL nodes show v1.29.x
  □ kubectl version --short → client and server match
  □ Run kube-bench to verify no CIS regressions from upgrade
  □ Verify all anihpj pods are running and healthy

Critical Rules for Safe Upgrades

⬆️
One Minor at a Time

Never skip versions. v1.28→v1.29→v1.30. Skipping causes API version incompatibilities that break the cluster.

💾
Always Backup etcd

Before ANY upgrade: etcdctl snapshot save. If the upgrade corrupts etcd, the snapshot is your only recovery path.

🔄
Drain Before Worker Upgrades

Pods are rescheduled to other nodes during drain. Use --ignore-daemonsets for DaemonSet pods that must run on every node.

Real Upgrade Output — What You Actually See During kubeadm upgrade

Annotated kubeadm upgrade apply output — learn to read it
  $ kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.5

  [preflight] Running pre-flight checks.
  [upgrade] Reading configuration from the cluster...
  [upgrade] FYI: You can look at this config with kubectl -n kube-system
          get cm kubeadm-config -o yaml
  [upgrade/version] You have chosen to upgrade to version "v1.29.5"
  [upgrade/versions] Cluster version: v1.28.10
  [upgrade/versions] kubeadm version: v1.29.5
  [upgrade] Checking cluster health...
  [upgrade/health] All control plane components are healthy ✅
  [upgrade/etcd] Upgrading etcd from 3.5.6 to 3.5.10
  [upgrade/static-pods] Preparing for "kube-apiserver" upgrade
  [upgrade/static-pods] Renewing "apiserver" certificate  ← Certs renewed!
  [upgrade/static-pods] Renewing "apiserver-kubelet-client" certificate
  [upgrade/static-pods] Renewing "front-proxy-client" certificate
  [upgrade/static-pods] Waiting for the kubelet to restart each component
  [upgrade/static-pods] This might take a minute depending on your cluster
  [apiclient] Found 1 Pods for label selector component=kube-apiserver
  [apiclient] All control plane components are healthy after upgrade ✅

  [upgrade] SUCCESS! Control plane upgraded to v1.29.5
  [upgrade] Now upgrade kubelet on all nodes:
            apt-get install -y kubelet=1.29.5-00 && systemctl restart kubelet

  🔑 WHAT TO WATCH FOR:
  • "preflight" checks failing → fix before proceeding (wrong kubeadm version?)
  • "etcd" upgrade → etcd data migration happens here — this is why you backup
  • "Renewing certificates" → certs are rotated during upgrade — this is normal
  • "All control plane components are healthy" → wait for this line before proceeding

Upgrade Urgency Decision Tree — When Must You Upgrade?

🔴 Has a CRITICAL CVE (CVSS 9.0+) been announced affecting your version?
🚨 YES → UPGRADE IMMEDIATELY. Do not wait for the maintenance window. This is an emergency. The exploit is already being scanned for.
No critical CVE. Continue.
📅 Is your version more than 12 months old (approaching EOL)?
⚠️ YES → Plan upgrade within 2 months. You are close to losing patch support.
Not near EOL. Continue.
⬆️ Is there a new minor version with security features you need (e.g., bound tokens in 1.24)?
✅ YES → Test in staging → upgrade within 3 months to gain the security feature.
🎉 Your cluster is current, patched, and secure. Next review: when the next patch is released.

12.3 Security Patches vs Minor Upgrades

Not all upgrades are equal. Understanding the difference between a patch release (security fix) and a minor release (new features) determines your response timeline:

Patch vs Minor — When to Act

🔴 PATCH RELEASE (1.29.0 → 1.29.5)
⏰ Security fixes + bug fixes only
📅 Released every 4-6 weeks
🚨 ACTION: Apply IMMEDIATELY when CVE is in release notes
✅ No breaking changes — safe to apply directly
🟡 MINOR RELEASE (1.28 → 1.29)
⏰ New features + API changes + deprecations
📅 Released every ~4 months
🧪 ACTION: Test in staging → upgrade within 6-8 months
⚠️ May have breaking changes — read release notes carefully

Kubernetes Release Cycle — Strategic Timeline

When each type of release happens and how you should respond
  PATCH RELEASE (e.g., 1.29.0 → 1.29.5):
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Contains: Security fixes, bug fixes only. ZERO new features.
  Frequency: Every 4-6 weeks.
  ACTION: Apply IMMEDIATELY, especially when the release notes
          mention a CVE fix. These are zero-risk upgrades.
          $ apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.29.5-00 kubelet=1.29.5-00

  MINOR RELEASE (e.g., 1.28 → 1.29):
  ────────────────────────────────────
  Contains: New features, API changes, some deprecations.
  Frequency: Every ~4 months (3 releases per year).
  ACTION: Test in staging environment first. Plan upgrade within
          6-8 months of release to stay within the N-2 window.

  EOL: Running version N-3 or older:
  ──────────────────────────────────
  Status: NO MORE PATCHES. Critical CVEs will NOT be fixed.
  ACTION: URGENT — upgrade immediately. You are running known
          vulnerabilities with publicly available exploit code.

  📅 TYPICAL ONE-YEAR UPGRADE PLAN:
  Q1: Upgrade from v1.28 to v1.29 (staging tested, production applied)
  Q2: Apply v1.29 patch releases as they come (1.29.1, 1.29.2, ...)
  Q3: Upgrade from v1.29 to v1.30 (staging tested, production applied)
  Q4: Apply v1.30 patch releases as they come

Version Compatibility — What Changes Between Minor Versions

ComponentVersion ConstraintWhat Happens If Mismatched
kube-apiserver → kubeletAPI server must be ≥ kubelet minor versionKubelet cannot communicate — node goes NotReady
kubelet → kube-apiserverKubelet can be ONE minor version BEHIND API server (skew policy)Works, but upgrade kubelet soon
kubectl → kube-apiserverkubectl must be within ±1 minor version of API serverMay work, but some features unavailable
CNI PluginMust be compatible with target K8s versionNetworkPolicy enforcement may break
etcdMust be at a version supported by the API serverAPI server cannot connect to etcd — cluster down

📊 Chapter 12 Visual Summary

📅 14-Month Window K8s supports N, N-1, N-2. EOL = no patches. Stay within 2 versions of latest.
🐛 4 Notable CVEs Big Bird (9.8), RBAC bypass (8.1), hostPath escape (8.1), node MITM (7.6)
⬆️ One Minor at a Time Never skip versions. Control plane first, then workers. Drain before upgrading.
🚨 Patch = Immediate Security patches: apply NOW. Minor releases: test, then upgrade within 6-8 months.
💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam version management questions are practical: you will be given a cluster on an outdated version and asked to upgrade it. The workflow is always: (1) kubeadm upgrade plan to see available versions, (2) upgrade kubeadm binary first, (3) kubeadm upgrade apply on the control plane, (4) upgrade kubelet and kubectl, (5) drain worker nodes one at a time and upgrade them. Never skip versions. Always backup etcd before upgrading the control plane.

Kubernetes Version Skew Policy — Why You Can't Skip Versions

Kubernetes enforces a strict version skew policy that governs which versions can communicate with each other. This is not arbitrary — it exists because the API server, kubelet, and kubectl use versioned protobuf APIs that change between releases. Breaking the skew policy results in silent failures, API version mismatches, and corrupted etcd data:

Kubernetes Version Skew Policy — What Can Talk to What
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SKEW POLICY RULES (from kubernetes.io/docs/setup/version-skew-policy)   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RULE 1: kube-apiserver MUST be at version X or X+1 (one minor ahead)   │
  │          relative to kubelet.                                             │
  │  Example: API server at 1.29 → kubelet can be 1.28 or 1.29.              │
  │           API server at 1.29 → kubelet CANNOT be 1.27 (2 versions behind)│
  │                                                                          │
  │  RULE 2: kubelet MUST NOT be NEWER than kube-apiserver.                  │
  │  Example: kubelet 1.30 + API server 1.29 → BROKEN.                       │
  │           Kubelet may use APIs that don't exist yet.                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RULE 3: kubectl MUST be within one minor version (newer OR older)       │
  │          of kube-apiserver.                                               │
  │  Example: kubectl 1.30 + API server 1.29 → OK.                           │
  │           kubectl 1.31 + API server 1.29 → BROKEN.                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚡ THE UPGRADE ORDER EXISTS BECAUSE OF THESE RULES:                     │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────                       │
  │  1. Upgrade kubeadm FIRST (the upgrade tool itself).                     │
  │  2. kubeadm upgrade apply → upgrades API server, controller-manager,    │
  │     scheduler, and etcd (control plane components).                       │
  │  3. Upgrade kubelet and kubectl on control plane nodes.                  │
  │  4. Drain worker nodes one at a time. For each worker:                   │
  │     a) Upgrade kubeadm on worker.                                        │
  │     b) kubeadm upgrade node (updates kubelet config).                    │
  │     c) Upgrade kubelet + kubectl on worker.                              │
  │     d) Uncordon worker.                                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WHY THIS ORDER:                                                         │
  │  • API server must be upgraded BEFORE kubelets (Rule 1).                 │
  │  • Kubelets must NOT be newer than API server (Rule 2).                  │
  │  • Worker components should be upgraded AFTER control plane.             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

How kubeadm upgrade apply Actually Works — Step by Step Inside the Control Plane

When you run kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.5, kubeadm orchestrates a complex sequence across multiple components. Understanding this sequence helps you troubleshoot when upgrades fail — which they do, frequently, on the CKS exam:

1
Preflight Checks

kubeadm verifies: cluster is healthy, all nodes are Ready, kubeadm version matches target, no pending certificate expirations, etcd is healthy. If any check fails, kubeadm REFUSES to proceed. Fix the issue before retrying.

2
etcd Backup (if configured)

kubeadm takes a snapshot of etcd before making changes. If the upgrade fails catastrophically, you can restore from this snapshot. The snapshot is stored on the control plane node's filesystem.

3
Renew Certificates (if needed)

If certificates are near expiry, kubeadm renews them during the upgrade. This is automatic but can be controlled with flags.

4
Upgrade Static Pod Manifests

kubeadm writes NEW manifests to /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ with updated image tags (e.g., v1.28.0 → v1.29.5). The kubelet detects the changes and restarts each static pod with the new image. Order: etcd → API server → controller-manager → scheduler.

5
Upgrade kubelet and kubectl Binaries

kubeadm upgrade apply does NOT upgrade kubelet/kubectl binaries. You must do this separately with apt/yum. This is the #1 mistake on the CKS exam — candidates upgrade the control plane but forget to upgrade kubelet, and the version skew breaks node communication.

Chapter 13: Reducing the OS Attack Surface — Node Hardening

Kubernetes nodes run real Linux operating systems — Ubuntu, RHEL, Flatcar, or similar — and every package installed on those nodes, every service listening on a port, and every user account with SSH access is a potential entry point for an attacker. If a container escapes its sandbox (and container escapes do happen — CVE-2022-0185, CVE-2022-0492, CVE-2024-21626 all enabled kernel-level breakouts), the attacker lands directly on the node OS. What they find there determines whether the breach stops at one pod or escalates to every workload on every node in your cluster. This chapter teaches you the OS-level hardening techniques that form the last line of defense below Kubernetes — techniques that every CKS exam tests and every production cluster needs.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🖥️ System Hardening 🛡️ OS Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why the node OS is the last line of defense — and what happens when it fails
  • ✅ How to audit and remove unnecessary services, packages, and daemons from every node
  • ✅ How to lock down open ports with firewall rules — exposing ONLY what Kubernetes requires
  • ✅ How to harden SSH, create dedicated admin users, and eliminate shared root access
  • ✅ How to verify every hardening step against the CIS Linux Benchmark
  • ✅ How to apply OS hardening to the anihpj/jobpost cluster nodes
🎓 CKS Relevance
System Hardening 15% Minimize Vulnerabilities 20% CIS Benchmarks Covered
🧠 OS Hardening in the CKS Exam — What They Actually Test

The CKS exam does not ask you to memorize every Linux service. It tests your ability to execute a hardening workflow:

  • If the question says "reduce the attack surface of the worker node" → audit services with systemctl list-units --type=service, stop/disable unnecessary ones, and verify with ss -tlnp.
  • If the question says "harden SSH access to cluster nodes" → edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config: disable root login, disable password auth, restrict to key-only, add AllowUsers.
  • If the question says "restrict which processes can run on nodes" → remove unnecessary packages with apt remove / yum remove and verify with dpkg -l / rpm -qa.
  • The exam terminal gives you root SSH access to nodes. Use it to check EVERYTHING before submitting.

13.1 The Node OS Is Your Last Line of Defense

Picture this: an attacker exploits a remote code execution vulnerability in the anihpj Django application. They gain a shell inside the Django container. They discover they're running as root (because the pod spec didn't set runAsNonRoot: true). They find a kernel exploit — say, CVE-2022-0185, a heap overflow in the Linux kernel's legacy_parse_param function that allows an unprivileged user to escape containers and gain root on the host. They run the exploit. They are now on your Kubernetes node's operating system.

Container Escape → What Happens Next Depends on OS Hardening

🚨 UNHARDENED NODE — Full Cluster Compromise
  • Attacker finds 200+ installed packages → picks unpatched services to exploit
  • ss -tlnp shows 15+ open ports → finds vulnerable services to pivot through
  • Password SSH on port 22 → brute-forces from stolen /etc/shadow hashes
  • root login allowed via SSH → lateral movement to every other node
  • iptables/ufw absent → unrestricted network access to all cluster nodes
  • Docker socket mounted → attacker spawns privileged containers on ANY node
  • Result: Cluster-wide compromise in under 5 minutes
🛡️ HARDENED NODE — Blast Radius Contained
  • Minimal packages installed → no extra services to exploit
  • ss -tlnp shows only kubelet(10250), CRI socket, and SSH — all firewalled
  • SSH key-only, AllowUsers restricted → brute-force impossible
  • PermitRootLogin no → even with stolen key, root SSH blocked
  • iptables default-deny inbound → attacker's reverse shell can't phone home
  • No Docker socket, no unnecessary mounts → no container escape path to other nodes
  • Result: Attacker trapped on one node, unable to pivot, detected by Falco in seconds

The Container Escape Kill Chain — and Where OS Hardening Stops It

Every stage of a container escape attack — and the OS-level defense at each point
  STAGE 1: INITIAL ACCESS — Attacker exploits app vulnerability (RCE in anihpj Django)
  │
  ├─ 🛡️ OS DEFENSE: Minimal packages → fewer exploit targets. If the app runs as
  │    non-root (Chapter 18), most kernel exploits require privilege escalation first.
  │
  ▼
  STAGE 2: CONTAINER ESCAPE — Attacker runs kernel exploit (CVE-2022-0185, CVE-2024-21626)
  │
  ├─ 🛡️ OS DEFENSE: Seccomp profile (Chapter 15) blocks the specific syscalls the
  │    exploit needs. AppArmor profile (Chapter 14) denies access to /proc and /sys.
  │    If the kernel is patched (Chapter 12), the vulnerability doesn't exist at all.
  │
  ▼
  STAGE 3: SHELL ON NODE OS — Attacker now has a root shell on the Kubernetes node
  │
  ├─ 🛡️ OS DEFENSE: ⬅⬅⬅ THIS CHAPTER (13) ⬅⬅⬅
  │    • Unnecessary services removed → nothing extra to exploit for persistence
  │    • Open ports firewalled → attacker can't listen or connect out
  │    • SSH hardened → attacker can't add their own SSH key or brute-force accounts
  │    • IAM restricted → attacker finds only one non-root admin user, no shared root
  │
  ▼
  STAGE 4: LATERAL MOVEMENT — Attacker tries to reach other nodes, etcd, cloud metadata
  │
  ├─ 🛡️ OS DEFENSE: iptables rules restrict node-to-node traffic. No cloud metadata
  │    endpoint reachable (Chapter 16). kubelet auth requires TLS cert the attacker
  │    doesn't have (Chapter 11).

  ├─ 🛡️ OS DEFENSE: Filesystem mounted read-only where possible (Chapter 31).
  │    Falco (Chapter 29) detects unexpected process spawns and file writes.
  │    Audit log (Chapter 28) records every command for forensic analysis.

  ▼

     The blast radius is ONE node, not the entire cluster.
