CIS Benchmarks for Linux — What Applies to Kubernetes Nodes

The CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark complements the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark. While Chapter 4 focused on the K8s-specific benchmark (API server flags, etcd encryption, kubelet config), the Linux benchmark covers the OS layer beneath Kubernetes. Key sections that apply to K8s nodes:

📦
CIS §1: Filesystem

Mount options (nodev, nosuid, noexec on /tmp and /var/tmp), sticky bit on world-writable directories, separate partitions for critical paths.

🔧
CIS §2: Services

Disable services not required for Kubernetes: autofs, avahi-daemon, cups, dhcpd, slapd, named, vsftpd, httpd, dovecot, smb, squid, snmpd, rsync, nis.

🌐
CIS §3: Network

Disable unused network protocols (DCCP, SCTP, RDS, TIPC). Enable firewall (iptables/ufw). Disable IP forwarding unless explicitly needed.

📝
CIS §4: Logging

Configure auditd to log critical system events. Ensure rsyslog or journald is collecting logs. Logs must be shipped off-node (Chapter 28).

👤
CIS §5: Access/Auth

SSH hardening, password policy enforcement (pam_pwquality), restrict su to wheel group, lock inactive accounts, set TMOUT.

🛠️
CIS §6: Maintenance

Verify package integrity with rpm -Va / dpkg --verify. Check for unowned files. Verify file permissions against RPM/DEB database.

The 80/20 Rule of Node Hardening

⚡ You Don't Need to Memorize 200 CIS Checks

The CKS exam focuses on four high-impact categories that eliminate 80% of the OS attack surface:

  1. Package minimization (Section 13.2) — Every removed package is a removed attack vector
  2. Port lockdown (Section 13.3) — Only the 5-6 ports Kubernetes needs should be open
  3. SSH hardening (Section 13.4) — Key-only auth, no root login, restricted users
  4. User/IAM restriction (Section 13.4) — Dedicated admin accounts, no shared root, sudo logging

Master these four, and you can handle any CKS OS hardening task. The remaining CIS Linux checks are important for production but rarely tested directly on the exam.

The Physics of a Container Escape — How Kernel Exploits Actually Work

To understand WHY OS hardening matters, you need to understand what happens at the kernel level when a container escape succeeds. A container is NOT a virtual machine — there is no hypervisor, no hardware virtualization, no separate kernel. Every container on a node shares the exact same Linux kernel. The only thing separating a container from the host is a collection of Linux namespace and cgroup constructs — and these are security boundaries, not impenetrable walls. A kernel exploit that breaks through a namespace boundary gives the attacker direct access to the host kernel — and from there, to every process, file, and network connection on the node.

Namespaces: The Invisible Walls That Containers Live Inside

Linux namespaces are the kernel feature that makes containers possible. When you run docker run or crictl run, the container runtime asks the kernel to create a set of namespaces for the new process:

Namespace TypeWhat It IsolatesWithout ItExploit Target?
Mount (mnt)Filesystem view — the container sees its own / rootContainer sees host's entire filesystem including /etc/shadow, /var/lib/kubelet, /var/lib/etcdYES — CVE-2024-21626 exploited mount namespace via WORKDIR
PIDProcess tree — container only sees its own processesContainer sees EVERY process on the host — can kill -9 kubelet, containerd, sshdYES — PID namespace escape via /proc access
Network (net)Network stack — container has its own interfaces, IP, routesContainer shares host's network namespace — can sniff ALL node traffic including etcd TLSYES — hostNetwork: true bypasses this
UTSHostname and domain nameContainer can change node's hostname — potential for impersonation attacksPartial
IPCInter-process communication (shared memory, semaphores)Container can read/write host processes' shared memory segmentsYES — IPC namespace escape possible
UserUID/GID mapping — root in container (UID 0) can be mapped to UID 65534 (nobody) on hostRoot in container = root on host. This is how most escapes work.YES — THE most common escape vector
CgroupResource limits (CPU, memory) visibilityContainer can see and modify other containers' limits — DoS attacks possiblePartial — CVE-2022-0492 exploited cgroup v1
How CVE-2022-0185 Actually Worked — A Step-by-Step Reconstruction

Let's walk through the most impactful container escape of 2022 — not in abstract terms, but in concrete technical steps. Understanding this one exploit will teach you why EVERY OS hardening measure in this chapter matters.

CVE-2022-0185 — Linux Kernel Heap Overflow Escape, Step by Step
  THE SETUP:
  ──────────
  • Attacker has a shell inside a container (via compromised Django RCE in anihpj)
  • Container runs as root (UID 0 inside container = UID 0 inside this user namespace)
  • Kernel version: 5.10.x (unpatched — K8s node hasn't been upgraded since 2022)
  • Seccomp: not configured (Chapter 15 — not yet applied in our story)
  • AppArmor: not configured (Chapter 14 — not yet applied)

  STEP 1: ATTACKER RECONNAISSANCE INSIDE THE CONTAINER
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ uname -r                    → 5.10.0-15-amd64
  $ cat /proc/self/status | grep -i seccomp
  Seccomp: 0                    → Seccomp is DISABLED. All 300+ syscalls available.
  $ cat /proc/self/attr/current → unconfined
  → AppArmor profile is "unconfined." No restrictions at all.

  FINDING: No seccomp, no AppArmor, old kernel. Perfect conditions.

  STEP 2: ATTACKER LOADS THE EXPLOIT
  ──────────────────────────────────
  The exploit for CVE-2022-0185 targets the legacy_parse_param() function
  in the Linux kernel's filesystem mounting code. This function is called
  when mounting certain filesystem types (like tmpfs) with specific options.

  key technical detail: The function allocates a 4096-byte (PAGE_SIZE) buffer
  with kmalloc(), then copies user-controlled data into it WITHOUT checking
  the size. Input > 4096 bytes overflows the heap buffer.

  The attacker crafts a payload that:
  a) Triggers the overflow by mounting a tmpfs with oversized options
  b) Overwrites a function pointer on the kernel heap with a controlled address
  c) Redirects execution to attacker-controlled kernel code
  d) That code calls commit_creds(prepare_kernel_cred(0)) → gives root

  STEP 3: EXECUTION — THE ESCAPE
  ──────────────────────────────
  $ unshare -U -m -p -f /bin/bash    # Create new user+mount+PID namespaces
  $ mount -t tmpfs -o "size=4096,...[OVERSIZED OPTIONS]..." none /tmp/escape
  → KERNEL PANICS... but the exploit has already:
    1. Overwritten the heap → redirected kernel code execution
    2. Called commit_creds(prepare_kernel_cred(0)) → attacker process now
       has root credentials (UID 0, GID 0) in the INITIAL (host) user namespace
    3. Escaped the container's namespaces → now sees the HOST filesystem

  STEP 4: ATTACKER NOW HAS ROOT ON THE HOST NODE
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  $ ls /                          → This is the HOST root filesystem
  /bin /boot /dev /etc /home /lib /media /mnt /opt /proc /root /run /sbin
  /srv /sys /tmp /usr /var

  $ cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  → Now the attacker can read the API server manifest, find etcd certs,
    read every Secret in etcd, and pivot to other nodes.

  WHAT WOULD HAVE STOPPED THIS:
  ────────────────────────────
  ✅ PATCHED KERNEL (Ch12):       The vulnerability was fixed in 5.10.96.
                                  If kubeadm upgrade had been run, exploit fails.
  ✅ SECCOMP (Ch15):              The unshare() syscall would have been blocked
                                  by a restrictive seccomp profile → exploit
                                  cannot even begin.
  ✅ APPARMOR (Ch14):             The mount attempt would have been denied by
                                  an AppArmor profile that blocks mount() for
                                  the Django container.
  ✅ OS HARDENING (Ch13):         Even after escape, attacker finds minimal
                                  packages, firewalled ports, hardened SSH,
                                  and no compilers to build further exploits.

  LESSON: Defense in depth. Each layer ALONE might fail. ALL layers together
  make exploitation exponentially harder.
Why Root in Container = Root on Host — The User Namespace Problem

This is the single most misunderstood concept in container security. When you run a container as root (UID 0) without user namespace remapping, that root user is the same UID 0 as the host's root user. The container's root can do anything that the host's root can do — IF it can escape the namespace boundaries. And if there's a kernel bug (like CVE-2022-0185), those boundaries are paper-thin.

User namespace remapping (userns-remap in Docker, or UserNamespacesSupport in containerd) maps UID 0 inside the container to a high, unprivileged UID on the host (like 65534 = nobody). Even if the container escapes, the attacker lands as an unprivileged user on the host — not root. This is why Chapter 18 (Security Contexts) insists on runAsNonRoot: true and why Chapter 21 covers user namespace remapping in depth.

⚡ The Root-in-Container Reality Check

Run this command on ANY of your nodes right now:

kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '[.items[].spec.containers[] | select(.securityContext.runAsNonRoot != true)] | length'

That number is how many containers in your cluster are running as root — and therefore have the potential to exploit a kernel escape vulnerability. Every one of those containers should have runAsNonRoot: true set, unless there is an extremely specific reason why the application requires UID 0.

Filesystem Hardening — Mount Options and Why They're Critical

The CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark §1 specifies mount options that should be applied to every partition on a Kubernetes node. These options are not just bureaucratic checkboxes — each one prevents a specific class of attack. Here's what they actually do and why they matter:

🚫
nodev

Blocks: Device files on this filesystem

Attack prevented: Attacker creates a device node for /dev/sda on an unsecured partition, then reads/writes the raw disk — bypassing file permissions entirely.

Where: /tmp, /var/tmp, /home, any user-writable partition

CIS check: §1.1.2-1.1.5

🚫
nosuid

Blocks: setuid/setgid bits on executables

Attack prevented: Attacker uploads a setuid-root binary to /tmp, executes it, and immediately gains root. Without nosuid, the kernel ignores the setuid bit on this partition.

Where: /tmp, /var/tmp, /home

CIS check: §1.1.3, 1.1.6-1.1.7

🚫
noexec

Blocks: Execution of ANY binary on this filesystem

Attack prevented: Attacker downloads a compiled exploit to /tmp and tries to run it. With noexec, the kernel refuses to execute anything on that mount — even with +x permissions.

Where: /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm (shared memory — commonly used for exploit staging)

CIS check: §1.1.4-1.1.5, 1.1.8-1.1.15

The pattern is: any filesystem location that a non-root user (or a compromised container process) can write to should have nodev, nosuid, and noexec set. These three mount options alone have stopped more post-exploitation attacks than any other single hardening measure. Here's how to apply them:

Bash — Applying CIS-recommended mount options on K8s nodes 
# Check current mount options for /tmp
mount | grep " /tmp "
# Example output: /dev/sda2 on /tmp type ext4 (rw,relatime)
# Missing: nodev, nosuid, noexec → VULNERABLE

# METHOD 1: Remount with options (immediate, non-persistent)
mount -o remount,nodev,nosuid,noexec /tmp
mount -o remount,nodev,nosuid,noexec /var/tmp
mount -o remount,nodev,nosuid,noexec /dev/shm

# METHOD 2: Add to /etc/fstab (persistent across reboots)
# Add these lines to /etc/fstab:
# /dev/sda2  /tmp       ext4  defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec  0  0
# /dev/sda3  /var/tmp   ext4  defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec  0  0
# tmpfs      /dev/shm   tmpfs defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec  0  0

# METHOD 3: Use a separate partition for /tmp (prevents /tmp from filling root)
# This also satisfies CIS §1.1.2 — separate /tmp partition

# Verify after applying:
mount | grep -E '/tmp|/var/tmp|/dev/shm'
# Should show: (rw,nodev,nosuid,noexec,relatime)

13.2 Removing Unused Services and Packages

Every package installed on a Kubernetes node is a potential attack surface. A web server package like nginx or apache2 has no business being on a K8s node — the pods run those services, not the node itself. Yet production clusters are routinely found with hundreds of unnecessary packages because nodes were provisioned from general-purpose OS images that included "kitchen sink" package sets. The rule is simple: if Kubernetes doesn't need it to run pods, it should not be installed on the node.

The Audit Workflow — Find, Stop, Remove, Verify

1
FIND — List what's running

systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
Shows every active service on the node. Every line you don't recognize is a candidate for removal.

2
STOP — Disable unnecessary services

systemctl stop <service> && systemctl disable <service>
Stops the service immediately AND prevents it from restarting on reboot.

3
REMOVE — Uninstall the package

apt remove --purge <package> (Debian) or yum remove <package> (RHEL). Purge removes config files too — leaving configs behind is a security risk.

4
VERIFY — Confirm nothing's left

systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running | wc -l — count should decrease. dpkg -l | grep <package> — should return nothing.

Services to CHECK and REMOVE on Kubernetes Nodes

The table below lists the most common unnecessary services found on Kubernetes nodes. These are pulled from real-world node audits and the CIS Distribution Independent Linux Benchmark. Every service in the "Remove on K8s Node" column should be investigated — some may be required by your specific infrastructure, but most are not.

Service / PackageWhat It DoesWhy It's on a NodeAction on K8s NodeVerification Command
apache2 / httpd / nginxWeb serverDefault in many OS imagesREMOVE — pods serve web trafficdpkg -l | grep apache2
vsftpd / proftpdFTP serverLegacy provisioningREMOVE — use SCP/SFTPsystemctl status vsftpd
avahi-daemonmDNS / Zeroconf discoveryDesktop-oriented distrosREMOVE — not needed on serverssystemctl status avahi-daemon
cups / cups-browsedPrinting serviceDesktop-oriented distrosREMOVE — no printers on K8s nodessystemctl status cups
snapdSnap package managerUbuntu defaultEVALUATE — may auto-update kernelsnap list
docker (daemon)Docker enginePre-K8s 1.24 installsREMOVE — K8s 1.24+ uses containerdsystemctl status docker
rpcbind / nfs-commonNFS/RPC servicesNFS storage backendsKEEP if using NFS volumessystemctl status rpcbind
bluetoothBluetooth daemonDesktop distro defaultREMOVE — no Bluetooth on serverssystemctl status bluetooth
ModemManagerMobile broadbandDesktop distro defaultREMOVE — no modems on serverssystemctl status ModemManager
whoopsieUbuntu error reportingUbuntu desktop defaultREMOVE — phones home with error datasystemctl status whoopsie

Complete Node Audit — Real Commands for the CKS Exam

Bash — Complete OS audit for a Kubernetes node (SSH into node as root) 
#!/bin/bash
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# KUBERNETES NODE OS AUDIT — Run on every node after provisioning
# This script identifies unnecessary services, packages, and open ports
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

echo "=== 1. LIST ALL RUNNING SERVICES ==="
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager

echo ""
echo "=== 2. COUNT RUNNING SERVICES (target: < 15) ==="
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager | grep -c "loaded active running"

echo ""
echo "=== 3. CHECK FOR KNOWN UNNECESSARY SERVICES ==="
UNNEEDED="apache2 httpd nginx vsftpd proftpd avahi-daemon cups cups-browsed \
          bluetooth ModemManager whoopsie docker snapd squid dhcpd named \
          dovecot postfix smbd nmbd xinetd telnet rsh-server"
for svc in $UNNEEDED; do
    if systemctl is-active --quiet $svc 2>/dev/null; then
        echo "❌ FOUND UNNECESSARY: $svc is RUNNING — STOP AND REMOVE"
    fi
done

echo ""
echo "=== 4. LIST ALL INSTALLED PACKAGES (Debian/Ubuntu) ==="
dpkg -l | wc -l
echo "Total packages installed. Target: as few as possible (< 500 ideal)"

echo ""
echo "=== 5. CHECK FOR LEGACY PACKAGES ==="
# telnet, rsh, ftp clients should never be on a K8s node
for pkg in telnet rsh-client ftp nfs-common; do
    if dpkg -l | grep -q "^ii.*$pkg "; then
        echo "❌ LEGACY PACKAGE: $pkg installed — REMOVE with apt remove --purge"
    fi
done

echo ""
echo "=== 6. VERIFY NO COMPILERS ARE INSTALLED ==="
for compiler in gcc g++ make cmake; do
    if which $compiler &>/dev/null; then
        echo "⚠️  COMPILER FOUND: $compiler — REMOVE (attackers use compilers to build exploits)"
    fi
done

echo ""
echo "=== AUDIT COMPLETE ==="

Stop, Disable, and Remove — The Hardening Commands

Bash — Removing unnecessary services and packages on a K8s node 
# STEP 1: STOP the service (immediate effect)
systemctl stop apache2
systemctl stop vsftpd
systemctl stop avahi-daemon

# STEP 2: DISABLE the service (prevent restart on reboot)
systemctl disable apache2
systemctl disable vsftpd
systemctl disable avahi-daemon

# STEP 3: MASK the service (prevent ANY start, even manual or dependency-triggered)
# Use mask for services you are CERTAIN should never run
systemctl mask apache2

# STEP 4: REMOVE the package (Debian/Ubuntu)
apt remove --purge -y apache2 apache2-bin apache2-data apache2-utils
apt remove --purge -y vsftpd
apt remove --purge -y avahi-daemon avahi-utils

# STEP 5: AUTOREMOVE orphaned dependencies
apt autoremove --purge -y

# STEP 6: VERIFY nothing remains
dpkg -l | grep -E 'apache2|vsftpd|avahi'    # Should return NOTHING

# For RHEL/CentOS/AlmaLinux:
# yum remove -y httpd vsftpd avahi
# rpm -qa | grep -E 'httpd|vsftpd|avahi'     # Should return NOTHING

Before / After — Visual Impact of Package Minimization

🔴 BEFORE: General-Purpose Ubuntu Image
Running services:28 services
Installed packages:1,247 packages
Compilers present:gcc, g++, make
Attack surface:High — 28 attack vectors
CIS score:~60% — Failing
🟢 AFTER: Hardened K8s Node
Running services:8 services
Installed packages:342 packages
Compilers present:NONE
Attack surface:Low — 8 known vectors
CIS score:~92% — Passing

That's a 73% reduction in installed packages and a 71% reduction in running services — achieved in under 10 minutes of auditing.

⚠️ Critical Pre-Removal Check — Don't Break the Cluster

Before removing any package, verify it's not a dependency of containerd, kubelet, or your CNI plugin:

# Check reverse dependencies (Debian/Ubuntu)
apt-cache rdepends <package-name>
# Example: if removing 'libseccomp2' would break containerd, DON'T DO IT
apt-cache rdepends libseccomp2 | grep -E 'containerd|kubelet|runc'

Golden rule: If you're not 100% sure a package is unnecessary, STOP the service but DON'T purge the package. A stopped service can be restarted. A purged package requires reinstallation — which might not work if networking is broken.

How Attackers Weaponize Unnecessary Services — Three Real Attack Chains

It's easy to think "it's just a printing service, who cares?" But every service is a piece of software written by humans — and all software has bugs. Let's trace three real attack chains that started with "unnecessary" services on Kubernetes nodes:

🔴 ATTACK CHAIN 1: CUPS (Printing Service) → Privilege Escalation

The setup: CUPS runs as root (it needs to access printer devices) and listens on port 631. It was installed by default on the Ubuntu 20.04 image used for K8s nodes. Nobody thought to remove it — "it's just a printer service."

The attack:

  1. Attacker escapes a container to the host (kernel exploit, or misconfigured hostPath volume)
  2. Runs ss -tlnp → finds CUPS listening on 127.0.0.1:631
  3. CUPS has a history of RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2024-47176, CVSS 9.1 — unauthenticated RCE via cups-browsed)
  4. Attacker sends a malicious IPP packet to localhost:631 → gains code execution as root (CUPS runs as root)
  5. Now has root on the node through a service that never should have been there

Prevention: systemctl stop cups cups-browsed && apt remove --purge cups cups-browsed — 10 seconds of work eliminates this entire attack surface forever.

🔴 ATTACK CHAIN 2: Avahi-Daemon (mDNS) → Network Reconnaissance

The setup: avahi-daemon implements mDNS (Multicast DNS) and DNS-SD (Service Discovery) via the Zeroconf protocol. It broadcasts service information over the network and responds to queries. Installed by default on Ubuntu Server — yes, even server editions.

The attack:

  1. Attacker compromises any pod in the cluster (e.g., via a vulnerable npm package in a frontend pod)
  2. From the pod, sends an mDNS query to 224.0.0.251:5353 (multicast address that avahi responds to)
  3. avahi-daemon responds with: hostname, IP address, OS version, and a list of services running on the node
  4. Attacker now has a complete inventory of the node — which K8s components are running, what version of Ubuntu, and network topology — without ever leaving their pod
  5. This is pure reconnaissance. No exploit needed. avahi is designed to broadcast this information.

Prevention: systemctl stop avahi-daemon && systemctl mask avahi-daemon — mDNS has zero legitimate use on a Kubernetes node. Containers handle their own service discovery via CoreDNS. avahi is pure attack surface.

🔴 ATTACK CHAIN 3: Compilers (gcc/g++) → Building Exploits on the Node

The setup: gcc and g++ were installed as part of build-essential — a common meta-package that DevOps engineers install to compile kernel modules or troubleshoot. The node has full C/C++ compilation capability.

The attack:

  1. Attacker escapes to the node (any method — kernel exploit, misconfigured volume, stolen SSH key)
  2. Discovers they are not root — they are uid 1000 (unprivileged user). Need privilege escalation.
  3. Without gcc: attacker would need to find a pre-compiled exploit binary that works on this exact kernel version and architecture. This is slow and unreliable.
  4. With gcc: attacker downloads exploit source code (publicly available on exploit-db.com), compiles it with gcc -o exploit exploit.c -static, and runs it. The whole process takes under 30 seconds.
  5. Compiles a local privilege escalation exploit (like Dirty Pipe — CVE-2022-0847) → gains root on the node

Prevention: apt remove --purge build-essential gcc g++ make — removing compilers forces attackers to use pre-compiled binaries that may not match your kernel/architecture, dramatically slowing their attack. Many modern container-optimized Linux distributions (Flatcar, Bottlerocket, Talos) ship with NO compilers at all.

systemd Mask vs Disable — Understanding the Dependency Chain Deeply

When you run systemctl disable <service>, you are telling systemd "don't start this service automatically at boot." But the service can STILL be started — by another service that depends on it, by a socket activation trigger, by a D-Bus message, or by a manual systemctl start. A disabled service is dormant, not dead.

systemctl mask <service> goes further: it symlinks the service unit file to /dev/null. Now the service CANNOT be started under ANY circumstances — not manually, not by dependencies, not by triggers. The kernel literally cannot find the unit file to load.

systemd Service States — The Lifecycle of a Service From Installed to Obliterated
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  systemd SERVICE STATES — weakest to strongest restriction              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  1. INSTALLED & ENABLED (package just installed)                        │
  │     └→ systemctl status → "active (running)" or "inactive (dead)"       │
  │     └→ STARTS automatically at boot                                     │
  │     └→ CAN be started manually: systemctl start <service>               │
  │     └→ Dependencies CAN trigger it to start                             │
  │     └→ RISK: HIGH — service runs whenever it or its dependencies want   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  2. STOPPED but ENABLED (service stopped manually)                      │
  │     └→ systemctl stop <service>                                         │
  │     └→ WILL restart at next boot (because it's enabled)                 │
  │     └→ RISK: MEDIUM — stops now, comes back on reboot                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  3. DISABLED (no automatic start, but CAN be started)  ⬅ EXAM FOCUS    │
  │     └→ systemctl disable <service>                                      │
  │     └→ Does NOT start at boot                                           │
  │     └→ CAN still be started manually: systemctl start <service>         │
  │     └→ Socket activation TRIGGERS it (if .socket unit exists)           │
  │     └→ Dependencies PULL it in: if "Wants=" or "Requires=" references   │
  │         this service, it WILL start when the dependent starts           │
  │     └→ RISK: MEDIUM — manual/dependency start still possible            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  4. MASKED (CANNOT be started by ANYTHING)  ⬅ STRONGEST                │
  │     └→ systemctl mask <service>                                         │
  │     └→ Creates symlink: /etc/systemd/system/<service>  →  /dev/null     │
  │     └→ Manual start FAILS: "Failed to start <service>: Unit is masked"  │
  │     └→ Dependencies IGNORE it — "Wants=masked-service" does nothing     │
  │     └→ Socket activation BLOCKED — even if socket gets traffic          │
  │     └→ RISK: ZERO — service is functionally deleted from systemd        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  5. PURGED (package removed from disk) ⬅ ULTIMATE                       │
  │     └→ apt remove --purge <package>                                     │
  │     └→ Binary, config files, unit files, man pages — ALL gone           │
  │     └→ Even if an attacker wants to start it, there's nothing to start  │
  │     └→ RISK: NEGATIVE — cannot be exploited because it doesn't exist    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CKS EXAM PATTERN:
  • "Disable the service" → systemctl disable (prevent boot start)
  • "Stop and disable the service" → systemctl stop && systemctl disable
  • "Ensure the service cannot be started" → systemctl mask
  • "Remove the package" → apt remove --purge (RHEL: yum remove)

13.3 Limiting Open Ports and Network Interfaces

Every open port on a Kubernetes node is a listening door. An attacker who escapes a container or compromises a node-level process can connect to any port that's bound to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces). Worse, they can open their own listening port for a reverse shell, command-and-control channel, or cryptocurrency miner. A hardened Kubernetes node should have exactly 5-8 ports open — the minimum required for the control plane, worker components, and SSH. Everything else should be blocked at the firewall level.

Port Audit — What's Listening on Your Node?

Bash — Auditing open ports on a Kubernetes node 
# METHOD 1: ss (socket statistics) — modern replacement for netstat
ss -tlnp
# -t = TCP, -l = listening, -n = numeric (no DNS resolution), -p = show process

# Sample output from a hardened K8s worker node:
# State  Recv-Q  Send-Q  Local Address:Port    Process
# LISTEN 0       128     127.0.0.1:10248       kubelet
# LISTEN 0       128     0.0.0.0:10250         kubelet
# LISTEN 0       128     127.0.0.1:10256       kube-proxy
# LISTEN 0       128     0.0.0.0:22            sshd

# METHOD 2: Check which INTERFACE each port is bound to
ss -tlnp | awk '{print $4}' | sort -u
# 127.0.0.1:XXXX  → localhost only (safe)
# 0.0.0.0:XXXX    → ALL interfaces (NEEDS FIREWALL)
# 192.168.x.x:XXXX → specific interface (better than 0.0.0.0)

# METHOD 3: Count open ports by process (spot anomalies)
ss -tlnp | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
# Shows how many ports each process has open — any process with
# unexpected ports is a red flag

Firewall Configuration — Two Approaches for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam expects you to know both iptables (direct kernel firewall) and higher-level tools like ufw (Uncomplicated Firewall, Ubuntu) or firewalld (RHEL). iptables is the lowest common denominator — it works on EVERY Linux distribution and is always available. Use iptables when the exam explicitly asks for it; use ufw/firewalld when the exam gives you a choice.

Bash — iptables firewall for a Kubernetes worker node (anihpj worker-1) 
#!/bin/bash
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# iptables HARDENING for K8s WORKER NODE
# This locks down a worker node to ONLY kubelet + SSH + CNI ports
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# STEP 1: SET DEFAULT POLICIES — DENY ALL INBOUND
iptables -P INPUT DROP
iptables -P FORWARD DROP
iptables -P OUTPUT ACCEPT  # Allow outbound (pods need internet access)

# STEP 2: ALLOW LOOPBACK (critical for local communication)
iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT

# STEP 3: ALLOW ESTABLISHED CONNECTIONS (responses to outbound traffic)
iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# STEP 4: ALLOW SSH FROM ADMIN JUMP HOST ONLY (not the whole internet!)
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp -s 10.0.0.100 --dport 22 -j ACCEPT

# STEP 5: ALLOW KUBELET API — from control plane nodes only
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp -s 10.0.0.10 --dport 10250 -j ACCEPT  # cp-1
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp -s 10.0.0.11 --dport 10250 -j ACCEPT  # cp-2
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp -s 10.0.0.12 --dport 10250 -j ACCEPT  # cp-3

# STEP 6: ALLOW CNI (Calico BGP) from other cluster nodes
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp -s 10.0.0.0/24 --dport 179 -j ACCEPT

# STEP 7: ALLOW NODEPORT RANGE — only if needed
# iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 30000:32767 -j ACCEPT

# STEP 8: LOG AND DROP everything else
iptables -A INPUT -j LOG --log-prefix "IPTABLES-DENIED: " --log-level 4
iptables -A INPUT -j DROP

# STEP 9: SAVE RULES (persistent across reboots)
# Debian/Ubuntu:
apt install -y iptables-persistent
iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4
# RHEL/CentOS:
# iptables-save > /etc/sysconfig/iptables

# STEP 10: VERIFY RULES
iptables -L -v -n
Bash — ufw (Uncomplicated Firewall) for Ubuntu nodes — simpler syntax 
# ufw is a friendlier frontend to iptables
# Default: DENY incoming, ALLOW outgoing
ufw default deny incoming
ufw default allow outgoing

# Allow SSH from admin subnet only
ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/28 to any port 22 proto tcp

# Allow kubelet API from control plane
ufw allow from 10.0.0.10 to any port 10250 proto tcp
ufw allow from 10.0.0.11 to any port 10250 proto tcp
ufw allow from 10.0.0.12 to any port 10250 proto tcp

# Allow Calico BGP from cluster nodes
ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/24 to any port 179 proto tcp

# Enable the firewall
ufw --force enable

# Verify
ufw status verbose

Port Decision Flowchart — "Should This Port Be Open?"

🔍 Is a Kubernetes component (kubelet, kube-proxy, CNI, etcd, apiserver) listening on this port?
✅ YES → Verify it's bound to localhost (127.0.0.1) if possible. If it MUST bind to 0.0.0.0, add an iptables rule restricting source IPs to cluster-internal ranges.
❓ No. Continue.
🔍 Is this SSH (port 22)?
✅ YES → Restrict to admin jump host IPs ONLY. Never expose SSH to 0.0.0.0/0. Use AllowUsers in sshd_config.
🚫 NO and NOT a K8s component → STOP THE SERVICE and CLOSE THE PORT. If the process is essential, firewall the port to specific source IPs, then investigate why it's listening.

Disable Unused Network Protocols

The CIS benchmark also requires disabling unused kernel network protocols. Each protocol module loaded in the kernel is a potential attack surface. The commands below disable protocols that Kubernetes nodes should never need:

Bash — Disabling unused kernel network protocols 
# Disable DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol)
echo "install dccp /bin/true" >> /etc/modprobe.d/CIS-dccp.conf

# Disable SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol)
echo "install sctp /bin/true" >> /etc/modprobe.d/CIS-sctp.conf

# Disable RDS (Reliable Datagram Sockets)
echo "install rds /bin/true" >> /etc/modprobe.d/CIS-rds.conf

# Disable TIPC (Transparent Inter-Process Communication)
echo "install tipc /bin/true" >> /etc/modprobe.d/CIS-tipc.conf

# Disable IP forwarding (unless this node is a router — K8s nodes should NOT be)
echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0" >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-cis.conf
echo "net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 0" >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-cis.conf
sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-cis.conf

# Verify all four modules are blacklisted
lsmod | grep -E 'dccp|sctp|rds|tipc'
# Should return NOTHING

iptables Deep Dive — How Packets Flow Through Chains

Every network packet that arrives at or leaves a Linux node passes through the kernel's netfilter framework, which iptables configures. Understanding this flow is critical because a single misconfigured rule — a DROP where you need ACCEPT — can take down your entire cluster. Let's trace exactly what happens to a packet from the moment it hits the network interface:

iptables Packet Flow — The Complete Path Through the Kernel
  INCOMING PACKET (e.g., kubectl command arriving at kube-apiserver:6443)
  │
  ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. PREROUTING CHAIN (raw → mangle → nat)                          │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────                          │
  │  Purpose: DNAT (destination NAT) happens here.                      │
  │  • If the packet is for a NodePort service (30000-32767), DNAT      │
  │    rewrites the destination from the node IP to the pod IP.         │
  │  • If the packet is for a ClusterIP service, same thing.            │
  │  ⚡ CKS RELEVANCE: NodePort rules live in PREROUTING nat chain.     │
  │     If you DROP here, you break ALL NodePort services.              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼  ROUTING DECISION: Is this packet for THIS node? Or should we forward it?
  │
  ├─ YES, for this node:
  │    │
  │    ▼
  │    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │    │  2. INPUT CHAIN (mangle → filter)  ⬅⬅⬅ THIS IS WHERE YOUR RULES GO │
  │    │  ─────────────────────────────────                                   │
  │    │  Purpose: Filter packets DESTINED for local processes.               │
  │    │  • iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 6443 -s 10.0.0.0/24 -j ACCEPT  │
  │    │  • iptables -A INPUT -j DROP   ← default-deny everything else       │
  │    │  ⚡ CKS RELEVANCE: Every hardening rule you write goes in INPUT.     │
  │    │     The order matters: ACCEPT rules FIRST, then DROP at the end.     │
  │    │     If DROP comes first, EVERYTHING is dropped — including SSH.      │
  │    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │    │
  │    ▼  Delivered to local process (e.g., kubelet on port 10250)
  │
  └─ NO, this node is a router:
       │
       ▼
       ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │  3. FORWARD CHAIN (mangle → filter)                                 │
       │  ─────────────────────────────────────                              │
       │  Purpose: Filter packets passing THROUGH this node (masquerade).    │
       │  • K8s workers forward traffic between pods on different nodes.     │
       │  • iptables -P FORWARD DROP is SAFE for workers (they don't route)  │
       │  • iptables -P FORWARD DROP on control plane is usually safe too    │
       │  ⚡ CKS RELEVANCE: If your node is a router/bridge, FORWARD must     │
       │     remain ACCEPT or pod-to-pod cross-node traffic will break.      │
       └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
       ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │  4. POSTROUTING CHAIN (mangle → nat)                                │
       │  ────────────────────────────────────────                           │
       │  Purpose: SNAT (source NAT) happens here — masquerading.            │
       │  • Pod traffic leaving the node gets SNAT'd to the node's IP.       │
       │  ⚡ CKS RELEVANCE: If you mess with POSTROUTING, pod egress breaks.  │
       └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  OUTGOING PACKET (locally generated):
  │
  ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  5. OUTPUT CHAIN (raw → mangle → nat → filter)                      │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────                     │
  │  Purpose: Filter packets GENERATED BY local processes.               │
  │  • iptables -P OUTPUT ACCEPT is the default and generally safe.     │
  │  • Restrictive OUTPUT rules can break pod egress, DNS, etc.         │
  │  ⚡ CKS RELEVANCE: Don't set OUTPUT to DROP on K8s nodes unless      │
  │     you have a VERY specific reason and tested pod networking.       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KEY TAKEAWAY FOR THE CKS EXAM:
  ─────────────────────────────────
  iptables -P INPUT DROP      → Blocks incoming traffic by default (GOOD)
  iptables -P FORWARD DROP    → Usually safe (nodes don't route)
  iptables -P OUTPUT ACCEPT   → Keep this ACCEPT (pods need to talk out)

  Then add ACCEPT rules in INPUT chain for: SSH, kubelet, CNI
  The ORDER is: ACCEPT rules first → LOG denied → DROP at the very end

Why Binding to 127.0.0.1 vs 0.0.0.0 Matters — A Network-Level Analysis

When a process opens a socket with bind(), it specifies which IP address(es) to listen on. This is not just a configuration detail — it is a fundamental security boundary. The difference between binding to 127.0.0.1 and 0.0.0.0 is the difference between "only processes on this machine can reach this port" and "any machine on the network can reach this port."

🔴 0.0.0.0 (INADDR_ANY) — All Interfaces

The process binds to every network interface on the node:

  • lo (127.0.0.1) — localhost
  • eth0 (10.0.0.5) — primary network
  • caliXXX (pod network) — CNI interfaces
  • tunl0 (tunnel) — overlay network

Attacker impact: Can reach this port from a pod on ANOTHER node (10.0.1.x → 10.0.0.5:10250), from the internet (if the node has a public IP), or from any compromised machine on the network.

🟢 127.0.0.1 — Localhost Only

The process binds ONLY to the loopback interface:

  • lo (127.0.0.1) — localhost ONLY

Attacker impact: Even if they are on the same node (container escape), they can only reach this port from the host itself. An attacker on a different node or the internet cannot reach it at all — the kernel drops the packets at the network layer before the process ever sees them.

Look at the Kubernetes port table above again — notice that kube-scheduler (10259) and kube-controller-manager (10257) bind to 127.0.0.1. This is intentional: only the API server (running on the same control plane node) needs to talk to them. No one else — not even other pods on the same node — should be able to reach the scheduler or controller manager. If an attacker on a compromised pod could reach port 10259 and send a malicious scheduling request, they could influence where pods land — potentially placing privileged pods on compromised nodes.

Container Escape Scenario — Why Node Hardening Is Your Last Line

ATTACK SCENARIO What Happens When a Container Escapes to an Unhardened vs Hardened Node
1
Attacker escapes container via CVE in runc

Using CVE-2024-21626, the attacker breaks out of the container namespace and lands on the host node as root (or a non-root user). They now have direct access to the node OS.

2
On an UNHARDENED node:

Attacker finds SSH running with password auth → brute-forces credentials. Finds gcc installed → compiles a kernel exploit. Finds docker still installed (not containerd) → accesses other containers directly. Finds FTP server running → exfiltrates data. The node has 200+ unnecessary packages installed — every one is a potential privilege escalation or persistence vector.

🛡️
On a HARDENED node (per this chapter):

SSH is key-only, root login disabled → brute-force impossible. No compilers (gcc removed) → cannot compile exploits. Only containerd (no docker) → no direct container access. No FTP/printing/Bluetooth → no exfiltration channels. Only 12 essential packages → minimal attack surface. The attacker is trapped on a stripped-down OS with virtually no tools to escalate. Node hardening turned a catastrophic breach into a contained incident.

Automated Node Audit Script — Run This on Every Node Weekly

Bash — Complete node security audit in one script
#!/bin/bash
# node-audit.sh — Run weekly on every Kubernetes node
echo "=== NODE SECURITY AUDIT: $(hostname) — $(date) ==="

# 1. Check for unnecessary services running
echo "[1/8] Checking unnecessary services..."
BAD_SVCS="cups vsftpd apache2 nginx avahi-daemon bluetooth snapd"
for svc in $BAD_SVCS; do
  if systemctl is-active --quiet $svc 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "  ❌ $svc is RUNNING — should be removed"
  fi
done

# 2. Check open ports (only K8s-required ports should be listening)
echo "[2/8] Checking open ports..."
ALLOWED_PORTS="6443 2379 2380 10250 10256 179 4240"
ss -tlnp | while read line; do
  port=$(echo "$line" | grep -oP ':\d+' | tr -d ':' | head -1)
  if [ -n "$port" ] && ! echo "$ALLOWED_PORTS" | grep -qw "$port"; then
    echo "  ⚠️  Unexpected port $port is listening"
  fi
done

# 3. Check SSH configuration
echo "[3/8] Checking SSH hardening..."
grep -q "^PermitRootLogin no" /etc/ssh/sshd_config || echo "  ❌ Root login allowed"
grep -q "^PasswordAuthentication no" /etc/ssh/sshd_config || echo "  ❌ Password auth enabled"

# 4. Check for unnecessary users
echo "[4/8] Checking user accounts..."
for user in $(awk -F: '$3>=1000{print $1}' /etc/passwd); do
  if ! id -nG "$user" | grep -qw "k8s-admins"; then
    echo "  ⚠️  User $user exists but not in k8s-admins group"
  fi
done

# 5. Check kernel hardening
echo "[5/8] Checking kernel parameters..."
[ "$(sysctl -n net.ipv4.ip_forward)" = "0" ] || echo "  ⚠️  IP forwarding enabled (only needed if pod networking uses it)"

# 6. Check for compilers
echo "[6/8] Checking for compilers (should be absent)..."
which gcc 2>/dev/null && echo "  ❌ gcc installed — remove with: apt remove gcc"
which make 2>/dev/null && echo "  ⚠️  make installed"

# 7. Check AppArmor
echo "[7/8] Checking AppArmor status..."
aa-status --enabled 2>/dev/null || echo "  ❌ AppArmor not enabled"

# 8. Summary
echo "[8/8] Audit complete. Review findings above."

13.4 User and IAM Hardening on Nodes

Who can SSH into your Kubernetes nodes? If the answer is "anyone with the root password" or "everyone in the DevOps team using the same key," your nodes are one stolen credential away from total compromise. Kubernetes ServiceAccounts control pod identity inside the cluster (Chapter 10), but Linux user accounts control who can access the node OS itself. These are entirely separate identity systems, and both must be hardened.

Kubernetes ServiceAccounts vs Linux User Accounts — Two Different Worlds

🔑 ServiceAccounts (Chapter 10)
  • Scope: Inside the Kubernetes cluster
  • Identity for: Pods, CI/CD pipelines, operators
  • Managed by: Kubernetes RBAC
  • Authentication: JWT tokens, bound tokens
  • Access: API server (kubectl, controllers)
  • Example: system:serviceaccount:anihpj:django-sa
🐧 Linux Users (This Chapter)
  • Scope: The node operating system
  • Identity for: Human admins, automation agents
  • Managed by: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, PAM
  • Authentication: SSH keys, passwords, PAM modules
  • Access: SSH shell, file system, systemctl
  • Example: k8s-admin (uid 1001, in sudo group)

A compromised ServiceAccount gives access to the Kubernetes API. A compromised Linux user gives access to the node OS itself — which is far more dangerous because it bypasses ALL Kubernetes security controls. This section focuses on preventing the latter.

The Node Access Hardening Checklist

🚫
No Root SSH

Set PermitRootLogin no in sshd_config. Root should only be accessible via sudo from a dedicated admin account.

🔑
Key-Only Auth

Set PasswordAuthentication no. SSH keys are immune to brute-force. Passwords are not.

👤
AllowUsers Restriction

Whitelist exactly which users can SSH. Every other user is denied before authentication even begins.

🔄
Rotate Keys

Rotate SSH keys quarterly. Remove keys for departed team members immediately. Audit ~/.ssh/authorized_keys monthly.

SSHD Hardening — The Complete Configuration

Bash — Hardening /etc/ssh/sshd_config for Kubernetes nodes 
#!/bin/bash
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# SSHD HARDENING for KUBERNETES NODES
# Run on every node (control plane AND worker)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# STEP 0: BACKUP THE ORIGINAL CONFIG
cp /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak.$(date +%Y%m%d)

# STEP 1: APPLY HARDENED SETTINGS
cat >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-cks-hardening.conf << 'EOF'
# ── CKS Node Hardening ──

# AUTHENTICATION
PermitRootLogin no              # NEVER allow direct root SSH
PasswordAuthentication no       # Key-based auth ONLY
PubkeyAuthentication yes        # Enable SSH keys
ChallengeResponseAuthentication no  # No keyboard-interactive
KerberosAuthentication no       # No Kerberos
GSSAPIAuthentication no         # No GSSAPI

# ALLOW ONLY SPECIFIC USERS (whitelist approach)
AllowUsers k8s-admin ansible-deploy

# PROTOCOL AND CIPHERS
Protocol 2                      # SSHv2 ONLY (v1 is insecure)
Ciphers chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com,aes256-gcm@openssh.com
MACs hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com
KexAlgorithms curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org

# SESSION HARDENING
ClientAliveInterval 300         # Timeout idle sessions after 5 min
ClientAliveCountMax 2           # 2 x 300s = 10 min total before disconnect
MaxAuthTries 3                  # Only 3 auth attempts per connection
MaxSessions 5                   # Limit concurrent sessions per user
LoginGraceTime 30               # 30 seconds to authenticate after connecting
MaxStartups 10:30:60            # Rate-limit unauthenticated connections

# DISABLE UNNECESSARY FEATURES
X11Forwarding no                # No X11 on servers
AllowAgentForwarding no         # Prevent SSH agent hijacking
AllowTcpForwarding no           # Prevent SSH tunneling (bypasses firewalls)
PermitTunnel no                 # No SSH tunnels
PermitUserEnvironment no        # No user env vars via SSH
PrintMotd no                    # No message-of-the-day (info leak)
UsePAM yes                      # Keep PAM for session logging
EOF

# STEP 2: TEST THE CONFIGURATION (CRITICAL — don't skip this!)
sshd -t
# If this returns "Syntax OK", the config is valid.

# STEP 3: RELOAD SSHD (don't restart — reload keeps existing sessions alive)
systemctl reload sshd

# STEP 4: VERIFY FROM ANOTHER TERMINAL (before closing your current session!)
# Open a NEW terminal and try to SSH in. If it works, your config is valid.
# If it FAILS, you still have your original session to fix the config.

echo "✅ SSHD hardened. VERIFY by opening a new SSH session before closing this one."

Creating a Dedicated Admin User — No More Shared Root

Bash — Creating a hardened admin user on each K8s node 
#!/bin/bash
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# CREATE A HARDENED ADMIN USER (DO THIS ON EVERY NODE)
# Replaces shared root access with individual, auditable admin accounts
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# STEP 1: CREATE THE ADMIN USER
useradd -m -s /bin/bash k8s-admin
# -m = create home directory, -s = set shell

# STEP 2: SET A STRONG PASSWORD (used only as backup, SSH keys are primary)
passwd k8s-admin
# Enter a 16+ character random password

# STEP 3: ADD TO SUDO GROUP (with password requirement for sudo)
usermod -aG sudo k8s-admin       # Debian/Ubuntu
# usermod -aG wheel k8s-admin    # RHEL/CentOS

# STEP 4: SET UP SSH KEY AUTHENTICATION
mkdir -p /home/k8s-admin/.ssh
chmod 700 /home/k8s-admin/.ssh
# Copy the admin's PUBLIC key (NOT the private key!)
echo "ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAI..." > /home/k8s-admin/.ssh/authorized_keys
chmod 600 /home/k8s-admin/.ssh/authorized_keys
chown -R k8s-admin:k8s-admin /home/k8s-admin/.ssh

# STEP 5: CONFIGURE SUDO WITH AUDIT LOGGING
cat > /etc/sudoers.d/k8s-admin << 'EOF'
# k8s-admin — Kubernetes node administrator
# All sudo commands are logged to /var/log/sudo.log
Defaults:k8s-admin logfile=/var/log/sudo.log
Defaults:k8s-admin log_input,log_output
Defaults:k8s-admin !requiretty
k8s-admin ALL=(ALL) ALL
EOF
chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/k8s-admin

# STEP 6: SET PASSWORD POLICIES (via PAM)
# Enforce strong passwords for ANY local user
apt install -y libpam-pwquality
cat >> /etc/security/pwquality.conf << 'EOF'
minlen = 14
dcredit = -1          # At least 1 digit
ucredit = -1          # At least 1 uppercase
lcredit = -1          # At least 1 lowercase
ocredit = -1          # At least 1 special character
maxrepeat = 3         # Max 3 repeated characters
EOF

# STEP 7: LOCK INACTIVE ACCOUNTS (auto-lock after 30 days of inactivity)
useradd -D -f 30

# STEP 8: SET SESSION TIMEOUT (auto-logout after 15 min of inactivity)
echo "TMOUT=900" >> /etc/profile.d/cks-timeout.sh
echo "readonly TMOUT" >> /etc/profile.d/cks-timeout.sh
echo "export TMOUT" >> /etc/profile.d/cks-timeout.sh

echo "✅ Admin user 'k8s-admin' created. Use this account instead of root."

Verify Node Hardening — The CKS Exam Verification Pattern

Bash — CKS exam verification checklist — run BEFORE submitting each task 
#!/bin/bash
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# NODE HARDENING VERIFICATION — Run on EVERY node before exam submission
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

echo "=== 1. SSH CONFIGURATION ==="
echo "PermitRootLogin: $(grep '^PermitRootLogin' /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null)"
echo "PasswordAuth:   $(grep '^PasswordAuthentication' /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null)"
echo "AllowUsers:     $(grep '^AllowUsers' /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null)"

echo ""
echo "=== 2. RUNNING SERVICES (should be < 12) ==="
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager | grep -c "loaded active running"

echo ""
echo "=== 3. LISTENING PORTS ==="
ss -tlnp

echo ""
echo "=== 4. FIREWALL STATUS ==="
iptables -L INPUT -v -n | head -20
# OR: ufw status verbose

echo ""
echo "=== 5. USERS WITH SHELL ACCESS ==="
grep -v '/nologin\|/false\|/sync\|/halt\|/shutdown' /etc/passwd | cut -d: -f1

echo ""
echo "=== 6. SUDOERS (who has sudo access?) ==="
grep -v '^#\|^$' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/* 2>/dev/null

echo ""
echo "=== ✅ VERIFICATION COMPLETE ==="

The PAM Authentication Stack — How Linux Actually Authenticates Users

When you type ssh k8s-admin@node-01, you are not just hitting a password prompt. Behind the scenes, Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) orchestrates a chain of checks — each module in the chain must succeed for authentication to proceed. Understanding PAM is essential because misconfiguring it can lock you out of nodes permanently. Here's what happens when an SSH connection arrives:

PAM Authentication Flow — What Happens When You SSH Into a Node
  SSH CONNECTION REQUEST: k8s-admin@node-01
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. TCP CONNECTION established (port 22)                        │
  │     └→ iptables ALLOWED this source IP  ✓                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  2. SSHD checks AllowUsers / DenyUsers / AllowGroups            │
  │     └→ "k8s-admin" IS in AllowUsers → CONTINUE                 │
  │     └→ If NOT in AllowUsers → Connection CLOSED immediately     │
  │     ⚡ KEY INSIGHT: AllowUsers blocks BEFORE authentication even │
  │        begins. The attacker never sees a password prompt. This  │
  │        is why AllowUsers is more secure than just key-only auth. │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  3. PAM STACK: /etc/pam.d/sshd is consulted                     │
  │     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │     │  pam_nologin.so     → Check if /etc/nologin exists       │ │
  │     │  pam_env.so         → Set environment variables          │ │
  │     │  pam_unix.so        → THE MAIN AUTH MODULE:              │ │
  │     │    • For PASSWORD auth: checks /etc/shadow hash          │ │
  │     │    • For KEY auth: checks ~/.ssh/authorized_keys         │ │
  │     │  pam_pwquality.so   → Enforce password complexity        │ │
  │     │  pam_tally2.so      → Count failed attempts (lockout)    │ │
  │     │  pam_faillock.so    → Alternative lockout module         │ │
  │     │  pam_limits.so      → Apply ulimits (max processes, etc) │ │
  │     │  pam_lastlog.so     → Update /var/log/lastlog            │ │
  │     │  pam_motd.so        → Print /etc/motd (if enabled)       │ │
  │     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                  │
  │  THE CRITICAL PAM RULE: Each module returns one of:              │
  │  • success   → this module passed                                │
  │  • auth_err  → authentication failed (bad password/key)          │
  │  • acct_exp  → account expired / locked                          │
  │  • perm_denied → permission denied (user not in allowed group)   │
  │                                                                  │
  │  The STACK determines what happens:                              │
  │  • required   → module MUST succeed, but continue checking others│
  │  • requisite  → module MUST succeed, STOP on failure             │
  │  • sufficient → if this module succeeds, authentication PASSES   │
  │    (even if other modules fail)                                  │
  │  • optional   → result doesn't matter for success/failure        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  4. SESSION OPENED                                              │
  │     • pam_systemd.so → registers session with systemd-logind    │
  │     • pam_umask.so → sets file creation mask (default: 022)     │
  │     • Shell spawned: /bin/bash for k8s-admin                    │
  │     • TMOUT=900 → auto-logout after 15 minutes of inactivity    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CKS EXAM RELEVANCE:
  ────────────────────
  The exam may ask you to:
  • "Configure password complexity" → edit /etc/security/pwquality.conf
  • "Lock accounts after 5 failed attempts" → configure pam_tally2 or pam_faillock
  • "Set account expiration" → chage -E 2026-12-31 k8s-admin
  • "Restrict which users can use su" → edit /etc/pam.d/su, add pam_wheel.so

The SSH Agent Forwarding Attack — A Deeper Explanation

When we set AllowAgentForwarding no in sshd_config, we are preventing a devastating attack that most engineers don't understand until it happens to them. SSH agent forwarding allows you to use your LOCAL SSH key on a REMOTE server — the remote server forwards authentication requests back to your local SSH agent. It's convenient. It's also a trap.

🔴 HOW SSH AGENT FORWARDING COMPROMISE WORKS

Scenario: Alice is a DevOps engineer. She connects to the K8s bastion host with agent forwarding enabled: ssh -A alice@bastion.k8s.internal

  1. Alice's SSH agent socket (/tmp/ssh-XXXXXX/agent.1234) is forwarded to the bastion host at /tmp/ssh-XXXXXX/agent.5678
  2. An attacker who previously compromised the bastion host (or any intermediate jump host) can see this socket
  3. The attacker runs: SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/ssh-XXXXXX/agent.5678 ssh root@prod-db-01
  4. SSH asks Alice's LOCAL agent to sign the authentication challenge with her private key
  5. Alice's agent does it — it's designed to do exactly this
  6. The attacker now has root access to prod-db-01, authenticated as Alice
  7. Alice never sees a prompt, never knows her key was used

What makes this so dangerous: The attacker doesn't steal Alice's private key. They use it while it's still in Alice's possession, through the forwarded socket. Alice's key never leaves her machine — but the ability to use it is forwarded to a compromised host.

This is why AllowAgentForwarding no is on the hardening checklist. The alternative — using ProxyJump (ssh -J bastion prod-node) — achieves the same result without exposing the agent socket to intermediate hosts. ProxyJump tunnels the SSH connection through the jump host without forwarding the agent.

Why Shared Root Is Dangerous — The Audit Trail Problem

When five DevOps engineers all SSH into nodes as root, and one of them accidentally runs kubectl delete namespace production at 3 AM, who did it? With shared root, the answer is: nobody knows. The audit log shows:

Feb 14 03:17:42 node-01 sudo: root : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/root ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/kubectl delete namespace production

Every engineer uses the same account. Every command looks identical in logs. There is zero accountability. Now compare that to dedicated admin accounts with sudo logging:

Feb 14 03:17:42 node-01 sudo: k8s-alice : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/k8s-alice ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/kubectl delete namespace production
Feb 14 03:17:42 node-01 sudo: k8s-alice : COMMAND=/usr/bin/kubectl delete namespace production [INPUT: y\n]

Now you know exactly who ran the command, when they ran it, from which directory, and even what they typed as input. This is not just about security — it's about operational maturity. In regulated environments (PCI-DSS, SOC2, HIPAA), the ability to attribute every administrative action to a specific individual is a compliance requirement, not a nice-to-have.

The log_input and log_output sudo options (which we configured in the admin user creation script) capture even more: every keystroke the user types into the sudo session and every byte of output. This creates a complete replayable record of every administrative session. Combined with shipping logs off-node (Chapter 28), this means even if an attacker compromises a node and deletes local logs, the audit trail survives on the central log server.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

OS hardening tasks on the CKS exam follow a four-step workflow: (1) SSH to the node, (2) audit what's there (services, ports, packages, users), (3) apply the specific hardening the question asks for (stop services, close ports, harden SSH, create users), (4) verify with the commands shown above. Always verify before submitting. The exam terminal gives you full root access to the nodes — use it. And remember: if you lock yourself out of SSH, you'll have to restart the exam scenario. Always test SSH access from a second terminal before closing your original session.
