💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

Node minimization on the CKS exam is about systematic auditing and removal. The exam workstation gives you SSH access to nodes. Use it to: (1) audit running services with systemctl list-units --type=service, (2) audit open ports with ss -tlnp, (3) audit installed packages with dpkg -l, (4) audit kernel modules with lsmod, (5) apply hardening via the commands in this chapter. Always verify after every change. And remember: AIDE is explicitly on the CKS curriculum — install it, initialize the database, and run a check. The exam may ask you to verify that specific system files have not been modified.

Chapter 17: Pod Security Standards — Admission-Level Enforcement

Before Pod Security Standards (PSS), Kubernetes used PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) — a complex, confusing, and ultimately deprecated mechanism for controlling pod security. PSS, introduced in Kubernetes 1.22 and stable in 1.25, replaces PSP with a simple, namespace-scoped, label-based system with three predefined security levels: Privileged, Baseline, and Restricted. PSS is enforced at admission time — when a pod is created, the API server checks whether the pod spec violates the namespace's PSS level. If it does, the pod is rejected BEFORE it ever reaches a node. This chapter teaches you to apply the right PSS level to every namespace in your anihpj cluster — ensuring that every pod in production runs with Restricted-level security, while system namespaces (kube-system) maintain the flexibility they need.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 📋 Admission Control 🛡️ Pod Hardening

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What PSS is and how it replaced PodSecurityPolicy — the three security levels
  • ✅ What each PSS level allows and blocks — Privileged, Baseline, and Restricted compared
  • ✅ How to apply PSS to namespaces via labels — enforce, audit, and warn modes
  • ✅ The decision flowchart for choosing the right PSS level for any namespace
  • ✅ How to configure PSS Restricted for anihpj-prod and verify compliance
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities 20% System Hardening 15%
🧠 PSS in the CKS Exam — What They Actually Test

The CKS exam tests PSS in a practical, namespace-level way:

  • Apply PSS labels to a namespace: Add pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted label. The exam expects you to know the exact label keys.
  • Fix a non-compliant pod: The exam may give you a pod that violates Baseline or Restricted. You must identify which fields are violating and fix them (add runAsNonRoot, drop capabilities, etc.).
  • Understand the label format: pod-security.kubernetes.io/<MODE>: <LEVEL> where MODE = enforce | audit | warn and LEVEL = privileged | baseline | restricted.
  • CRITICAL EXAM FACT: PSS labels go on the NAMESPACE, not the pod. The pod spec itself doesn't declare a PSS level — the namespace decides.

17.1 What Are Pod Security Standards (PSS)?

Pod Security Standards define three security levels that restrict what pods can do. These levels are cumulative — Baseline includes everything in Privileged plus restrictions, and Restricted includes everything in Baseline plus more. Importantly, PSS is enforced by a built-in admission controller (PodSecurity), not by an external webhook. This means it works out of the box on any Kubernetes cluster 1.23+ without installing anything extra.

The Three PSS Levels — What Each Allows and Blocks

PSS Security Levels — From Most Permissive to Most Restrictive
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  🔴 PRIVILEGED — No Restrictions (least secure)                          │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                            │
  │  • Allows everything: hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC, privileged mode     │
  │  • Allows all Linux capabilities, including dangerous ones               │
  │  • Allows running as root (UID 0)                                        │
  │  • Allows hostPath volumes, /proc mount, /dev access                     │
  │  • Allows custom AppArmor/SELinux/seccomp profiles (or none)             │
  │  ⚡ USE CASE: kube-system pods (CNI, CSI drivers, node exporters)        │
  │  ⚡ NEVER USE: For user-facing workloads like anihpj                     │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  🟡 BASELINE — Prevents Known Privilege Escalations (medium)             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────                   │
  │  • DISABLES: hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC (prevents container escape)   │
  │  • DISABLES: privileged containers                                       │
  │  • DISABLES: hostPath volumes (prevents host filesystem access)          │
  │  • DISABLES: CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW, and other dangerous caps        │
  │  • ALLOWS: running as any user (root or non-root)                        │
  │  • ALLOWS: most Linux capabilities                                       │
  │  ⚡ USE CASE: Dev/staging namespaces, workloads being migrated to        │
  │     Restricted that still need flexibility                               │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  🟢 RESTRICTED — Maximum Security (strongly recommended for production)   │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────    │
  │  • ALL Baseline restrictions, PLUS:                                       │
  │  • REQUIRES: runAsNonRoot: true                                           │
  │  • REQUIRES: seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault (or Localhost)               │
  │  • REQUIRES: capabilities: drop: [ALL]                                    │
  │  • RESTRICTS: volume types to ConfigMap, Secret, EmptyDir, PVC, and      │
  │    projected volumes only (no hostPath, no flexVolume, no CSI ephemeral) │
  │  • RESTRICTS: /proc mount type to default only                            │
  │  • REQUIRES: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (unless exception)              │
  │  ⚡ USE CASE: anihpj-prod, any production namespace                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

PSS vs PSP — Why the Switch Matters

FeaturePodSecurityPolicy (PSP - Deprecated)Pod Security Standards (PSS - Current)
Status❌ Removed in K8s 1.25✅ GA since 1.25
Where appliedCluster-wide (RBAC-based)Namespace-level (label-based)
ConfigurationComplex YAML with 30+ fieldsThree predefined levels (Privileged/Baseline/Restricted)
GranularityPer-user/per-ServiceAccountPer-namespace
Built-inRequired enabling admission pluginBuilt-in PodSecurity admission controller
ExtensibilityCould create custom policiesFixed predefined levels (use OPA/Kyverno for custom)
CKS ExamMay appear as theory question✅ Hands-on — apply labels, fix violations

Side-by-Side — What Each Level Enforces on a Typical Pod Spec

Pod Spec FieldPrivilegedBaselineRestricted
hostNetwork✅ Allowed❌ Blocked❌ Blocked
hostPID / hostIPC✅ Allowed❌ Blocked❌ Blocked
privileged: true✅ Allowed❌ Blocked❌ Blocked
hostPath volumes✅ Allowed❌ Blocked❌ Blocked
runAsNonRootNot requiredNot required✅ REQUIRED
seccompProfileNot requiredNot required✅ REQUIRED (RuntimeDefault)
capabilities.dropNot required⚠️ Drops dangerous caps✅ REQUIRED (drop ALL)
readOnlyRootFilesystemNot requiredNot required✅ REQUIRED
Volume types allowedAll types⚠️ Most (no hostPath)⚠️ Limited (no hostPath, flexVol, CSI ephemeral)

How the PodSecurity Admission Controller Works Internally

When a pod is created, the PodSecurity admission controller runs as part of the API server's admission chain. It checks the pod spec against the namespace's PSS labels and returns ALLOW or DENY. Understanding this internal logic helps you troubleshoot when pods are unexpectedly rejected or when violations aren't caught:

PodSecurity Admission Controller — Internal Validation Logic
  kubectl apply -f pod.yaml (namespace: anihpj-prod)
  │
  ▼
  API SERVER receives the CREATE Pod request
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 1: LOOK UP NAMESPACE LABELS                                        │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────                                        │
  │  The PodSecurity controller reads the namespace object for "anihpj-prod":│
  │  labels:                                                                  │
  │    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted                         │
  │    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.29                      │
  │                                                                           │
  │  STEP 2: DETERMINE THE APPLICABLE POLICY                                  │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────                                │
  │  enforce=restricted → The controller loads the "restricted" policy        │
  │  definition for version v1.29 from its built-in policy library.           │
  │  The policy is a set of CHECKS, not a single rule. Each check validates   │
  │  one aspect of the pod spec.                                              │
  │                                                                           │
  │  STEP 3: RUN EACH CHECK AGAINST THE POD SPEC                              │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                             │
  │  The controller iterates through ~15 checks for the Restricted level:     │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CHECK 1: runAsNonRoot                                                    │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                    │
  │  Reads: pod.spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot                             │
  │  AND: container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot (for EACH container)         │
  │  Rule: At least one must be explicitly set to true.                        │
  │  If BOTH are unset → FAIL: "runAsNonRoot != true"                         │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CHECK 2: seccompProfile                                                  │
  │  ────────────────────────                                                  │
  │  Reads: pod.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type                      │
  │  AND: container.securityContext.seccompProfile.type                       │
  │  Rule: type must be "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost".                      │
  │  If type is "Unconfined" or unset → FAIL                                 │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CHECK 3: capabilities                                                    │
  │  ──────────────────────                                                    │
  │  Reads: container.securityContext.capabilities.drop                       │
  │  Rule: drop must include ALL.                                              │
  │  If drop is missing or doesn't include ALL → FAIL                        │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CHECK 4: allowPrivilegeEscalation                                        │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────                                        │
  │  Reads: container.securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation                │
  │  Rule: must be explicitly set to false.                                    │
  │  If unset or true → FAIL                                                  │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CHECK 5-15: readOnlyRootFilesystem, volume types, /proc mount type,     │
  │  hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC, privileged, hostPath volumes,             │
  │  AppArmor profile, SELinux type, sysctls, procMount...                    │
  │                                                                           │
  │  STEP 4: AGGREGATE RESULTS                                                │
  │  ─────────────────────────                                                │
  │  ALL checks must pass → request is ALLOWED.                               │
  │  ANY check fails → ALL failures are aggregated into a single error        │
  │  message (so you see ALL violations at once, not one at a time).          │
  │                                                                           │
  │  STEP 5: RETURN DECISION                                                  │
  │  ────────────────────────                                                  │
  │  enforce mode: DENY → returns 403 Forbidden with violation details.       │
  │  audit mode: ALLOW → logs violation to audit log.                         │
  │  warn mode: ALLOW → returns warning to kubectl user.                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

17.2 Applying PSS to Namespaces

PSS is applied by adding labels to the Namespace object. Each label controls a specific enforcement mode for a specific security level. The label format is: pod-security.kubernetes.io/<MODE>: <LEVEL>. You can apply multiple modes simultaneously — for example, enforce at Baseline but warn at Restricted to prepare for a future upgrade.

The Three Enforcement Modes

🚫
enforce

Violations are REJECTED. The pod is not created. The API server returns a 403 Forbidden error with details about which fields violated the policy. This is the mode you use in production.

📝
audit

Violations are LOGGED to the audit log but the pod is ALLOWED. Use this to discover which pods would fail a stricter level without breaking anything. This is how you prepare to upgrade from Baseline to Restricted.

⚠️
warn

Violations trigger a WARNING to the user who created the pod (visible in kubectl output), but the pod is ALLOWED. Use this to educate developers without blocking their work.

Namespace Label Examples — All Modes, All Levels

Bash — Applying PSS labels to namespaces 
# ── PRODUCTION: Enforce Restricted (maximum security) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-prod \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29

# ── STAGING: Enforce Baseline, Warn on Restricted ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-staging \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29

# ── DEV: Audit Restricted (log violations, don't block) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-dev \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29

# ── KUBE-SYSTEM: Privileged (system pods need host access) ──
kubectl label namespace kube-system \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29

# ── VERIFY labels are applied ──
kubectl get namespace anihpj-prod --show-labels
# Look for: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

# ── REMOVE PSS labels (revert to no enforcement) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-dev \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce- \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn- \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-

Testing PSS — What Happens When a Pod Violates Restricted

Bash — Test that PSS Restricted blocks a non-compliant pod 
# Create a namespace with Restricted enforcement
kubectl create namespace pss-test
kubectl label namespace pss-test pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

# Try to create a pod that runs as root (violates Restricted)
kubectl apply -n pss-test -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-root
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:latest
    # ❌ MISSING: runAsNonRoot: true (required by Restricted)
    # ❌ MISSING: seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault (required by Restricted)
    # ❌ MISSING: capabilities: drop: [ALL] (required by Restricted)
EOF

# OUTPUT: Error from server (Forbidden): pods "test-root" is forbidden:
# violates PodSecurity "restricted:v1.29": unrestricted capabilities
# (container "nginx" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"]),
# runAsNonRoot != true (pod or container "nginx" must set
# securityContext.runAsNonRoot=true), seccompProfile (pod or container
# "nginx" must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault"
# or "Localhost")

# ✅ FIX the pod and try again
kubectl apply -n pss-test -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-fixed
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:latest
    securityContext:
      runAsNonRoot: true
      runAsUser: 1000
      capabilities:
        drop: [ALL]
      seccompProfile:
        type: RuntimeDefault
EOF
# Pod created successfully ✅

The Admission Plugin Chain — Where PSS Fits in the Request Pipeline

PSS is just one admission plugin among many. When a pod creation request reaches the API server, it passes through a CHAIN of admission plugins, each with a specific responsibility. Understanding the order helps you troubleshoot: if a pod is rejected, was it PSS? NodeRestriction? An OPA webhook? Here's the exact chain:

Pod Creation Admission Chain — Every Plugin in Order
  CREATE POD REQUEST ENTERS ADMISSION CHAIN
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  MUTATING PHASE (plugins can MODIFY the pod spec)                        │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────                            │
  │  1. NamespaceLifecycle — Ensures namespace exists, is not terminating.   │
  │  2. MutatingAdmissionWebhook — External webhooks (Istio sidecar inject,  │
  │     Kyverno mutate rules). Can ADD containers, volumes, labels.          │
  │  3. PodSecurity (MUTATING) — Adds default seccompProfile if unset,       │
  │     adds default runAsNonRoot based on namespace policy (if configured). │
  │  ... (other mutating plugins)                                             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  VALIDATING PHASE (plugins can ACCEPT or REJECT, but NOT modify)         │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────                │
  │  4. PodSecurity (VALIDATING) ← ⬅⬅⬅ PSS CHECKS RUN HERE                   │
  │     Checks the (possibly mutated) pod spec against namespace PSS labels. │
  │     If enforce=restricted → REJECTS violations.                           │
  │  5. NodeRestriction — Ensures kubelets only modify their own pods/nodes. │
  │  6. ValidatingAdmissionWebhook — External webhooks (OPA, Kyverno verify).│
  │  7. ResourceQuota — Ensures namespace resource limits not exceeded.      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚡ KEY INSIGHT: PSS runs AFTER mutating webhooks. This means:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • If Istio injects a sidecar, PSS validates the sidecar too.
  • If Kyverno adds a default seccompProfile, PSS sees the default.
  • BUT: If the original pod spec violates Restricted and a mutating webhook
    is supposed to fix it, PSS might reject the pod BEFORE the webhook runs
    (because PSS runs in BOTH mutating and validating phases).
  • The mutating PSS plugin runs FIRST in the mutating phase and can add
    defaults, then the validating PSS plugin runs later to check compliance.

17.3 PSS for the anihpj Namespace

Now let's apply PSS to the anihpj namespaces. The production namespace gets Restricted — every pod must run as non-root, with no capabilities, with RuntimeDefault Seccomp. The dev namespace gets Baseline (enforced) with Restricted warnings — developers can work freely but see warnings when their pods would fail production.

PSS Level Decision Flowchart — Which Level for Which Namespace?

🔍 Does this namespace contain workloads that NEED host-level access? (CNI plugins, CSI drivers, node exporters, monitoring daemons)
✅ YES → Use PRIVILEGED. But restrict with NetworkPolicy (Ch6) and RBAC (Ch9) to limit who can deploy to this namespace. Example: kube-system.
❓ No — the pods are user workloads. Continue.
🔍 Can ALL containers in this namespace run as non-root? (Dockerfiles have USER 1000 or equivalent)
❌ NO — some containers still need root → Use BASELINE (enforce). Add warn=restricted to nudge toward fixing. Example: anihpj-dev.
✅ YES — all containers are non-root ready. Continue.
🔍 Can ALL containers run with read-only root filesystem, drop ALL capabilities, and RuntimeDefault Seccomp?
❌ NO → Use BASELINE (enforce) + audit=restricted. Review the audit logs to identify what needs fixing.
🎉 YES → Use RESTRICTED! This is the maximum security level. All new pods will be validated against it. Example: anihpj-prod.

Complete PSS Configuration for anihpj Namespaces

Bash — Configure PSS for all anihpj namespaces 
#!/bin/bash
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# PSS CONFIGURATION FOR ANIHPJ CLUSTER
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# ── PRODUCTION: RESTRICTED (maximum security) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-prod \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29 \
  --overwrite

# ── STAGING: RESTRICTED (same as prod — test what you deploy) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-staging \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29 \
  --overwrite

# ── DEV: BASELINE enforce + RESTRICTED warn (flexibility + education) ──
kubectl label namespace anihpj-dev \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.29 \
  --overwrite

echo "✅ PSS configured for all anihpj namespaces"
echo ""
echo "Verification:"
kubectl get namespace anihpj-prod --show-labels | grep pod-security
kubectl get namespace anihpj-staging --show-labels | grep pod-security
kubectl get namespace anihpj-dev --show-labels | grep pod-security

Compliant anihpj Pod Spec for Restricted Level

YAML — anihpj Django deployment compliant with PSS Restricted 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
  namespace: anihpj-prod  # ← This namespace has enforce=restricted
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-django
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-django
    spec:
      # ── PSS RESTRICTED COMPLIANCE ──
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true           # ✅ Required by Restricted
        runAsUser: 1000               # ✅ Specific non-root UID
        runAsGroup: 1000              # ✅ Specific non-root GID
        fsGroup: 1000                 # ✅ Filesystem group
        seccompProfile:               # ✅ Required by Restricted
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:v2.0.0
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # ✅ Required by Restricted
          capabilities:
            drop: [ALL]                    # ✅ Required by Restricted
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true     # ✅ Required by Restricted
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp            # Writable emptyDir for temp files
        - name: media
          mountPath: /app/media      # Writable PVC for uploads
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}                 # ✅ Allowed volume type
      - name: media
        persistentVolumeClaim:       # ✅ Allowed volume type
          claimName: anihpj-media

Migrating from Baseline to Restricted — A Real-World Scenario

Most organizations start with Baseline and gradually migrate to Restricted. This is not a one-day task — it requires updating Dockerfiles, fixing application code, and testing. Here's the systematic migration playbook:

🟡 SCENARIO: Migrating anihpj Namespaces from Baseline to Restricted

Current state: anihpj-prod has enforce=baseline. Pods run as root (UID 0) because the Dockerfile doesn't specify a USER. Seccomp is not configured. Capabilities are not dropped.

Goal: enforce=restricted without breaking production.

Migration playbook — 4 phases over 2 sprints:

  1. PHASE 1: DISCOVERY (Sprint 1, Week 1)
    • Add audit=restricted and warn=restricted labels to anihpj-prod (keep enforce=baseline).
    • For 1 week, collect audit logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-* | grep "would violate PodSecurity"
    • Identify ALL pods that would violate Restricted. Document which fields need fixing for each.
  2. PHASE 2: FIX (Sprint 1, Week 2)
    • For each non-compliant pod, fix the root cause:
      • Dockerfile: Add USER 1000 at the end
      • Deployment YAML: Add runAsNonRoot: true, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault, capabilities: drop: [ALL]
      • Identify writable paths: Add emptyDir or PVC volumes for /tmp, /var/log, etc.
    • Deploy fixes to staging (anihpj-staging) first. Verify pods start successfully with enforce=restricted.
  3. PHASE 3: ENFORCE (Sprint 2)
    • Change anihpj-prod label: enforce=restricted
    • Roll out fixed deployments one at a time (canary deployment).
    • Monitor: any pod that still violates Restricted will fail to create. Roll back and fix.
  4. PHASE 4: LOCK (Ongoing)
    • Add OPA/Kyverno policy (Ch24) to verify Dockerfiles have USER directives in CI/CD.
    • Add CI/CD check: every Deployment YAML must pass kubectl apply --dry-run=server against a Restricted namespace.
    • Goal: Prevent non-compliant pods from ever reaching the API server.

Common migration pitfalls:

  • Forgotten writable directories: App writes to /var/log/app.log but rootfs is read-only → crash. Fix: mount emptyDir at /var/log.
  • Port binding below 1024: App binds to port 80 as non-root → EACCES. Fix: use port 8000 or add NET_BIND_SERVICE capability (but then you lose Restricted).
  • Third-party images: The postgres:15 image runs as root by default. Fix: use postgres:15-alpine which runs as postgres user, or set securityContext explicitly.

📊 Chapter 17 Visual Summary — Pod Security Standards at a Glance

🔴
Privileged

Use for: kube-system pods (CNI, CSI)
Blocks: Nothing
Allows: Everything including host access
Risk: Highest — full node access

🟡
Baseline

Use for: Dev/staging namespaces
Blocks: hostNetwork, hostPID, privileged, hostPath
Allows: Root containers, most capabilities
Risk: Medium — known exploits blocked

🟢
Restricted

Use for: Production (anihpj-prod)
Blocks: Root, all capabilities, writable rootfs
Requires: non-root, Seccomp, drop ALL
Risk: Lowest — maximum pod hardening

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

PSS tasks on the CKS exam follow a three-step workflow: (1) Label the namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=<level>, (2) Identify which fields in a given pod spec violate the level, (3) Fix the pod spec by adding the required fields (runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile, drop ALL, readOnlyRootFilesystem). Remember: the labels go on the NAMESPACE, not the pod. The pod spec must comply with the namespace's level. And the enforce-version label is important — it determines which version of the PSS policy definitions are used. Without it, the API server uses the latest built-in version, which may have slightly different rules.

PSS Selection Flowchart — Which Level Should You Choose?

Decision Tree: Privileged → Baseline → Restricted
  START: I need to secure my namespace
         │
         ▼
  Q1: Does this workload NEED host-level access?
      (hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC, privileged?)
  YES → Use PRIVILEGED (but ask: is there another way?)
  NO  ↓
  Q2: Can the workload run as a non-root user?
      (Does the Dockerfile have USER 1000?)
  NO  → Use BASELINE (allows root, blocks known exploits)
  YES ↓
  Q3: Can the container run with read-only root filesystem?
      (Writable dirs handled via emptyDir / PVC mounts?)
  NO  → Use BASELINE (allows writable root fs)
  YES ↓
  Q4: Can you drop ALL Linux capabilities?
      (Does the app need NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN, etc.?)
  NO  → Use BASELINE + specific capabilities allowed
  YES ↓
  🎉  Use RESTRICTED — Maximum security for this workload!

  RECOMMENDED FOR ANIHPJ:
  ─────────────────────
  anihpj-prod → RESTRICTED (public job listings)
  anihpj-dev  → BASELINE (developer flexibility)
  kube-system → PRIVILEGED (CNI plugins NEED host access)
      → But: apply NetworkPolicy to restrict who reaches them

PSS Three Levels — Side-by-Side Visual Comparison

Privileged vs Baseline vs Restricted — What Each Allows
  ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐
  │  🔴 PRIVILEGED       │ │  🟡 BASELINE         │ │  🟢 RESTRICTED    │
  │  (Most permissive)   │ │  (Moderate security) │ │  (Maximum security)│
  ├─────────────────────┤ ├─────────────────────┤ ├───────────────────┤
  │                     │ │                     │ │                    │
  │  ✅ Allowed:        │ │  ❌ Blocked:        │ │  ❌ Blocked:       │
  │  • root user        │ │  • hostNetwork      │ │  • ALL in Baseline │
  │  • ALL caps         │ │  • hostPID          │ │  • runAsNonRoot=   │
  │  • hostNetwork      │ │  • hostIPC          │ │    false           │
  │  • hostPID          │ │  • privileged=true  │ │  • volume types:   │

Chapter 18: Security Contexts — Locking Down Containers at Runtime

A pod's SecurityContext is the single most impactful set of YAML fields you can configure for container security. It controls who the container runs as (UID/GID), what Linux capabilities it has, whether it can escalate privileges, whether its root filesystem is writable, and what Seccomp/AppArmor profiles apply. Without a SecurityContext, every container runs as root with 38+ Linux capabilities — the exact conditions that make container escapes possible. This chapter teaches you every field in the SecurityContext, explains the security impact of each one, and shows you the exact configuration that PSS Restricted requires for the anihpj Django application.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours ⚙️ Container Hardening 🛡️ Runtime Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What a SecurityContext is — pod-level vs container-level settings
  • ✅ Why running as non-root is the single most important security setting
  • ✅ What Linux capabilities are, which ones are dangerous, and how to drop ALL
  • ✅ How allowPrivilegeEscalation prevents setuid-based privilege escalation
  • ✅ How readOnlyRootFilesystem enforces container immutability
  • ✅ The complete hardened pod spec for anihpj — every field explained
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities 20% System Hardening 15%
🧠 SecurityContext in the CKS Exam — What They Actually Test
  • Fix a pod that runs as root: Add runAsNonRoot: true and runAsUser: 1000. The exam may give you a pod spec without these and ask you to harden it.
  • Drop ALL capabilities: Add capabilities: drop: [ALL]. If the app needs a specific capability, add it back individually — never grant more than one.
  • Set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false: This must be set for PSS Restricted compliance. The exam will check this.
  • Configure readOnlyRootFilesystem: Mount emptyDir or PVC volumes for writable paths. The exam may give you a pod that crashes because /tmp is read-only.

18.1 What Is a Security Context?

A SecurityContext is a section of the Kubernetes pod/container spec that defines privilege and access control settings for the pod and its containers. It can be set at two levels: pod-level (applies to all containers) and container-level (overrides pod-level for that specific container). The fields control everything from the Linux UID the process runs as, to which Linux capabilities are available, to whether the filesystem is writable:

SecurityContext Fields — Complete Annotated Reference

Every SecurityContext Field — Pod-Level and Container-Level
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  spec:
    # ── POD-LEVEL securityContext (applies to ALL containers) ──
    securityContext:
      runAsNonRoot: true          # ❌ Refuse to start if container runs as UID 0
      runAsUser: 1000             # 👤 Linux UID for ALL containers
      runAsGroup: 1000            # 👥 Linux GID for ALL containers
      fsGroup: 1000               # 📁 Filesystem group for volume ownership
      fsGroupChangePolicy: "OnRootMismatch"  # 🔄 When to chown volumes
      seccompProfile:             # 🔍 Syscall filter for ALL containers
        type: RuntimeDefault
      supplementalGroups: [2000]  # 👥 Additional Linux groups

    containers:
    - name: anihpj
      # ── CONTAINER-LEVEL securityContext (overrides pod-level) ──
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true              # ❌ (container-specific)
        runAsUser: 1000                 # 👤 Override pod-level UID
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false # ⬆️  Block setuid binaries
        capabilities:                   # 🧢 Linux capabilities
          drop: [ALL]                   #    Remove ALL (best practice)
          add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]       #    Add back only what's needed
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true    # 🧊 Make / read-only
        privileged: false               # 🚫 NOT a privileged container
        procMount: "Default"            # 📂 /proc mount type (Default or Unmasked)

Pod-Level vs Container-Level — Inheritance Rules

📦
Pod-Level securityContext

Applies to ALL containers. Set common security settings here: runAsUser, fsGroup, seccompProfile. Every container inherits these unless it explicitly overrides them.

🔧
Container-Level securityContext

Overrides pod-level for that specific container. Use for container-specific settings: different UID, specific capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem (init containers may need write access).

18.2 Running as Non-Root — The Most Important Setting

If you take ONE thing from this entire guide, make it this: never run containers as root. Root in the container is the same UID 0 as root on the host. If a container escape occurs (kernel exploit, misconfigured volume, runtime bug), the attacker lands on the host as root — able to read every file, modify every process, and pivot to every other node. Running as non-root means the attacker lands as an unprivileged user — massively limiting what they can do even after a successful escape.

Root vs Non-Root — What Changes After a Container Escape

🔴 ROOT CONTAINER (UID 0)
  • Attacker escapes to host → lands as UID 0 (root)
  • Can read /etc/shadow, /var/lib/etcd, all Secrets
  • Can install kernel modules, rootkits, backdoors
  • Can modify system binaries (replace /usr/bin/kubectl)
  • Can access all host network interfaces
  • Can kill any process, including kubelet and containerd
🟢 NON-ROOT CONTAINER (UID 1000)
  • Attacker escapes to host → lands as UID 1000
  • Cannot read /etc/shadow (mode 000, root:shadow)
  • Cannot install kernel modules (needs CAP_SYS_MODULE)
  • Cannot modify system binaries (/usr/bin is root-owned)
  • Cannot open raw sockets (needs CAP_NET_RAW)
  • Must find a LOCAL PRIVILEGE ESCALATION exploit first

Configuring Non-Root — The Pod Spec and Dockerfile Must Match

YAML + Dockerfile — Non-root pod spec with matching Dockerfile USER 
# ── POD SPEC ──
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true    # Kubernetes REFUSES to start if container is root
    runAsUser: 1000       # The Linux UID to run as
    runAsGroup: 1000      # The Linux GID to run as
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:v2.0.0
# ── DOCKERFILE (must match the UID in pod spec) ──
FROM python:3.12-slim

# Create a non-root user with the SAME UID as the pod spec
RUN groupadd -r -g 1000 anihpj && useradd -r -u 1000 -g anihpj anihpj

# ... install dependencies, copy code ...

# ⬅⬅⬅ THIS IS CRITICAL: must be at the END of the Dockerfile
USER 1000

# ⚡ IMPORTANT: USER must come AFTER any commands that need root
# (apt-get, pip install --system, chown, mkdir in /etc)
# All COPY commands after USER will be owned by UID 1000

Why Root-in-Container = Root-on-Host — The UID Namespace Problem

This is the most misunderstood concept in container security. Linux UIDs are global within a user namespace. By default, a container shares the host's user namespace — meaning UID 0 inside the container IS UID 0 on the host. Docker/containerd can remap container UIDs to different host UIDs via user namespace remapping, but Kubernetes does not enable this by default. Until user namespace support becomes GA in Kubernetes (alpha in 1.25, beta in 1.27, GA targeted for 1.30), the ONLY protection is runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser: >0:

UID Mapping — With and Without User Namespaces
  WITHOUT USER NAMESPACES (Kubernetes default, all versions through 1.29):
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Container UID space = Host UID space (shared user namespace)

  Container: UID 0 (root) ───→ Host: UID 0 (root) — SAME USER
  Container: UID 1000       ───→ Host: UID 1000      — SAME USER

  ⚡ RESULT: If the container process escapes to the host, it keeps the
     SAME UID. Root in container = root on host. No translation occurs.

  WITH USER NAMESPACES (available in containerd, coming to Kubernetes):
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Container UID space is REMAPPED to a RANGE of high host UIDs:

  Container: UID 0 (root) ───→ Host: UID 65536 (unprivileged)
  Container: UID 1000       ───→ Host: UID 66536 (unprivileged)

  ⚡ RESULT: Even if the container runs as "root" (UID 0 inside the
     container), on the HOST it is UID 65536 — an unprivileged user.
     Container escape lands as an unprivileged user automatically.

  CURRENT STATE (Kubernetes 1.29):
  ────────────────────────────────
  • User namespaces in K8s are BETA (feature gate: UserNamespacesSupport)
  • Most production clusters run WITHOUT user namespace remapping
  • THEREFORE: runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser: >0 is ESSENTIAL
  • When user namespaces become GA, runAsNonRoot is less critical —
    but still a best practice (defense in depth)

18.3 Linux Capabilities — Dropping What You Don't Need

Linux capabilities break the monolithic "root" privilege into ~40 granular permissions. Instead of "root can do anything," capabilities say "this process can bind to low ports, but cannot load kernel modules." By default, Docker/containerd grants containers a set of ~14 capabilities. PSS Restricted requires dropping ALL of them. A Django web application needs zero additional capabilities — it binds to port 8000 (above 1024, so no CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE needed), doesn't modify network settings, and doesn't touch kernel parameters.

Dangerous Capabilities — What They Allow, Why You Drop Them

CapabilityWhat It AllowsAttack ScenarioNeeded by anihpj?
CAP_SYS_ADMINMount filesystems, swapon, setdomainname, and dozens of other privileged opsAttacker mounts host filesystem into container, reads /etc/shadow❌ NEVER
CAP_NET_RAWCreate raw sockets (craft arbitrary packets)Attacker runs ARP spoofing, TCP hijacking, or network scanning from inside container❌ NEVER
CAP_SYS_PTRACETrace arbitrary processes, read their memoryAttacker attaches to kubelet process, reads sensitive data from its memory❌ NEVER
CAP_SYS_MODULELoad/unload kernel modulesAttacker loads a malicious kernel module that hides their processes❌ NEVER
CAP_DAC_OVERRIDEBypass file permission checksAttacker reads /etc/shadow despite mode 000❌ NEVER
CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICEBind to ports below 1024Not dangerous by itself, but unnecessary if app uses port 8000+⚠️ Only if port < 1024
CAP_CHOWNChange file ownershipMinor — mostly needed for init containers that set up volume permissions⚠️ Init containers only

The drop ALL + add-back Pattern

YAML — Drop ALL capabilities, add back only what's needed 
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]                    # Remove ALL 14 default capabilities
    add: []                        # anihpj Django needs NONE
    # If the app needed NET_BIND_SERVICE:
    # add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]      # Add back ONLY this one

How the Kernel Checks Capabilities — The Internals That Make drop: [ALL] Work

When a containerized process attempts a privileged operation, the Linux kernel does NOT check "is this root?" It checks "does this process have the required capability in its capability bounding set?" Understanding this mechanism explains why drop: [ALL] is so effective — it strips every capability from every set, making even UID 0 processes unable to perform privileged operations:

Linux Capability Sets — What drop: [ALL] Actually Removes
  EVERY LINUX PROCESS HAS 5 CAPABILITY SETS:
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. PERMITTED SET (pP')
     • Capabilities the process is ALLOWED to use.
     • Can be added to the Effective set when needed.
     • drop: [ALL] clears this set completely.

  2. EFFECTIVE SET (pE)
     • Capabilities the process is USING RIGHT NOW.
     • The kernel checks this set on every privileged syscall.
     • If CAP_SYS_ADMIN is not in pE → mount() syscall returns EPERM.

  3. BOUNDING SET (pB)
     • Ultimate limit — no capability can ever be in pP' if not in pB.
     • drop: [ALL] clears this set. Once cleared, CANNOT be restored.
     • Even a setuid-root binary cannot regain capabilities outside pB.

  4. INHERITABLE SET (pI)
     • Capabilities passed to child processes across execve().
     • Cleared by drop: [ALL] — children get no capabilities.

  5. AMBIENT SET (pA)
     • Capabilities preserved across execve() of non-setuid binaries.
     • Allows unprivileged programs to retain specific capabilities.
     • Cleared by allowPrivilegeEscalation: false.

  WHAT HAPPENS WITH drop: [ALL]:
  ────────────────────────────
  Before: pP' = {CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, NET_BIND_SERVICE, SYS_ADMIN, ...} (14 caps)
  After:  pP' = {} — ALL sets are empty
           pE = {}
           pB = {}
           pI = {}
           pA = {}

  Root (UID 0) with empty capability sets:
  ───────────────────────────────────────
  • Can read/write any file (DAC — UID 0 still bypasses file permissions)
  • Can send signals to any process
  • But CANNOT: mount filesystems, load kernel modules, change network
    settings, bind to ports < 1024, change system time, or any other
    operation that requires a specific capability.

  ⚡ THIS IS WHY drop: [ALL] + runAsNonRoot: true is the golden combination:
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Non-root: cannot bypass file permissions (DAC restricts access)
  • No capabilities: cannot perform ANY privileged kernel operation
  • Combined effect: The process is a normal Unix user with ZERO special powers

Root vs Non-Root Container — Security Impact Comparison

❌ ROOT CONTAINER

securityContext: {}
→ runs as UID 0 (root)

Container escape → root on node:

  • Can read ALL files on host
  • Can install rootkits
  • Can modify system files
  • Can access host network
  • Can load kernel modules
✅ NON-ROOT CONTAINER

runAsNonRoot: true
runAsUser: 1000
runAsGroup: 1000

Container escape → UID 1000 on node:

  • Very limited permissions
  • Cannot install rootkits
  • Cannot modify system files
  • Cannot access host network
  • Cannot load kernel modules

18.4 Privilege Escalation — The allowPrivilegeEscalation Flag

allowPrivilegeEscalation: false prevents a process from gaining more privileges than its parent process through setuid binaries or other privilege escalation mechanisms. A setuid binary (like /usr/bin/passwd) runs with the privileges of the file owner (typically root), not the user who executed it. If an attacker finds a vulnerable setuid binary inside the container, they can exploit it to gain root — even if the container started as non-root. Setting this flag to false blocks ALL setuid execution.

YAML — Block privilege escalation in the container 
securityContext:
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # Block setuid binaries
  # Also blocks: file capabilities, ambient capabilities
  # and any other mechanism that would increase privileges

18.5 Read-Only Root Filesystem — Immutability in Practice

readOnlyRootFilesystem: true makes the container's root filesystem (/) read-only. The container cannot write to any path that is part of the image — no modifying binaries, no creating files in /etc, no writing logs to /var/log. This enforces the immutability principle: containers should not change after they start. If a container needs to write, it must use explicitly mounted volumes (emptyDir, PVC, ConfigMap) — which are visible and auditable.

Making anihpj Django Work with Read-Only Root Filesystem

YAML — Identify writable paths and mount volumes for each 
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    securityContext:
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true  # / is READ-ONLY
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp               # ✅ Writable: session files, upload staging
    - name: media
      mountPath: /app/media         # ✅ Writable: user-uploaded files
    - name: staticfiles
      mountPath: /app/staticfiles   # ✅ Writable: collected static files
    - name: cache
      mountPath: /var/cache/nginx   # ✅ Writable: HTTP cache
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}                    # Ephemeral — cleared on pod restart
  - name: media
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: anihpj-media       # Persistent — survives pod restarts
  - name: staticfiles
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: cache
    emptyDir:
      sizeLimit: 256Mi              # Limited size to prevent disk fill

Container Escape & Defense Tree — 6 Attack Paths, 12 Defenses

Every Escape Path Blocked by at Least Two Layers
  🔴 ATTACKER INSIDE CONTAINER — tries to escape to host node

  PATH 1: Exploit kernel vulnerability
  Attacker runs: exploit_linux_kernel.py
  → Needs dangerous syscalls (ptrace, mount, kexec_load)
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: Seccomp profile blocks those syscalls
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: gVisor/Kata sandbox (different kernel)

  PATH 2: Mount host filesystem
  Attacker runs: mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/host → reads /etc/shadow
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: cap drop ALL (no CAP_SYS_ADMIN)
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: privileged: false (no host mounts)

  PATH 3: Access host network
  Attacker runs: tcpdump on host interface → sniffs other pods
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: hostNetwork: false (pod has own namespace)
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: cap drop ALL (no CAP_NET_RAW)

  PATH 4: Write malicious binary
  Attacker writes: /usr/bin/backdoored-gunicorn
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (write fails)
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: AppArmor blocks writes to /usr/bin/

  PATH 5: setuid privilege escalation
  Attacker runs: /bin/setuid-root-backdoor → child runs as root
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: runAsNonRoot: true (pod starts non-root)

  PATH 6: Access Docker socket
  Attacker mounts: /var/run/docker.sock → creates privileged container
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: never mount docker.sock in user pods
  🛡️  STOPPED BY: PSS Restricted (no hostPath)

  🏁  Every escape path blocked by at least TWO layers.
      Defense-in-depth: even if one layer fails, another stops it.

18.6 Complete Security Context for anihpj — The Hardened Pod Spec

Here is the complete security-hardened pod spec for the anihpj Django application. Every field is explained with its security purpose. This is the reference configuration that satisfies PSS Restricted and represents the gold standard for production pod security:

YAML — Complete hardened pod spec for anihpj Django 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
      # POD-LEVEL SECURITY CONTEXT (applies to all containers)
      # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true            # ❌ Block root containers
        runAsUser: 1000               # 👤 Django runs as UID 1000
        runAsGroup: 1000              # 👥 GID 1000
        fsGroup: 1000                 # 📁 Volume files owned by GID 1000
        seccompProfile:               # 🔍 Block dangerous syscalls
          type: RuntimeDefault

      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:v2.0.0
        # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        # CONTAINER-LEVEL SECURITY CONTEXT
        # ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # ⬆️  Block setuid binaries
          privileged: false                # 🚫 Not a privileged container
          capabilities:
            drop: [ALL]                    # 🧢 No Linux capabilities
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true     # 🧊 / is read-only
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
        - name: media
          mountPath: /app/media
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: media
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: anihpj-media

📊 Chapter 18 Visual Summary — Security Contexts at a Glance

👤
Non-Root (18.2)

runAsNonRoot: true
runAsUser: 1000
Container escape → attacker is UID 1000, not root

🧢
Drop ALL Caps (18.3)

capabilities.drop: [ALL]
Removes all 14 default capabilities
Django needs ZERO

⬆️
No Priv Esc (18.4)

allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
Blocks setuid binaries
Prevents gaining root via suid

🧊
Read-Only FS (18.5)

readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
Cannot modify binaries or configs
Writes only to mounted volumes

🛡️
Complete Hardening (18.6)

All fields combined
Satisfies PSS Restricted
Defense-in-depth at runtime

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

SecurityContext tasks are the most common PSS-related questions on the CKS exam. The exam expects you to read a pod spec, identify which fields violate PSS Restricted, and fix them. The violations are always the same: missing runAsNonRoot, missing seccompProfile, capabilities not dropped, allowPrivilegeEscalation not set to false, readOnlyRootFilesystem not true. Memorize these five fields. If the exam gives you a pod that runs as root with no securityContext, you must add ALL five. And remember: capabilities are ADDITIVE when set at both pod and container level — if the pod drops ALL but the container adds NET_RAW, the container gets NET_RAW. Container-level overrides pod-level.

Chapter 19: Secrets Management — Encryption at Rest

Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted. This is the most dangerous default in Kubernetes — and the most commonly misunderstood. Anyone who can access etcd (the cluster's database) can read every Secret in plaintext by simply base64-decoding the values. If you have a database password stored as a Secret, and an attacker gains etcd access through a misconfigured RBAC rule, a compromised control plane node, or a stolen etcd backup — they have your database password instantly. This chapter teaches you to enable encryption at rest — encrypting Secrets with AES-GCM before they are written to etcd, so that even someone with direct etcd access sees only ciphertext. It also covers encryption provider selection, key rotation, and best practices for the anihpj application.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1 hour 🔐 Encryption 🗄️ etcd Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why base64 is NOT encryption — and why that matters for etcd security
  • ✅ How to create and apply an EncryptionConfiguration resource
  • ✅ The difference between encryption providers: identity, aescbc, aesgcm, secretbox, kms
  • ✅ How to verify encryption is working by reading directly from etcd
  • ✅ How to rotate Secrets after enabling encryption (existing Secrets are NOT auto-encrypted)
  • ✅ Secrets management best practices for the anihpj Django application
🎓 CKS Relevance
Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities 20% System Hardening 15%
🧠 Encryption at Rest in the CKS Exam — What They Actually Test
  • Create an EncryptionConfiguration file: Write the YAML, place it at /etc/kubernetes/enc.yaml on the control plane node.
  • Configure the API server: Add --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc.yaml to the API server manifest and mount the file.
  • Rotate existing Secrets: Run kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f - to rewrite all Secrets with encryption applied.
  • Verify encryption: Check etcd directly with etcdctl get /registry/secrets/... — the value should be binary garbage (encrypted), not readable base64.

19.1 The Problem: Secrets in etcd Are Stored in Plaintext (By Default)

The first time most engineers learn this, they don't believe it. Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted. Base64 is a character encoding — it transforms binary data into printable ASCII characters. It provides ZERO security. Anyone who can read the Secret can decode it instantly:

Base64 ≠ Encryption — The Dangerous Default
  kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
    --from-literal=password=supersecret123 \
    --from-literal=username=anihpj-admin

  kubectl get secret db-creds -o yaml
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Secret
  data:
    password: c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=     ← "Looks encrypted?" ❌
    username: YW5paHBqLWFkbWlu         ← "Looks encrypted?" ❌

  ⚡ ONE COMMAND reveals the plaintext:
  ─────────────────────────────────────
  echo "c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=" | base64 -d
  → supersecret123

  echo "YW5paHBqLWFkbWlu" | base64 -d
  → anihpj-admin

  WHAT BASE64 ACTUALLY IS:
  ────────────────────────
  • Base64 is an ENCODING, not ENCRYPTION.
  • Purpose: safely transport binary data in text-only formats (JSON, YAML, email)
  • Security: ZERO. It's mathematically reversible without any key.
  • It's like writing your password in a slightly different alphabet — anyone
    who knows the alphabet (everyone) can read it.

  WITHOUT ENCRYPTION AT REST:
  ────────────────────────────
  etcd stores: c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=  (plain base64)
  Attacker with etcd access: base64 -d → supersecret123
  Attacker with etcd backup: same thing
  Attacker with disk access: same thing

  WITH ENCRYPTION AT REST:
  ────────────────────────
  etcd stores: 
  Attacker with etcd access: sees random bytes, cannot decode
  Attacker with etcd backup: same — backup contains ciphertext
  Attacker with disk access: same — disk contains ciphertext

Who Can Access etcd? — The Attack Vectors

👑
Control Plane Compromise

Anyone with SSH access to a control plane node can read /var/lib/etcd/ directly. If the node is compromised, etcd data is exposed.

📋
etcd Backup Theft

etcd snapshots are taken for disaster recovery. If a backup file is stored in an insecure location (S3 bucket, shared drive), all Secrets in it are exposed.

🔐
RBAC Misconfiguration

A misconfigured RBAC rule granting get secrets to an untrusted user lets them read all Secrets through the API. Encryption doesn't prevent API access — it protects at the storage layer.

How etcd Stores Secrets — The Write Path Without and With Encryption

Understanding exactly where encryption happens in the API server's write path helps you troubleshoot when it doesn't work. The encryption layer is a transparent wrapper around etcd — the API server encrypts data before sending it to etcd, and decrypts it when reading it back. Other components (kubectl, controllers) never see the encryption — they always work with plaintext Secrets:

Secret Write Path — Without Encryption vs With aesgcm Encryption
  WITHOUT ENCRYPTION (identity provider):
  ───────────────────────────────────────
  kubectl create secret → API server receives Secret → validates →
  base64-encodes values → writes raw base64 to etcd
  │
  etcd stores: {"password":"c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM="}   ← READABLE base64
  │
  Attacker with etcd access: base64 -d → supersecret123

  WITH ENCRYPTION (aesgcm provider):
  ───────────────────────────────────
  kubectl create secret → API server receives Secret → validates →
  base64-encodes values → 🔐 AES-GCM ENCRYPTS the entire Secret value →
  prepends "k8s:enc:aesgcm:v1:key1:" header → writes ciphertext to etcd
  │
  etcd stores: "k8s:enc:aesgcm:v1:key1:"
  │
  Attacker with etcd access: sees binary garbage. Cannot decode.
  │
  ON READ: API server reads from etcd → detects "k8s:enc:" prefix →
  looks up provider "aesgcm", key "key1" → decrypts → base64-decodes →
  returns plaintext Secret to kubectl

  ⚡ THE ENCRYPTION HEADER (stored in etcd with the encrypted data):
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  k8s:enc:aesgcm:v1:key1:
  │     │      │   │
  │     │      │   └── Key name (which key encrypted this value)
  │     │      └────── API version
  │     └───────────── Provider name (which algorithm to use for decryption)
  └─────────────────── Magic prefix (identifies encrypted data)

  This header means the API server ALWAYS knows how to decrypt a value,
  even if the EncryptionConfiguration changes. It stores the provider
  and key name with every encrypted Secret.

19.2 Enabling Encryption at Rest

Encryption at rest is configured via an EncryptionConfiguration resource — a YAML file that tells the API server which resources to encrypt and which encryption provider to use. The file is passed to the API server via the --encryption-provider-config flag and must be mounted into the API server's static pod.

Complete Encryption Setup — 4 Steps

Bash + YAML — Enable encryption at rest for Secrets 
# STEP 1: Generate a 32-byte encryption key
ENCRYPTION_KEY=$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)
echo "Key: $ENCRYPTION_KEY"
# Example: aGVsbG93b3JsZHRoaXNpc2F0aGlydHl0d29ieXRla2V5Zm9yYWVz

# STEP 2: Create the EncryptionConfiguration file
cat > /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml << EOF
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
    providers:
      - aesgcm:                    # ← Encrypt with AES-GCM (recommended)
          keys:
            - name: key1
              secret: ${ENCRYPTION_KEY}
      - identity: {}               # ← Fallback: allow unencrypted reads
EOF
# STEP 3: Configure the API server to use the encryption config
# Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml:
# 1. Add the flag:
#    --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
# 2. Mount the file:
#    volumeMounts:
#    - name: encryption-config
#      mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#      readOnly: true
# 3. Add the volume:
#    volumes:
#    - name: encryption-config
#      hostPath:
#        path: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#        type: File
# 4. Wait for API server to restart (kubelet detects manifest change)

# STEP 4: Rotate ALL existing Secrets (critical!)
# Existing Secrets are NOT automatically encrypted — only NEW Secrets are.
kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -
# This reads every Secret, decrypts with the old provider (identity/plaintext),
# and rewrites it encrypted with the new provider (aesgcm).

Verifying Encryption Is Working

Bash — Verify that Secrets are encrypted in etcd 
# METHOD 1: Check etcd directly (requires etcdctl and certs)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/anihpj-prod/db-creds \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
# If encrypted: output is binary garbage (k8s:enc:aesgcm:v1:key1:...)
# If NOT encrypted: output contains readable base64 (c3VwZXJzZWNyZXQxMjM=)

# METHOD 2: Check API server logs for encryption config
kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-cp-1 | grep "encryption"
# Should show: "Loaded encryption provider" or similar

# METHOD 3: Create a new Secret and check
kubectl create secret generic test-encryption -n default \
  --from-literal=test=hello123
# Then verify via etcdctl that /registry/secrets/default/test-encryption
# contains k8s:enc:aesgcm:v1:key1: prefix

19.3 Encryption Providers — Which to Use

Kubernetes supports multiple encryption providers, each with different security and performance characteristics. The CKS exam expects you to know the differences:

ProviderAlgorithmKey SizeSecurityPerformanceWhen to Use
identityNone (plaintext)N/A❌ NONEN/ANEVER for production. Use only as fallback during migration.
aesgcmAES-GCM (authenticated)16/24/32 bytes✅ Strong✅ FastRecommended. Authenticated encryption — detects tampering. Must rotate key every 200K writes.
aescbcAES-CBC (unauthenticated)32 bytes⚠️ Good✅ FastUse if aesgcm is not available. No tamper detection — prefer aesgcm.
secretboxXSalsa20 + Poly130532 bytes✅ Strong✅ Very FastGood alternative to aesgcm. Faster on CPUs without AES-NI.
kmsExternal KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault)Managed by KMS✅ Strongest⚠️ Network latencyEnterprise best practice. Keys never touch the cluster. Envelope encryption.

KMS Envelope Encryption — How External KMS Works

The KMS provider uses envelope encryption — a two-layer system where a Data Encryption Key (DEK) encrypts the actual data, and the KMS encrypts the DEK. This means the encryption key material never touches the Kubernetes cluster at all:

KMS Envelope Encryption — Two-Layer Key System
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WRITE PATH: kubectl create secret generic db-creds                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  1. API server generates a random DEK (Data Encryption Key — 256-bit).   │
  │  2. DEK encrypts the Secret value using AES-GCM.                         │
  │  3. API server sends the DEK to AWS KMS / GCP KMS / Azure Key Vault:    │
  │     "Please encrypt this DEK with the customer-managed key"              │
  │  4. KMS encrypts the DEK and returns the encrypted DEK.                  │
  │  5. API server stores BOTH in etcd:                                      │
  │     {                                                                     │
  │       "encrypted_data": "",                           │
  │       "encrypted_dek": ""                              │
  │     }                                                                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  READ PATH: kubectl get secret db-creds                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  1. API server reads encrypted blob + encrypted DEK from etcd.          │
  │  2. Sends encrypted DEK to KMS: "Please decrypt this DEK"               │
  │  3. KMS decrypts the DEK and returns it (only if the API server's       │
  │     IAM role has kms:Decrypt permission).                                │
  │  4. API server uses the DEK to decrypt the Secret value.                │
  │  5. Returns plaintext Secret to kubectl.                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚡ ADVANTAGES:                                                           │
  │  ─────────────                                                            │
  │  • Key material NEVER stored in the cluster.                              │
  │  • Key rotation: rotate the KMS key → KMS re-encrypts all DEKs.         │
  │  • Audit trail: KMS logs every encrypt/decrypt operation.               │
  │  • Access control: IAM policies control who can decrypt (even with      │
  │    full etcd access, an attacker cannot decrypt without KMS access).    │
  │  • Revocation: disable the KMS key → ALL encrypted Secrets become       │
  │    permanently unreadable (emergency kill-switch for breaches).          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

19.4 Secrets Management in anihpj — Best Practices

Beyond encryption at rest, the anihpj Django application needs a comprehensive Secrets management strategy. Here are the best practices, applied to anihpj's specific configuration needs:

YAML — Complete secure Secret management for anihpj 
# ── DATABASE CREDENTIALS (used by Django settings.py) ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-creds
  namespace: anihpj-prod
type: Opaque
stringData:
  DATABASE_URL: postgres://anihpj:${DB_PASSWORD}@postgres:5432/anihpj

# ── DJANGO SECRET_KEY (used for sessions, CSRF tokens) ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: django-secret
  namespace: anihpj-prod
type: Opaque
stringData:
  SECRET_KEY: django-insecure-50chars-random-string-here

# ── MOUNT SECRETS AS ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES ──
spec:
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    envFrom:
    - secretRef:
        name: db-creds              # Injects DATABASE_URL as env var
    - secretRef:
        name: django-secret         # Injects SECRET_KEY as env var

# ⚡ NEVER store cloud credentials as Secrets — use IRSA/Workload Identity
# ⚡ NEVER commit Secret YAML to git — use sealed-secrets or external secrets
# ⚡ ALWAYS enable encryption at rest for the anihpj-prod namespace

Audit Who Can Read Secrets — The RBAC Check

Bash — Audit which users and ServiceAccounts can read Secrets 
# Find ALL RoleBindings/ClusterRoleBindings that grant secret access
kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name | test(".*secret.*|.*admin.*|cluster-admin|edit")) | "\(.kind): \(.metadata.name) → \(.subjects)"'

# Check if a specific user can read secrets in anihpj-prod
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n anihpj-prod --as=developer@anihpj.com
# Must return: no

# Check if a ServiceAccount can read secrets across all namespaces
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --all-namespaces \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:ci-cd:deployer-sa
# Must return: no (CI/CD should NOT need to read Secrets — only create/update)

Key Rotation — When and How to Rotate Encryption Keys

Encryption keys should be rotated regularly — not because the algorithm is weak, but because the longer a key is used, the more data is encrypted with it, and the greater the impact if the key is compromised. AES-GCM also has a safety limit: you should not encrypt more than ~2³² values with the same key (the birthday bound for GCM's nonce). For Kubernetes Secrets, this is unlikely, but key rotation is still a best practice:

Bash — Rotating encryption keys for Secrets 
# Generate a NEW key
NEW_KEY=$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)

# Update EncryptionConfiguration — ADD the new key FIRST, keep old key
cat > /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml << EOF
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
    providers:
      - aesgcm:
          keys:
            - name: key2           # ← NEW key FIRST (used for WRITES)
              secret: ${NEW_KEY}
            - name: key1           # ← OLD key SECOND (used for READS only)
              secret: 
      - identity: {}
EOF

# The API server will NOW:
# • Write NEW Secrets with key2 (first key in list)
# • Read OLD Secrets with key1 (still available for decryption)

# Re-encrypt ALL existing Secrets with the new key
kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -
# This reads every Secret (decrypted with key1) and rewrites it
# (encrypted with key2).

# Once all Secrets are re-encrypted, you can REMOVE key1 from the config.
# Verify: check etcd — no values should have the old key name header.
# Then remove key1 and restart the API server.

📊 Chapter 19 Visual Summary — Encryption at Rest at a Glance

⚠️
The Problem (19.1)

Default: Secrets are base64 (NOT encrypted)
Risk: etcd access = all Secrets exposed
Fix: EncryptionConfiguration

🔧
Setup (19.2)

Generate: 32-byte key
Configure: EncryptionConfiguration YAML
Flag: --encryption-provider-config
Rotate: kubectl replace all Secrets

🔐
Providers (19.3)

Recommended: aesgcm
Enterprise: kms (external)
Fallback: identity (plaintext — unsafe)

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

Encryption at rest tasks on the CKS exam follow a five-step workflow: (1) Generate a random 32-byte key with openssl or /dev/urandom, (2) Create the EncryptionConfiguration YAML with the aesgcm provider, (3) Add --encryption-provider-config to the API server manifest AND mount the file, (4) Wait for the API server to restart, (5) Rotate ALL existing Secrets with kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -. Never skip step 5: existing Secrets are NOT auto-encrypted when you enable encryption. They remain in plaintext until rewritten. And remember: the identity provider in your EncryptionConfiguration should always be the LAST provider in the list — it's used as a fallback for READING old unencrypted data during migration, not for writing.
