⚠️ DEPRECATED Plugins You Must Know for CKS

PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) — Removed in Kubernetes 1.25. Replaced by PodSecurity admission plugin. If a CKS exam question mentions PSP, it's a trap — the correct answer is PodSecurity (PSS). SecurityContextDeny — Removed in 1.27. Used to deny pods that set privileged securityContext fields. Replaced by PodSecurity restricted profile. NamespaceAutoProvision — Deprecated. Automatically creating namespaces on-the-fly is considered dangerous. Modern clusters should pre-create namespaces.

Security-Critical Built-in Admission Plugins — Deep Dive for CKS

PluginTypeWhat It DoesCKS Exam Scenario
NodeRestriction Validating Limits a kubelet's API access to ONLY its own node's pods, secrets, and configmaps. A kubelet on node-01 cannot read secrets from pods on node-02. This is the primary defense against a compromised kubelet reading cross-node secrets. "A compromised kubelet is reading secrets from other nodes. How do you prevent this?" → Enable NodeRestriction.
PodSecurity Validating Enforces Pod Security Standards (PSS) at the namespace level. Three levels: privileged (no restrictions), baseline (minimal hardening — blocks hostPath, hostNetwork, privileged containers), restricted (maximum hardening — requires runAsNonRoot, seccomp, drops ALL capabilities). Replaces the deprecated PSP. "Ensure all pods in namespace 'anihpj' comply with the restricted PSS profile." → Label namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted.
LimitRanger Mutating + Validating Two-phase operation: (1) MUTATE: Sets default resource requests/limits for containers that don't specify them. (2) VALIDATE: Rejects containers that exceed min/max limits defined in the namespace's LimitRange object. "Pods without resource limits are starving other workloads. How do you enforce defaults?" → Create a LimitRange object.
ResourceQuota Validating Enforces aggregate resource consumption caps per namespace: total CPU, memory, PVC count, Secrets count, ConfigMaps, Services. If creating a new pod would exceed the namespace quota, the request is denied BEFORE the pod is created. "The 'anihpj' namespace is consuming all cluster resources. Cap it at 10 CPUs and 20Gi memory." → Create a ResourceQuota.
ServiceAccount Mutating Three automatic actions: (1) If pod.spec.serviceAccountName is empty → sets it to "default". (2) If automountServiceAccountToken is not false → adds a projected volume for the SA token. (3) Adds the token volume mount to each container. This is why pods get a default token even when you don't configure it. Always enabled by default. Know that it exists. To disable: set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the pod or SA.
MutatingAdmissionWebhook Mutating Calls external HTTPS webhooks in sequence. Each webhook can modify the object using JSON Patch (RFC 6902). Used by Kyverno mutate rules, Istio sidecar injection, and custom defaulting logic. Reinvocation policy controls whether webhooks re-run after other mutations. "How does Istio automatically inject the Envoy sidecar?" → MutatingAdmissionWebhook calls Istio sidecar injector.
ValidatingAdmissionWebhook Validating Calls external HTTPS webhooks that can accept/reject. All validating webhooks run in PARALLEL (not sequential). If ANY webhook returns DENY, the object is rejected. Used by OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno validate rules. "Block any pod that uses an image from Docker Hub." → Deploy OPA Gatekeeper with ValidatingWebhookConfiguration.
ImagePolicyWebhook Validating A specialized, simpler admission plugin that calls an external webhook specifically for IMAGE approval. Unlike ValidatingAdmissionWebhook (which gets the entire object), ImagePolicyWebhook sends ONLY image information. The backend decides: is this image allowed? Simpler to implement than full OPA/Kyverno but less flexible. "Only allow images signed by our CI/CD pipeline, without deploying a full policy engine." → Configure ImagePolicyWebhook backend.

Configuring Built-in Admission Plugins on the API Server

YAML — API server manifest with recommended admission plugins for CKS 
# /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: kube-apiserver
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  containers:
  - name: kube-apiserver
    image: registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.30.0
    command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,LimitRanger,ResourceQuota,ServiceAccount,MutatingAdmissionWebhook,ValidatingAdmissionWebhook
    - --disable-admission-plugins=DefaultStorageClass
    - --admission-control-config-file=/etc/kubernetes/admission-control.yaml
    volumeMounts:
    - name: admission-config
      mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/admission-control.yaml
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: admission-config
    hostPath:
      path: /etc/kubernetes/admission-control.yaml
      type: File

How to Verify Which Admission Plugins ARE Active — Three Methods

Bash — Verify admission plugins from the API server (no direct node access needed) 
# ── METHOD 1: Check API server pod spec (requires node access) ──
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml \
  | grep enable-admission-plugins
# Or, from any machine with kubectl:
kubectl get pod -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver \
  -o json | jq '.items[0].spec.containers[0].command[] | select(contains("enable-admission"))'

# ── METHOD 2: kubectl api-versions (shows enabled API groups, not plugins) ──
# This shows which RESOURCE TYPES are available — admission plugins
# control HOW those types are processed, not which ones exist.

# ── METHOD 3: API server metrics (most reliable) ──
# If Prometheus metrics are enabled:
curl -sk https://localhost:6443/metrics | grep apiserver_admission_controller
# Shows latency and count per admission plugin per operation

# ── METHOD 4: Check logs at startup ──
kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver- | grep "Loaded"
# Shows: "Loaded 12 mutating admission controllers and 15 validating admission controllers"
# Then lists each one with its initialization status
⚠️ CKS Exam Critical: Enabling Admission Plugins

On the CKS exam, you may be asked to enable specific admission plugins. Remember: (1) The API server manifest is at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. (2) Edit --enable-admission-plugins. (3) The API server pod restarts automatically (static pod). (4) Always include existing plugins when adding new ones — the flag is a COMPLETE LIST, not additive. If you replace --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction with --enable-admission-plugins=PodSecurity, you LOST NodeRestriction and everything else. (5) Some plugins have dependencies: ServiceAccount plugin should run BEFORE MutatingAdmissionWebhook. (6) Verify with kubectl describe pod kube-apiserver-<node> -n kube-system and check logs for "Loaded N mutating admission controllers."

24.2 Dynamic Admission Control — Webhooks Explained

Built-in admission plugins are powerful but limited — they can only enforce what the Kubernetes authors built into them. For custom organizational policies, you need dynamic admission control: webhooks that call an external HTTPS server. The API server sends the admission request to your webhook, and your webhook responds with "allow" or "deny." This is how OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno, and custom policy engines integrate. Understanding the webhook protocol deeply — TLS, AdmissionReview, timeouts, failurePolicy — is essential for both the CKS exam and production operations.

Mutating vs Validating Webhooks — Two Different Purposes, Different Execution Models

Mutating vs Validating Webhook — When and How They Fire
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     ADMISSION WEBHOOK PHASES                              │
  │                                                                           │
  │  kubectl apply → API Server                                               │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ├── AuthN + AuthZ ────────────────────── ✅ Pass                    │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗    │
  │  ║  PHASE 1: MUTATING WEBHOOKS — Run SEQUENTIALLY                    ║    │
  │  ║  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ║    │
  │  ║  Webhook A runs → modifies object → Webhook B sees MODIFIED obj  ║    │
  │  ║  Webhook B runs → modifies object → Webhook C sees both changes  ║    │
  │  ║                                                                   ║    │
  │  ║  Each webhook receives AdmissionReview with the current object:   ║    │
  │  ║  {                                                                 ║    │
  │  ║    "request": {                                                   ║    │
  │  ║      "uid": "abc123",                                            ║    │
  │  ║      "operation": "CREATE",                                      ║    │
  │  ║      "object": { ... },       ← Original or previously-mutated   ║    │
  │  ║      "oldObject": null        ← Only for UPDATE/DELETE ops       ║    │
  │  ║    }                                                               ║    │
  │  ║  }                                                                 ║    │
│  ║                                                                   ║    │
│  ║  Webhook responds with JSON Patch to modify the object:            ║    │
│  ║  {                                                                  ║    │
│  ║    "response": {                                                   ║    │
│  ║      "uid": "abc123",                                             ║    │
│  ║      "allowed": true,                                             ║    │
│  ║      "patchType": "JSONPatch",                                    ║    │
│  ║      "patch": "W3sib3AiOiJhZGQiLC..."  ← base64(JSON Patch)      ║    │
│  ║    }                                                                ║    │
│  ║  }                                                                  ║    │
│  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝    │
│       │ Object has been MODIFIED                                          │
│       ▼                                                                    │
│  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗    │
│  ║  PHASE 2: VALIDATING WEBHOOKS — Run in PARALLEL                    ║    │
│  ║  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  ║    │
│  ║  ALL validating webhooks receive the SAME final object and run    ║    │
│  ║  concurrently. If ANY returns DENY → request is rejected.         ║    │
│  ║                                                                   ║    │
│  ║  Webhook Response:                                                 ║    │
│  ║  {                                                                 ║    │
│  ║    "response": {                                                  ║    │
│  ║      "uid": "abc123",                                            ║    │
│  ║      "allowed": true,           ← false → 403 Forbidden          ║    │
│  ║      "status": {                                                  ║    │
│  ║        "code": 403,                                              ║    │
│  ║        "message": "image not from approved registry"             ║    │
│  ║      }                                                             ║    │
│  ║    }                                                               ║    │
│  ║  }                                                                 ║    │
│  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝    │
│       │                                                                    │
│       ├── ALL ALLOWED ✅ → Object persisted to etcd                      │
│       └── ANY DENIED ❌ → 403 Forbidden                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔑 CRITICAL: MUTATING IS SEQUENTIAL, VALIDATING IS PARALLEL
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Mutating: Each webhook sees the output of the previous one.
    Order is determined by the MutatingWebhookConfiguration name.
  • Validating: All webhooks receive the identical final object.
    They run concurrently for maximum throughput.
  • If a mutating webhook TIMES OUT, the chain STOPS.
  • If a validating webhook TIMES OUT, it depends on failurePolicy.

Webhook TLS Certificate Management — The Most Common Production Problem

Every admission webhook requires mutual TLS: the API server must verify the webhook server's certificate, and the webhook server must verify the API server's client certificate. The caBundle field in the webhook configuration contains the CA certificate (base64-encoded PEM) that the API server uses to verify the webhook's TLS certificate. This is the single most common source of webhook failures in production:

Webhook TLS Handshake — What Actually Happens
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     WEBHOOK TLS SETUP                                 │
  │                                                                       │
  │  STEP 1: Generate CA + certificates                                   │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  # Create a self-signed CA                                     │    │
  │  │  openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -days 365 -nodes \       │    │
  │  │    -keyout ca.key -out ca.crt \                               │    │
  │  │    -subj "/CN=admission-ca"                                    │    │
  │  │                                                                 │    │
  │  │  # Create webhook server cert (signed by CA)                   │    │
  │  │  openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout server.key \     │    │
  │  │    -out server.csr -subj "/CN=gatekeeper-webhook-service.\    │    │
  │  │    gatekeeper-system.svc"    ← MUST match Service DNS name     │    │
  │  │                                                                 │    │
  │  │  openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key \  │    │
  │  │    -CAcreateserial -out server.crt -days 365                   │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                       │
  │  STEP 2: Store in Kubernetes Secret                                   │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  kubectl create secret tls gatekeeper-webhook-server-cert \   │    │
  │  │    --cert=server.crt --key=server.key \                       │    │
  │  │    -n gatekeeper-system                                        │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                       │
  │  STEP 3: Configure ValidatingWebhookConfiguration                     │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  clientConfig:                                                 │    │
  │  │    service:                                                    │    │
  │  │      name: gatekeeper-webhook-service                          │    │
  │  │      namespace: gatekeeper-system                              │    │
  │  │      path: /v1/admit                                           │    │
  │  │    caBundle:      ← API server uses this CA   │    │
  │  │                                      to VERIFY server cert    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                       │
  │  🔑 TLS VERIFICATION FLOW:                                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  1. API server connects to gatekeeper-webhook-service:443     │    │
  │  │  2. Webhook server presents server.crt                        │    │
  │  │  3. API server checks: Is server.crt signed by ca.crt?        │    │
  │  │  4. API server checks: Does CN/SAN match the service DNS?     │    │
  │  │     → CN must be: gatekeeper-webhook-service.gatekeeper-      │    │
  │  │       system.svc (or use SANs for wildcard: *.gatekeeper-     │    │
  │  │       system.svc)                                             │    │
  │  │  5. If EITHER check fails → TLS error → webhook call fails    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔴 The #1 Webhook Failure: CN/SAN Mismatch

The most common webhook deployment error is a certificate CN that doesn't match the Kubernetes Service DNS name. The API server connects to the webhook using the service DNS name: <service-name>.<namespace>.svc. If the server certificate's CN (or SAN) doesn't match this EXACT name, TLS verification fails. Solution: always use the full service DNS name in the certificate's CN field, or add it as a Subject Alternative Name (SAN). With cert-manager, use a Certificate resource with the correct DNS name automatically.

Webhook Configuration — Every Field Explained

YAML — ValidatingWebhookConfiguration with ALL fields annotated 
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: anihpj-image-policy
webhooks:
- name: image-policy.anihpj.com
  # ── RULES: Which API operations trigger this webhook? ──
  rules:
  - apiGroups:   [""]
    apiVersions: ["v1"]
    operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]   # Also: DELETE, CONNECT
    resources:   ["pods"]               # Also: "pods/status", "pods/ephemeralcontainers"
    scope:       "Namespaced"           # "Cluster" or "*" (both)

  # ── NAMESPACE SELECTOR: Filter by namespace labels ──
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      admission.anihpj.com/enabled: "true"
    # matchExpressions also supported for complex matching

  # ── OBJECT SELECTOR: Filter by object labels (K8s 1.15+) ──
  # More granular than namespaceSelector. Only sends objects
  # that match these labels to the webhook.
  objectSelector:
    matchLabels:
      security.anihpj.com/scan: "required"

  # ── CLIENT CONFIG: Where is the webhook? ──
  clientConfig:
    # Option A: Kubernetes Service (production)
    service:
      name: gatekeeper-webhook-service
      namespace: gatekeeper-system
      path: /v1/admit
      port: 443
    # Option B: External URL (for external policy engines)
    # url: https://policy-engine.anihpj.com/admit
    caBundle: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi...

  # ── WEBHOOK BEHAVIOR ──
  admissionReviewVersions: ["v1", "v1beta1"]  # v1 preferred, v1beta1 as fallback
  sideEffects: None               # None | NoneOnDryRun | Unknown
  # None: webhook has NO side effects (safe for dry-run)
  # NoneOnDryRun: webhook has side effects but NOT during dry-run
  # Unknown: must specify sideEffectClass for dry-run compatibility

  failurePolicy: Fail             # Fail | Ignore
  # Fail: if webhook UNREACHABLE → DENY request (secure, but risky)
  # Ignore: if webhook UNREACHABLE → ALLOW request (available, but insecure)

  timeoutSeconds: 10              # 1-30 seconds. Webhook must respond in this time.
  # If timeout is exceeded:
  #   failurePolicy=Fail → request DENIED
  #   failurePolicy=Ignore → request ALLOWED

  # ── MATCH POLICY: How rules are interpreted ──
  matchPolicy: Equivalent         # Equivalent | Exact
  # Equivalent: match resources even if API group/version differs
  # Exact: only match the EXACT apiGroups/apiVersions specified

  # ── REINVOCATION POLICY (MutatingWebhookConfiguration only) ──
  # reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded  # Never | IfNeeded
  # Controls whether mutating webhooks re-run after other mutations

failurePolicy Deep Dive — The Most Important CKS Decision

failurePolicy: Fail (Secure — Fail CLOSED)
  SCENARIO: Policy engine pod crashes

  Developer: kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
  → API Server → AuthN/AuthZ ✅
  → Mutating phase ✅
  → Validating phase:
    → API Server tries POST /validate to Gatekeeper
    → Gatekeeper pod is DOWN → TCP connection refused
    → API Server retries (up to timeoutSeconds)
    → After 10s timeout: webhook call FAILED
    → failurePolicy: Fail → DENY request

  RESULT: 403 Forbidden
  "admission webhook 'image-policy.anihpj.com'
   denied the request: webhook unreachable"

  IMPACT: NO pods can be created/updated cluster-wide
  MITIGATION: Run webhook with 3+ replicas, PDB,
              health checks, and alerting on webhook failures

  WHEN TO USE: Security-critical policies
  (image allowlist, PSS enforcement, RBAC validation)
failurePolicy: Ignore (Available — Fail OPEN)
  SCENARIO: Policy engine pod crashes

  Developer: kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
  → API Server → AuthN/AuthZ ✅
  → Mutating phase ✅
  → Validating phase:
    → API Server tries POST /validate to webhook
    → Webhook pod is DOWN → connection refused
    → After 10s timeout: webhook call FAILED
    → failurePolicy: Ignore → ALLOW request

  RESULT: Pod CREATED (even if it violates policy!)
  Developer sees: Pod created successfully
  Security team sees: Nothing (no alert, no log)

  IMPACT: All pods are deployed WITHOUT validation
  MITIGATION: Only use for non-security policies
              (default labels, annotations, formatting)

  WHEN TO USE: Non-critical policies
  (default labels, annotation injection, cosmetic checks)

Debugging Webhook Failures — The CKS Troubleshooting Flow

1Check webhook pod status

kubectl get pods -n gatekeeper-system → Are all webhook pods Running? If CrashLoopBackOff → check logs.

2Check webhook Service endpoints

kubectl get endpoints -n gatekeeper-system gatekeeper-webhook-service → Are there ready endpoints? If empty → Service selector doesn't match pods.

3Check TLS certificate

openssl s_client -connect gatekeeper-webhook-service.gatekeeper-system.svc:443 → Does the certificate CN match? Is it valid? Is it signed by the CA in caBundle?

4Check API server logs

kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-<node> | grep webhook → Look for "failed calling webhook" or "x509: certificate signed by unknown authority" errors.

5Check webhook configuration

kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations → Is failurePolicy: Fail set? Are there namespaceSelectors blocking your namespace? Is timeoutSeconds too low?

6Test webhook directly

Use curl to send a test AdmissionReview to the webhook. If it returns 200 with allowed:true/false → webhook is working. If connection refused → TLS or network issue.

24.3 OPA Gatekeeper — Policy as Code for Kubernetes

OPA (Open Policy Agent) is a CNCF-graduated general-purpose policy engine. Gatekeeper is the Kubernetes-native implementation of OPA — it integrates via ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and lets you write policies in Rego, a declarative logic programming language. Gatekeeper introduces two Kubernetes-native CRDs: ConstraintTemplate (defines the policy logic in Rego) and Constraint (applies the policy to specific resources with parameters). The separation of template (what to check) from constraint (what to apply it to) allows platform teams to define policy templates once and let application teams instantiate them with their own parameters.

Rego Language Fundamentals — The Logic Programming Paradigm

Rego is NOT a procedural language. You don't write "if X then Y" — you write logical rules that evaluate to TRUE or FALSE. If a rule evaluates to TRUE, it generates a value. If it evaluates to FALSE (or is undefined), it generates nothing. This is the logic programming paradigm — the same paradigm as Prolog and Datalog. Understanding this is the key to writing correct Rego policies:

Rego Language Concepts — From Basic to Production Patterns
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  CONCEPT 1: RULES — Named boolean expressions
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # A rule named "deny" that generates a message if the condition is true
  deny[msg] {
      input.request.object.spec.hostNetwork == true
      msg := "hostNetwork is not allowed"
  }

  # HOW IT WORKS:
  # 1. Rego evaluates the body (between { })
  # 2. If ALL expressions in the body are TRUE → rule SUCCEEDS
  # 3. The rule generates the value assigned to deny (msg)
  # 4. If ANY expression is FALSE or UNDEFINED → rule FAILS → no value
  # 5. The rule "deny" collects ALL generated messages
  # 6. If deny has ANY values → request is REJECTED

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  CONCEPT 2: ITERATION — The [_] Operator (Comprehensions)
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # [_] iterates over ALL elements of an array or set
  containers := input.request.object.spec.containers

  # Iterate over ALL containers. For EACH container, check conditions.
  deny[msg] {
      container := containers[_]        # _ binds to each index
      container.securityContext == null  # No securityContext?
      msg := sprintf("container '%v' missing securityContext", [container.name])
  }

  # If there are 3 containers and NONE have securityContext,
  # this rule generates 3 deny messages.

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  CONCEPT 3: NOT — Negation (Absence of Fact)
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # not X means: "X is undefined or false"
  # This is DIFFERENT from procedural "!X" — it's logical negation

  deny[msg] {
      container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
      not container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot  # runAsNonRoot not set
      msg := "runAsNonRoot must be true"
  }

  # not container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot succeeds if:
  # - securityContext is missing (runAsNonRoot is undefined), OR
  # - securityContext exists but runAsNonRoot is not set, OR
  # - runAsNonRoot is explicitly false

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  CONCEPT 4: INCREMENTAL DEFINITIONS — Multiple Bodies
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # A rule can have MULTIPLE bodies. A value is generated if
  # ANY body evaluates to true (logical OR).

  deny[msg] {
      container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
      container.securityContext.privileged == true
      msg := "privileged containers are not allowed"
  }

  deny[msg] {
      container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
      startswith(container.image, "docker.io/")
      msg := sprintf("image '%v' from docker.io not allowed", [container.image])
  }

  # deny will collect messages from ALL matching bodies

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  CONCEPT 5: FUNCTIONS — Reusable Logic
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # Functions are just rules with arguments

  is_privileged(container) = true {
      container.securityContext.privileged == true
  }

  deny[msg] {
      container := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]
      is_privileged(container)
      msg := sprintf("container '%v' is privileged", [container.name])
  }

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  CONCEPT 6: SET COMPREHENSIONS — Building Sets
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  # Collect all container images into a set
  images := {c.image | c := input.request.object.spec.containers[_]}

  # Check if ANY image is from an unapproved registry
  deny[msg] {
      image := images[_]
      not startswith(image, "registry.anihpj.com/")
      msg := sprintf("image '%v' not approved", [image])
  }

OPA Gatekeeper Architecture — How Rego Policies Become Kubernetes Rules

Gatekeeper Architecture — ConstraintTemplate → Constraint → Enforcement
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    GATEKEEPER POLICY ENFORCEMENT                           │
  │                                                                           │
  │  STEP 1: Platform Team creates a ConstraintTemplate (defines the CHECK)  │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1                            │  │
  │  │  kind: ConstraintTemplate                                           │  │
  │  │  metadata:                                                          │  │
  │  │    name: k8srequiredregistry                                        │  │
  │  │  spec:                                                              │  │
  │  │    crd:                                                             │  │
  │  │      spec:                                                          │  │
  │  │        names:                                                       │  │
  │  │          kind: K8sRequiredRegistry  ← Creates a NEW CRD in cluster  │  │
  │  │    targets:                                                         │  │
  │  │    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh                            │  │
  │  │      rego: |                     ← THE REGO POLICY (the logic)      │  │
  │  │        package k8srequiredregistry                                  │  │
  │  │        violation[{"msg": msg}] {                                    │  │
  │  │          input.review.object.spec.containers[container]             │  │
  │  │          not startswith(image, "registry.anihpj.com/")             │  │
  │  │          msg := sprintf("image not from approved registry: %v",     │  │
  │  │                         [image])                                     │  │
  │  │        }                                                             │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       │  Gatekeeper reads the ConstraintTemplate and CREATES a new CRD:   │
  │       │  → K8sRequiredRegistry.constraints.gatekeeper.sh                   │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  STEP 2: Application Team creates a Constraint (APPLIES the check)        │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1                      │  │
  │  │  kind: K8sRequiredRegistry          ← Uses the CRD from template    │  │
  │  │  metadata:                                                          │  │
  │  │    name: require-anihpj-registry-only                               │  │
  │  │  spec:                                                              │  │
  │  │    match:                                                           │  │
  │  │      kinds:                                                         │  │
  │  │      - apiGroups: [""]                                              │  │
  │  │        kinds: ["Pod"]                                               │  │
  │  │      namespaces: ["anihpj", "anihpj-staging"]                      │  │
  │  │    parameters:              ← Parameters passed INTO the Rego policy │  │
│  │      allowedRegistries:                                               │  │
│  │      - registry.anihpj.com                                            │  │
│  │      - gcr.io/anihpj-project                                          │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│       │                                                                    │
│       ▼                                                                    │
│  STEP 3: Gatekeeper enforces the policy in REAL TIME                       │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Developer: kubectl apply -f pod-using-dockerhub.yaml                │  │
│  │  → Pod has image: nginx:latest (from docker.io)                      │  │
│  │  → Gatekeeper webhook runs the Rego policy                           │  │
│  │  → violation: image "nginx:latest" does NOT start with any allowed   │  │
│  │    registry prefix                                                    │  │
│  │  → Returns: {"allowed": false, "message": "image not from approved   │  │
│  │    registry: nginx:latest"}                                           │  │
│  │  → Developer sees: Error from server (Forbidden): admission webhook  │  │
│  │    "validation.gatekeeper.sh" denied the request: image not from     │  │
│  │    approved registry: nginx:latest                                   │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Rego Policy Deep Dive — Image Registry Allowlist for anihpj

Rego — Full ConstraintTemplate: Deny images not from approved registries 
package k8srequiredregistry

# ── Parameterized violation rule ──
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
    container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
    image := container.image
    allowed := input.parameters.allowedRegistries
    not registry_match(image, allowed)
    msg := sprintf("REJECTED: image '%v' not from an allowed registry. Allowed: %v",
                   [image, allowed])
}

# ── Check initContainers too ──
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
    container := input.review.object.spec.initContainers[_]
    image := container.image
    allowed := input.parameters.allowedRegistries
    not registry_match(image, allowed)
    msg := sprintf("REJECTED: initContainer image '%v' not from allowed registry",
                   [image])
}

# ── Check ephemeral containers (K8s 1.25+) ──
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
    container := input.review.object.spec.ephemeralContainers[_]
    image := container.image
    allowed := input.parameters.allowedRegistries
    not registry_match(image, allowed)
    msg := sprintf("REJECTED: ephemeral container image '%v' not from allowed registry",
                   [image])
}

# ── Helper: match image against allowed registries ──
registry_match(image, registries) {
    registry := registries[_]
    startswith(image, registry)
}
YAML — Constraint: Apply the registry policy to the anihpj namespace 
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredRegistry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-approved-registries-only
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      kinds: ["Pod"]
    - apiGroups: ["apps"]
      kinds: ["Deployment", "StatefulSet", "DaemonSet"]
    - apiGroups: ["batch"]
      kinds: ["Job", "CronJob"]
    namespaces:
    - anihpj
    - anihpj-staging
  parameters:
    allowedRegistries:
    - registry.anihpj.com
    - 12345.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj
    - gcr.io/anihpj-project

Additional Gatekeeper Policies — Real-World Patterns

Rego — ConstraintTemplate: Require resource limits on all containers 
package k8srequirelimits

violation[{"msg": msg}] {
    container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
    not container.resources.limits.cpu
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' missing CPU limit", [container.name])
}

violation[{"msg": msg}] {
    container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
    not container.resources.limits.memory
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' missing memory limit", [container.name])
}

violation[{"msg": msg}] {
    container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
    not container.resources.requests.cpu
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' missing CPU request", [container.name])
}
Rego — ConstraintTemplate: Deny hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC 
package k8sdenyhostnamespace

violation[{"msg": "hostNetwork is not allowed"}] {
    input.review.object.spec.hostNetwork == true
}

violation[{"msg": "hostPID is not allowed"}] {
    input.review.object.spec.hostPID == true
}

violation[{"msg": "hostIPC is not allowed"}] {
    input.review.object.spec.hostIPC == true
}

# Also check ALL containers for privileged access
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
    container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
    container.securityContext.privileged == true
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' is privileged — not allowed", [container.name])
}

Gatekeeper Audit and Dry-Run Modes — Testing Policies Safely

Gatekeeper Audit Mode vs Enforce Mode — The Safe Rollout Pattern
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    GATEKEEPER POLICY ROLLOUT                          │
  │                                                                       │
  │  PHASE 1: AUDIT MODE — Discover existing violations                   │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  1. Deploy ConstraintTemplate and Constraint                  │    │
  │  │  2. Gatekeeper scans ALL existing resources against policy   │    │
  │  │  3. Results are stored in ConstraintStatus/PodStatus CRs:    │    │
  │  │                                                               │    │
  │  │  $ kubectl get k8srequiredregistry require-anihpj-only \     │    │
  │  │    -o json | jq '.status'                                     │    │
  │  │  {                                                            │    │
  │  │    "totalViolations": 5,  ← 5 existing pods violate policy  │    │
  │  │    "violations": [                                            │    │
  │  │      {"name": "old-app", "namespace": "anihpj",              │    │
  │  │       "message": "image 'nginx:latest' not approved"},       │    │
  │  │      ...                                                       │    │
  │  │    ]                                                           │    │
  │  │  }                                                            │    │
  │  │                                                               │    │
  │  │  4. EXISTING pods are NOT blocked (audit only reports)        │    │
  │  │  5. NEW pods ARE blocked if they violate the policy          │    │
  │  │     (enforcementMode: deny is active for new requests)       │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                       │
  │  PHASE 2: DRY-RUN MODE — Test without blocking                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  enforcementAction: dryrun  # (instead of deny)               │    │
  │  │                                                               │    │
  │  │  • Policies are EVALUATED but NEVER block requests           │    │
  │  │  • Violations are logged and reported in status              │    │
  │  │  • Used to test new policies without risking production      │    │
  │  │  • Once confidence is high → switch to enforcementAction: deny│   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                       │
  │  PHASE 3: ENFORCE MODE — Full blocking                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  enforcementAction: deny                                      │    │
  │  │                                                               │    │
  │  │  • ALL violating requests are BLOCKED                        │    │
  │  │  • Audit results still available in ConstraintStatus         │    │
  │  │  • This is the production security posture                   │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔴 ATTACK SCENARIO: Without Admission Control — The Crypto Miner Pod

ATTACK SCENARIO What Happens When You Don't Have Image Admission Control
1
Compromised CI/CD Token

A developer accidentally commits a ServiceAccount token to a public GitHub repo. The token has edit permissions in the anihpj namespace. The attacker finds the token via automated GitHub scanning bots within seconds.

2
Deploying a Malicious Pod

The attacker uses the stolen token to create a pod with image: attacker/crypto-miner:latest from Docker Hub. RBAC allows it — the SA has create pods permission.

3
Without Admission Control — Pod Deploys

No ValidatingWebhookConfiguration. No Gatekeeper. Pod is created. Crypto miner consumes 100% CPU. Cloud bill spikes by $50,000/month.

🛡️
With Admission Control — BLOCKED

Gatekeeper runs Rego policy: image not from approved registry → violation. Returns {"allowed": false}. API server returns 403 Forbidden. Pod NEVER created. Attack stopped at the admission gate.

24.4 Kyverno — Simpler Kubernetes-Native Policies

OPA Gatekeeper is powerful but requires learning Rego, a functional logic programming language that many teams find challenging. Kyverno (Greek for "govern") takes a different approach: policies are written in pure YAML using Kubernetes-native patterns. No new language to learn. No separate template/constraint separation. Kyverno supports four policy types: Validate (deny non-compliant resources), Mutate (auto-fix missing fields), Generate (create additional resources like default NetworkPolicies), and VerifyImages (check image signatures with Cosign/Notary). For teams already comfortable with Kubernetes YAML, Kyverno offers a gentler learning curve.

Kyverno Architecture — How YAML Becomes Admission Control

Kyverno Internals — From ClusterPolicy to Admission Decision
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    KYVERNO ARCHITECTURE                                │
  │                                                                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  Kyverno Controller  │     │  Kyverno Webhook Server           │   │
  │  │  (background loop)   │     │  (admission endpoint)             │   │
  │  │                      │     │                                   │   │
  │  │  • Watches CRDs:     │     │  • Receives AdmissionReview from  │   │
  │  │    - ClusterPolicy   │     │    API server                     │   │
  │  │    - Policy          │     │  • Evaluates policies against     │   │
  │  │  • Generates webhook │     │    the request object             │   │
  │  │    configurations    │     │  • Returns AdmissionResponse      │   │
  │  │  • Runs background   │     │  • Mutate: returns JSON Patch     │   │
  │  │    scans (audit)     │     │  • Validate: returns allow/deny   │   │
  │  │  • Generates Policy  │     │                                   │   │
  │  │    Reports           │     │                                   │   │
  │  └─────────────────────┘     └──────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                       │
  │  REQUEST FLOW:                                                        │
  │  ─────────────                                                        │
  │  API Server → POST /mutate → Kyverno mutating webhook → JSON Patch   │
  │            → POST /validate → Kyverno validating webhook → allow/deny│
  │                                                                       │
  │  POLICY EVALUATION ENGINE:                                            │
  │  ──────────────────────────                                          │
  │  Kyverno uses JMESPath (JSON Matching Expression Paths) for          │
  │  condition evaluation. JMESPath is a query language for JSON:        │
  │                                                                       │
  │  {{ request.object.spec.containers[].image }}                         │
  │  → ["registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2", "redis:7-alpine"]              │
  │                                                                       │
  │  Kyverno evaluates JMESPath expressions against the AdmissionReview  │
  │  request and determines if conditions match. This is the YAML-native │
  │  equivalent of Rego's input.review.object.spec.containers[_].        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Kyverno Policy Types — Four Actions You Can Take

🚫
Validate

Check resources and DENY non-compliant ones. Equivalent to OPA's violation rules. Uses validate.deny.conditions with JMESPath expressions.

🔧
Mutate

Automatically MODIFY resources via patchStrategicMerge or patchesJson6902. Auto-add securityContext, labels, annotations when developers forget.

✨
Generate

CREATE additional resources when a trigger fires. Auto-create NetworkPolicy for new namespaces. Clone secrets across namespaces. Sync ConfigMaps.

✍️
VerifyImages

Check container image SIGNATURES (Cosign, Notary, Sigstore). Only allow images signed by your CI/CD pipeline's key. Covered in Ch26.

Kyverno Validate Policy — Image Registry Allowlist

YAML — Kyverno ClusterPolicy: Deny images from unapproved registries 
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-approved-registry
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  background: true
  rules:
  - name: check-image-registry
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: [Pod, Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob]
    exclude:
      any:
      - resources:
          namespaces: [kube-system, kyverno, gatekeeper-system]
    validate:
      message: >-
        Image {{ request.object.spec.containers[].image }} is not from
        an approved registry. Allowed: registry.anihpj.com, gcr.io/anihpj-project
      deny:
        conditions:
          any:
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.initContainers[].image }}"
            operator: NotIn
            value: ["registry.anihpj.com/*", "gcr.io/anihpj-project/*"]
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.containers[].image }}"
            operator: NotIn
            value: ["registry.anihpj.com/*", "gcr.io/anihpj-project/*"]
          - key: "{{ request.object.spec.ephemeralContainers[].image }}"
            operator: NotIn
            value: ["registry.anihpj.com/*", "gcr.io/anihpj-project/*"]

Kyverno Mutate Policy — Auto-Add securityContext

YAML — Kyverno ClusterPolicy: Auto-add securityContext if developer forgot it 
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: add-default-securitycontext
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: add-runAsNonRoot
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
    mutate:
      patchStrategicMerge:
        spec:
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
            fsGroup: 1000
          containers:
          - (name): "*"
            securityContext:
              allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
              readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
              capabilities:
                drop: ["ALL"]
          initContainers:
          - (name): "*"
            securityContext:
              allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
              readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
              capabilities:
                drop: ["ALL"]

Kyverno Generate Policy — Auto-Create NetworkPolicy on New Namespace

YAML — Kyverno Generate Policy: Auto-create a default-deny NetworkPolicy for every new namespace 
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: auto-create-default-deny-networkpolicy
spec:
  rules:
  - name: generate-default-deny
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Namespace"]
    # ── EXCLUDE system namespaces ──
    exclude:
      any:
      - resources:
          names: [kube-system, kube-public, kyverno]
    # ── GENERATE: Create a NetworkPolicy in the new namespace ──
    generate:
      apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
      kind: NetworkPolicy
      name: default-deny-all
      namespace: "{{ request.object.metadata.name }}"  # Target: the new namespace
      synchronize: true  # If someone deletes the NP, Kyverno recreates it
      data:
        spec:
          podSelector: {}        # Selects ALL pods in the namespace
          policyTypes:
          - Ingress
          - Egress
          # No ingress/egress rules = DENY ALL traffic by default
          # Individual apps must have their own NetworkPolicies to allow traffic

Kyverno CLI Testing — Test Policies Before Deploying

Bash — Kyverno CLI: Test policies locally before cluster deployment 
# ── Test a policy against a resource (dry run) ──
kyverno apply /path/to/policy.yaml --resource /path/to/pod.yaml

# ── Test a policy against a Kubernetes resource in-cluster ──
kyverno apply /path/to/policy.yaml --cluster --namespace anihpj

# ── Test with expected results (unit test style) ──
# tests.yaml:
#   - name: test-approved-registry
#     policies:
#     - require-approved-registry.yaml
#     resources:
#     - good-pod.yaml
#     - bad-pod.yaml
#     results:
#     - policy: require-approved-registry
#       rule: check-image-registry
#       resource: good-pod
#       result: pass
#     - policy: require-approved-registry
#       rule: check-image-registry
#       resource: bad-pod
#       result: fail

kyverno test /path/to/tests.yaml

# ── Generate Policy Reports for compliance auditing ──
kyverno apply /path/to/policies --cluster --policy-report

OPA Gatekeeper vs Kyverno — Choosing the Right Policy Engine

FeatureOPA GatekeeperKyverno
Policy LanguageRego — Logic programming. Powerful, expressive, but steep learning curve.YAML + JMESPath — Kubernetes-native. Familiar syntax. Lower barrier to entry.
Policy TypesValidate only (mutating needs separate webhook)Validate, Mutate, Generate, VerifyImages — all in one
Template/Instance Split✅ ConstraintTemplate + Constraint (separation of concerns)❌ Single ClusterPolicy/Policy resource (simpler but less reusable)
Image VerificationRequires external Cosign webhook or custom solutionBuilt-in VerifyImages with Cosign, Notary, Sigstore support
Mutating❌ Not natively supported. Separate MutatingWebhook needed.✅ Built-in mutate via patchStrategicMerge or patchesJson6902
Generate❌ Not supported✅ Auto-create resources on triggers (NetworkPolicies, secrets, ConfigMaps)
Policy Testing✅ gator test CLI with unit test framework✅ kyverno test CLI with test manifests
Audit & Reports✅ ConstraintStatus per constraint✅ PolicyReport + ClusterPolicyReport CRDs with structured results
Learning Curve🔴 Steep — new language paradigm (logic programming)🟢 Gentle — YAML anyone can read; JMESPath adds complexity for advanced use
Flexibility🟢 Extremely flexible — Rego is Turing-complete🟡 Good for 95% of K8s use cases; complex logic hits JMESPath limits
EcosystemCNCF Graduated. Rego reusable beyond K8s (Terraform, Envoy, etc.)CNCF Incubating. K8s-focused. Growing community.
CKS Exam✅ Know Rego basics, violation pattern, ConstraintTemplate/Constraint structure✅ Know YAML structure, validate/mutate/generate rule types, JMESPath basics
Best ForLarge orgs with platform teams, multi-domain policies, teams already using OPATeams wanting K8s-native experience, auto-mutation, built-in image verification

Decision Tree: OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno?

Policy Engine Selection Framework
  START: I need a Kubernetes admission policy engine
  │
  ├─ Does my team already know Rego or use OPA elsewhere? → OPA Gatekeeper
  ├─ Do I need MULTI-DOMAIN policies (K8s + Terraform + CI/CD)? → OPA (Rego is portable)
  ├─ Do I need auto-mutation of resources? → Kyverno (built-in mutate)
  ├─ Do I need image signature verification? → Kyverno (built-in VerifyImages)
  ├─ Do I need to auto-GENERATE resources on triggers? → Kyverno (Generate rules)
  ├─ Is my team YAML-native and resistant to learning Rego? → Kyverno
  └─ Need MAXIMUM flexibility for complex logic? → OPA Gatekeeper

  🟢 MANY ORGS USE BOTH: Kyverno for mutate/generate/verify, OPA for complex validation

Complete Admission Control Flow — OPA + Kyverno in Action

End-to-End Admission Pipeline — anihpj Pod Creation with Both Engines
  kubectl apply -f anihpj-pod.yaml
  │  Pod spec: image=registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
  │  (no securityContext, no resource limits)
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ✅ AuthN: Token valid → identity: system:serviceaccount:anihpj     │
  │  ✅ AuthZ: RBAC allows "create pods" in namespace "anihpj"          │
  │                                                                       │
  │  MUTATING PHASE (sequential):                                         │
  │  1. ServiceAccount plugin → sets SA to "default"                     │
  │  2. Kyverno Mutate → add-default-securitycontext fires               │
  │     → Adds runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, capabilities.drop=[ALL]          │
  │                                                                       │
  │  VALIDATING PHASE (parallel):                                         │
  │  3. PodSecurity → restricted PSS check → ✅                         │
  │  4. OPA Gatekeeper → K8sRequiredRegistry → image approved ✅        │
  │  5. Kyverno Validate → require-approved-registry → ✅               │
  │  6. ResourceQuota → namespace has capacity → ✅                     │
  │                                                                       │
  │  ✅ ALL CHECKS PASSED → Pod persisted → Scheduler → Running          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📊 Chapter 24 Visual Summary — Admission Control at a Glance

🚪
Built-in Plugins (24.1)

~30 plugins, 8 critical for CKS. Plugin chain runs mutating first (sequential), validating second (parallel). Configured via --enable-admission-plugins on API server. Always keep existing plugins when adding new ones.

🪝
Webhooks (24.2)

Mutating: sequential. Validating: parallel. TLS certs require CN matching Service DNS. failurePolicy: Fail = secure but risky. Ignore = available but insecure. objectSelector for fine-grained matching.

📜
OPA Gatekeeper (24.3)

Rego language. Logic programming paradigm. ConstraintTemplate defines logic, Constraint applies it with parameters. Audit mode for safe rollout. Rego reusable across K8s, Terraform, CI/CD.

🏛️
Kyverno (24.4)

Pure YAML. Validate/Mutate/Generate/VerifyImages. Auto-create NetworkPolicies for new namespaces. PolicyReport CRDs for compliance. CLI testing with kyverno test.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam tests admission control in multiple ways: (1) Enable admission plugins — edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, modify --enable-admission-plugins, keep existing plugins, verify with kubectl describe. (2) Configure ValidatingWebhookConfiguration — know clientConfig.service, caBundle (base64 CA cert), failurePolicy (Fail vs Ignore), namespaceSelector, objectSelector. (3) Write OPA ConstraintTemplate in Rego — know the violation[{"msg": msg}] pattern, iterate with containers[_], use input.review.object path, handle initContainers and ephemeralContainers. (4) Write Kyverno ClusterPolicy in YAML — know validate.deny.conditions, JMESPath expressions like {{ request.object.spec.containers[].image }}, mutate with patchStrategicMerge. (5) Order matters: Mutating runs BEFORE validating. Mutations are visible to validators. If a mutating webhook times out with failurePolicy: Fail, the request is denied before validators even run.

Chapter 25: Static Analysis — Scanning Manifests Before Deployment

Admission controllers (Ch24) catch bad configurations at the API server gate. But by the time a manifest reaches the API server, developers have already written it, reviewed it, merged it, and deployed it. The best security is prevention at the source: catching misconfigurations the moment a developer writes them — in their IDE, in their pull request, before they ever reach a cluster. This is Shift Left Security: moving security checks as close to the developer as possible. Static analysis tools — kube-linter, kubesec, and conftest — scan Kubernetes YAML manifests for security issues without ever touching a live cluster. They find privileged containers, missing securityContexts, writable root filesystems, and images with floating tags before they become production incidents. The cheapest vulnerability to fix is the one that never reaches production.

🟢 Beginner-Friendly ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔍 Static Analysis 📦 Supply Chain

🎯 What You'll Learn — Core-Level Mastery

  • ✅ Shift Left Security: Why catching misconfigurations at YAML level is 100x cheaper than fixing them in production — the security testing pyramid explained
  • ✅ kube-linter internals: How the template-based check engine works, 30+ built-in checks, creating custom checks, pre-commit hook integration
  • ✅ kubesec scoring deep dive: The full scoring algorithm, HTTP server mode for CI/CD, score tracking over time, comparison with kube-score and polaris
  • ✅ conftest Rego patterns: Fixture-based testing, Dockerfile + Terraform policies, data/warn rules beyond deny, IDE integration
  • ✅ Production CI/CD patterns: Pre-commit hooks for local dev, decision tree for tool selection, performance optimization, artifact-based score tracking
🎓 CKS Relevance
Supply Chain Security 20%

25.1 Why Static Analysis of YAML Matters — Shift Left Security

Every Kubernetes security incident begins with a YAML file. A developer writes a Deployment, sets privileged: true "just to make it work," commits it, and six months later that privileged container is the entry point for a cluster-wide breach. In February 2018, Tesla's Kubernetes cluster was breached because an unprotected dashboard allowed attackers to deploy crypto-mining pods — a misconfiguration that static analysis would have caught instantly. Static analysis catches these mistakes before they become incidents. Unlike admission controllers (which catch problems at deploy time) and runtime detection (which catches problems after they're exploited), static analysis works at the earliest possible moment — when the YAML is written.

The Cost of Finding Security Issues — Why Earlier Is Exponentially Cheaper

Shift Left — The Cost of Fixing a Security Issue by Detection Stage

  │  COST TO FIX                                                            │
  │  (log scale)    │                                                         │
  │                 │                                              🔴 $10,000+
  │                 │                                          ╱  (Incident
  │                 │                                     ╱      Response +
  │                 │                                ╱          Forensic +
  │                 │                           ╱               Post-Mortem)
  │                 │                      ╱
  │                 │                 ╱    🟠 $1,000
  │                 │            ╱        (Rollback +
  │                 │       ╱              Redeploy +
  │                 │  ╱   🟡 $100         Emergency Fix)
  │                 │╱     (PR Fix +
  │    🟢 $10       │       CI Re-run)
  │   (IDE plugin   │
  │    catches it   │
  │    instantly)   │
  │                 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  │                 IDE      PR/CI      Staging    Production   Incident
  │                 Write    Check      Deploy     Running      Response
  │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  │  STAGE              │  TOOL                  │  COST TO FIX        │
  │  ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
  │  │  IDE (developer writes)│  VS Code kube-linter  │  $0 (instant fix)   │
  │  │  PR/CI (code review)  │  kube-linter + kubesec │  $10 (re-push)      │
  │  │  Staging deploy       │  OPA/Kyverno admission │  $100 (re-deploy)   │
  │  │  Production running   │  Falco runtime alert   │  $1,000 (incident)  │
  │  │  Breach detected      │  IR team, forensics    │  $10,000+ (breach)  │
  │  └─────────────────────┴────────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘
  │
  │  🔑 THE INSIGHT: Every hour you delay finding a vulnerability
  │     multiplies its cost by ~10x. Static analysis at the YAML level
  │     is the cheapest, fastest, and most developer-friendly security
  │     check you can implement.
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Static Analysis vs Admission Control — Complementary, Not Competing

DimensionStatic Analysis (Ch25)Admission Control (Ch24)
WhenBefore commit, during CI/CDAt kubectl apply time
WhereDeveloper machine, CI runnerAPI server
What it seesYAML files on diskLive API requests
Can modify?No (analysis only)Yes (mutating webhooks)
Cluster required?No (works offline)Yes (must reach API server)
False negatives?Possible (e.g., Helm template not rendered)Very rare (sees final rendered object)
Best forDeveloper feedback, CI/CD gatesEnforcement, default injection
StrategyShift LEFT: Catch earlyShift RIGHT: Enforce at gate

BOTH are essential. Static analysis catches problems the developer can fix in seconds. Admission control catches problems that slip through CI/CD. Together they form a defense-in-depth strategy: catch early, enforce always.

The Static Analysis Tool Landscape — What Each Tool Checks

🔍
kube-linter

Linter for K8s YAML. 30+ built-in checks. Detects: privileged containers, missing limits, hostNetwork, writable root FS, latest tags. Written by StackRox (Red Hat).

📊
kubesec

Risk scorer (0-10). Scores manifests on security posture. Checks: capabilities, seccomp, readOnlyRoot, runAsNonRoot, AppArmor, serviceAccount.

📜
conftest

OPA Rego policy testing. Test any YAML/JSON against Rego policies. Not K8s-specific — works with Dockerfiles, Terraform, etc.

🛡️
checkov

Multi-cloud scanner. Bridgecrew's IaC scanner. Checks K8s, Terraform, CloudFormation, Helm. 750+ built-in policies. Graph-based analysis.

📝 Real-World Incident: Tesla Kubernetes Breach (2018)

In February 2018, attackers discovered an unprotected Kubernetes dashboard in Tesla's AWS environment. The dashboard had no authentication and was exposed to the internet. Attackers deployed pods running crypto-mining software, consuming Tesla's cloud resources. Static analysis would have caught: (1) the dashboard deployment with no authentication configuration, (2) pods with no resource limits (allowing crypto miners to consume unlimited CPU), (3) missing network policies (allowing pods to reach external mining pools). The breach was discovered by RedLock (now Palo Alto) cloud security monitoring — but static analysis at the YAML level would have prevented it entirely.

25.2 kube-linter — Kubernetes YAML Security Analysis

kube-linter (by StackRox, now Red Hat) is a static analysis tool that checks Kubernetes YAML manifests against 30+ built-in security checks. It's designed to be fast, opinionated, and CI/CD-friendly. Unlike kubesec (which gives a numeric score), kube-linter produces a simple pass/fail result for each check with actionable error messages.

How kube-linter Works Internally — Template Engine + Object Traversal

kube-linter Architecture — From YAML File to Lint Result
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    KUBE-LINTER INTERNALS                               │
  │                                                                       │
  │  STEP 1: YAML PARSE + OBJECT DETECTION                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  kube-linter reads anihpj-deployment.yaml                     │    │
  │  │  → Detects: Kind=Deployment, apiVersion=apps/v1              │    │
  │  │  → Parses the full object tree into memory                    │    │
  │  │  → Identifies: Pod template, containers, volumes, etc.       │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │                         ▼                                             │
  │  STEP 2: CHECK REGISTRY — Which checks apply to this object?         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  For Object: Deployment → applies to:                          │    │
  │  │  • Deployment-level checks (host-network, host-pid, etc.)     │    │
  │  │  • Pod template checks (container-level)                      │    │
  │  │  • Container-level checks (privileged, run-as-non-root, etc.) │    │
  │  │                                                                 │    │
  │  │  Each check is a Go template or Rego rule that traverses       │    │
  │  │  the object tree looking for specific patterns.                │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                         │                                             │
  │                         ▼                                             │
  │  STEP 3: CHECK EXECUTION — Run each matching check                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  check: privileged-container                                   │    │
  │  │    target: containers[].securityContext.privileged             │    │
  │  │    logic: if value == true → FAIL                              │    │
  │  │    result: container "anihpj" has privileged=true → ❌         │    │
  │  │                                                                 │    │
  │  │  check: run-as-non-root                                         │    │
  │  │    target: containers[].securityContext.runAsNonRoot            │    │
  │  │    logic: if not set or false → FAIL                            │    │
  │  │    result: runAsNonRoot not set → ❌                             │    │
  │  │                                                                 │    │
  │  │  check: latest-tag                                              │    │
  │  │    target: containers[].image                                   │    │
  │  │    logic: if image ends with :latest or has no tag → FAIL       │    │
  │  │    result: image "anihpj-django:latest" → ❌                    │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

kube-linter Built-in Checks — The Most Important Ones for CKS

Check NameWhat It DetectsSeverityWhy It Matters
privileged-containerContainer has securityContext.privileged: trueCriticalPrivileged containers have ALL Linux capabilities and access to all host devices. Equivalent to root on the node.
no-read-only-root-filesystemreadOnlyRootFilesystem is not set or is falseHighWritable root FS allows attackers to install tools, write scripts, and modify binaries after exploitation.
run-as-non-rootrunAsNonRoot is not set to trueHighContainers running as root (UID 0) can escape the container via kernel exploits or misconfigured volumes.
host-networkPod has hostNetwork: trueHighHost network access bypasses all NetworkPolicies and exposes pod to host interfaces.
host-pidPod has hostPID: trueHighHost PID namespace access allows listing and signaling all processes on the node.
latest-tagContainer image uses :latest tagMediumFloating tags are mutable — you don't know which image version is actually running.
dangling-serviceService selector matches no podsMediumIndicates a misconfiguration — the Service has no backends.

Running kube-linter — Local, CI/CD, Pre-Commit, and Helm

Bash — kube-linter commands for all scanning scenarios 
# ── Install ──
brew install kube-linter
# Or: curl -LO https://github.com/stackrox/kube-linter/releases/latest/download/kube-linter-linux

# ── Scan a single YAML file ──
kube-linter lint anihpj-deployment.yaml

# ── Scan all YAML files in a directory ──
kube-linter lint ./k8s-manifests/

# ── Scan a Helm chart ──
kube-linter lint ./anihpj-helm-chart/

# ── Scan with specific checks ──
kube-linter lint --include privileged-container,run-as-non-root ./manifests/
kube-linter lint --exclude latest-tag ./manifests/

# ── JSON output for CI/CD ──
kube-linter lint --format json ./manifests/ > kube-linter-report.json

Pre-Commit Hook — Catch Issues Before They Leave Your Machine

YAML — .pre-commit-config.yaml — Run kube-linter on every git commit 
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
- repo: local
  hooks:
  - id: kube-linter
    name: kube-linter
    entry: kube-linter lint
    language: system
    files: \.(yaml|yml)$
    pass_filenames: false    # Lint all k8s/ files, not just changed ones
    args: ['k8s/']

# Setup:
# pip install pre-commit
# pre-commit install
# Now EVERY git commit runs kube-linter.
# If it finds issues → commit is BLOCKED.

🔴 Example: What kube-linter Catches in an Insecure anihpj Deployment

INSECURE MANIFEST — anihpj-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-django
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      hostNetwork: true          # ❌ host-network
      hostPID: true              # ❌ host-pid
      containers:
      - name: anihpj
        image: anihpj-django:latest  # ❌ latest-tag
        securityContext:
          privileged: true       # ❌ privileged-container
          runAsUser: 0           # ❌ run-as-non-root
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80      # ❌ privileged-ports
kube-linter OUTPUT — 5 Issues Found
$ kube-linter lint anihpj-deployment.yaml

anihpj-deployment.yaml: (object: anihpj/anihpj-django)
  ❌ "host-network" — hostNetwork set to true
  ❌ "host-pid" — hostPID set to true
  ❌ "privileged-container" — container "anihpj"
     is privileged
  ❌ "run-as-non-root" — container "anihpj"
     does not have runAsNonRoot set
  ❌ "latest-tag" — container "anihpj" uses
     image with ":latest" tag

Error: found 5 lint errors
Exit code: 1 → CI/CD pipeline BLOCKED 🛡️

Creating Custom kube-linter Checks — Extend Beyond Built-ins

YAML — .kube-linter.yaml — Custom check: require team annotation on all resources 
# .kube-linter.yaml
checks:
  addAllBuiltIn: true
  exclude:
  - "dangling-service"
  - "no-extensions-v1beta"

  # ── CUSTOM CHECK: Require 'team' annotation ──
  customChecks:
  - name: "required-annotation-team"
    template: "required-annotation"
    params:
      key: "team"
      value: ".*"           # Any value is acceptable

  # ── CUSTOM CHECK: Deny specific namespace ──
  - name: "deny-default-namespace"
    template: "disallowed-object"
    params:
      kind: "Deployment"
      # All Deployments must be in a non-default namespace

  # ── CUSTOM CHECK: Require specific label ──
  - name: "required-label-app"
    template: "required-label"
    params:
      key: "app"
      value: "anihpj-.*"   # Must match pattern

ignorePaths:
- "vendor/"
- "test/fixtures/"

Decision Tree: Which Static Analysis Tool for Which Scenario?

Static Analysis Tool Selection for Kubernetes YAML
  START: I need to check Kubernetes YAML for security issues
  │
  ├─ Do I want BUILT-IN CHECKS with NO configuration?
  │  └─ YES → kube-linter (30+ checks out of the box, zero config needed)
  │
  ├─ Do I want a NUMERIC SECURITY SCORE for each manifest?
  │  └─ YES → kubesec (0-10 score, track improvement over time)
  │
  ├─ Do I need CUSTOM ORGANIZATIONAL POLICIES in Rego?
  │  ├─ YES → conftest (write your own Rego rules)
  │  └─ Also consider: kube-linter customChecks (simpler template-based)
  │
  ├─ Do I need to scan TERRAFORM, DOCKERFILES, or other IaC?
  │  ├─ For K8s + Terraform + Dockerfile → conftest (multi-parser)
  │  ├─ For Terraform specifically → checkov (graph-based, 750+ policies)
  │  └─ For Dockerfile only → hadolint (specialized Dockerfile linter)
  │
  ├─ Am I in CI/CD (PR gate)?
  │  ├─ Lightweight + fast → kube-linter (fastest, simplest)
  │  ├─ Score threshold → kubesec (numeric gate: score ≥ 4)
  │  └─ Custom policies → conftest (organization-specific rules)
  │
  └─ 🟢 RECOMMENDATION: Use ALL THREE in CI/CD
     kube-linter for built-in checks (fast, broad coverage)
     kubesec for scoring threshold (numeric quality gate)
     conftest for custom policies (organization-specific)

25.3 kubesec — Security Risk Analysis for K8s Manifests

While kube-linter gives you pass/fail checks, kubesec (by ControlPlane) gives you a numeric risk score from 0 to 10. Each check contributes or subtracts points, and the final score represents the overall security posture of your manifest. This is invaluable for measuring security improvement over time: "Last month our deployment scored 3/10. After adding securityContexts, it's 7/10."

kubesec Scoring Algorithm — How Points Are Calculated

kubesec Scoring Breakdown — What Adds and Subtracts Points
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    KUBESEC SCORING MODEL (0-10)                            │
  │                                                                           │
  │  SCORE = SUM(points) / MAX_POSSIBLE_POINTS * 10                           │
  │                                                                           │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  CHECK                          │  POINTS  │  CRITICALITY          │  │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────┼──────────┼───────────────────────┤  │
  │  │  containers[].securityContext   │          │                        │  │
  │  │    .runAsNonRoot = true         │  +1      │  CRITICAL (blocks LPE) │  │
  │  │    .readOnlyRootFilesystem=true │  +1      │  HIGH (blocks writes)  │  │
  │  │    .allowPrivilegeEscalation=fls│  +1      │  HIGH (blocks setuid)  │  │
  │  │    .privileged = false          │  +1      │  CRITICAL              │  │
  │  │    .capabilities.drop = [ALL]   │  +1      │  CRITICAL              │  │
  │  │    .capabilities.add = []       │  +1      │  HIGH                  │  │
  │  │    .seccompProfile = set        │  +1      │  HIGH                  │  │
  │  │    .appArmorProfile = set       │  +1      │  MEDIUM                │  │
  │  ├─────────────────────────────────┼──────────┼───────────────────────┤  │
  │  │  DEDUCTIONS (negative points):  │          │                        │  │
  │  │    privileged = true            │  -5      │  IMMEDIATE FAIL        │  │
  │  │    allowPrivilegeEscalation=true│  -3      │  CRITICAL              │  │
  │  │    runAsNonRoot = false         │  -3      │  CRITICAL              │  │
  │  │    capabilities.add includes    │          │                        │  │
  │  │      SYS_ADMIN or NET_ADMIN     │  -3      │  HIGH                  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                           │
  │  SCORE INTERPRETATION:                                                    │
  │  ─────────────────────                                                    │
  │  0-3:  🔴 CRITICAL — Do not deploy. Missing essential controls.           │
  │  4-5:  🟠 HIGH — Only dev/staging. Needs improvement.                     │
  │  6-7:  🟡 MEDIUM — Acceptable for production with monitoring.             │
  │  8-9:  🟢 LOW — Good security posture.                                    │
  │  10:   ✅ IDEAL — All recommended controls. Rare.                         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Running kubesec — CLI, HTTP Server, and CI/CD Integration

Bash — kubesec commands, HTTP server mode, and CI/CD score gating 
# ── CLI: Scan a manifest file ──
kubesec scan anihpj-deployment.yaml

# ── CLI: Pipe from kubectl or helm ──
kubectl get deployment anihpj-django -n anihpj -o yaml | kubesec scan -
helm template ./anihpj-chart | kubesec scan -

# ── HTTP SERVER MODE: Run kubesec as a service (for CI/CD) ──
kubesec server --port 8080 &
curl -sSX POST --data-binary @anihpj-deployment.yaml \
  http://localhost:8080/scan | jq .

# ── CI/CD SCORE GATE ──
SCORE=$(kubesec scan anihpj-deployment.yaml | jq -r '.[0].score')
if [ "$SCORE" -lt 4 ]; then
  echo "❌ Score $SCORE below threshold (≥4 required)"
  exit 1
fi

# ── TRACK SCORE OVER TIME: Save score as CI artifact ──
kubesec scan k8s/*.yaml | jq '[.[] | {object: .object, score: .score}]' \
  > kubesec-scores-$(date +%Y%m%d).json
# Archive this artifact — track score trends across builds

Interpreting kubesec Output — anihpj Before and After Hardening

kubesec Scan Result — anihpj Deployment Before and After Hardening

Featurekubeseckube-scorepolaris
