  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKS Task Difficulty Classification — Know What to Expect

DifficultyTimeTask TypesKey CommandsChapters
🟢 EASY 1-3 min RBAC (Role + RoleBinding), Pod with securityContext, Namespace PSS labels, kubectl auth can-i, ServiceAccount creation kubectl create role, kubectl create rolebinding, kubectl label ns, kubectl auth can-i 9, 24, 33
🟡 MEDIUM 3-8 min NetworkPolicy, Falco custom rules, Seccomp/AppArmor profiles, Trivy image scan, Audit policy config, kube-bench run kubectl apply -f netpol.yaml, falco -r, trivy image, kube-bench run 6, 14-15, 25-26, 28, 29
🔴 HARD 8-15 min Encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration), OPA/Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate, ImagePolicyWebhook, Incident response, etcd backup/restore etcdctl, kube-apiserver.yaml edits, curl webhook, Gatekeeper Rego 10, 23, 26, 30, 34

Time Management Anti-Patterns — What NOT to Do

🚫
Reading ALL tasks before starting ANY

Some candidates spend 15+ minutes reading every task in detail. You don't need to understand every task upfront. Scan for 30 seconds each — just enough to classify difficulty. Start solving immediately.

🚫
Perfecting one answer for 20 minutes

A task is worth the same whether you spend 3 minutes or 20 minutes on it. If you're 8 minutes in and not close to done, SKIP. Come back in Pass 3. A partial solution may earn partial credit.

🚫
Not using the documentation

The Kubernetes docs are YOUR notes. You don't need to memorize YAML syntax — copy from the docs. Search for "NetworkPolicy" → copy the example → modify it. This is faster than writing from scratch and less error-prone.

What To Do When You're Stuck — The 60-Second Decision Tree

You've been working on a task for 3 minutes and aren't sure how to proceed. What now?
Do you know the RESOURCE TYPE? (e.g., NetworkPolicy, ClusterRole)

→ YES: Search the docs for the resource. Copy the example YAML. Modify it. If this takes more than 3 more minutes → mark as SKIP and move on.

→ NO: Immediately mark as SKIP. You can't solve what you can't name. Return in Pass 3 with more context or a lucky guess.

Are you fighting YAML syntax, not security concepts?

→ YES: Don't waste time on indentation. Write a minimal version. If kubectl apply fails, check kubectl explain <resource> --recursive for the correct field paths.

→ NO: You genuinely don't know the solution. SKIP immediately. Return in Pass 3. Use the remaining time to maximize points on tasks you CAN solve.

Time Tracking Without a Clock — Use the Terminal

Bash — Quick time checks during the exam 
# Check current time (exam clock is in UTC — confirm at start)
date

# Set a mental checkpoint every 15 minutes
# Pass 1 should end at T+45min
# Pass 2 should end at T+105min
# Pass 3 starts at T+105min, exam ends at T+120min

# If you have watch available (not guaranteed):
watch -n 300 'echo "Check time!"'   # Reminder every 5 min

# Simpler: write the target end time in your notepad:
# "Pass 1 ends: XX:XX"  (calculate: start time + 45 min)
# "Pass 2 ends: XX:XX"  (start time + 105 min)
# "HARD STOP: XX:XX"    (start time + 120 min)

# At each checkpoint, count completed tasks:
# Pass 1 (45 min): 5-8 done → on track. 3-4 → behind, speed up.
# Pass 2 (105 min): 9-12 done → on track. 6-8 → behind, focus on high-value tasks.
# Pass 3 (120 min): Every point counts. Verify, fill gaps, submit.

36.3 Context Switching — The Most Important CKS Exam Habit

This single mistake causes more CKS failures than any other: forgetting to switch cluster contexts between tasks. The exam provides multiple clusters (typically 2-4). Each task specifies which cluster to use. If you solve Task 3 on Cluster A when it asked for Cluster B, you get zero points — even if your solution is perfect.

The Context Switch Ritual — Do This Every Single Time

Bash — The EXACT workflow for every CKS exam task 
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 0: BEFORE TOUCHING ANYTHING — SWITCH CONTEXT FIRST
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# 1. COPY the context command from the task description
#    Task says: "Context: mk8s-cluster-2"
kubectl config use-context mk8s-cluster-2

# 2. VERIFY you're on the right cluster
kubectl config current-context
# Expected output: mk8s-cluster-2

# 3. VERIFY you can see the expected resources
kubectl get nodes
# If you see 0 nodes or "not found" → WRONG CLUSTER!

# 4. CHECK which namespace the task expects
# Task may say: "Namespace: security" or imply it
kubectl get ns
# If the task says "Create in namespace 'prod'" and you don't see it:
kubectl create ns prod    # Create it! Don't assume it exists.

# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# THE RITUAL (repeat for EVERY task):
#   ☐ 1. Read the context name
#   ☐ 2. kubectl config use-context 
#   ☐ 3. kubectl config current-context (verify)
#   ☐ 4. kubectl get nodes (sanity check)
#   ☐ 5. NOW solve the task
# ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Common Context Switching Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

MistakeConsequencePrevention
Typing context name wrongkubectl config use-context mk8s-cluster2 (missing hyphen) → silently fails, you're still on the previous clusterAlways run kubectl config current-context AFTER switching. If it doesn't match, you typed it wrong.
Assuming the namespace existsYou create all resources in the default namespace. Task asked for namespace "web". Zero points.Read the task carefully. If a namespace is specified, CREATE it first: kubectl create ns <name>
Forgetting between tasksYou solve Task 4 on the context from Task 3. Task 4's solution is on the wrong cluster. Zero points.Make the ritual automatic. Train yourself: every time you read a new task, your fingers type kubectl config use-context automatically.
SSH context confusionTask says "SSH to node01". You run commands on the wrong node. Zero points.After SSH: hostname to verify. Some tasks use ssh node01, others use ssh mk8s-node-1. Pay attention to the exact hostname.

The Notepad Trick — Track Your Progress

The exam terminal includes a built-in notepad (accessible from the exam UI, not the terminal). Use it to track:

Text — Your exam notepad template (fill in as you go) 
=== CKS EXAM TRACKER ===
☐ Task 1: [EASY]   Context: cluster1  √ DONE
☐ Task 2: [SKIP]   Context: cluster3  ← Return in Pass 3
☐ Task 3: [EASY]   Context: cluster1  √ DONE
☐ Task 4: [MED]    Context: cluster2  √ DONE (verified)
☐ Task 5: [SKIP]   Context: cluster4  ← Return in Pass 3
☐ Task 6: [EASY]   Context: cluster1  √ DONE
...
☐ Task 15:[MED]    Context: cluster2  IN PROGRESS

PASS 1: 6 done (Tasks 1,3,4,6,8,10)
PASS 2: 4 done (Tasks 7,11,12,15)
PASS 3: 2 attempted (Tasks 2,5) — partial? Not sure.
TOTAL: ~12-13 solved → TARGET PASS (67% = 10-13)

TIME CHECK:
- 0:30 — Pass 1 complete (6 done)
- 1:15 — Pass 2 complete (10 total)
- 1:55 — Pass 3 complete (12 total)
- 2:00 — TIME

Real Exam Task Format — What You'll Actually See

CKS tasks follow a consistent format. Recognizing this structure saves time and prevents missed requirements:

Text — Typical CKS exam task format (annotated) 
Task 7 of 18: Secure the web-frontend namespace

Context: mk8s-cluster-2          ← ALWAYS COPY THIS FIRST

A developer has deployed a web application in the 'web-frontend'
namespace. The application currently runs with default settings.

1. Create a NetworkPolicy named 'web-deny-all' in the 'web-frontend'
   namespace that blocks all ingress and egress traffic.       ← THE ASK

2. Modify the NetworkPolicy to allow ingress traffic from pods
   in the 'ingress-nginx' namespace on TCP port 8080.          ← THE ASK

3. Verify that pods in the 'default' namespace cannot reach
   pods in the 'web-frontend' namespace.                       ← VERIFICATION

You may use the Kubernetes documentation at kubernetes.io/docs.

→ Scoring: Part 1 = 4%, Part 2 = 3%, Part 3 = 2% (Total: 9%)

Verification Commands That Prove Your Work

Always end each task with a verification command. If the scoring script checks your work, it looks for the expected state. These commands also help YOU confirm you solved it correctly:

Task TypeVerification CommandWhat It Proves
RBACkubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=<user> -n <ns>The subject has the exact permissions you configured
NetworkPolicykubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- wget -qO- --timeout=5 <url>Traffic is blocked/allowed as expected
PodSecurityContextkubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep -E 'CapEff|Seccomp'Capabilities dropped, Seccomp active
Encryption at restETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/<ns>/<name> | hexdump -CSecret is encrypted (garbled) in etcd
Falco rulecat /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml or falco --validate <file>Rule file exists and is syntactically valid
Audit policycat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq . | head -50Audit logs are being generated
Image scantrivy image <image> --severity CRITICAL — shows 0 resultsNo CRITICAL CVEs in scanned image

36.4 File Locations You Must Know (No Internet Search Needed)

In the CKS exam, searching the Kubernetes documentation for file paths wastes precious minutes. These paths appear in nearly every exam task. Memorize them. Write them on a piece of paper and review them 5 minutes before your exam starts (during the check-in process, you'll have a few minutes while the proctor verifies your ID).

Critical File Paths — Categorized by Component

File / DirectoryComponentPurposeCommon Task
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kubeletStatic pod manifests directory. Any YAML here is automatically run as a static pod.Edit API server, controller-manager, scheduler, or etcd configuration
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yamlAPI ServerAPI server static pod manifest. Add flags here to configure encryption, audit, admission plugins.Enable encryption at rest, configure audit policy, disable anonymous auth
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yamlController ManagerController manager static pod manifest.Configure ServiceAccount token signing, enable/disable controllers
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yamletcdetcd static pod manifest. Configure TLS, peer URLs, data directory.Enable TLS for etcd, change data directory
/var/lib/kubelet/config.yamlkubeletKubelet configuration file (YAML). Contains authentication, authorization, cgroup driver settings.Disable anonymous auth, enable webhook authorization, set Seccomp default
/etc/kubernetes/pki/PKICluster certificate authority and key files.Inspect certificate expiration, rotate certificates
/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/etcd PKIetcd-specific certificates and keys.Configure etcd TLS, verify peer certificates
/var/lib/etcd/etcdetcd data directory. Contains the actual key-value store data.Backup, restore, check data size
/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yamlAPI ServerAudit policy file. Defines WHAT to log and at what detail level.Create or modify audit policy, enable audit logging
/etc/falco/falco.yamlFalcoFalco main configuration file. Output channels, rules files, engine settings.Change output format, enable/disable rules, configure alerting
/etc/falco/falco_rules.yamlFalcoDefault Falco rules. Shipped with Falco installation.View default rules for reference when writing custom rules
/etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yamlFalcoLOCAL custom rules file. Add your custom rules here (never edit the default file).Write custom Falco rules for specific applications
/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/kubeletDirectory for local Seccomp profiles. Place custom JSON profiles here.Create and apply custom Seccomp profiles
/etc/apparmor.d/AppArmorAppArmor profile directory. Place custom AppArmor profiles here.Load and apply custom AppArmor profiles to pods
/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yamlAPI ServerEncryptionConfiguration file. Defines encryption providers and keys.Enable encryption at rest for Secrets

Memorization Strategy — How to Remember These Paths

🧠
Group by Parent Directory

Most paths live under 3 parents: /etc/kubernetes/ (API server, PKI, audit), /var/lib/kubelet/ (kubelet config, Seccomp), and /etc/falco/ (Falco rules). Memorize the 3 parents first, then the specific files under each.

📝
Write Them Before Starting

During the NDA/check-in screen (you have a few minutes), mentally recite these paths. As soon as the terminal appears, type them into the notepad: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/, /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml. Your future self will thank you.

🔗
Associate with Tasks

Don't memorize in isolation. Link each path to a specific task: "If I need to enable encryption → edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml". "If I need to write a custom Falco rule → edit /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml". The association makes it stick.

Additional Critical Paths — The Extended Reference

File / DirectoryComponentWhy You Need It
/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yamlSchedulerStatic pod for kube-scheduler. May need to edit for profiling, authentication settings.
/var/lib/kubelet/config.yamlKubeletTHE kubelet config file. Contains authentication, authorization, seccompDefault, rotateCertificates. Edit this for most kubelet hardening tasks.
/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crtPKICluster CA certificate. Used to verify API server TLS, etcd TLS, and service account tokens.
/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crtAPI ServerAPI server certificate. Check expiration: openssl x509 -in <file> -text -noout | grep -A2 Validity
~/.kube/configkubectlKubeconfig file. Contains clusters, users, and contexts. kubectl config view to see all configured contexts.
/etc/containerd/config.tomlcontainerdContainer runtime configuration. May need to check for insecure registries or runtime settings.
/etc/kubernetes/admission-control/API ServerDirectory for admission webhook configurations (ImagePolicyWebhook, etc.).
/usr/local/bin/SystemWhere tools like trivy, kube-bench, etcdctl are installed. Check with which <tool>.

Exam Task → File Path Quick Reference

Every CKS exam task maps to one or more of these files. Here's the cheat sheet:

🔐
Encryption Tasks

Create /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml → Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml → Add --encryption-provider-config flag + volume mount → Verify with etcdctl get

📝
Audit Tasks

Create /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml → Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml → Add --audit-policy-file + --audit-log-path flags + volume mounts → Check /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log

🛡️
Kubelet Hardening

Edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml → Set authentication.anonymous.enabled: false, authorization.mode: Webhook, readOnlyPort: 0 → Restart kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet

🔍
Falco Tasks

Edit /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml → Write custom rules → Validate: falco --validate <file> → Restart Falco: systemctl restart falco or kill -1 $(pidof falco)

📦
Seccomp Tasks

Create profile in /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ → Reference in Pod securityContext.seccompProfile.localhostProfile → Verify: kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp

🛡️
AppArmor Tasks

Create profile in /etc/apparmor.d/ → Load: apparmor_parser -r <file> → Reference in Pod annotation → Verify: cat /proc/<pid>/attr/current

Chapter 37: Mock Scenarios & Practice Labs

Reading about security is not enough. You must practice. This chapter contains 28 hands-on tasks (4 per exam domain) plus a complete 17-task mock exam — all with detailed step-by-step solutions. Each task is structured like a real CKS exam question: a context, an objective, and verification steps. Do these tasks on a real cluster. Use minikube, kind, or a cloud sandbox. Time yourself. Build the muscle memory that will carry you through exam day.

🔴 Hands-On ⏱️ ~4 hours 🧪 Practice 📋 28 Tasks

🎯 What You'll Practice — Exam-Ready Skills

  • ✅ Domain 1 (Cluster Setup): Run kube-bench, apply NetworkPolicies, configure TLS Ingress, secure Dashboard access
  • ✅ Domain 2 (Cluster Hardening): Disable anonymous auth, configure audit logging, create minimal RBAC, disable automount
  • ✅ Domain 3 (System Hardening): Apply AppArmor + Seccomp profiles, harden kubelet, remove unnecessary services
  • ✅ Domain 4 (Microservice Vulnerability): Enforce PSS, harden pod securityContext, enable encryption at rest, apply sandbox runtime
  • ✅ Domain 5 (Supply Chain): Scan images with Trivy, write OPA policies, sign with cosign, configure ImagePolicyWebhook
  • ✅ Domain 6 (Runtime Security): Configure Falco rules, write custom rules, investigate alerts, analyze audit logs

37.1 Domain 1: Cluster Setup Practice Tasks (10% of exam)

Task A: Run kube-bench on Control Plane, Fix Top 3 FAIL Items

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-1 | Time: 8 min | Points: 5
📋
Objective: Run kube-bench against the control plane. Identify the top 3 FAIL items and fix them. Verify each fix.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Run kube-bench on the control plane node
ssh control-plane-1
kube-bench run --targets master --benchmark cis-1.23

# Step 2: Identify failures (example: 1.1.1, 1.1.3, 1.2.6)
# Fix 1: 1.1.1 — API server anonymous auth enabled
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add/change: - --anonymous-auth=false
# Wait ~30 seconds for the API server to restart automatically

# Fix 2: 1.1.3 — Controller manager pod spec permissions not 600
sudo chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml
sudo chown root:root /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml

# Fix 3: 1.2.6 — API server profiling enabled
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Change: - --profiling=true  →  - --profiling=false

# Step 3: Re-run kube-bench to verify
kube-bench run --targets master --benchmark cis-1.23
# Verify: The 3 FAIL items are now PASS

Task B: Apply NetworkPolicy Set to Isolate a Namespace

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-1 | Time: 10 min | Points: 7
📋
Objective: Create NetworkPolicies in namespace "isolated" that block all ingress/egress, then allow DNS and a specific pod-to-pod connection.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create namespace
kubectl create ns isolated

# Step 2: Default deny all ingress + egress
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: isolated
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
EOF

# Step 3: Allow DNS
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: isolated
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}, {protocol: TCP, port: 53}]
EOF

# Step 4: Test
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -n isolated -- nslookup kubernetes.default
# ✅ Should WORK (DNS allowed)
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -n isolated -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 google.com
# ❌ Should FAIL (external blocked)

Task C: Configure Ingress with TLS for a Test Service

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-1 | Time: 10 min | Points: 6
📋
Objective: Deploy a test web app, create a TLS Secret, and configure an Ingress to serve it over HTTPS. Verify with curl.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Deploy a test app + service
kubectl create ns web-test
kubectl create deployment nginx --image=nginx -n web-test
kubectl expose deployment nginx --port=80 -n web-test

# Step 2: Generate a self-signed TLS certificate
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt \
  -subj "/CN=test.example.com/O=test"

# Step 3: Create TLS Secret
kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key -n web-test

# Step 4: Create Ingress with TLS
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: nginx-tls
  namespace: web-test
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - test.example.com
    secretName: web-tls
  rules:
  - host: test.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: nginx
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

# Step 5: Verify
curl -k https://test.example.com
# Should return nginx welcome page (use -k to skip CA verification for self-signed)

Task D: Secure Kubernetes Dashboard Access with Token + NetworkPolicy

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-1 | Time: 10 min | Points: 6
📋
Objective: Deploy Kubernetes Dashboard, create a ServiceAccount with cluster-admin access, obtain its token, and apply a NetworkPolicy restricting access to a specific IP range.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Deploy Dashboard
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/dashboard/v2.7.0/aix/deploy/recommended.yaml

# Step 2: Create admin ServiceAccount + ClusterRoleBinding
kubectl create sa dashboard-admin -n kubernetes-dashboard
kubectl create clusterrolebinding dashboard-admin \
  --clusterrole=cluster-admin \
  --serviceaccount=kubernetes-dashboard:dashboard-admin

# Step 3: Create long-lived token (K8s v1.24+)
kubectl create token dashboard-admin -n kubernetes-dashboard --duration=24h

# Step 4: Restrict access with NetworkPolicy
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: restrict-dashboard
  namespace: kubernetes-dashboard
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      k8s-app: kubernetes-dashboard
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 192.168.1.0/24   # Only office network
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8443
EOF

# Step 5: Access dashboard
kubectl proxy &
# Open: http://localhost:8001/api/v1/namespaces/kubernetes-dashboard/services/https:kubernetes-dashboard:/proxy/
# Login with the token from Step 3
💡 Domain 1 Exam Tips — Cluster Setup (10%)

kube-bench: Memorize the 3 most common FAIL items (anonymous-auth, file permissions, profiling). You can fix these in <2 minutes. NetworkPolicy: The exam always tests default-deny + DNS + specific allow. Practice this pattern until it's muscle memory. TLS Ingress: Know openssl req -x509 by heart. The command is long but you'll use it on every CKS exam. Dashboard: CKS may ask you to secure it — NetworkPolicy + token auth is the standard answer. See Chapter 6 (NetworkPolicy), Chapter 33 (hardening).

37.2 Domain 2: Cluster Hardening Practice Tasks (15% of exam)

Task A: Disable Anonymous Auth on API Server, Verify

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-2 | Time: 4 min | Points: 4
📋
Objective: Disable anonymous authentication on the Kubernetes API server. Verify that anonymous requests are rejected.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: SSH to control plane node
ssh control-plane-1

# Step 2: Edit API server manifest
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Find: - --anonymous-auth=true  (or add if missing)
# Change to: - --anonymous-auth=false
# Save and exit

# Step 3: Wait for API server to restart (~30 seconds)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep apiserver
# Should show a new pod with AGE of a few seconds

# Step 4: Verify — anonymous request should FAIL
kubectl get pods --as=system:anonymous
# Expected: Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden: User "system:anonymous" cannot list

# Step 5: Verify authenticated request still works
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
# Should return pod list normally

Task B: Create Audit Policy, Enable Audit Logging, Verify Log Output

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-2 | Time: 8 min | Points: 6
📋
Objective: Create an audit policy that logs all Secret reads at Metadata level. Enable audit logging. Create and read a Secret to verify logs are generated.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create audit policy file on control plane node
sudo mkdir -p /etc/kubernetes/audit
sudo tee /etc/kubernetes/audit/policy.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
- level: Metadata
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["secrets"]
EOF

# Step 2: Edit API server manifest to enable audit logging
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# ADD these flags:
#   - --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit/policy.yaml
#   - --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
#   - --audit-log-maxage=7
#   - --audit-log-maxbackup=3
#   - --audit-log-maxsize=100

# ADD volumeMounts:
#   - mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/audit
#     name: audit-policy
#     readOnly: true
#   - mountPath: /var/log/kubernetes
#     name: audit-log
#     readOnly: false

# ADD volumes:
#   - name: audit-policy
#     hostPath:
#       path: /etc/kubernetes/audit
#       type: DirectoryOrCreate
#   - name: audit-log
#     hostPath:
#       path: /var/log/kubernetes
#       type: DirectoryOrCreate

# Step 3: Wait for API server restart, then test
kubectl create secret generic test-audit --from-literal=key=secretvalue -n default
kubectl get secret test-audit -n default -o yaml > /dev/null

# Step 4: Verify audit log contains the secret read
sudo cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="secrets") | {verb, user: .user.username, secret: .objectRef.name, time: .stageTimestamp}'
# Should show: {"verb":"get","user":"kubernetes-admin","secret":"test-audit","time":"..."}

Task C: Create Minimal RBAC for a Given Service Account

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-2 | Time: 5 min | Points: 5
📋
Objective: Create a ServiceAccount "reader" in namespace "app". Grant it permission to get, list, and watch pods in that namespace ONLY. Verify with kubectl auth can-i.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create namespace and ServiceAccount
kubectl create ns app
kubectl create sa reader -n app

# Step 2: Create Role (pod reader only)
kubectl create role pod-reader -n app \
  --verb=get,list,watch \
  --resource=pods

# Step 3: Bind Role to ServiceAccount
kubectl create rolebinding pod-reader-binding -n app \
  --role=pod-reader \
  --serviceaccount=app:reader

# Step 4: Verify permissions (what this SA CAN do)
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:app:reader -n app
# Expected: yes

# Step 5: Verify restrictions (what this SA CANNOT do)
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:app:reader -n app
# Expected: no
kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:app:reader -n default
# Expected: no
kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:app:reader -n app
# Expected: no

Task D: Configure ServiceAccount with automount Disabled

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-2 | Time: 5 min | Points: 4
📋
Objective: Create a ServiceAccount "no-api" with automountServiceAccountToken: false. Create a pod using this SA and verify the token is NOT mounted.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create SA with automount disabled
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: no-api
  namespace: default
automountServiceAccountToken: false
EOF

# Step 2: Create pod using this SA
kubectl run test-no-api --image=nginx -n default \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"no-api"}}'

# Step 3: Verify token is NOT mounted
kubectl exec test-no-api -n default -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
# Expected: ls: cannot access '...': No such file or directory
# ✅ Token correctly NOT mounted

# Step 4: For comparison, check a pod with default SA (token IS mounted)
kubectl run test-default --image=nginx -n default
kubectl exec test-default -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
# Expected: ca.crt  namespace  token  (token IS mounted)
💡 Domain 2 Exam Tips — Cluster Hardening (15%)

Anonymous auth: Always verify AFTER changing — use kubectl get pods --as=system:anonymous. If it returns pods, your fix didn't work. Audit policy: The API server manifest edit is the hardest part — you need BOTH the flag AND the volume mount. Missing either = audit logging silently broken. RBAC: Always test with kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>. Test BOTH positive (allowed) and negative (denied) cases. Common mistake: Creating a ClusterRoleBinding instead of RoleBinding — this grants cross-namespace access and loses points. See Chapter 9 (RBAC), Chapter 28 (Audit).

37.3 Domain 3: System Hardening Practice Tasks (15% of exam)

Task A: Load AppArmor Profile and Apply to a Pod

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-3 | Time: 8 min | Points: 6
📋
Objective: Create a custom AppArmor profile that denies writing to /tmp. Load it on the node. Create a pod with this profile and verify writes to /tmp are blocked.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: SSH to worker node where pod will run
ssh worker-1

# Step 2: Create AppArmor profile
sudo tee /etc/apparmor.d/deny-tmp-write <<EOF
#include <tunables/global>
profile deny-tmp-write flags=(attach_disconnected) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  /tmp/  r,
  /tmp/** r,
  deny /tmp/** w,
}
EOF

# Step 3: Load the profile
sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/deny-tmp-write
sudo aa-status | grep deny-tmp-write   # Verify loaded

# Step 4: Create pod with AppArmor annotation
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: apparmor-test
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/test: localhost/deny-tmp-write
spec:
  containers:
  - name: test
    image: nginx
EOF

# Step 5: Verify — write to /tmp should FAIL
kubectl exec apparmor-test -- touch /tmp/test-file
# Expected: touch: cannot touch '/tmp/test-file': Permission denied

Task B: Apply Seccomp RuntimeDefault Profile to a Pod

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-3 | Time: 5 min | Points: 4
📋
Objective: Create a pod that uses the RuntimeDefault Seccomp profile. Verify the profile is active by checking /proc/1/status.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create pod with seccompProfile
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: seccomp-test
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: test
    image: nginx
EOF

# Step 2: Verify Seccomp is active
kubectl exec seccomp-test -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp
# Expected: Seccomp:  2
# 0 = disabled, 1 = strict, 2 = filter (RuntimeDefault = filter mode)

# Compare with a pod WITHOUT seccomp
kubectl run no-seccomp --image=nginx
kubectl exec no-seccomp -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp
# Expected: Seccomp:  0 (disabled)

Task C: Harden Kubelet — Disable Anonymous Auth, Enable Webhook

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-3 | Time: 7 min | Points: 5
📋
Objective: SSH to a worker node. Edit the kubelet config to disable anonymous authentication and enable Webhook authorization. Restart kubelet. Verify the changes.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: SSH to worker node
ssh worker-1

# Step 2: Edit kubelet config
sudo vi /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# Change/add these settings:
# authentication:
#   anonymous:
#     enabled: false
#   webhook:
#     enabled: true
# authorization:
#   mode: Webhook
# readOnlyPort: 0

# Step 3: Restart kubelet
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
sudo systemctl status kubelet  # Verify running

# Step 4: Verify — anonymous request should FAIL
curl -k https://localhost:10250/pods
# Expected: Unauthorized (anonymous auth disabled)

# Step 5: Verify kubelet is still working (pods are running)
kubectl get nodes
# Worker-1 should show Ready status

Task D: Remove Unnecessary Services from a Node

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-3 | Time: 5 min | Points: 4
📋
Objective: On a worker node, identify and stop unnecessary services (e.g., FTP, Telnet). Disable them from auto-starting on boot. Verify they are stopped.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: SSH to worker node
ssh worker-1

# Step 2: List active services, identify unnecessary ones
sudo systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running | grep -E 'ftp|telnet|smtp|nfs|rpc'

# Step 3: Stop and disable identified services
sudo systemctl stop vsftpd     # FTP server
sudo systemctl disable vsftpd
sudo systemctl stop telnet     # Telnet daemon (if xinetd-based)
sudo systemctl disable telnet.socket

# Step 4: Verify services are stopped
sudo systemctl status vsftpd
# Expected: Active: inactive (dead)

# Step 5: Verify the node is still functional
kubectl get nodes
# Should still show Ready
💡 Domain 3 Exam Tips — System Hardening (15%)

AppArmor: The profile MUST exist on the NODE where the pod runs. If the pod is stuck in ContainerCreating, the profile is missing or has a syntax error. Seccomp: /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp is your verification friend. 2=filter (good), 0=disabled (bad). Kubelet hardening: After editing /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, ALWAYS run systemctl restart kubelet — the config is NOT hot-reloaded. Check systemctl status kubelet for errors. Remove services: If systemctl stop works but systemctl disable fails, check if the service is a dependency of another unit. See Chapter 13 (Node Hardening), Chapter 14 (AppArmor), Chapter 15 (Seccomp).

37.4 Domain 4: Microservice Vulnerability Practice Tasks (20% of exam)

Task A: Apply PSS Restricted to a Namespace, Fix Violating Pods

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-4 | Time: 6 min | Points: 5
📋
Objective: Label namespace "secure-app" with PSS Restricted enforcement. Create a pod that violates Restricted. Observe the rejection. Fix the pod to comply.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create namespace with PSS Restricted
kubectl create ns secure-app
kubectl label ns secure-app \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=v1.30

# Step 2: Try creating a pod that VIOLATES Restricted (runs as root)
kubectl run bad-pod --image=nginx -n secure-app
# Expected: Error: pods "bad-pod" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:v1.30":
#   runAsNonRoot != true, seccompProfile...

# Step 3: Fix the pod — add required securityContext
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: good-pod
  namespace: secure-app
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine   # Alpine nginx runs as non-root
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
EOF
# ✅ Pod created successfully

Task B: Add Full Security Context to Pod (Non-Root, Drop ALL Caps)

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-4 | Time: 8 min | Points: 7
📋
Objective: Create a pod with the full CKS security context: non-root, read-only filesystem, drop ALL capabilities, privilege escalation disabled. Verify each control is active.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create hardened pod
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hardened-app
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 1000
    fsGroup: 1000
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
    - name: cache
      mountPath: /var/cache/nginx
    - name: run
      mountPath: /var/run
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: cache
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: run
    emptyDir: {}
EOF

# Step 2: Verify non-root
kubectl exec hardened-app -- whoami
# Expected: whoami: unknown uid 1000 (not root)

# Step 3: Verify read-only filesystem
kubectl exec hardened-app -- touch /test
# Expected: touch: cannot touch '/test': Read-only file system

# Step 4: Verify writable emptyDir works
kubectl exec hardened-app -- touch /tmp/test
# Expected: SUCCESS (no output)

Task C: Enable Encryption at Rest for Secrets in etcd

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-4 | Time: 12 min | Points: 8
📋
Objective: Create an EncryptionConfiguration using aescbc. Enable it on the API server. Verify new secrets are encrypted in etcd. Rotate existing secrets.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Generate encryption key (32 bytes base64-encoded)
ENCRYPTION_KEY=$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)

# Step 2: Create EncryptionConfiguration on control plane
sudo tee /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources:
  - secrets
  providers:
  - aescbc:
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: ${ENCRYPTION_KEY}
  - identity: {}
EOF

# Step 3: Edit API server manifest
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add flag: - --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
# Add volumeMount:
#   - mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#     name: encryption-config
#     readOnly: true
# Add volume:
#   - name: encryption-config
#     hostPath:
#       path: /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
#       type: File

# Step 4: Wait for API server restart, test
kubectl create secret generic encrypted-test --from-literal=key=secretvalue -n default

# Step 5: Verify encryption in etcd
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  get /registry/secrets/default/encrypted-test | hexdump -C | head
# Look for "k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:key1:" prefix — that's the encrypted data!

# Step 6: Rotate existing secrets
kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
# ✅ All secrets now encrypted

Task D: Apply RuntimeClass gVisor to an Untrusted Workload

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-4 | Time: 8 min | Points: 6
📋
Objective: Create a RuntimeClass for gVisor. Create a pod using this RuntimeClass. Verify the pod is using gVisor by checking the kernel version inside the container.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create RuntimeClass (assumes gVisor is installed as runsc)
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc
EOF

# Step 2: Create pod using gVisor RuntimeClass
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sandboxed-app
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
EOF

# Step 3: Verify gVisor is active
kubectl exec sandboxed-app -- uname -r
# Expected: 4.4.0  (gVisor's sentry kernel, NOT the host kernel)
# Compare with regular pod:
kubectl run regular --image=nginx
kubectl exec regular -- uname -r
# Expected: 5.15.0-xxx  (the actual host kernel version)
💡 Domain 4 Exam Tips — Microservice Vulnerability (20%)

PSS Restricted: This is the SINGLE most tested topic on the CKS. Know the 3 required fields: runAsNonRoot: true, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault, capabilities.drop: [ALL]. If a pod is rejected, read the error message — it tells you exactly what's missing. SecurityContext: Practice writing the full 7-field securityContext from memory. On the exam, you don't want to waste time searching docs for each field. Encryption at rest: The hardest part is the API server manifest edit. Practice it 5 times before the exam. Remember: flag + volume mount + volume (3 pieces). gVisor/RuntimeClass: The verification is unique — uname -r returns a different kernel. This is how you prove it's working. See Chapter 24 (PSS), Chapter 33 (anihpj hardening), Chapter 23 (Encryption).

37.5 Domain 5: Supply Chain Security Practice Tasks (20% of exam)

Task A: Scan an Image with Trivy, Report CRITICAL CVEs

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-5 | Time: 8 min | Points: 6
📋
Objective: Scan the image nginx:1.21 with Trivy. Output a JSON report. Identify all CRITICAL CVEs. Count and report the total. Save results to /tmp/trivy-report.json.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Install Trivy (if not already installed)
curl -sfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/trivy/main/contrib/install.sh | sh

# Step 2: Scan the image, output JSON
trivy image nginx:1.21 --severity CRITICAL --format json -o /tmp/trivy-report.json

# Step 3: Count CRITICAL CVEs
cat /tmp/trivy-report.json | jq '[.Results[].Vulnerabilities[]? | select(.Severity=="CRITICAL")] | length'
# Expected: some number (depends on when you scan — CVEs accumulate over time)

# Step 4: List each CRITICAL CVE with ID and package
cat /tmp/trivy-report.json | jq -r '.Results[].Vulnerabilities[]? | select(.Severity=="CRITICAL") | "\(.VulnerabilityID): \(.PkgName) (\(.InstalledVersion))"'

# Step 5: Also scan for HIGH severity
trivy image nginx:1.21 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --format table

Task B: Create OPA ConstraintTemplate to Block Unapproved Images

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-5 | Time: 10 min | Points: 7
📋
Objective: Create a Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate + Constraint that only allows images from registry.k8s.io/* and nginx:alpine. Test by creating a pod with a disallowed image — it should be rejected.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create ConstraintTemplate
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sallowedrepos
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sAllowedRepos
      validation:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          properties:
            repos:
              type: array
              items:
                type: string
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8sallowedrepos
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        satisfied := [good | repo := input.parameters.repos[_]; good := startswith(container.image, repo)]
        not any(satisfied)
        msg := sprintf("container <%v> uses disallowed image <%v>", [container.name, container.image])
      }
EOF

# Step 2: Create Constraint
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sAllowedRepos
metadata:
  name: allowed-registries
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      kinds: [Pod]
  parameters:
    repos:
    - "registry.k8s.io/"
    - "nginx:alpine"
EOF

# Step 3: Test — allowed image should WORK
kubectl run test-allowed --image=nginx:alpine
# Expected: pod/test-allowed created ✅

# Step 4: Test — disallowed image should FAIL
kubectl run test-blocked --image=nginx:latest
# Expected: Error: admission webhook "validation.gatekeeper.sh" denied

Task C: Sign an Image with Cosign, Configure Kyverno to Verify It

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-5 | Time: 8 min | Points: 6
📋
Objective: Sign the nginx:alpine image with cosign (keyless). Create a Kyverno ClusterPolicy that verifies the signature. Verify the policy allows the signed image.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Install cosign
curl -sSL https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/releases/latest/download/cosign-linux-amd64 -o /usr/local/bin/cosign
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/cosign

# Step 2: Sign the image (keyless — uses OIDC)
# Note: For exam practice, you need a real OIDC provider (GitHub Actions).
# For local practice, generate a key pair:
cosign generate-key-pair
cosign sign --key cosign.key nginx:alpine

# Step 3: Create Kyverno verifyImages policy
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: verify-signed-images
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-signature
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences:
      - "nginx:alpine"
      attestors:
      - count: 1
        entries:
        - keys:
            publicKeys: |
              $(cat cosign.pub)
EOF

# Step 4: Test — signed image works
kubectl run signed-test --image=nginx:alpine
# ✅ Created (policy verified signature)

# Step 5: Test — unsigned image would be rejected
# (If you try a different tag, it will fail)

Task D: Deploy ImagePolicyWebhook, Test Image Rejection

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-5 | Time: 10 min | Points: 6
📋
Objective: Configure the ImagePolicyWebhook admission plugin on the API server. Point it to a webhook server. Test that images are checked against the webhook.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create kubeconfig for the webhook
cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/kubernetes/admission/imagepolicy-kubeconfig.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- cluster:
    server: https://webhook.example.com/image-policy
  name: image-policy-webhook
users:
- name: api-server
current-context: webhook
contexts:
- context:
    cluster: image-policy-webhook
  name: webhook
EOF

# Step 2: Edit API server manifest
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Add flags:
#   - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,ImagePolicyWebhook
#   - --admission-control-config-file=/etc/kubernetes/admission/imagepolicy-config.yaml
# Add volume mounts for the webhook config files

# Step 3: Create admission control config
cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/kubernetes/admission/imagepolicy-config.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: AdmissionConfiguration
plugins:
- name: ImagePolicyWebhook
  configuration:
    imagePolicy:
      kubeConfigFile: /etc/kubernetes/admission/imagepolicy-kubeconfig.yaml
      allowTTL: 300
      denyTTL: 300
      retryBackoff: 500
      defaultAllow: false
EOF

# Step 4: Test — images will be checked against the webhook
# (The webhook at webhook.example.com won't actually respond, so pods will fail)
kubectl run test-imagepolicy --image=nginx
# Expected: Error (webhook unreachable — this proves the plugin is active)
💡 Domain 5 Exam Tips — Supply Chain Security (20%)

Trivy: Know the difference between --severity filter and --exit-code. trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 FAILS if any CRITICAL CVEs exist. OPA/Gatekeeper: The ConstraintTemplate's Rego is the hardest part. Memorize the pattern: violation[{msg}] { container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]; ... }. Cosign + Kyverno: For the exam, generate a key pair (cosign generate-key-pair) rather than keyless (which requires GitHub OIDC). ImagePolicyWebhook: This is a CKS-specific topic — know the API server flags, the kubeconfig format, and the AdmissionConfiguration. See Chapter 25 (Trivy), Chapter 10 (OPA/Gatekeeper), Chapter 26 (Supply Chain).

37.6 Domain 6: Runtime Security Practice Tasks (20% of exam)

Task A: Configure Falco Audit Policy — Log Secret Reads

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-6 | Time: 7 min | Points: 5
📋
Objective: Edit the Kubernetes audit policy to log all Secret reads at Metadata level and pod exec at RequestResponse level. Enable the policy. Verify it works by reading a Secret and checking the audit log.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Create/update audit policy
sudo tee /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
rules:
- level: Metadata
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["secrets"]
- level: RequestResponse
  verbs: ["create"]
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["pods/exec"]
- level: None
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["pods", "services"]
EOF

# Step 2: Verify API server has audit flags
# (See Task 37.2B for full API server configuration)
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# Ensure flags: --audit-policy-file, --audit-log-path

# Step 3: Test — create and read a secret
kubectl create secret generic falco-audit-test --from-literal=key=demo -n default
kubectl get secret falco-audit-test -n default -o yaml > /dev/null

# Step 4: Verify audit log
sudo cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="secrets") | {verb, user: .user.username, secret: .objectRef.name}' | tail -5
# Should show the GET request for falco-audit-test

Task B: Write Falco Rule to Detect Shell in Specific Container

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-6 | Time: 8 min | Points: 7
📋
Objective: Write a custom Falco rule that detects any shell spawned in a container named "web". Place the rule in /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml. Test by creating a pod named "web" and running a shell inside it.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Write custom Falco rule
sudo tee /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml <<EOF
- rule: Shell in web container
  desc: Alert on any shell spawned in the web container
  condition: >
    spawned_process and container.name = "web"
    and proc.name in (bash, sh, zsh, dash)
  output: >
    🚨 Shell detected in web container! (user=%user.name
    pod=%pod.name cmdline=%proc.cmdline)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [web, shell, practice]
EOF

# Step 2: Validate rule syntax
sudo falco --validate /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml

# Step 3: Restart Falco (or send SIGHUP)
sudo systemctl restart falco
# Or: sudo kill -1 $(pidof falco)

# Step 4: Test — create web pod and exec a shell
kubectl run web --image=nginx
kubectl exec web -- sh -c "echo 'test shell'"

# Step 5: Check Falco logs for the alert
sudo journalctl -u falco --since "1 min ago" | grep "Shell in web"
# Or: sudo cat /var/log/falco.log | grep "Shell in web"

Task C: Investigate a Falco Alert — Identify the Suspicious Process

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-6 | Time: 8 min | Points: 7
📋
Objective: A Falco alert fired: "Unexpected outbound connection". Investigate: find the pod that triggered it, identify the suspicious process, capture the process details, and determine if it's malicious.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Read the Falco alert
# Alert output: "🌐 EXTERNAL connection! pod=test-pod container=app dest=198.51.100.23:4444 cmdline=sh"

# Step 2: Find the pod
kubectl get pods -A | grep test-pod
# Identified: pod test-pod in namespace default

# Step 3: Inspect the pod
kubectl describe pod test-pod -n default
# Check: which image? when created? what node?

# Step 4: Check running processes in the pod
kubectl exec test-pod -n default -- ps auxf
# Look for: sh process, or the process that made the connection

# Step 5: Check network connections
kubectl exec test-pod -n default -- ss -tunap
# Look for: connection to 198.51.100.23:4444

# Step 6: Capture forensic evidence
kubectl logs test-pod -n default --tail=500 > /tmp/incident-logs.txt
kubectl get pod test-pod -n default -o yaml > /tmp/incident-pod.yaml

# Step 7: Assessment
# The IP 198.51.100.23 is not in our allowed range → likely C2 server
# Action: isolate pod immediately (see Ch34, Ch30 for incident response)

Task D: Enable Audit Logging, Find Suspicious kubectl exec from Logs

TASKContext: mk8s-cluster-6 | Time: 8 min | Points: 7
📋
Objective: Enable audit logging with RequestResponse level for pods/exec. Execute kubectl exec into a pod. Find the exact audit log entry and identify the user who ran the command.
✅ Solution
# Step 1: Ensure audit policy includes pods/exec (from Task A)
sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml | grep -A2 "pods/exec"

# Step 2: Execute a kubectl exec (this will be logged)
kubectl run audit-test --image=nginx
kubectl exec audit-test -- ls /tmp

# Step 3: Find the audit log entry
sudo cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="pods" and .objectRef.subresource=="exec")' | jq '{user: .user.username, pod: .objectRef.name, command: .requestObject.command, time: .stageTimestamp}'

# Expected output:
# {
#   "user": "kubernetes-admin",
#   "pod": "audit-test",
#   "command": ["ls", "/tmp"],
#   "time": "2026-06-14T10:30:00Z"
# }

# Step 4: Check for suspicious exec commands (from unknown users or odd hours)
sudo cat /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq 'select(.objectRef.subresource=="exec") | select(.user.username != "kubernetes-admin")'

# Step 5: If you found a suspicious entry (e.g., from an unknown user at 3AM):
# → Investigate the user: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[].name=="suspicious-user")'
# → Rotate their credentials
# → Report incident
💡 Domain 6 Exam Tips — Runtime Security (20%)

Falco rules: Write rules in /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml — NEVER edit the default falco_rules.yaml (your changes will be overwritten on upgrade). Rule validation: Always run falco --validate after writing rules. A syntax error = the rule silently doesn't load. Audit log analysis: jq is your best friend. Practice jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="secrets")' and jq 'select(.verb=="create")' patterns. Common mistake: Forgetting to restart Falco after updating rules. New rules don't take effect until Falco reloads. Use kill -1 $(pidof falco) for a graceful reload without dropping events. See Chapter 29 (Falco), Chapter 28 (Audit).

Mock Exam Instructions

1Setup

Use a test cluster (minikube, kind, or cloud sandbox). Install required tools: Trivy, kube-bench, Falco, cosign, Gatekeeper, Kyverno. Ensure you have SSH access to at least one control plane and one worker node.

2Exam Rules

120-minute timer. Allowed: kubernetes.io/docs, falco.org, github.com/falcosecurity/falco. NOT allowed: personal notes, bookmarks, AI tools, StackOverflow. Score yourself honestly.

3Scoring

Each task is worth the listed points. Partial credit: if you complete 70% of a task, give yourself 70% of the points. Verification steps count — if the task asks you to verify, you MUST verify to get full points.

4Review

After finishing, review every task you missed. Re-do them until you can solve each one in the target time without help. Focus on your weakest domain.

Mock Exam Scoring Strategy — Maximize Your Score

StrategyDescriptionExpected Gain
Always attempt every taskNo negative scoring. Even writing kubectl create ns for the right namespace earns partial credit. Never leave a task completely blank.+5-10 points
Prioritize high-value tasksTasks 2 (7pts), 11 (8pts), 13 (7pts), 16 (7pts), 17 (7pts) are worth the most. Ensure you attempt these even if running short on time.+10-15 points
Verification = pointsAt least 20% of task points come from verification. If a task says "verify", you MUST run a verification command. kubectl get or kubectl describe is often enough.+5-10 points
Use the docs for YAMLDon't write YAML from memory. Search the docs, copy the example, paste into vi, modify only what you need. This saves time AND prevents syntax errors.+5 points (time saved)

Self-Assessment After the Mock Exam

📊
Score 85+

You're ready. Schedule your exam. Focus on speed — can you complete the same tasks 20% faster? Practice until each task takes 60-70% of the target time.

📊
Score 67-84

Close — borderline pass. Review every missed task. Identify your weak domain. Do ALL 4 tasks in that domain again. Take another mock exam in 3-5 days.

📊
Score <67

Not yet ready. Re-read the chapters for your weakest domains. Practice each task individually until you can solve it in the target time. Only then attempt another full mock.

How to Use This Cheat Sheet During the Exam

1Identify the domain

Read the task description. Does it mention kube-bench? → Domain 1. API server flags? → Domain 2. AppArmor/Seccomp? → Domain 3. PSS or encryption? → Domain 4. Trivy/cosign? → Domain 5. Falco/audit? → Domain 6. This mental mapping takes 5 seconds and tells you which section to scan.

2Scan the domain section

Each domain lists 4-6 commands. 90% of exam tasks can be solved with just these commands. If the exact command isn't listed, the DOMAIN tells you which tool to search for in the Kubernetes docs.

3Type — don't copy-paste

The PSI browser doesn't allow copy-paste from the exam content to your terminal. Memorize the command patterns, not the exact syntax. For example: kubectl create role NAME --verb=VERB --resource=RESOURCE -n NS — the pattern is what matters.

38.2 Critical kubectl Commands for CKS — The Top 40

These 40 commands cover 90% of what you'll type during the CKS exam. Practice each one until it's automatic.

  │                                                                   │
  │  🔑 GOLDEN RULE: kubectl config use-context BEFORE every task    │
  │  🔑 REMEMBER: No negative scoring — ALWAYS attempt every task    │
  │  🔑 SPEED: Copy YAML from docs, don't write from memory          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Command Pattern Recognition — Groups to Memorize

Instead of memorizing 40 individual commands, group them into 7 patterns. Each pattern has a consistent structure:

🔀
Context Pattern

kubectl config use-context NAME
kubectl config current-context
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get ns

ALWAYS run these first. Every single task.

📝
Create Pattern

kubectl create ns/role/rolebinding/sa/secret/configmap
All follow: kubectl create TYPE NAME [flags]
Use --dry-run=client -o yaml to preview.

🔍
Inspect Pattern

kubectl get/describe/logs/exec/top
get = what exists
describe = detailed state
logs = what happened
exec = go inside

🔐
Auth Pattern

kubectl auth can-i VERB RESOURCE --as=SA
ALWAYS test both positive (allowed) and negative (denied).
If the task creates RBAC, the verification is auth can-i.

🏷️
Label Pattern

kubectl label ns/resource NAME KEY=VALUE
kubectl label ns NAME KEY- (remove label)
PSS enforcement, NetworkPolicy selectors, all use labels.

🧪
Test Pattern

kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- CMD
Test NetworkPolicy, DNS, connectivity.
The --rm flag auto-cleans the test pod.

38.3 Security Context Quick Reference

The pod securityContext appears in 50% of CKS tasks. This is the 7-field pattern to memorize:

YAML — The CKS Golden SecurityContext Template (copy-paste, then customize) 
# Pod-level securityContext (applies to all containers)
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true              # ① MUST be true for PSS Restricted
    runAsUser: 1000                 # ② Specific UID (not 0)
    runAsGroup: 1000                # ③ Specific GID
    fsGroup: 1000                   # ④ Volume ownership
    seccompProfile:                 # ⑤ Kernel syscall filter
      type: RuntimeDefault          #    Required by PSS Restricted

  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myimage@sha256:abc...
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # ⑥ Block setuid binaries
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true     # ⑦ Block writes to root FS
      capabilities:
        drop:
        - ALL                          # ⑧ DROP ALL capabilities
      # ADD back only what's needed:
      # add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]     # For binding to ports <1024

    # Writable volumes (required with readOnlyRootFilesystem)
    volumeMounts:
    - name: tmp
      mountPath: /tmp
    - name: cache
      mountPath: /var/cache
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
  - name: cache
    emptyDir: {}

SecurityContext Verification Commands

What to CheckCommandExpected Output
Running as root?kubectl exec POD -- whoamiNOT "root"
Filesystem writable?kubectl exec POD -- touch /test"Read-only file system" error
Capabilities dropped?kubectl exec POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff0000000000000000
Seccomp active?kubectl exec POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp2 (filter mode)
Privilege escalation blocked?kubectl exec POD -- cat /proc/1/status | grep NoNewPrivs1
PSS compliance?kubectl label ns --dry-run=server POD --overrides='{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"securityContext":{"runAsNonRoot":false}}}}}'Error: violates PodSecurity

SecurityContext Decision Tree — Which Fields When?

What does the CKS task ask for?
"Apply PSS Restricted" or "Harden the pod"

→ Use ALL 7 fields: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, allowPrivilegeEscalation, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities.drop:ALL, seccompProfile:RuntimeDefault, fsGroup. This is the maximum-security configuration.

"Prevent privilege escalation" or "Non-root only"

→ Use: runAsNonRoot:true + allowPrivilegeEscalation:false + capabilities.drop:[ALL]. This is the minimum-viable security configuration.

"Read-only filesystem" or "Immutable container"

→ Use: readOnlyRootFilesystem:true + add emptyDir volumes for /tmp, /var/cache, /var/run. ALWAYS add volumes when setting readOnlyRootFilesystem — the app WILL break without them.

38.4 NetworkPolicy Quick Reference

The CKS exam ALWAYS tests NetworkPolicies. Memorize this 3-policy pattern:

YAML — The CKS NetworkPolicy Golden Trio (default-deny + DNS + app) 
---
# POLICY 1: Default deny all (ALWAYS start here)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: TARGET-NS
spec:
  podSelector: {}               # Applies to ALL pods
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress                      # Block ALL incoming
  - Egress                       # Block ALL outgoing
---
# POLICY 2: Allow DNS (required for service discovery)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: TARGET-NS
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
---
# POLICY 3: Allow specific traffic (customize for task)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-app
  namespace: TARGET-NS
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp               # Target pods
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: source-ns      # Source namespace
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080

NetworkPolicy Test Patterns — Verify Your Policies Work

✅
Test DNS (should work)

kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -n NS -- nslookup kubernetes.default
If this FAILS → you forgot the DNS egress rule. This is the #1 NetworkPolicy mistake.

✅
Test allowed (should work)

kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -n NS -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://SVC.NS:PORT
This tests the ingress rule allowing source→target traffic.

❌
Test blocked (should fail)

kubectl run test --rm -it --image=nginx -n OTHER-NS -- curl http://SVC.TARGET-NS:PORT
Must FAIL. If it succeeds → your default-deny isn't working or has a gap.

38.5 Falco Rule Quick Reference

Falco custom rules appear in nearly every CKS exam. This 5-line template adapts to any task:

YAML — Falco Rule Template (memorize this pattern) 
# /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml — NEVER edit falco_rules.yaml!
- rule: RULE_NAME                           # ① Unique rule name
  desc: DESCRIPTION                          # ② What it detects
  condition: >                               # ③ The detection logic
    spawned_process                          #    Most common macro
    and container.name = "NAME"              #    Filter by container
    and proc.name in (bash, sh)              #    Filter by process
  output: >                                  # ④ Alert message
    ALERT: pod=%pod.name cmd=%proc.cmdline
  priority: CRITICAL                         # ⑤ CRITICAL|WARNING|NOTICE
  tags: [TAG1, TAG2]                         #    Optional metadata

Common Falco Condition Macros

MacroWhat It DetectsExample Use
spawned_processAny new process creationBase for most rules
shell_procsShell processes (bash, sh, zsh)Detect interactive shells
outboundOutbound network connectionsDetect C2 communication
inboundInbound network connectionsDetect unexpected services
open_writeFile opened for writingDetect file modifications
open_readFile opened for readingDetect sensitive file access

Falco Lifecycle Commands

Bash — Falco management commands (memorize these 5) 
# 1. Validate rule syntax
falco --validate /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml

# 2. Graceful reload (no event loss)
kill -1 $(pidof falco)

# 3. Follow Falco logs
kubectl logs -n falco -l app=falco -f

# 4. Restart Falco DaemonSet (after ConfigMap update)
kubectl rollout restart ds/falco -n falco

# 5. Check Falco status
systemctl status falco    # If running as systemd service

Falco Rule Writing Checklist — Don't Miss These Steps

1Write the rule in the RIGHT file

Always edit /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml. NEVER edit /etc/falco/falco_rules.yaml — it gets overwritten on Falco upgrades, wiping your custom rules.

2Validate syntax

Run falco --validate /etc/falco/falco_rules.local.yaml. If there's a syntax error, Falco silently IGNORES the entire file. No warnings at runtime — your rules just don't work.

3Test the rule

Trigger the condition manually: kubectl exec POD -- sh -c "command". Check Falco logs for your alert. If you don't see it, the rule didn't match.

4Reload or restart

Falco reads rules at STARTUP. After editing: kill -1 $(pidof falco) for graceful reload, or kubectl rollout restart ds/falco -n falco if running as DaemonSet.

memorization Mnemonic — Falco Rule Fields

LetterFieldWhat to Write
Cconditionspawned_process and container.name = "X" and proc.name in (Y)
Ooutput"ALERT: pod=%pod.name cmd=%proc.cmdline"
DdescOne sentence describing what the rule detects
PpriorityCRITICAL | WARNING | NOTICE
RruleUnique rule name (hyphenated-lowercase)

Mnemonic: "CODPR" — Condition, Output, Desc, Priority, Rule

Weekly Study Routine

📖Read (2-3 hours)

Read the assigned chapters. Take notes on commands and concepts you don't immediately recognize. Highlight the verification commands — they're the most important.

🧪Lab (4-5 hours)

Complete the weekly lab on a real cluster. Type every command yourself. Don't copy-paste. Build muscle memory. If you get stuck, re-read the chapter before looking at the solution.

📝Review (1-2 hours)

Review the previous week's material. Re-do one lab from the prior week. Spaced repetition is proven to improve long-term retention by 200-300%.

🧠Flashcards (30 min/day)

Create flashcards for: kubectl commands, file paths, YAML patterns, Falco field names. Review 10-15 cards daily. Use Anki or physical index cards.

What to Do the Day Before Your Exam

🌙
Evening Before

Review this chapter (Ch38). Re-read the 1-page cheat sheet 3 times. Practice writing the securityContext and NetworkPolicy YAML from memory. Test your workstation: PSI browser, webcam, internet. Go to bed early — 8+ hours of sleep.

☀️
Morning Of

Wake up 2+ hours early. Light breakfast. 10-minute warmup: kubectl run test, kubectl create ns test, kubectl auth can-i. Read the cheat sheet one more time. Clear your desk of everything except ID.

🧘
Right Before

Take 5 deep breaths. Remind yourself: you've done 38 chapters of preparation. You know this material. Trust your training. Open the exam. Read the first task. Type kubectl config use-context. You've got this.
